# heki

> Static checker for Python that tracks side effects and mutations across function calls.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/

# heki

<p align="center">
  <img src="assets/heki-banner.png" alt="heki: a snake in front of a brick wall" width="600">
</p>

🧱 heki (壁, Japanese for "wall") checks the semantics of Python code. It does not replace Ruff or
your type checker (mypy, Pyright, Pyrefly, or ty): it is a third layer that runs next to them.
Ruff checks syntax and style, and the type checkers check declared types. heki follows aliases,
helpers, and file boundaries to find which function a call really runs, which state it changes,
and which effects it has. It is written in Rust and checks a 100,000-line project in a few
seconds.

This stops a pull request that passes the syntax checks and strict type checking but changes
what the code does. With no configuration, `heki check` reports a shared cache changed in place,
a read-only argument changed by a helper, a database query in a loop, a lock taken again while it
is held, and a blocking call in `async` code. The same run enforces the rules only your project
knows: who owns a piece of state, which change must invalidate a cache, and where I/O may happen.

You write those rules as [contracts](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#contracts). A contract uses the results of
the same analysis to decide, in every pull request, whether a change, a call, or an I/O is
allowed. The `async` checks are one use of that analysis among the others.

![heki check in a terminal: MUT114 reports, with no configuration, a dict that an lru_cache function returned and another file changes in place, and MUT201 a write to Order.items through a helper outside the functions a contract allows, with its call chain](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/assets/example-check.svg)

<p>
  <a class="md-button md-button--primary" href="getting-started/">Getting Started</a>
  <a class="md-button" href="rules/">Rules</a>
  <a class="md-button" href="configuration/#contracts">Contracts</a>
</p>

[![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/heki)](https://pypi.org/project/heki/)
[![Python versions](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/heki)](https://pypi.org/project/heki/)

[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-blue.svg)](https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki/blob/main/LICENSE)

⚡ Try it in your project's root, without installing: `uvx heki check`. Then follow
[Try it in 5 minutes](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/#try-it-in-5-minutes).

---

### A bug found with no configuration

Each file looks fine on its own, and the types are right: the bug is in what the cache shares.

```python
# app/config.py
from functools import lru_cache


@lru_cache(maxsize=64)
def base_headers(region: str) -> dict[str, str]:
    return {"Accept": "application/json", "X-Region": region}
```

```python
# app/api.py
from app.config import base_headers


def request_headers(region: str, token: str) -> dict[str, str]:
    headers = base_headers(region)
    headers["Authorization"] = f"Bearer {token}"
    return headers
```

`lru_cache` hands the same dict to every call with the same `region`. `request_headers` writes a
token into it, so a later caller of `base_headers` for that region sends the token of whoever
called `request_headers` last.

### A wall your project writes

Only the functions in `app.store` may change `Order.items`. Write that down once:

```toml
# heki.toml
[[write-owners]]
name = "order-store"
targets = ["app.models.Order.items"]
allowed-writers = ["app.store.*"]
message = "change Order.items through app.store"
fail = true   # a report of this contract fails the run
```

```python
# app/models.py
class Order:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.items: list[str] = []
```

```python
# app/store.py
from app.models import Order


def add_item(order: Order, item: str) -> None:
    order.items.append(item)
```

`app/checkout.py` changes the list through a helper in another file:

```python
# app/util.py
def append_to(items: list[str], item: str) -> None:
    items.append(item)
```

```python
# app/checkout.py
from app.models import Order
from app.util import append_to


def add_gift_wrap(order: Order) -> None:
    append_to(order.items, "gift-wrap")
```

tach and import-linter stop at the import layers, and every import here is allowed; heki follows
the write through the helper, as it follows any change, call, or I/O across helpers and aliases.

The image at the top is `heki check` on these examples: `MUT114` with no configuration, and
`MUT201` from the contract. The same code passes Ruff, and mypy, Pyright, Pyrefly, and ty in
strict mode (`mypy --strict`, Pyright's `strict`, Pyrefly's `strict` preset, every ty rule as an
error). Ruff with every rule on asks only for docstrings, copyright lines, and an `__init__.py`.

### Works alongside Ruff, your type checker, and import-linter

heki does not replace these tools: run it next to them. Each one models one layer of the code,
and heki checks what the code does across files.

| Tool | Models | heki adds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ruff | syntax and style | the behavior behind a call, across files: the state it changes, a shared cache changed in place, a database query in a loop, a lock taken again while it is held, I/O where it should not happen, a blocking call in `async` code |
| mypy, Pyright, Pyrefly, ty | declared types | in-place changes, through aliases and helpers, to `frozen`, `ReadOnly`, and `Final` fields and to `Sequence` / `Mapping` / `AbstractSet` arguments |
| tach, import-linter | the import layers: which modules may import which | which functions write or read a field, call a function, or reach I/O, and which changes must invalidate a cache, through helpers and aliases; import rules that know when each import runs (experimental); planned: reading these tools' contracts as heki contracts |

Its configuration, suppression comments, and output formats follow Ruff's.
[Design Philosophy](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/philosophy/) says why heki works this way and compares its checks with what
Rust and Haskell enforce.

## 🧭 What heki can do

### ✅ Bug checks with no configuration

These rules run by default, and each report shows the chain of calls that leads to it. Every
report they made on 378 packages (about 30.75 million lines) and on a frozen holdout of 100 more
was checked by hand, with no false claim ([Rule precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/#certifications)).

| What goes wrong | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| A list, dict, or set that an `lru_cache` / `cache` function returned, changed in place | [`MUT114`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-result-mutation/) |
| A `Sequence` / `Mapping` / `AbstractSet` argument changed in place by a helper | [`MUT110`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-param-mutation/) |
| A change of a builtin container that is lost because the object is new and nothing holds it (`list(xs).sort()`) | [`MUT119`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/change-lost-on-new-object/) |
| A database statement on every iteration of a loop over data | [`EFF103`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-db-query/) |
| A new HTTP, database, or RPC client (or a request without a session) on every iteration of a loop over data | [`EFF102`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-unpooled-client/) |
| A lock that is not reentrant, taken again while it is held, so the thread or task waits for itself | [`EFF109`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/lock-reacquired-while-held/) |
| A call of a generator function whose generator nothing iterates, so its body never runs | [`EFF116`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/generator-never-iterated/) |
| A blocking call that a call in an `async def` always runs, several helpers below | [`EFF101`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-blocking-call/) |
| A DataFrame or array concatenated with itself on every loop iteration | [`DATA101`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-carried-concat/) |
| A list rebuilt, or a dict or set merged, on every loop iteration, and a nested-loop join | `OPT101`, `OPT102`, `OPT113` ([fixes](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/fixes/)) |

The size-dependent rewrites (`OPT103`, `OPT110`, `OPT111`, `OPT120`, `OPT121`, `OPT130`) are exact
too, but opt-in. The other rules are heuristic or opt-in ([Rules](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/)).

A call on the result of a builtin or standard-library call is followed too
(`text.strip().lower()`, `shlex.split(line)[0].upper()`), with result types from typeshed's
stubs: heki infers a method's or function's result, a library attribute, an enumeration member and
its value, and a `match` class pattern's subject. It stays unresolved where overloads join to no
single type (`d.get(key).upper()`), for module variables, and for packages outside the standard
library ([How a call is resolved](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/scope/#how-a-call-is-resolved)).

`heki check --fix` applies an `OPT` rewrite only when it proves, under CPython's semantics, that
the program behaves the same ([Fixes and safety](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/fixes/)). More by problem:
[async and execution effects](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/effects/), [state ownership and mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/ownership/), and
[imports and module boundaries](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/imports/).

### 📜 Walls you write: contracts and coding agents

Write the rules your project keeps by review today as contract tables in `heki.toml` or under
`[tool.heki]`. heki follows aliases, helpers, and subclasses, with nothing added at run time.
Contract reports are heuristic, so they are warnings until the table sets `fail = true`.

| What you want to keep | Contract | Main keys |
| --------------------- | -------- | --------- |
| Only `app.store` changes `Order.items` | `write-owners` | `targets = ["Order.items"]`, `allowed-writers = ["app.store.*"]` |
| Only `app.billing` reads `Order.card_token` | `read-owners` | `targets = ["Order.card_token"]`, `allowed-readers = ["app.billing.*"]` |
| Only `app.admin` calls `app.db.reset` | `call-owners` | `targets = ["app.db.reset"]`, `allowed-callers = ["app.admin.*"]` |
| No caller changes the settings `load_settings` returns to everyone | `readonly-returns` | `producers = ["app.config.load_settings"]`, `deep = true` |
| Every change of `Order.items` is followed by `order_changed()` | `invalidation` | `targets = ["Order.items"]`, `invalidators = ["app.cache.order_changed"]` |
| Code in `app.render` makes no blocking call | `effect-boundaries` | `scopes = ["app.render.*"]`, `forbid = ["blocking"]` |
| `app.domain` imports nothing from `app.web`, even lazily or inside a function | `import-boundaries` (experimental) | `importers = ["app.domain.*"]`, `forbidden-imports = ["app.web", "app.web.*"]` |

See [Contracts](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#contracts) for every key. A coding agent can miss a rule written
in its instructions, but not a contract that `heki check` enforces:

- List `heki.toml` and `heki-baseline.toml` in `CODEOWNERS`: moving a wall takes a review.
- Run `heki check --report-suppressed <PATH>` in CI: it lists every inline `# heki: ignore` and `# noqa`
  that silences a report, so a change that goes around a wall shows in review ([details](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#auditing-inline-suppressions)).
- A contract's `message` starts the help line of its reports, so the agent reads it as the fix.
- A [Stop hook](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#a-stop-hook-for-claude-code) sends a failing check back before
  the agent ends its turn.
- [`heki inspect`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#what-a-function-does-heki-inspect-experimental)
  (experimental) shows what one function reaches, changes, and returns.
- [`heki recommend --focus types --diff`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/recommend/#applying-the-suggestions) (experimental) prints the exact type suggestions
  as one patch that `git apply` takes, annotations only.
- `--output-format json` gives every check as JSON, and the
  [Agent Skill](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#agent-skill-experimental) (experimental) teaches the routine
  after an edit. [Coding agents](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/) has the whole setup.

## 🚀 Try it in 5 minutes

1. In your project's root (the directory with `pyproject.toml`), run `uvx heki check`. An exact
   error, like `MUT114` above, fails the run (exit code 1). Warnings are printed but don't fail it
   unless you pass `--fail-on warning`.

2. Ask what fits the project with [`heki recommend`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/recommend/) (experimental). It writes no
   file and helps most when the first step finds nothing, as on heki's
   [sample service](https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki/tree/main/tests/sample_service):

    ```console
    $ uvx heki check
    All checks passed (4 file(s)).
    ...
    $ uvx heki recommend
    ...
    Contract candidates
      write-owners  app.models:Order.*  high
        written by 1 function(s), all in app.store (add_item), changed in place; read in 2 other module(s)
    ```

    Only `app.store` writes `Order.items`, so heki proposes that wall with the keys to add.
    [Getting Started](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/getting-started/#ask-what-fits-the-project) shows more of the report.

3. Keep it running with the [pre-commit hook](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#pre-commit) and a CI step, and record
   today's findings in a [Ratchet baseline](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#ratchet-baselines) so only new ones fail:
   `uvx heki==0.11.0 check --baseline heki-baseline.toml --update-baseline`. The
   [starter recipes](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#starter-recipes) have these setups ready to copy.

!!! warning "Pre-release"

    Rules, configuration keys, and output formats can change in any release, and the release
    notes list every change. The default rules are exact. Heuristic rules, experimental rules, and
    experimental commands run only when you ask for them, and every output labels heuristic
    reports. Please [report](https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki/issues) what heki gets wrong.

## 👉 Next steps

- 🎯 When heki isn't sure, it doesn't report: [scope and limitations](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/scope/).
- 📦 [Install heki](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/installation/), 🚀 [run it on a project](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/getting-started/), and ⚙️
  [configure](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/) rules and contracts.
- 📏 Browse the [rules](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/) and [how precise each one is](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/), and 🪜
  [adopt heki gradually](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/).
- 🖥️ Use it from [your editor](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/lsp/) or 🤖 [a coding agent](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/).

## 📛 Name

*heki* is 壁, "wall", in its Sino-Japanese (*on*) reading, the one used in compounds such as
防火壁 (*bōkaheki*, "firewall"). On its own the character is usually read *kabe*.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/installation/

# Installation

heki is a single executable: its Python package ships only that executable and installs no
Python dependencies into your environment. It is published as prebuilt wheels on PyPI for the
platforms listed below, so `uvx heki`, `pip install heki`, and the pre-commit hook need no Rust
toolchain and compile nothing.

## With uv, pipx, or pip

=== "uv"

    ```console
    $ uv tool install heki
    $ uvx heki check            # or run it without installing
    ```

=== "pipx"

    ```console
    $ pipx install heki
    ```

=== "pip"

    ```console
    $ pip install heki
    ```

As a development dependency of a project:

```console
$ uv add --dev heki
```

Wheels are published for these platforms:

| OS | Architectures |
| -- | ------------- |
| Linux | x86-64, AArch64, x86-64 musl |
| macOS | Apple silicon, Intel |
| Windows | x86-64 |

## Check the installation

```console
$ heki --version
$ heki rule --all
```

## Supported Python versions

- heki analyzes code written for Python 3.11 to 3.15.
- It does not need a Python interpreter to run.
- The version of the checked code comes from
  [`target-version`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#top-level-settings), or from `requires-python`; see
  [Scope](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/scope/#the-target-python-version) for what it changes.

## From source

??? note "Only for a platform without a wheel, or for development on heki"

    heki needs Rust 1.99 or newer:

    ```console
    $ git clone https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki
    $ cd heki
    $ cargo install --path crates/heki
    ```

    `pip install` of the source distribution builds the same executable with maturin.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/getting-started/

# Getting Started

This page runs heki on a project, reads a diagnostic, applies a fix, and picks the rules.

## Run it

From the root of a project (the directory with `pyproject.toml`):

```console
$ heki check
$ heki check --heuristic
```

The first command runs the exact rules that are not opt-in, and the rules of the
[contracts](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#contracts) you declare. An exact rule is certified: every report it
made on the development corpus and on a frozen holdout corpus was checked by hand, and none was
false ([Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/#certifications)). Without configuration, it runs:

- [`MUT110` (readonly-param-mutation)](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-param-mutation/)
- [`MUT114` (cached-result-mutation)](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-result-mutation/)
- [`MUT119` (change-lost-on-new-object)](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/change-lost-on-new-object/)
- [`EFF101` (async-blocking-call)](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-blocking-call/)
- [`EFF102` (loop-unpooled-client)](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-unpooled-client/)
- [`EFF103` (loop-db-query)](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-db-query/)
- [`EFF109` (lock-reacquired-while-held)](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/lock-reacquired-while-held/)
- [`EFF116` (generator-never-iterated)](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/generator-never-iterated/)
- [`DATA101` (loop-carried-concat)](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-carried-concat/)
- [`OPT101` (list-quadratic-concat)](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/list-quadratic-concat/)
- [`OPT102` (set-dict-quadratic-merge)](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/set-dict-quadratic-merge/)
- [`OPT113` (nested-loop-equijoin)](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/nested-loop-equijoin/)

`MUT101`, `MUT111`, and the size-dependent `OPT` rules (`OPT103`, `OPT110`, `OPT111`, `OPT120`,
`OPT121`, `OPT130`) are exact too, but run only when `select` or `extend-select` names them (in `pyproject.toml` or on the command
line, by code or name), or, for the five with a rewrite (not `OPT103`), when
`--include-size-dependent` is given: their reports were rarely harmful ([Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/)).

A report of an exact rule that did not establish every premise of its claim, such as an `OPT`
rewrite heki could not prove safe, is heuristic. A text run says how many heuristic rules and
reports it left out. `--heuristic` adds them; they can be wrong about the code, and every output
labels them.

heki checks every Python file under the current directory, except the
[excluded and ignored ones](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#which-files-are-checked). Pass directories to narrow
it, or files to look at: a file is checked in its project, so heki still analyzes the whole
project and shows the reports that touch the file.

```console
$ heki check src/
$ heki check app/api.py
```

## Ask what fits the project

`heki recommend` (experimental) analyzes the project as `heki check` does and says which
parameter types and contracts the code already keeps, which rules would report here, and what
heki could not see, with the keys to add to `[tool.heki]`. It writes no file. A run of `heki check` that shows nothing, on a
project without contracts or a baseline, ends with a line that points to it. On the
[sample service](https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki/tree/main/tests/sample_service) in heki's
tests:

```console
$ heki check
All checks passed (4 file(s)).
...
hint: `heki recommend` (experimental) lists the parameter types and contracts the code already keeps, the rules that fit this project, and what heki could not see
$ heki recommend
heki recommend (experimental) on .: 4 file(s), 11 function(s)
...
Types the code already keeps
  1 read-only parameter group(s), exact; 0 heuristic
  No type checker configuration found: half of each guard is a type checker's.
    app/report.py:8  total(prices)  list[float] -> Sequence[float]  public
...
What heki cannot see (no report either way)
  calls of packages heki's catalog does not cover: 1 call(s) of 1 name(s) in 1 package(s)
    name                  calls  async  loops  if it waits     if it sends a query
    stripe.Charge.create      1      1      0  EFF101 1 exact  -
...
Contract candidates
  write-owners  app.models:Order.*  high
    written by 1 function(s), all in app.store (add_item), changed in place; read in 2 other module(s)
...
```

`total` only reads `prices`, so its annotation can say so. heki's catalog doesn't say what
`stripe.Charge.create` does, so heki reports nothing through it. If the call waits on the
network, `EFF101` would report it in `async def checkout`. Only `app.store` writes `Order.items`,
so the report ends with the keys that make that a contract.

See [Configuration Advice](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/recommend/) for the whole report. To adopt heki in a repository,
start from the [starter recipes](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#starter-recipes).

## Read a diagnostic

```console
app/api.py:5:12: EFF101 (async-blocking-call) [error] `app.users.load_user` always runs the waiting call `requests.get` on the event loop (1 call down, on every path)
  |
5 |     user = load_user(user_id)
  |            ^
  = related: app/api.py:5:12: `handler` calls `app.users.load_user`
  = related: app/users.py:5:12: `load_user` calls `requests.get`
  = help: offload it with `asyncio.to_thread`, or use an async client
```

| Part | Meaning |
| ---- | ------- |
| `app/api.py:5:12` | where to look |
| `EFF101 (async-blocking-call)` | the rule's code and name |
| `[error]` | its severity: `error` for a bug that can be critical (a wrong result, an exception, a lost update, a deadlock, an event loop held up for every other task, as here, a broken contract), `warning` for slower code or for a bug that is rarely harmful. An exact error makes `heki check` fail; a warning is shown without failing it, unless `--fail-on warning` (`lint.fail-on = "warning"`) is set. A heuristic report adds `heuristic` (`[error, heuristic]`): it can be wrong about the code, as a premise of its claim can be open, so it counts as a warning and fails the run only with `--fail-on warning` |
| the message | what heki established, in one sentence: here, that the call to `load_user` always runs `requests.get`, a call that waits on the network, on the event loop |
| `related` lines | the hops of the chain of calls behind it, to follow it across files; editors show them as related information you can jump to |
| `help` line | what to do about it |

`heki rule EFF101` explains the rule, its exclusions, and what to do instead. The
[rules reference](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/) has the same text for every rule.

## Look at one function

`heki inspect` (experimental) answers "what does this function do, and who depends on it?" for
one function. It needs no configuration. Name the function as `module.Class.method`, a suffix
such as `Cart.add`, or `path.py:LINE`:

```text
$ heki inspect app.store.Cart.add
Cart.add  (app.store)
  app/store.py:10-13  method
  impure: effects, changes_self, changes_globals
effects
  blocking_net (called), 2 calls down, whenever it runs
    store.py:13         Cart.notify
    store.py:16         requests.post
changes
  self.items     directly
  global _CACHE  directly: store.py:12
callers   1
  web.handle  web.py:7  (in a loop)
reports   none
```

The sections are what it reaches (`effects`, with the chain of calls to each), what it changes,
who calls it, and what `heki check` reports in it. `--callers --depth 3` follows the callers up,
and `--output-format json` gives every field. [Coding agents](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#what-a-function-does-heki-inspect-experimental)
lists them all.

## Fix what heki can prove

`--fix` applies the rewrites heki proves safe and always faster (`OPT101`, `OPT102`), and
`--diff` shows them first:

```console
$ heki check --diff
--- a/app/report.py
+++ b/app/report.py
@@ -1,5 +1,5 @@
 def rows_of(items):
     rows = []
     for item in items:
-        rows = rows + [item]
+        rows.append(item)
     return rows
Would fix 1 issue(s) in 1 file(s).
$ heki check --fix
Fixed 1 issue(s) in 1 file(s).
```

`--fix` then reports what is left, such as the `EFF101` above, which has no automatic fix.

When heki cannot prove a fix safe, the help says why, nothing is rewritten, and the report is
heuristic whatever the rule's certainty. Here the list is also handed to other code inside the
loop:

```console
$ heki check --heuristic app/shared.py
app/shared.py:4:9: OPT101 (list-quadratic-concat) [warning, heuristic] `rows = rows + [...]` copies the whole list each time it runs in the loop
  |
4 |         rows = rows + [item]
  |         ^
  = help: append in place with `rows.append(...)` / `rows.extend(...)` [not auto-fixable: Unique(rows): it may be shared: passed to code heki cannot see (line 5)]

Found 1 diagnostic(s) in 1 file(s).
```

[Fixes and Safety](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/fixes/) lists which rules are fixed, and what a fix must prove.

## Silence a diagnostic

Append a suppression comment to the reported line:

```python
user = load_user(user_id)  # heki: ignore[EFF101]
```

The other forms (`# heki: ignore`, `# noqa: EFF101`) and `per-file-ignores` are in
[Inline suppressions](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#inline-suppressions).

## Choose the rules

```console
$ heki check --select EFF,MUT        # only these families
$ heki check --extend-select EFF105  # add an opt-in rule
$ heki check --ignore OPT113         # everything except one rule
```

Codes, code prefixes, and rule names (`async-blocking-call`) are accepted. A prefix does not
enable the opt-in rules, nor the heuristic ones without `--heuristic`: see
[Rule selection](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#rule-selection-toolhekilint).

## Output formats

```console
$ heki check --output-format json
```

| Format | Prints |
| ------ | ------ |
| `full` (default; `github` in GitHub Actions) | each diagnostic with its source line, call chain, and help |
| `concise` | one line per diagnostic: the message, without the help |
| `json` | every field: also the help, the evidence, the blocker that stops a fix, and the fix edits ([fields](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#after-an-edit-heki-check)) |
| `github` | GitHub Actions annotations with the message ([CI](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#continuous-integration)) |
| `sarif` | the message, the location, the call chain, and the help (`properties.help`), for code-scanning dashboards (no evidence or blocker) |

Without `--output-format`, `HEKI_OUTPUT_FORMAT` chooses the format, and in GitHub Actions
(`GITHUB_ACTIONS=true`) it is `github`.

Every format, `--diff`, and the errors of files that cannot be read or parsed print a file's
path relative to the working directory when the file is inside it (otherwise as given), as Ruff
does, and with `/` separators on every platform, Windows included.

### Colors

On a terminal, the `full` and `concise` output and `--diff` are colored as Ruff colors its
output: paths in bold, rule codes in red, the severity, the source frame and its caret, and the
lines a diff removes and adds. The same variables and option as Ruff's decide it, each row over
the rows above it:

| Setting | Colors |
| ------- | ------ |
| stdout is a terminal / a pipe or a file | on / off |
| `NO_COLOR` set (to anything), or `CLICOLOR=0` | off |
| `FORCE_COLOR` set to anything but the empty string, or `CLICOLOR_FORCE` to anything but `0` | on (for a CI log that shows colors) |
| `--color always` / `--color never` | on / off |

`json`, `github`, and `sarif` output never holds colors, and the summary and the errors heki
writes to stderr are not colored.

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
| ---- | ------- |
| `0` | no diagnostics, or only warnings and heuristic reports (they are printed) |
| `1` | an exact error found, or any report with `--fail-on warning` (`lint.fail-on = "warning"`), among the Ratchet regressions when a baseline is used; also when `--update-baseline` refuses a grown entry, a baseline entry matched nothing with [`report-unused-suppressions`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#unused-suppressions), or `--diff` would change files |
| `2` | configuration error, unknown rule, or a file that cannot be read or has a syntax error; with files given (`heki check src/app.py`, `--touched`), only one of those files fails the run, and the others are named in a note |


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/ownership/

# State Ownership and Mutation

heki finds in-place changes of read-only parameters, cached results, and frozen fields, and enforces your own rules about who may change, read, or call what.

Python has no owner for a value: any code that reaches an object can change it. Type checkers see a change made on a value of a read-only type. heki follows the value through aliases and helper calls, so it also sees the change that a function three calls below makes. This page has three parts: who may change, read, or call what, how to leave a borrowed or shared value alone, and values that may be used only once. A table at the end maps the ideas to the words Rust uses for them. [Contracts](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#contracts) has every key, and [Rules](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/) has one page per rule.

Each entry names its rule and its tier, as `heki rule --all` gives it. An exact rule states a fact about the code. A heuristic rule can be wrong about the code, runs with `--heuristic` (or `lint.heuristic = true`) when it is on by default, and its reports count as warnings. An opt-in rule is off until you name it in `extend-select`, for example `--extend-select MUT115`; a prefix such as `MUT` or `ALL` never enables it. An experimental rule can change or go away between releases, and [Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/) says why each one is marked.

## 📜 Who may change, read, or call what

Some rules belong to your project, not to Python: only `app.store` may append to `Order.items`, only `app.billing` reads a card token, nothing changes the settings object that `load_settings` returns. Write them down once and `heki check` enforces them across files, aliases, and helpers.

| You want | Contract | Rules | Tier |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Only some functions change an attribute or container | `write-owners` | [`MUT201`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/write-owner-violation/), [`MUT205`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-write/) | heuristic, contract |
| Only some functions read an attribute | `read-owners` | [`MUT203`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/read-owner-violation/), [`MUT206`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-read/) | heuristic, contract |
| Only some functions call a function, method, or class | `call-owners` | [`MUT204`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/call-owner-violation/), [`MUT207`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-call/) | heuristic, contract |
| Nobody changes a shared value that a producer returns | `readonly-returns` | [`MUT202`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-return-mutation/) | heuristic, contract |
| Every change of an attribute is followed by a call that announces it | `invalidation` | [`MUT208`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/write-without-invalidation/) | heuristic, contract |

The second rule of each owner contract (`MUT205`, `MUT206`, `MUT207`) is its strict mode. It reports what heki cannot place: an attribute named like a target that is written on an object of unknown class. Set `unresolved = "report"` in the contract to get it.

A contract rule is on as soon as a contract table exists. Its reports are warnings until you set `fail = true` in the table. Record today's findings in a [Ratchet baseline](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#ratchet-baselines) first, so only new breaks fail.

### Only the store changes the order

```toml
# heki.toml
[[write-owners]]
name = "order-store"
targets = ["app.models.Order.items"]
allowed-writers = ["app.store.*"]
message = "change Order.items through app.store"
fail = true
```

A function in `app/api.py` appends to `order.items` through a helper:

```console
$ heki check
app/api.py:9:5: MUT201 (write-owner-violation) [error, heuristic] `add_gift_wrap` writes `app.models.Order.items` (through a helper) via `app.api._append` outside the write owners of `order-store`
  |
9 |     _append(order.items, "gift-wrap")
  |     ^
  = related: app/api.py:9:5: `add_gift_wrap` calls `app.api._append`
  = help: change Order.items through app.store; allowed writers of `app.models.Order.items`: `app.store.add_item`

Found 1 diagnostic(s) in 4 file(s).
```

The run exits with code 1. `read-owners` and `call-owners` take the same shape with `allowed-readers` and `allowed-callers`. A target covers the subclasses of its class too, and a read or call through a value typed with a project `Protocol` that only the class and its subclasses implement: with `Order` the one class implementing `HasItems`, `cart.items` with `cart: HasItems` reads `Order.items` ([`read-owners`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#read-owners)).

### Every change must be announced

```toml
# heki.toml
[[invalidation]]
name = "order-total"
targets = ["app.models.Order.items"]
invalidators = ["app.cache.order_changed"]
message = "call order_changed() after changing Order.items"
```

`add` appends and then calls `order_changed()`. `remove` does not:

```console
$ heki check
app/cart.py:11:5: MUT208 (write-without-invalidation) [error, heuristic] `remove` writes `app.models.Order.items` (in place) and returns on some path without calling an invalidator of `order-total`
   |
11 |     order.items.remove(name)
   |     ^
  = help: call order_changed() after changing Order.items; announcing writers of `app.models.Order.items`: `app.cart.add`
...
```

Without `fail = true` this run exits with code 0, because a heuristic report counts as a warning.

### Which contract do I need?

| If the rule you have in mind says | Use |
| --- | --- |
| "only X may change this field" | `write-owners` |
| "only X may read this field" | `read-owners` |
| "only X may call this function" or "only X may construct this class" | `call-owners` |
| "nobody may change what this function returns" | `readonly-returns`, with `producers = [...]` and `deep = true` for what is below the result |
| "after changing this field, always call that function" | `invalidation` |
| "this code must not write, read, or call anything of that kind, however deep" | `effect-boundaries`, see [Async and Execution Effects](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/effects/#contracts-for-execution-effects) |

A contract names a method as `Class.method`, and a subclass that overrides the method is another function. Set `include-overrides = true` on a contract (or in its [defaults table](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#defaults-for-the-tables-of-a-kind)) and an entry naming a method in `allowed-*`, `forbidden-*`, `exempt-methods`, `invalidators`, or `exempt-writers` also names the overrides of it in the project subclasses of `Class`. The key is off by default because it allows a subclass written later to do what its base class may, with no change of the configuration. See [Allowed and forbidden functions](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#allowed-and-forbidden-functions).

A value that an annotation declares as a union (`Model | Node`, `Optional[...]`, a `TypeAlias`, a `TypeVar` bound) is each of its classes when it has at most eight, and a method call on it runs the method of each. A value that different assignments join keeps at most three classes. Past the limit the value has no class, and a write on it stays an unresolved write. A loop that writes the keys of a `TypedDict` (`for name, value in td.items(): setattr(obj, name, value)`) writes the keys the class declares only when the `TypedDict` is closed (`closed=True`, PEP 728, or a base that is closed). A `TypedDict` without it is open: a subclass value may be passed where it is declared, so the write names an attribute at run time, as for a plain `dict`.

`lru_cache` and `cache` results are protected without a contract. A `readonly-returns` entry adds the producers that are not cached, such as a function that returns a module-level dict.

## 🤝 Not breaking a value you borrowed or share

A function that receives a list did not make it, and a function that gets a cached result did not make that either. Changing such a value changes it for everyone who holds it. These rules report the change.

```toml
# heki.toml
[lint]
extend-select = ["MUT113", "MUT115"]
```

### A read-only parameter changed by a helper

A parameter annotated `Sequence`, `Mapping`, or `AbstractSet` promises that the function only reads it. `MUT110` reports a call that hands such a parameter, as itself, to a function that changes it in place. Tier: exact, default ([`MUT110`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-param-mutation/)).

```python
# app/stock.py
from collections.abc import Sequence


def sort_names(names) -> None:
    if isinstance(names, list):
        names.sort()


def prepare(names: Sequence[str]) -> list[str]:
    sort_names(names)
    return list(names)
```

```console
$ heki check
app/stock.py:10:5: MUT110 (readonly-param-mutation) [warning] `prepare` passes its read-only parameter `names` to `app.stock.sort_names`; whenever line 6 of `sort_names` runs, it changes the caller's object in place
   |
10 |     sort_names(names)
   |     ^
  = related: app/stock.py:10:5: `prepare` calls `app.stock.sort_names`
  = related: app/stock.py:6:9: `sort_names` changes the object in place here
  = help: pass a copy (`list(names)` / `dict(names)` / `set(names)`), or annotate the helper's parameter with a mutable type
...
```

`MUT110` is a warning, because the bug it reports is rarely harmful, so it does not fail the run. Copy the parameter to a local list, sort the copy, and return it, so the caller's object stays as it was:

```python
def prepare(names: Sequence[str]) -> list[str]:
    ordered = list(names)
    sort_names(ordered)
    return ordered
```

Or annotate the helper's parameter with a mutable type, so the type checker shows the mismatch at the call.

### A cached result changed in place

A function under `lru_cache` or `cache` hands the same list, dict, or set to every caller with the same arguments. `MUT114` reports a change of that object. Tier: exact, default ([`MUT114`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-result-mutation/)).

```python
# app/stock.py
from functools import lru_cache


@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def default_tags(shop: str) -> list[str]:
    return ["new", shop]


def tag(shop: str, item: str) -> list[str]:
    tags = default_tags(shop)
    tags.append(item)
    return tags
```

```console
$ heki check
app/stock.py:11:5: MUT114 (cached-result-mutation) [error] `tag` changes in place the list that `default_tags` returned; `default_tags` is cached by `functools.lru_cache`
   |
11 |     tags.append(item)
   |     ^
  = help: change a copy (`list(...)`) instead
...
```


`MUT114` is an error, so it fails the run. A producer that is not cached, such as a function that returns a module-level dict, is covered by a `readonly-returns` contract.

### A shared return value changed

For a value that is shared without a cache, name its producers in a `readonly-returns` contract, with `deep = true` to cover what is below the result. `MUT202` reports a change of what a producer returned, directly or through the functions that return it. Tier: heuristic, contract ([`MUT202`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-return-mutation/)).

```toml
# heki.toml
[[readonly-returns]]
name = "schemas"
producers = ["registry.schema"]
deep = true
```

```python
# app/m.py
from registry import schema


def schema_of(name: str) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
    return schema(name)


def extend(name: str) -> None:
    s = schema_of(name)
    s["fields"].append("extra")
```

heki reports: `extend` mutates the shared object returned by read-only producer `registry.schema` through `app.m.schema_of`. Change a `copy.deepcopy` of the value instead.

### A shallow copy shares its items

`dict(x)`, `x.copy()`, and `copy.copy(x)` copy one level. The inner lists are the same objects, so a change below the copy changes the original too. `MUT115` reports it when the original is state that outlives the call. Tier: heuristic, opt-in ([`MUT115`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/shallow-copy-nested-mutation/)).

```python
def with_base(options: dict[str, list[str]], base: str) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
    result = options.copy()
    result["bases"].append(base)  # changes the list `options["bases"]` holds
    return result
```

heki reports: `with_base` changes in place an object that its shallow copy of `options` (`.copy()`, line 2) shares with `options`. Rebuild the inner value instead: `result["bases"] = [*result["bases"], base]`.

### A container changed while it is iterated

A dict, set, or deque that a loop is iterating raises `RuntimeError` at the next step once something changes it. `MUT113` reports a method that suspends at a `yield` inside such a loop while another method changes the container. Tier: heuristic, experimental, opt-in ([`MUT113`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/iterated-container-mutation/)).

```python
class Subscriptions:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.by_node: dict[str, object] = {}
        self._cursor = self._cycle()

    def _cycle(self):
        while self.by_node:
            yield from self.by_node.values()  # MUT113

    def next_subscriber(self) -> object | None:
        subscriber = next(self._cursor, None)
        if subscriber is None:
            self._cursor = self._cycle()  # no subscribers: return None, start over next time
        return subscriber

    def drop(self, node: str) -> None:
        self.by_node.pop(node, None)
```

heki reports: `Subscriptions._cycle` suspends at a `yield` while iterating `self.by_node`, which `Subscriptions.drop` changes in place, so resuming it after that change raises `RuntimeError`. Iterate over a snapshot: `yield from list(self.by_node.values())`.

### Other rules about values that change under you

| Rule | Reports | Tier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`MUT119`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/change-lost-on-new-object/) | an in-place change of a new container that nothing keeps, such as `list(xs).sort()`: the change is lost | exact, default |
| [`MUT118`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/sentinel-lost-in-deepcopy/) | `copy.deepcopy` of an instance whose `object()` sentinel a function tests by identity | heuristic, runs with `--heuristic` |
| [`MUT108`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-type-mutation/) | an in-place change of a field that a standard type declares read-only: a frozen dataclass, a `NamedTuple`, `Final` and `ReadOnly` attributes, `ReadOnly` `TypedDict` keys | heuristic, opt-in |
| [`MUT107`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/hash-attr-mutation/) | a method other than an initializer that changes an attribute the class's `__hash__` reads | heuristic, opt-in |
| [`MUT120`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-view-mutation/) | a change of a value held through a read-only view (a protocol of properties without setters) that a type checker does not see | heuristic, experimental, opt-in |
| [`MUT112`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/conditional-ownership-mutation/) | an in-place change of a value that is new on one path and borrowed state on another | heuristic, experimental, opt-in |
| [`MUT101`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-property-stale-mutation/), [`MUT111`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-property-stale-read/) | an attribute that a `@cached_property` reads, changed without invalidating the cache, and a read of such a stale property | exact, experimental, opt-in |

A write is a plain store, one premise of an exact `MUT101` or `MUT111` report, only when every base of the class is a project class, a plain one, or a library base the ecosystem catalog lists as keeping what its subclasses' code stores in the instance. Django's `models.Model` is one: neither it nor its metaclass defines attribute hooks, so a write of an attribute a model's code sets (in `__init__` or a method) is a plain store, and a stale `@cached_property` over it is an exact report once the rules are switched on. A class-body field (`expires = models.DateTimeField()`, which Django replaces with a descriptor) and `pk` (a property of `Model`) keep the report heuristic.

## 🔂 Single-use values used twice or not at all

An iterator or a generator gives each item once. Reading it a second time sees nothing, and a generator that nobody iterates never runs its body.

### An iterator consumed twice

`rows` below is a generator expression. `sum` uses it up, and the list comprehension after it sees no items. `MUT106` reports the second pass. Tier: heuristic, opt-in ([`MUT106`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/iterator-double-consumption/)).

```python
def summarize(lines: list[str]) -> tuple[int, list[str]]:
    rows = (line.strip() for line in lines)
    count = sum(1 for _ in rows)
    kept = [r for r in rows if r]  # MUT106: `rows` was consumed by `sum`
    return count, kept
```

heki reports: `rows` is a single-pass iterator already consumed at line 3, so this pass sees no items. Build a list when the value is read more than once.

### A generator that is never iterated

Calling a generator function only creates the generator. Its body runs when something iterates it. `EFF116` reports a call whose generator is dropped: a statement, a value only tested for truth, a function handed to a thread, an `atexit` handler, or a `filter` predicate. Tier: exact, default, a warning; its heuristic reports, where a call may run another implementation, appear with `--heuristic` ([`EFF116`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/generator-never-iterated/)).

```python
def parse_extra(text: str):
    for line in text.splitlines():
        yield line.strip()


def check(text: str) -> None:
    if not parse_extra(text):  # EFF116
        print("nothing to parse")
```

heki reports: only a truth test reads what `parse_extra` returns, and `parse_extra` is a generator function: a generator is always true, and the body does not run. Iterate it, as in `if not list(parse_extra(text))`.

## 👉 Next steps

- [Configuration: contracts](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#contracts) lists every key of the five contracts.
- [Adopting heki in a code base](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/) shows how to start with a baseline.
- [Adoption recipes](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#starter-recipes) have contracts to copy for a web service and a layered application.
- [Coding agents](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/) shows how the same contracts keep an agent out of the files it must not change.
- `heki inspect app.cart.remove` (experimental) shows what one function changes, keeps, and returns.

## 🦀 If you know Rust

Nothing here is enforced when Python compiles the code. heki reports the places where the code breaks the expectation that a Rust compiler would hold it to. [What Python leaves open](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/philosophy/#what-python-leaves-open) puts these next to the effect and immutability checks.

| Rust | Closest in heki | How Python differs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ownership: one owner decides who may change a value | `write-owners`, `read-owners`, `call-owners` (`MUT201`, `MUT203`, `MUT204`) | Any code can reach any object. A contract names the owners, and heki reports the code outside them. |
| Shared borrow `&T` | `Sequence`, `Mapping`, `AbstractSet`, and `ReadOnly` parameters (`MUT110`); shared return values (`MUT114`, `MUT202`) | The annotation promises nothing at run time. heki reports the helper that changes the value anyway. |
| Exclusive borrow `&mut T`, no change while borrowed | a container changed while it is iterated (`MUT113`); a shallow copy that shares its items (`MUT115`) | Nothing stops the change, and it shows up later as a `RuntimeError` or a surprising value. |
| Move: a moved value cannot be used again | a single-use iterator or generator (`MUT106`, `EFF116`) | The name stays usable after the value is used up, and the second use sees nothing. |
| Lifetime: a reference does not outlive what it points to | cleanup that cancellation cuts short ([`EFF118`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/effects/#resource-and-cancellation-lifetimes)) | A Python object stays alive while a name refers to it, so nothing dangles. What can end early is the work around a resource. |


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/effects/

# Async and Execution Effects

heki finds blocking calls in async code, database queries and clients in loops, and lock and task hazards, keeps scopes free of an effect with `effect-boundaries`, and reports functions that gained an effect with `heki snapshot`.

An effect is what a call does besides returning a value: it waits on the network, sends a query, takes a lock, writes a field. heki follows effects through helper calls and across files, so a report names the function that does the work and the chain of calls that leads to it. [Rules](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/) has one page per rule, and [Contracts](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#contracts) has every contract key.

## 🔍 What runs without configuration

Three rules are exact and run by default, and two more are exact by default and are described with the problems they belong to. Their reports show the call chain, and an error fails `heki check`.

| Rule | Reports | Tier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`EFF101`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-blocking-call/) | a call in an `async def` that always runs a network, database, subprocess, or sleep call that waits on the event loop, however many helpers below | exact, default |
| [`EFF102`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-unpooled-client/) | a loop over data whose every iteration makes an HTTP, database, or RPC client, or a sessionless request | exact, default |
| [`EFF103`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-db-query/) | a loop over data whose every iteration sends a database statement | exact, default |

`EFF102` and `EFF103` also have heuristic reports, where a premise of the claim is open (a loop that can make a client or run a query on every iteration). They appear with `--heuristic`.

`EFF103` knows Django's model managers from the ecosystem catalog. `Model.objects`, read on a model class or on `cls`, is the `Manager` Django adds, or the manager the model's body declares (`objects = StreamManager()`, a project subclass of `models.Manager`). Its query methods (`get`, `count`, `create`, `get_or_create`, `update`, ...) send a statement on every call, so calling one per item of a loop over data is an exact, default `EFF103` report; `filter`, `exclude`, and `all` only build a `QuerySet`. A method the manager adds is followed as project code. Some managers keep the report heuristic (with `--heuristic`) or unknown:

- a manager that binds a name its query methods use (`get_queryset`, `_queryset_class`, `__init__`) runs its own code under them: heuristic. So is a model's default `objects` while the project defines such a manager, since heki takes a `Manager` to be possibly an instance of any project subclass;
- a project `QuerySet` subclass (`models.QuerySet` is the catalog's `QuerySet`) that binds a name a query method looks up on the queryset (`get`'s `filter` and `_fetch_all`, `acount`'s `count`) runs its own code under that method: a call of it on a `QuerySet` is heuristic, since heki takes a `QuerySet` to be possibly an instance of any project subclass. A subclass that only adds methods keeps every row, on its own instances too;
- `create` and `acreate` save a new instance of the model: while a project model binds `save` (or a method `save` reaches, `save_base`, `_save_table`, ...) otherwise than as a method calling `super().save(...)` on every path, they are heuristic. `get_or_create` and `update_or_create` query by `get` first on every call, and `QuerySet.delete` never calls the model's `delete`, so a model's overrides leave them exact;
- a manager `from_queryset()` or `as_manager()` builds, one of a class outside the project, and related managers (`question.choice_set`, a many-to-many field read on an instance) are unknown: they add no effect.

`EFF109` (a lock taken again while it is held) is under [Exclusive use and lock safety](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/effects/#a-lock-taken-again-while-it-is-held), and `EFF116` (a generator that nothing iterates) is on [State Ownership and Mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/ownership/#a-generator-that-is-never-iterated). Both are exact and run by default.

Two rules run by default only when you pass `--heuristic` (or set `lint.heuristic = true`), because they can be wrong about the code. They are about locks and cancellation: `EFF117` is under [Exclusive use and lock safety](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/effects/#exclusive-use-and-lock-safety), and `EFF118` under [Resource and cancellation lifetimes](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/effects/#resource-and-cancellation-lifetimes).

The knowledge base names the calls that wait. Besides `requests` and `httpx.Client`, it lists the synchronous clients of Xinference (`xinference_client.RESTfulClient` and the handles of its models) and of Supabase and PostgREST (`supabase.Client`, `postgrest.SyncPostgrestClient`): building a table query, including through `.not_`, sends nothing, and `execute()` waits for the server, so `EFF101` and `EFF103` report it there. Tier: exact, default ([`EFF101`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-blocking-call/), [`EFF103`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-db-query/)).

`DATA101` (exact, default, [`loop-carried-concat`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-carried-concat/)) also reports an array grown through `numpy.r_[...]` or `numpy.c_[...]` on every iteration (`arr = np.r_[arr, chunk]`), also when a helper returns that concatenation (`arr = grow(arr, chunk)`), as it does for `numpy.hstack`.

A function handed to a thread or process pool runs once per item for these rules:
`executor.submit(f, ...)` in a loop counts as a call of `f` on every iteration, and
`executor.map(f, items)` as one call of `f` per item, for the `concurrent.futures` executors;
`loop.run_in_executor(executor, f, ...)` in a loop is the same. `EFF102` then reports a client `f`
makes per item, and `EFF103` a query `f` sends per item. Through a pool both reports are heuristic
(with `--heuristic`), since the pool runs `f` after `submit` returns. A worker in another process
(`ProcessPoolExecutor`, `anyio.to_process.run_sync`) runs on copies of its arguments, so what it
changes in them does not reach the caller, and rules that follow changes to the caller's objects
do not follow it there.

The first page of the docs shows [`EFF101` two helpers below an `async def` and `EFF103` one helper below a loop](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/), with their output.

The chain a blocking-call report shows (`EFF101`, both tiers, and `EFF105`) is one real path to the call, chosen in this order: a path the call's arguments allow (a helper that dispatches on `isinstance(item, Response)` shows the branch an argument of known class takes), then a path on the normal flow before one through cleanup code (an `except` handler or a `finally` body), then the shortest. Which path is shown never decides whether the report exists or its tier. Output folds many reports into one (`(+N more)`) only when they reach the same blocking call through the same helper: sites that call one API directly still fold together, and sites that reach different blocking calls through different helpers stay separate groups.

## 🔧 Rules to switch on

These rules are off by default. Name one in `extend-select` or with `--extend-select EFF105`. A prefix such as `EFF` or `ALL` never enables them.

```toml
# heki.toml
[lint]
extend-select = ["EFF105", "EFF107"]
```

| Rule | Reports | Tier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`EFF105`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-blocking-fs/) | a call in an `async def` that always runs blocking local file I/O on the event loop | exact, opt-in |
| [`EFF107`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unretained-async-task/) | an `asyncio.create_task` result bound to a local variable that is never awaited, returned, or stored; a call whose result is discarded is not reported | heuristic, opt-in |
| [`EFF112`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/set-order-output/) | the iteration order of a set of strings, which changes between runs, reaching a file, a stream, or a serializer | heuristic, experimental, opt-in |
| [`EFF114`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/recursion-error-as-value/) | an `except` around a recursion that takes the `RecursionError` and goes on, so the result depends on the stack depth | heuristic, experimental, opt-in |
| [`EFF115`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-def-as-sync-callback/) | an `async def` handed to a library call that does not await it (a thread target, an executor function, a signal handler), so the body never runs | heuristic, experimental, opt-in |

Experimental rules can change or go away between releases. [Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/) says why each one is marked.

## 🔒 Exclusive use and lock safety

Some objects allow one user at a time: a lock, a stream reader, a database connection. These rules report code that breaks that. The opt-in ones (`EFF106` and `EFF110`) are off until you name them in `extend-select`, for example `--extend-select EFF106`. A prefix such as `EFF` or `ALL` never enables them.

```toml
# heki.toml
[lint]
extend-select = ["EFF106", "EFF110"]
```

### An exclusive object used by tasks started together

A stream reader, an asyncpg connection, or a WebSocket runs one operation at a time. `EFF110` reports tasks started together (`asyncio.gather`, a task group) that all use the same one, so the second call raises. Tier: heuristic, experimental, opt-in ([`EFF110`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/exclusive-object-fanout/)).

```python
import asyncio


class FrameClient:
    def __init__(self, reader: asyncio.StreamReader) -> None:
        self._reader = reader

    async def read_frame(self) -> bytes:
        return await self._reader.readexactly(4)

    async def read_frames(self, count: int) -> list[bytes]:
        return await asyncio.gather(*(self.read_frame() for _ in range(count)))  # EFF110
```

heki reports: `FrameClient.read_frames` starts a task for every item, each using `self._reader` (`asyncio.gather`); `asyncio.StreamReader` allows one operation at a time, so the second task's call raises. Read the frames one after another instead.

### A lock taken again while it is held

`threading.Lock` and `asyncio.Lock` are not reentrant. A method that holds the lock and calls another method that takes it waits for itself. `EFF109` reports the second take, directly or through a call. Tier: exact, default; its heuristic reports, where a helper takes the lock on some paths only, appear with `--heuristic` ([`EFF109`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/lock-reacquired-while-held/)).

```python
# app/m.py
import threading


class Registry:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        self._items: dict[str, int] = {}

    def size(self) -> int:
        with self._lock:
            return len(self._items)

    def add(self, key: str) -> int:
        with self._lock:
            self._items[key] = 1
            return self.size()  # EFF109
```

heki reports: `Registry.add` calls `app.m.Registry.size`, which takes `self._lock` while `Registry.add` holds it (taken at line 14); `threading.Lock` is not reentrant, so this waits forever. Move the body of `size` into a helper that does not take the lock, and call that one.

### A write without the lock its other writes hold

When one method changes a field holding a lock, every method that changes it needs the same lock. `EFF117` reports a write that holds none while another write of the same state holds a thread lock, and a thread heki resolves can run one of them. An update can be lost. Tier: heuristic, runs with `--heuristic` ([`EFF117`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unlocked-write-of-guarded-state/)).

```python
import threading


class Stats:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        self.received = 0

    def start(self) -> None:
        threading.Thread(target=self._read).start()

    def _read(self) -> None:
        with self._lock:
            self.received += 1

    def reset(self) -> None:
        self.received = 0  # EFF117
```

heki reports: `Stats.reset` assigns `self.received` where heki finds no lock held, while `Stats._read` assigns it holding `self._lock`; `Stats._read` can run on another thread, so the two writes can interleave and one can lose the other's update. Take the lock in `reset` too.

### I/O while holding a lock

A lock held across a network call or an `await` makes every other user of the lock wait for the slow call. `EFF106` reports an `await` or blocking network I/O while a `threading` lock or a database transaction is held. Tier: heuristic, opt-in ([`EFF106`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/lock-or-tx-held-across-io/)).

```python
# app/sync.py
import threading

import requests

_lock = threading.Lock()


def refresh(url: str) -> str:
    with _lock:
        return requests.get(url, timeout=5).text
```

```console
$ heki check
app/sync.py:10:16: EFF106 (lock-or-tx-held-across-io) [error, heuristic] `refresh` calls `requests.get` (blocking network I/O) while holding the synchronous `threading.Lock` taken at line 9
   |
10 |         return requests.get(url, timeout=5).text
   |                ^
  = related: app/sync.py:10:16: `refresh` calls `requests.get`
  = help: make the request before taking the lock and hold it only for the update

Found 1 diagnostic(s) in 2 file(s).
...
```

Make the request before taking the lock and hold it only for the update.

## ⏳ Resource and cancellation lifetimes

Work around a resource can end early. A cancelled task stops at its next checkpoint, and cleanup that runs after the cancellation can be stopped the same way, so the resource is never released. Each rule in this part reports one way the end of a scope leaves a resource in the wrong state. The rules are listed as entries of their own, so a new one is one more entry.

### Cleanup that stops at a cancellation checkpoint

A `finally` body, an `except` that takes the cancellation, or an `__aexit__` that awaits a call reaching an AnyIO or Trio cancellation checkpoint is cut short in a cancelled scope: the await raises the cancellation again and the rest of the cleanup does not run. `EFF118` reports it when no shield is on the way. A shield is a `CancelScope` with `shield=True` by the public name (`anyio.CancelScope`) or by the path that defines it (`anyio._core._tasks.CancelScope`). Tier: heuristic, runs with `--heuristic` ([`EFF118`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unshielded-cleanup-checkpoint/)).

```python
# app/m.py
import anyio


async def delete_group(name: str) -> None:
    await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(delete_container_group, name)


async def run(name: str) -> None:
    try:
        await watch(name)
    finally:
        await delete_group(name)  # EFF118
        log_deleted(name)
```

heki reports: `run` awaits `app.m.delete_group` in a `finally` body, which reaches the cancellation checkpoint `anyio.to_thread.run_sync` 2 calls down with no shield on the way: in a cancelled scope the await raises the cancellation and the rest of the cleanup does not run. Shield the cleanup:

```python
    finally:
        with anyio.CancelScope(shield=True):
            await delete_group(name)
        log_deleted(name)
```

## 📜 Contracts for execution effects

`effect-boundaries` marks code that must stay free of an effect: a render function that makes no blocking call, a decision pass that writes no model state, a generator that does not read the environment. Any function in scope that reaches the effect, directly or through calls, is reported as [`EFF201`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/effect-boundary-violation/) (heuristic, contract).

```toml
# heki.toml
[[effect-boundaries]]
name = "pure-render"
scopes = ["app.render.*"]
forbid = ["blocking"]
message = "render from data the caller already loaded"
fail = true
```

`render_page` in `app/render.py` calls `load_title`, which calls `requests.get`:

```console
$ heki check
app/render.py:5:19: EFF201 (effect-boundary-violation) [error, heuristic] `render_page` reaches blocking_net (`requests.get` via `app.loader.load_title`), which effect boundary `pure-render` forbids
  |
5 |     return f"<h1>{load_title(page_id)}</h1>"
  |                   ^
  = related: app/render.py:5:19: `render_page` calls `app.loader.load_title`
  = related: app/loader.py:5:12: `load_title` calls `requests.get`
  = help: render from data the caller already loaded

Found 1 diagnostic(s) in 3 file(s).
```

The run exits with code 1. `forbid` takes tokens such as `blocking`, `blocking-net`, `blocking-db`, `sleep`, `mutates-params`, `writes-targets`, `reads-targets`, `calls`, and `reads-environment`. [`effect-boundaries`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#effect-boundaries) lists them all with their extra keys.

A value that an annotation declares as a union of up to eight classes is each of them, so a call on it reaches the method of each class; a union that different assignments join keeps three. A loop over a `TypedDict`'s keys or items that calls `setattr(obj, name, value)` writes the keys the class declares only for a closed `TypedDict` (`closed=True`, or a base that is closed). For an open one the write stays an attribute named at run time (`unresolved-writes`), because a subclass value may carry more keys.

A `scopes` or `allowed-callees` entry naming a method (`Class.method`) names that method only. With `include-overrides = true` in the boundary (or in its [defaults table](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#defaults-for-the-tables-of-a-kind)) it also names the overrides in the project subclasses of `Class`, nested scopes included, so a subclass written later is in scope or allowed with no change of the configuration. The key is off by default for that reason.

## 📸 Public API effect changes across pull requests

A change in what a public function does is worth a review even when no rule fires: it starts changing an argument, or doing network I/O. `heki snapshot` saves the effect summaries of the project, and `MUT103` ([`summary-effect-regression`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/summary-effect-regression/), heuristic, opt-in) reports each function that gained an effect since.

```console
$ heki snapshot --write    # writes .heki-summary-snapshot.json
```

Commit the file. Later, `total` starts to sort its argument, and so does `checkout`, which calls it:

```console
$ heki check --select MUT103 --fail-on warning
app/billing.py:1:1: MUT103 (summary-effect-regression) [error, heuristic] `total` gained side effects since the summary snapshot: mutates parameter `prices`
  |
1 | def total(prices: list[int]) -> int:
  | ^
  = help: if the change is intended, refresh the snapshot with `heki snapshot --write`

app/billing.py:6:1: MUT103 (summary-effect-regression) [error, heuristic] `checkout` gained side effects since the summary snapshot: mutates parameter `prices`
  |
6 | def checkout(prices: list[int]) -> int:
  | ^
  = help: if the change is intended, refresh the snapshot with `heki snapshot --write`

Found 2 diagnostic(s) in 2 file(s).
```

The run exits with code 1. When the new effect is intended, refresh the snapshot in the same pull request, so the diff of the JSON file shows reviewers what changed. A pull request can also be compared with a snapshot of its base branch, with `heki check --snapshot PATH`. [Effect snapshots](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#effect-snapshots-mut103) has both workflows.

## 👉 Next steps

- [Configuration: effect-boundaries](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#effect-boundaries) lists every key and `forbid` token.
- [Adopting heki in a code base](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/) shows how to start with a baseline, and has the [blocking and database-write contracts of a web service](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#an-async-web-or-database-service) to copy.
- `heki inspect app.render.render_page` (experimental) shows what one function reaches, with the call chains. See [Coding agents](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#what-a-function-does-heki-inspect-experimental).
- [State Ownership and Mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/ownership/) covers the contracts about who may change, read, or call a thing, and the rules for borrowed, shared, and single-use values.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/imports/

# Imports and Module Boundaries

heki finds import cycles, import-order crashes, and test or development code loaded by a package, enforces `import-boundaries` contracts, and shows what a module loads with `heki inspect --imports` (all experimental).

The import rules know when each import runs: while its module loads, when a function runs, or only under `TYPE_CHECKING`. The rules and the contract can change between releases, and none of them runs without configuration. [Rules](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/) has one page per rule, and [Imports](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#imports-toolhekiimports) has the settings that say which imports count.

## 🔁 Cycles and import-order crashes

Two modules that import each other while they load are an import cycle. The cycle itself can work, until one import order makes a `from M import name` run before `M` has bound the name. Then Python raises `ImportError`, often only in a test run or an entry point that imports the modules in another order.

```toml
# heki.toml
[lint]
extend-select = ["IMP101", "IMP102"]
fail = ["IMP101", "IMP102"]
```

`fail` makes the reports of those rules fail the run, whatever their tier. Without it, a heuristic report is a warning.

```python
# pkg/a.py
from pkg.b import make_b


def make_a() -> str:
    return "a" + make_b()
```

```python
# pkg/b.py
from pkg.a import make_a


def make_b() -> str:
    return "b"


def both() -> str:
    return make_a()
```

```console
$ heki check --output-format concise
pkg/a.py:1:19: IMP102 [heuristic] `<module>` imports `make_b` from `pkg.b` while `pkg.b` is still loading, at its import of `pkg.a`, and has not bound it: importing `pkg.b` while no module of the import cycle has loaded raises `ImportError` here
pkg/b.py:1:19: IMP101 [heuristic] `<module>` imports `pkg.a` while `pkg.b` loads, which closes the import cycle `pkg.a` -> `pkg.b` -> `pkg.a`
pkg/b.py:1:19: IMP102 [heuristic] `<module>` imports `make_a` from `pkg.a` while `pkg.a` is still loading, at its import of `pkg.b`, and has not bound it: importing `pkg.a` while no module of the import cycle has loaded raises `ImportError` here
Found 3 diagnostic(s) in 3 file(s).
```

This output is from heki 0.9.0. The full format adds the source line and a `help`. When one import is on every cycle of the modules, the help names it, as here, where each of the two imports is:

```text
  = help: every import cycle of these modules goes through this import: move it into the functions that use it, or make it `lazy`
```

heki names an import only after one search of the import graph without it finds the cycle gone, and only a change that takes it out of what the rule counts: `lazy` from Python 3.15 on, where Python allows the keyword, and neither change for a class of imports `cycle-edges` counts. It names no import whose name code running while its module loads may read: the module body with its class bodies, decorators, defaults, bases, and the annotations the target version evaluates in place, the module's functions these call or apply as decorators, and its `__all__`. Moved into a function, such an import leaves that read unbound, and made `lazy`, it loads at the read, still while the module loads. Nor does it name one whose name another project module takes while that module loads: by `from m import name`, a star import of the module (for a public name), an attribute read off the module object (`import m`, then `m.name`), or the module object passed anywhere else (for any name, private ones too), also through a package that re-exports the name. A later statement of the module rebinding the name takes the import out of this only when no code runs between them (no other import, no call), so that no other module can see the import's binding. Moved, the import leaves the module without the name, so the move is offered only while no other module reads it at all; a read in a function leaves `lazy`, which loads at that read. Otherwise the help names the general ways out: import the name inside the function that uses it, import the module and read the name where it is used, or bind the name before the import of the cycle. `IMP301` and `IMP302` name the one import every chain from the package to the reported module goes through, and `IMP201` with `reach = "import-time"` the one every chain to the forbidden module goes through, each checked the same way.

## 📦 What package code loads while it loads

A package that works in the repository can fail after `pip install`: it imports a test helper, a development dependency, or a module that only an extra provides. These rules compare the imports that run while a module loads with the files of the project and the dependencies in `pyproject.toml`.

```toml
# heki.toml
[lint]
extend-select = ["IMP104", "IMP301"]
```

```python
# pkg/core.py
from tests.helpers import fake
```

```python
# pkg/fixtures.py
from faker import Faker
```

With `faker` declared only in the `dev` dependency group:

```console
$ heki check --output-format concise
pkg/core.py:1:27: IMP104 [heuristic] `<module>` imports `tests.helpers` while `pkg.core` loads, test code outside the package (`tests/helpers.py`) that the installed package does not include
pkg/fixtures.py:1:19: IMP301 [heuristic] `<module>` imports `faker` while `pkg.fixtures` loads, and the project declares `faker`, which provides it, only in the development group `dev`
Found 2 diagnostic(s) in 5 file(s).
```

heki matches a module to its distribution by name (`PyYAML` provides `yaml`, `Pillow` provides `PIL`). For any other module, `module-distributions` in `[tool.heki.imports]` says which distribution provides it.

## 🧱 Architecture import boundaries

`import-boundaries` says which modules may import which. It counts every import that runs, including one inside a function.

```toml
# heki.toml
[[import-boundaries]]
name = "domain-leaf"
importers = ["app.domain.*"]
forbidden-imports = ["app.web", "app.web.*"]
message = "the domain must not know the web layer"
fail = true
```

`app/domain/orders.py` imports the web layer inside a function:

```console
$ heki check
app/domain/orders.py:2:31: IMP201 (import-boundary-violation) [error, heuristic] `total` imports `app.web.views.render` when it runs, a forbidden import of `domain-leaf`
  |
2 |     from app.web.views import render
  |                               ^
  = help: the domain must not know the web layer

Found 1 diagnostic(s) in 5 file(s).
```

The run exits with code 1. A table can also list `allowed-imports` (with `<stdlib>` for the standard library) so that everything else is forbidden. With `unresolved = "report"`, an import whose module heki cannot name is reported as `IMP202`.

## 🔬 Inspecting the module load graph

`heki inspect --imports` takes a module name or a glob. For each project module it lists every import with the time it runs and what it loads, and what loading the module loads while it loads:

```console
$ heki inspect --imports app.domain.orders
app.domain.orders (app/domain/orders.py, open code)
  imports:
    2:31  from-import of `render`: app.web.views (project)  [function, in `total`, unconditional]
  loads while it loads, at least:
    project modules: none
    other modules: none
```

The import is in `total`, so it runs when `total` runs, and loading `app.domain.orders` loads no other module. Use it to see why an import cycle exists, or what an entry point pulls in at start-up. The command is experimental, like the rest of `heki inspect`.

## 📋 The rules and the contract

| Rule | Reports | Tier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [`IMP101`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/import-cycle/) | project modules that import each other while they load, once per group | heuristic, experimental, opt-in |
| [`IMP102`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/circular-import-failure/) | a `from M import name` that raises `ImportError` when a module of its cycle is imported first | heuristic, experimental, opt-in |
| [`IMP104`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/development-code-import/) | a module of the distributed package that imports test code, or a module outside the source roots of a `src` layout | heuristic, experimental, opt-in |
| [`IMP301`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/development-dependency-at-import-time/) | a package module that loads, while it loads, a module provided only by a development dependency | heuristic, experimental, opt-in |
| [`IMP302`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/optional-dependency-at-import-time/) | an import of a top-level package or an entry point's module that loads a module provided only by an extra | heuristic, experimental, opt-in |
| [`IMP201`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/import-boundary-violation/) | an import that an `import-boundaries` contract forbids or does not allow | heuristic, experimental, contract |
| [`IMP202`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-import/) | strict mode of `import-boundaries`: an import whose module heki cannot name | heuristic, experimental, contract |

[Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/) says why each one is marked. Which imports count for `IMP101` is the `cycle-edges` setting of `[tool.heki.imports]`: `"body"` by default, and `"lazy"`, `"function"`, and `"type-checking"` on request.

## 👉 Next steps

- [Configuration: import-boundaries](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#import-boundaries) lists every key of the contract.
- [Configuration: imports](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#imports-toolhekiimports) lists `cycle-edges` and `module-distributions`.
- [Adopting heki in a code base](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/) shows how to start with a baseline, and has a [domain boundary with a read-only settings contract](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#a-layered-application) to copy.
- [State Ownership and Mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/ownership/) and [Async and Execution Effects](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/effects/) cover the other contracts.

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/fixes/

# Fixes and Safety

`heki check --fix` rewrites an `OPT` finding only when heki proves that the rewrite keeps what
the program does. This page shows the fix commands, what each finding offers, and what a fix
must prove.

## Fix commands

```console
$ heki check --diff                              # preview (exit code 1 when something would change)
```
