```console
$ heki check --fix                               # apply safe, unconditional fixes
$ heki check --fix --include-size-dependent      # also the proven-safe size-dependent rewrites
$ heki check --fix --unsafe-fixes                # also the unsafe fixes
```

- A fix comes with a report: `--fix` applies only the fixes of the reports shown. A report whose
  rewrite heki proves safe has a safe fix, and it is [exact](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/#certifications) only
  when its other premises hold too: an `OPT120` report in a `while` loop is heuristic even when
  its rewrite is proven safe, because the loop's trip count is open. `OPT101` and `OPT102`
  run by default, so a run without configuration applies their fixes. Over another loop than one
  the data sizes, an `OPT101` or `OPT102` rewrite is heuristic, and its fix applies with
  `--heuristic` or when its rule is selected.
- The size-dependent rules (`OPT103`, `OPT110`, `OPT111`, `OPT120`, `OPT121`, `OPT130`) are
  opt-in: their rewrites are proven, but the loops they report were rarely large enough to matter
  ([Rule precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/#certifications)).
- `--include-size-dependent` runs the size-dependent rules with a rewrite (`OPT110`, `OPT111`,
  `OPT120`, `OPT121`, `OPT130`; not `OPT103`, which has no rewrite), as if `extend-select`
  named them. The flag alone changes no file: with `--fix` it applies their proven
  rewrites in every function (with `--diff`, it shows them), also over a loop whose trip count
  the data does not decide. After the fixes, the run lists their reports it could not rewrite, each with the obligation that
  blocks it.
- An unsafe fix may change what the program does, and applies only with `--unsafe-fixes`. One
  rule has one: a [`MUT118`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/sentinel-lost-in-deepcopy/) report for a Python 3.15
  target replaces the `object()` sentinel with `sentinel("NAME")`, whose type, repr, and
  pickling differ ([Fix safety](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/sentinel-lost-in-deepcopy/#fix-safety)).
- `--diff` takes the same flags as `--fix` and writes nothing.
- With `--touched`, or files given as paths, `--fix` and `--diff` rewrite only those files. A
  shown report in another file (one whose call chain reaches a touched file) keeps its fix, and
  the run says how many it left: a pre-commit hook never rewrites a file the commit left alone.

## What each finding offers

Every `OPT` rule finds a quadratic or linear-per-iteration pattern that has a faster equivalent.
Two independent questions decide whether heki offers the rewrite:

| Question | Possible answers |
| -------- | ---------------- |
| **Safety:** does the rewrite keep the program's behavior? | every proof obligation is `Established`, `Blocked` (cannot be proven here), or `Disproved` (a concrete counterexample shape exists) |
| **Profitability:** is the rewrite faster for every input? | unconditional, or size-dependent (it can be slower for tiny inputs or for loops that run zero times) |

### Safety

A rewrite keeps the program's behavior when the function returns an equal result or raises the
same exception type, makes the same calls into other code in the same order, changes shared
objects the same way, and ends the same way. Run time, memory, `id()` values, traceback line
numbers, and the messages of builtin exceptions are not kept
([observational equivalence](https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md#31-observational-equivalence)):
after an `OPT120` fix, `q[0]` of an empty queue still raises `IndexError`, with the message of a
`deque`.

| Obligations | What you get |
| ----------- | ------------ |
| All established | A diagnostic with a fix. A statement whose shape heki does not rewrite (a parenthesized `x = (x + [i])`, an annotated `x: list = x + [i]`) gets a diagnostic saying the rewrite is proven safe, to be made by hand. |
| One blocked | A diagnostic naming the first blocking obligation, and no fix. |
| One disproved | Nothing: the pattern only looks quadratic, and rewriting it would be a bug. |

### Profitability

| Profitability | Rules | Certainty | Applied by |
| ------------- | ----- | --------- | ---------- |
| Unconditional (faster from the first iteration) | `OPT101`, `OPT102` | exact (the proven reports) | `heki check --fix` |
| Size-dependent | `OPT110`, `OPT111`, `OPT120`, `OPT121`, `OPT130` (opt-in) | exact (the proven reports over a loop the data sizes) | `heki check --fix --include-size-dependent` |
| Size-dependent, no rewrite | `OPT103` (opt-in), `OPT112`, `OPT113` | `OPT103` exact (the proven reports over a loop the data sizes), `OPT113` exact (its exact tier), `OPT112` heuristic | none: suggestion only |

### When the size is fixed

A size-dependent rule reports nothing when the code fixes the size:

- the container holds at most 16 items and nothing grows it past that or lets it escape. It
  is a display without `*` / `**` unpacking, a string constant, a builtin constructor of an
  iterable the code fixes (`list(range(7))`, `tuple(".;:")`, `sorted(NAMES)`, `list()`), a
  slice with constant bounds (`cases[:3]`, `paths[-2:]`), or a comprehension over fixed
  iterables (`[c for c in LABELS if c in wanted]`). Shrinking it (`expected.pop(0)` on
  `expected = [b"a", b""]`) and read-only builtins are fine, and so is filling a new list a
  fixed number of times (`ids.append(card["id"])` in a loop over at most 6 cards). A tuple or
  a string stays fixed whatever other code does with it, unless other code rebinds its name
  (`cfg.STATEMENTS = tuple(rows)`). This holds also through local names,
  module constants, and other modules' module-level displays and class attributes, read in a
  function or in a module body;
- the loop runs a fixed number of times: over such a container, a `range` of constants with at
  most 16 steps, or an iterable a test on every path to the loop caps (`if not 1 <= len(cards)
  <= 6: raise ValueError(...)`, `assert len(xs) <= 3`, also after a loop that shrinks it, when
  nothing on the way to the loop grows it or hands it to other code);
- the list is rebuilt in every iteration;
- the loop's own test caps the accumulator: `while len(buf) < 10`.

These facts decide profitability only, never safety. A size known only at run time does not
count: a list whose size depends on the input is reported even when it always holds three items.

## What a fix must prove

The analysis behind the `OPT` rules is separate from the one behind the other rules, and
deliberately conservative:

| Obligation | Why | Example |
| ---------- | --- | ------- |
| No type annotation is trusted | a subclass can override `__contains__` or `__add__` | `x: list[int] = WeirdList(...)` is not a list for heki |
| The object is created in the function and never escapes | heki counts anything it cannot see as shared: parameters, globals, attributes, values passed to unknown functions, names captured by closures | `sink(rows)` inside the loop blocks `rows.append(...)` |
| Access is exclusive: no other variable, iterator, or view still refers to the old object after the statement | an in-place update would change what they see | `for v in x: x = x + [v]` ends, but `x.append(v)` would loop forever, so heki reports nothing |
| Evaluation order and exceptions are kept | a rewrite must not call anything earlier or later | `{**d, f(): g()}` becomes `d.update({f(): g()})`, not `d[f()] = g()`, which would call `g` first |
| Builtin names are the builtins | the module can rebind them | trusted only while nothing rebinds them: an assignment, a `global` store, `from m import *`, any call of `globals()`, or a module that patches `builtins` (a `.pyi` stub never runs, so its `import builtins` does not count) |
| Locals change only through the code | `eval`, `exec`, `locals()`, `sys._getframe`, and frame attributes can change them behind any analysis | candidates in such functions are always blocked; `heki assumptions` lists these places in a project |

The scope analysis is checked against CPython's `symtable`, and adversarial programs that break a
naive rewrite are run on CPython: see [Development](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/development/#checks-against-cpython).

## How `--fix` applies fixes

1. It applies the fixes that do not overlap.
2. It analyzes the result again and repeats until nothing changes, at most ten passes: a fix that
   becomes provable after another one is applied too.
3. It reports what is left.

| Case | What happens |
| ---- | ------------ |
| A suppressed diagnostic (`# heki: ignore[...]`) | It is never fixed. |
| A file that changed on disk meanwhile (an editor saved it) | It is not written: the run keeps that save, reports an error, and exits with code 2. Run `--fix` again. |
| Fixes of a pass that would leave a file that does not parse | None of them is applied to that file, and the run exits with code 2 (a heki bug to report). |
| `\n`, `\r\n`, or lone `\r` line breaks | Fixes work the same, and the lines they insert use the file's own line break. |

`--diff` prints the paths every other output format prints (relative to the working directory),
so `patch -p1` applies it where heki ran. It writes the lines in the file's own encoding (a
PEP 263 Latin-1 declaration included), as `--fix` writes the file, so the patch matches its bytes.

## Fixes keep type checkers and isort satisfied

A `collections.deque` rewrite (`OPT120`, `OPT121`) also rewrites the variable's annotation and
adds the import:

```console
$ heki check --diff --include-size-dependent jobs.py
--- a/jobs.py
+++ b/jobs.py
@@ -1,11 +1,12 @@
 """Job queue."""
 
+import collections
 import os
 
 
 def drain(jobs: list[int]) -> int:
-    queue: list[int] = list(jobs)
+    queue: collections.deque[int] = collections.deque(list(jobs))
     total = 0
     while queue:
-        total += queue.pop(0)
+        total += queue.popleft()
     return total
Would fix 1 issue(s) in 1 file(s).
```

- An annotation the fix cannot rewrite (`Sequence[int]`, a union), or another annotated
  declaration of the variable, blocks the fix.
- So does a variable the list reaches that is also bound to another object (`s = [...]` before
  `s = queue`, or a parameter `s`): a type checker gives the variable one type, which would
  not accept the deque.
- `import collections` goes into the module's block of standard-library imports, in the order
  that block follows: straight imports first, or sorted by module as with
  `force-sort-within-sections`.
- Without such a block, it starts one before the other imports. In a module without imports, it
  follows the docstring and `__future__` imports, with the blank lines isort expects.
- It never goes above a shebang, an encoding declaration, or a `from __future__` import, and only
  imports run before it, so the rewritten function cannot run before `collections` is bound.
- An existing `from collections import deque` or `import collections` is reused only when it runs
  unconditionally (not under `if TYPE_CHECKING:`), nothing else binds or deletes the name (no
  other store, no `del` in a function declaring it `global`, no star import that may rebind it),
  and it names the standard library's module (not `from .collections import deque`).


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/recommend/

# Configuration Advice

!!! warning "Experimental"

    `heki recommend` is experimental: what it prints, its policies, and its JSON object can
    still change in any release. See [Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/).

`heki recommend` analyzes a project as `heki check` does and prints advice on its
configuration, with counts from the project and the keys to add to `[tool.heki]`. It writes no
file and runs none of the project's code.

```console
$ heki recommend
$ heki recommend app --output-format json
```

It takes the options of `heki check` that decide what is analyzed: `--select`,
`--extend-select`, `--ignore`, `--heuristic` / `--no-heuristic`, `--config`,
`--target-version`, and `--baseline`. The advice is relative to that configuration. `--all`
shows every block of contracts, where the report shows the first 3 of each kind, lists up
to 50 of the sites that keep blocks at `unresolved = "ignore"`, where it lists 5, lists every
suggestion group, the heuristic ones too, where the text lists the first 3 exact ones, and names
every rule without reports. `--focus types` prints the [suggestions](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/recommend/#suggestions) alone, with
every exact group, and `--focus types --diff` prints them as a patch
([below](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/recommend/#applying-the-suggestions)).

## What it prints

- **The project**: the root, and the files and functions analyzed.
- **The takeaways**: at most three numbered lines, one of each kind: the quickest safety win,
  the smallest wall for a coding agent, and the biggest blind spot. Each repeats what a part
  further down says, names that part, and ends with the command or the setting that acts on it.
  A kind with nothing behind it has no line ([below](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/recommend/#the-takeaways)).
- **Reports now**: what `heki check` prints with the configuration, as exact and heuristic
  reports (reports sharing a root cause count once, as `heki check` folds them), the heuristic
  reports of exact rules that `lint.heuristic = false` withholds, and the heuristic rules it
  leaves off. With a baseline, the reports it allows and the regressions.
- **Types the code already keeps**: the [suggestions](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/recommend/#suggestions), counted exact and
  heuristic, and whether heki found a type checker's configuration (without one, half of each
  guard is missing). The first 3 exact groups by rank are listed, each on one line with its
  place, function and parameter, the annotation now and as proposed, and its labels;
  `--focus types` lists every exact group, and `--all` every group, the heuristic ones last with
  the premises they leave open. The lines under them say what each group states, what reports a
  later change of the type it writes, what each label shown means, and the command that applies
  the exact groups. The edits are in the JSON object; none of it enters the block.
- **Rules worth enabling here**: every rule the configuration leaves off, and every exact rule
  whose heuristic reports it withholds, with the reports naming it in `extend-select` would add
  (exact and heuristic, and with a baseline the regressions among them), its consequence, and
  the published measurement of how often its reports are right about the code
  ([Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/)), or "not measured". A rule that runs now and withholds its
  heuristic reports says so. A line under the rows gives the `heki check --extend-select` command
  that shows the reports they count (with the paths given; a rule the configuration ignores is
  left out of it, since `ignore` wins). The rules without reports here are on one line: how
  many, the exact ones by code, the experimental exact ones apart, and the number of heuristic
  ones, which `--all` names. `--all`, or a saved summary snapshot, also shows how to run
  `MUT103`.
- **What heki cannot see**: where heki is silent, so no count of reports applies (see
  [below](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/recommend/#what-heki-cannot-see)). The source-root candidates, the one part that enters the
  block, come first.
- **Contract candidates**: the `write-owners`, `read-owners`, and `effect-boundaries`
  contracts the code already keeps, as blocks: the candidates whose entries differ only in their
  targets or scopes are one entry. Each block has its confidence, evidence, and the trial run of
  its rules that verified it, and the class patterns tried for it ([below](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/recommend/#blocks-and-class-patterns)).
  The first 3 blocks of each kind are shown and declared, and the others counted. Then the
  sites heki cannot tie to a class that keep blocks at `unresolved = "ignore"`, each once with
  the candidates and blocks it holds back, and the candidates a trial rejected, with the report
  it made.
- **Contract entries that match nothing**: the entries of the contracts configured now that name
  no definition, attribute, method, or `__dict__` key in the analyzed files, with the existing
  names like each, as `heki check` warns about them
  ([Entries that match nothing](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#entries-that-match-nothing)). They are listed
  whatever `lint.unmatched-contract-entries` says, and the section is left out when there is
  none.
- **What keeps reports heuristic**: the heuristic reports of exact claims (the heuristic reports
  of exact rules), counted by the premise of the claim each leaves open and why ([Rule
  Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/)), or by the condition of the exact tier that is no premise
  ("Trip count open": the claim holds, and the change pays off only over a loop the data
  sizes). Each row says what the cause states, how many reports leave it open, how many leave
  nothing else open, and what closes it: an annotation, which must be true; a change of the
  code; heki's catalog, which no configuration sets (the row says where to report the case);
  or nothing you can apply. None of it enters the block. A report whose rule records no cause
  is counted as "not recorded", never given a guessed one.
- **Notes**: what to know to weigh the advice. How many of the reports shown now (with a
  baseline, the regressions) make `heki check` fail, with the Ratchet baseline that records them
  so that only new ones fail; and at the default `fail-on`, how many do not (warnings, and
  heuristic reports, which count as warnings), which `fail-on = "warning"` would make fail it.
  When contract candidates are listed, a note says that they are invariants the code keeps today,
  not architectural intent: adopt only the boundaries you intend to keep, give each an actionable
  `message`, set `fail = true` on each kept table (unless `fail-on = "warning"` is set), and consider
  a `CODEOWNERS`-protected `heki.toml`, with the legacy violations of a stricter wall in a Ratchet
  baseline, not in an `allowed-*` list.
  When the paths given leave out Python files below the project root, the note names them: heki
  takes the files it analyzed as the whole project, so what it says about callers, readers, and
  writers holds for those files only. It counts up to 50 such files, among the first 10,000
  entries below the root.
- **The keys to add or change**, for the file the project reads its configuration from:
  `[tool.heki...]` tables in a `pyproject.toml`, tables at the top level in `heki.toml`,
  `.heki.toml`, or a `--config` file. Without a configuration file, the keys go into a new
  `pyproject.toml`. The block only adds: an array the file already sets is written whole, with
  the additions named in a comment, since TOML cannot append to an array.

## The takeaways

Each line is chosen from counts the report already has, so it adds no claim, and `--all` starts
with the same lines:

- **Quickest safety win**: of the rules the block enables, the one with the most exact reports
  of a bug here, with the `heki check --extend-select` command that shows them (with a baseline,
  the regressions among its reports). When no such rule adds an exact report: the exact report
  of a bug that `heki check` shows now (with a baseline, a regression) naming the fewest other
  places (the hops of its call chain, a definition), with the `heki check` command that shows
  it.
- **Smallest wall for a coding agent**: the contract block that, with `fail = true` on its table,
  guards the most code an edit could cross it from (a wall as
  [Coding Agents](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#architecture-rules-with-agents) describes them). Of the blocks
  shown without `--all`, a high one before a medium one, then the one with the most other
  modules reading its targets (`write-owners`), using their classes (`read-owners`), or calling
  into its scopes (`effect-boundaries`), then the one with the fewest targets. With
  `fail-on = "warning"`, its reports fail `heki check` without `fail = true`. Without a
  candidate (when the block sets `src`, for one), there is no line.
- **Biggest blind spot**: a source root the block adds, with its `src` key. Otherwise the part
  of "What heki cannot see" with the most calls among those something you can write removes:
  the calls of library names without a catalog entry (an `[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]` entry, for a
  name whose effects you know), the calls of names heki's catalog lacks in packages it covers
  (an entry in heki's catalog, asked for at its issue tracker), and the calls heki does not
  resolve through a parameter without annotation or a value annotated `Any` or `object` (an
  annotation naming the class). The other calls heki does not resolve, and the functions with
  an A1 hazard, have no such remedy and make no line.

A source root the block adds comes first: it renames modules, so the other counts, and the
contract candidates, come from a run with it. Otherwise the lines come in the order above.

## What heki cannot see

heki reports nothing through a call it cannot follow, so these parts list calls, not reports.
For each call it says how many are awaited, how many may hold up an event loop (not awaited, in
an `async def` or in a function one runs on its thread), and how many run in a loop or below
one.

- **Calls of packages heki's catalog does not cover**, by the name an entry of
  `[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]` needs (entries are looked up by that exact name, without
  inheritance or aliases). heki takes such a call to have no effect. For the 64 names with the
  most reach, a trial run gives each a catalog entry that waits on the network and sends a
  database query (`effects = ["blocking_net", "db_query"]`) and says what `heki check` would
  then print through it, exact and heuristic: "if it waits" (`EFF101`) and "if it sends a query"
  (`EFF103`). heki cannot know what a library call does, so no entry enters the block, and the
  trial's counts are kept out of every count of reports: add an entry if you know what the call
  does. The text lists the names whose trial changes a report, the most exact reports first,
  then the most heuristic ones, then by reach, and counts the others on a line each: the names
  whose trial changes no report, with the first few by reach, and the names not tried.
- **Names heki's catalog lacks in packages it covers**: the same, for the names the trial shows
  heki would report through. If such a call waits or sends a query, report it at heki's issue
  tracker: the catalog should list it.
- **Calls heki does not resolve**, by function and reason: a parameter without annotation, an
  annotation that names no class heki knows, a value annotated `Any`, `object`, or `Callable`, a
  name nothing heki sees binds, a protocol whose implementations heki cannot list, a call's
  result or an attribute heki gives no class, a method named at run time, more implementations
  than heki follows, or a member heki does not find. An annotation would resolve most of them;
  an annotation is an edit of the program, so none enters the block. The text lists the calls in
  test code, as `relax-async-in-tests` finds it, after the others, and counts those it leaves out.
- **Source roots**: a directory below the project root, neither a source root nor a regular
  package (a directory with `__init__.py` is imported by its own name, so heki never takes one
  for a source root), below which the dotted path of an import that names no project module is a
  file (`backend/config/env.py` for `import config.env`) is a candidate for `src`. An import of
  the standard library or of a package heki's catalog covers is no candidate's, and neither is
  one whose path is below several directories none of which holds the importing file. The first
  8 candidates by imports are tried, each added to `src` with those already taken (the source
  roots heki detects are written out with them, since setting `src` turns detection off). A
  trial computes the module names with the directory added for every Python file below the
  project root, those the paths given leave out included (heki reads them for this; when they
  are more than the 50 it reads, no directory is tried), resolves each import as heki's index
  does, and takes the directory into the block only when the imports it was tried for name its
  own files, no two files of one kind then define one module unless just those files did before,
  every import that names a module of the project now, and every import a directory already
  taken was taken for, still names the same module of the same file, and every contract of the
  configuration and every baseline entry still names what it names now (the rules' matchers
  judge each definition by its name now and its name with the directory; a baseline entry must
  not spell a module whose name would change). The block is then checked whole: when it would
  make some other import resolve into a file below a source root that does not hold the
  importing file (`import utils` in `tool.py`, below `svc_a/` and `svc_b/`, would name
  `svc_a/utils.py`), the directory that file is below stays out and the others are tried again.
  heki cannot tell such a file is the one meant, and the block holds only what the trial
  checked. The calls of names of those files are left out of the library names.
- **Functions with an A1 hazard** (frame introspection, `exec`, a body too large to model):
  the Soundness lane proves nothing in them. `heki assumptions` lists them.

## Which rules the block enables

A rule enters the block when it reports here, is not experimental, reports bugs (its severity
is `error`), and no published measurement shows real harm below 10%. The other rules are
listed with the reason they stay out:

- slower code, and bugs that are rarely harmful, are worth reading but not worth failing a run
  for;
- experimental rules are listed apart, under "Optional", and never enabled;
- a rule the configuration ignores stays ignored;
- `MUT103` compares with a summary snapshot you save with `heki snapshot --write`;
- contract rules run when their contract is declared, so they are not listed here.

## Which contracts the block declares

Candidates are drawn from what the code does, never from names:

- `write-owners`: an attribute of a project class written after its object is constructed only
  by functions of one module, and read in at least two other modules. The entry allows the
  smallest of `module:Class.*` and `module:*` that covers the writers. An attribute written
  only while its objects are constructed (by an initializer, or by a function filling the object
  it constructs) gets an entry that allows no writer.
- `read-owners`: a private attribute (`_name`) read only by functions of its class's module,
  whose class is used in at least two modules. The entry allows the readers as above.
- An ownership candidate is judged by the accesses of its class's family, the class and its
  project subclasses, since its target covers them: their writers and readers, and the modules
  reading the attribute on objects of any of them. A method accessing the attribute only
  through its own receiver (`self.items.append(x)` in a subclass) may be in any module: when one
  is outside the owner's module, the entry sets `own-receiver = "allow"`.
- Test code never defines an owner: an attribute a test function writes (or a private one it
  reads) other than through its own receiver gets no candidate, since that access would be a
  report of the contract.
- `effect-boundaries`: a module whose functions reach no blocking call, with
  `forbid = ["blocking"]`; a package whose every module qualifies is one scope, which names the
  package's own module and the modules below it (`["pkg:*", "pkg.*:*"]`), also when it has no
  `__init__.py` yet. A scope has at least three functions. A package holding test code names its
  other modules one by one, not by a wildcard.

No candidate is drawn from a module holding test code, as `relax-async-in-tests` finds it: a
test file, or a file defining a `test_*` function or method (a test class in Django's
`tests.py`, for one). Its classes get no ownership contract and its functions no boundary. Nor
is one drawn from a module whose name, taken from its path, has a character a pattern cannot
spell literally: a `:`, or glob syntax (`routes/[id].py`).

What the configuration already declares is not proposed: an attribute a `write-owners` or
`read-owners` target names, and a module an effect boundary forbidding every blocking effect
covers. A kind whose rule the configuration ignores is not proposed either. When the block sets
`src`, no contract is proposed, and no verification run counts the block's rules: a new source
root renames modules and resolves imports heki does not resolve now, so run `heki recommend` again
once it is set. Each target has the
module-part form (`app.models:Order.items`), which never matches another project's names.

The contract trial declares every candidate at once, the ownership contracts with
`unresolved = "report"`, and runs their rules (`MUT201` and `MUT205`, `MUT203` and `MUT206`,
`EFF201`) as `heki check` would: inline suppressions and `per-file-ignores` apply, and the
reports inline suppressions drop are counted apart (a rule `per-file-ignores` turns off for a
file reports nothing there). A candidate the rule of its contract (`MUT201`, `MUT203`, `EFF201`)
reports is rejected and listed with the first report, and so is one that hides a report the
configuration's own contracts make now: a target lists its `__dict__` key, on its class and the
subclasses, for every contract, so a contract with `unlisted-dict-keys = "report"` stops
reporting a write of that key on an object of either (`Store.b` hides the report of a write of
`Child.b` when `Child` derives from `Store`). Reports of `MUT205` or `MUT206`, accesses on objects
of unknown class, reject no candidate: they make it medium (below). Of each kind, the trial
declares the first 32 candidates: `write-owners` with the attributes changed in place first, then
by the modules reading them; `read-owners` by the modules using the class; boundaries by their
functions times the functions calling into them from outside. The configuration's own
`write-owners` contracts take places of the 32.

| Confidence | When |
| ---------- | ---- |
| high | the trial reports nothing for the contract, every Python file below the project root was read, parsed, and analyzed (when the paths given leave part of the root out, the count of the files there got to its end and found none), and no function of a boundary's scopes reaches code heki does not see (a call it does not resolve, a library name without a catalog entry, a function it does not model) |
| medium | the trial reports no violation, but `MUT205` or `MUT206` reports accesses on objects of unknown class (they are listed), files were left out (or the count of them stopped before the end) or could not be parsed, or a scope function reaches code heki does not see (it is listed) |

Medium candidates are in the block too, an ownership one with `unresolved = "ignore"`: heki may
not see every access on objects of unknown class (in the files left out or not parsed, for one)
that the rule of such accesses would report. A high one sets `unresolved = "report"`, unless the
configuration ignores that rule (`MUT205`, `MUT206`): it stays ignored, so the entry sets
`unresolved = "ignore"` and the block does not select the rule. A candidate on a subclass is
left out when the one on its base class is kept: a target covers the subclasses of its class.
Every candidate carries the caveat that accesses inside code heki cannot follow are not seen.

### Blocks and class patterns

The kept candidates of one kind whose entries set the same keys but `name` and `targets` (or
`scopes`) are one block: its targets are theirs, and its trial their reports, each once. A
contract reports every access of one of its targets that it does not allow, whichever target it
is, so the block reports what its candidates do. A block's confidence is the lowest of its
candidates', and it is named after its one target or scope, or else after what accesses its
targets (`attributes written by app.store:Store.*`) or where its scopes are.

Where the census sees no function writing an attribute of a class or its subclasses (for
`read-owners`: reading one whose name starts with `_`) that the block does not allow, the block
may name them all by one pattern, `module:Class.*` (`module:Class._*`), which also names the
attributes the code adds later. The pattern trial declares each such pattern alone, with the
block's other keys and `unresolved = "report"`, and runs the rules of its kind: the block names
the pattern in place of the class's targets only when the trial reports nothing for it that they
did not, under the contract's rule, under the rule of accesses on objects of unknown class when
the block reports them (a pattern names any attribute a write of unknown class may add), and by
hiding a report of the configuration's own contracts. A refused pattern is listed with its first
report.

Blocks are ranked within each kind: `write-owners` with an attribute changed in place first,
then by the modules reading their targets times their candidates. The first 3 of each kind are
shown and declared; `--all` shows and declares every one. The sites of `MUT205` and `MUT206`
reports that keep blocks at `unresolved = "ignore"` are listed after the blocks, each once, with
the candidates whose trial reported it and the blocks they are in (shown or not), the first 5 by
the candidates they hold back (`--all`: up to 50). An annotation naming the object's class lets
heki judge such an access by that class.

The verification run then applies the whole block, the rules it enables and the contracts it
declares, as `heki check` would; the counts of the block's rules come from it.

## How the advice is kept honest

- Every count comes from the project, through the analysis `heki check` runs: inline
  suppressions, `per-file-ignores`, and the baseline apply as they do there. With the block
  applied, `heki check` prints the reports it promises.
- A contract enters the block only when the trial of its rules reports no violation of it on the
  code as it is, and hides no report the configuration's own contracts make; accesses on objects
  of unknown class make it medium, with `unresolved = "ignore"`. The verification run then
  applies the whole block as `heki check` would.
- How often a rule's reports are right is quoted only from published measurements, with their
  sample, interval, and date; a rule without one is "not measured". No score is computed.
- What keeps a report heuristic comes from the report itself, as the analysis decided its
  tier; a cause the analysis does not record is shown as not recorded, never guessed.
- No library catalog entry enters the block: heki cannot verify what a library call does. What
  a trial entry would make `heki check` print is said as a condition ("if it waits") and kept
  out of every count of reports. `src` enters only after its trial.
- The same input, configuration, and heki version give the same report, on any machine and
  with any number of threads.
- It writes nothing and keeps every value the configuration sets.

[ADR-020](https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki/blob/main/docs/DESIGN_HISTORY_AND_ADR.md#adr-020-heki-recommend-advice-on-the-configuration-from-the-projects-own-analysis)
records these rules and the decisions behind the command.

## Example

A project with three modules and a test file:

```python
# app/users.py
import requests

def fetch_name(user_id: int) -> str:
    return requests.get(f"https://api.example.com/users/{user_id}", timeout=5).text

def load_user(user_id: int) -> dict[str, str]:
    return {"id": str(user_id), "name": fetch_name(user_id)}

def known_names(names: list[str], source: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    known = list(source)
    found = []
    for name in names:
        if name in known:
            found.append(name)
    return found
```

```python
# app/report.py
def total_and_count(rows: list[int]) -> tuple[int, int]:
    items = (r for r in rows)
    total = sum(items)
    count = len(list(items))
    return total, count


def average(rows: list[int]) -> float:
    return sum(rows) / len(rows) if rows else 0.0


def spread(rows: list[int]) -> int:
    return max(rows) - min(rows) if rows else 0
```

```python
# app/api.py
from app.users import load_user

async def get_user(user_id: int) -> dict[str, str]:
    return load_user(user_id)
```

```python
# app/billing.py
import stripe

async def charge(amount: int) -> None:
    stripe.Charge.create(amount=amount)
```

```python
# tests/test_users.py
def test_load_user() -> None:
    pass
```

```console
$ heki recommend app
heki recommend (experimental) on .: 4 file(s), 13 function(s)

1. Quickest safety win: fix EFF101 at app/api.py:5 (get_user), the one exact report of a bug shown now, through 4 place(s): heki check app (Reports now)
2. Smallest wall for a coding agent: the effect-boundaries table "app.report without blocking calls" (medium): 3 function(s) of app.report reach no blocking call heki sees; with fail = true, heki check fails on an edit that makes one reach a blocking call (Contract candidates; the table is in the keys at the end)
3. Biggest blind spot: 1 call(s) of 1 library name(s) without a catalog entry, which heki takes to have no effect, such as stripe.Charge.create; an [[tool.heki.ecosystem]] entry for a name whose effects you know removes it (What heki cannot see)

Reports now  1 shown (1 exact, 0 heuristic), 0 heuristic withheld, 4 heuristic rule(s) off

Types the code already keeps
  2 read-only parameter group(s), exact; 2 heuristic (heki recommend app --all lists them)
  No type checker configuration found: half of each guard is a type checker's.
    app/report.py:2  total_and_count(rows)  list[int] -> Sequence[int]  public
    app/report.py:9  average(rows)          list[int] -> Sequence[int]  public
  Each group states that the parameter itself is never changed, in its function and in every function it is handed to, and that it does not leave them. The edits of a group go together; --output-format json has them.
  After the edit, a type checker reports a change of the parameter in the function and handing it to a `list`, `dict`, or `set` parameter; MUT110 (exact, on) reports handing it to a function without annotations that changes it.
  public: a name without a leading underscore along it; callers, overriders, and implementers outside the checked files are not known
  To apply the exact groups: heki recommend app --focus types --diff | git apply

Rules worth enabling here
  rule    reports  exact  consequence  right about the code (published)  real harm  block
  MUT106        1      -  bug          not measured                      -          yes
  OPT110        1      0  slowdown     78% (65-87%), n=50, 2026-11-21    6%         no: slower code, not a bug
  see the 2 report(s): heki check app --extend-select MUT106,OPT110
  No reports here: 29 rule(s); exact: EFF105, OPT103, OPT111, OPT120, OPT121, OPT130; experimental and exact: MUT101, MUT111; heki recommend --all names the 21 heuristic one(s)

What heki cannot see (no report either way)
  calls of packages heki's catalog does not cover: 1 call(s) of 1 name(s) in 1 package(s)
    name                  calls  async  loops  if it waits     if it sends a query
    stripe.Charge.create      1      1      0  EFF101 1 exact  -
  if it waits, if it sends a query: what heki check would print if the call waited on the network or sent a database query; a trial, not a fact (Notes)

Contract candidates
  effect-boundaries  app.report  medium
    3 function(s) in 1 module(s) reach no blocking call heki sees
    trial: EFF201 0
  For every block, accesses inside code heki cannot follow (unresolved calls, libraries without a catalog) are not seen.

What keeps reports heuristic
  1 heuristic report(s) of exact claims: OPT110 1
  premise: cause                                 reports  only open  closed by
  Rewrite proven safe: zero-trip-exception-safe        1          0  code
    the `set(...)` the rewrite builds before the loop may raise even when the loop runs no time: an element that may be unhashable, or a name that may be unbound there
    e.g. app/users.py:14 OPT110
  Rewrite proven safe: hash-consistent-probe           1          0  code
    the value looked up may compare otherwise through `hash` than through `==`: a custom `__eq__` / `__hash__`, or an unhashable value
    e.g. app/users.py:14 OPT110
  Nothing here enters the block: an annotation or a change of the code is an edit of the program.

Notes
  - 1 Python file(s) below the project root were not analyzed (tests/test_users.py): heki takes the analyzed files as the whole project, so what it says about callers, readers, and writers holds for those files only.
  - heki check fails on 1 report(s) shown now (exit code 1): a Ratchet baseline records them, so that it fails only on new ones (`heki check --baseline heki-baseline.toml --update-baseline`, then `baseline = "heki-baseline.toml"` in the configuration).
  - "if it waits" and "if it sends a query" come from a trial run that gives each library name tried a catalog entry with `effects = ["blocking_net", "db_query"]`: what `heki check` would print if the call waited on the network or sent a database query. heki cannot see what these calls do, so no entry for them is in the block; add one in `[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]` if you know.
  - the contract candidates are invariants the code keeps today, not architectural intent: adopt only the boundaries you intend to keep, give each an actionable `message`, and set `fail = true` on each kept table so that its reports fail `heki check`; consider a CODEOWNERS-protected heki.toml, and put the legacy violations of a stricter wall in a Ratchet baseline, not in an `allowed-*` list.

pyproject.toml: keys to add or change
  [tool.heki.lint]
  extend-select = ["MUT106"]  # adds MUT106

  [[tool.heki.effect-boundaries]]
  name = "app.report without blocking calls"
  scopes = ["app.report:*"]
  forbid = ["blocking"]
```

## Suggestions

A suggestion is a claim about the code and the annotation edit that writes it in standard
typing (ADR-023). It is no report: it has no rule code, severity, suppression, baseline entry,
or exit code, and `heki check` never prints one. Edits valid only together are one group: a
parameter and the parameters it is handed to, and the same parameter of every definition of an
override family. The text lists them under "Types the code already keeps", and the JSON object
under `suggestions`, with the edits.

The kind `readonly-parameter` suggests `Sequence`, `Mapping`, or `AbstractSet` for a parameter
annotated `list`, `dict`, or `set` that the function, and every function it hands it to, only
reads. What a suggestion states:

- **Only read here**, **Does not leave**, **Every call resolves and only reads**: the claim, from
  the facts `MUT110` reads, so the suggestion and its guard cannot disagree. When one is open,
  nothing is listed. A method called on a parameter annotated `Sequence`, `Mapping`, or
  `AbstractSet` reads as the same method of the builtin. An operator or a comparison can hand the
  object to the other operand's special method (`other == p` may run `other.__eq__(p)`, and which
  side Python tries first depends on the classes): only a builtin's keeps nothing, so the other operand is a value built in the function or of a
  builtin class no project class derives from. An item read of a `defaultdict` changes it.
- **The builtin's own reads**: the claim's last part (R2, read for the type the suggestion writes).
  A `Mapping` may be an instance of a project class deriving from `dict`, from a standard-library
  class of its family (`OrderedDict`, `defaultdict`, `Counter`, `UserDict`, `ChainMap`, ...), or
  from `Mapping` itself, or of a project class registered with one; a `Sequence` or an
  `AbstractSet` likewise. A `register` call heki cannot resolve, or a `__subclasshook__` in such
  a class, admits any class and leaves every parameter of the family out. The function's reads of the object, and those of the
  functions it hands it to, run that class's code if the class binds the method they run: item
  access (with `__missing__`), iteration (with the length hint `[*v]`, `f(*v)`, and `xs += v` take;
  `a, b = v` iterates too), size and truth, membership, comparison, conversion to text, operators,
  `keys()` and the items for `**v`, the length `case []` and `case {"k": v}` test and the `get` of
  the latter, the methods called by name (and `__getattribute__` for those), and what the catalog's
  `[[invokes]]` entry of a library call reading it names. A read with no such list (a library call
  without an entry, such as `bytes(v)`, or a method the builtin lacks) may run any member of the
  class. Such a class, or one a metaclass heki does not know creates, leaves the parameter out,
  counted by cause: `class Cache(dict)` with its own `__contains__` leaves out `k in m` on a `dict`
  parameter, not `m.get(k)`. So does a class deriving from `defaultdict` for an item read: the
  `__missing__` it inherits inserts the key. A class outside the project is taken to run what the
  builtin runs.
- **Literal container annotation**: a builtin `list`, `dict`, or `set`, or its `typing` form,
  after `Optional`, `| None`, and quotes; not `Annotated[...]`, a `Mutable*` ABC, or an alias.
  Its names are the module's: a name a function or class body around the `def` binds (`class
  list` in the enclosing function, a method `set` above it in the class) names that binding.
- **Abstract use**: every use exists on the read-only type; a set gives no iteration order.
- **Name bound once**, **Callees take it**, **Whole family** (no `Protocol` member, no
  `@overload`, a body that does something, the whole override family in the group), **Not
  replaced**, **Annotations stay unread** (every decorator in heki's table, of a `cached_property`
  the `functools` one only, no class machinery or base the catalog does not know, no use of the
  function as a value, no `dataclass` without a docstring for a constructor: it writes one from
  the constructor's signature), **A name for the type** (an import of the module is reused when
  it runs before the annotation is evaluated: above the `def`, or anywhere under `from __future__
  import annotations`; on a Python 3.14 target, whose annotations are deferred without it, an
  import below the `def` still leaves the premise open).
- **No fact lost**: the annotation trial. Each file of the groups is analyzed again with their
  edits applied in memory, as the JSON prints them; a group whose edits change the facts of a
  function they edit or the file's reports, every rule selected, is withheld, and `withheld` says
  what changed (`trial-limit`: heki stopped trying the file, after four analyses with other edits
  or two checks of its reports). With an `import-boundaries` contract that walks imports, the
  reports of the modules it judges are checked too: an import an edit adds may be reached from
  them. A heuristic group is tried by its facts only, so this premise is never established for
  one.
- **A file to edit**: no generated file (a leading comment with `generated` or `DO NOT EDIT`),
  no function a stub declares; these, and test code, are counted under `left_out`.

When the claim holds and only a premise of the edit is open, the group is heuristic, listed with
`--all` with the open premise and its place. A `list[str]` parameter is heuristic too: a
`Sequence[str]` also admits a plain `str`. heki looks for a type checker's configuration
(`[tool.ty]`, `ty.toml`, `[tool.mypy]`, `mypy.ini`, `[tool.pyright]`, `pyrightconfig.json`,
`[tool.pyrefly]`): half of each guard is the type checker's, the other half `MUT110`.

### Applying the suggestions

`heki recommend --focus types` prints the header and "Types the code already keeps" alone, with
every exact group; `--all` adds the heuristic ones. The analysis is the same as without it, so
the groups are too, and with `--output-format json` the object keeps every field, its
`suggestions.groups` holding every exact group past the cap of 50.

```console
$ heki recommend --focus types --diff | git apply
```

`--diff` prints the exact groups as one unified diff with the paths `heki check --diff`
prints, so `git apply` or `patch -p1` applies it from the same directory. It changes
annotations and adds the imports they name, nothing else: the edits of the JSON object, applied
as the annotation trial applied them. Each file keeps its line breaks and its declared encoding.
A heuristic group is never in it, and the diff is empty when no group is exact. The command
still writes nothing and exits with `0` (`2` when a file cannot be read or parsed); the count of
the groups goes to standard error. Run the project's formatter and type checker afterwards, as
after any `heki check --fix`.

## JSON output

`--output-format json` prints one object, described by the JSON Schema at
[schemas/recommend-3.json](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/schemas/recommend-3.json), the URL its `$schema` field names, which
`heki recommend --output-format-json-schema` prints. Version 3 lists contracts as blocks, with
`targets` in place of one `target`.
Within a `version`, fields are only added; the `version` changes when a field is removed or
changes meaning.

| Field | Content |
| ----- | ------- |
| `kind`, `version`, `heki` | `heki-recommend`, the version of the object, and the version of heki |
| `root`, `config_file`, `table_prefix` | the project root, the configuration file (`null` without one), and the table its keys are under (`tool.heki`, or empty) |
| `analyzed` | the files and functions analyzed, the files that could not be read or parsed, the paths given, and the Python files below the root they leave out |
| `runs` | the analyses the report was computed from: `discovery`, then `annotation-trial` (the files of the suggestions analyzed again with their edits) when there was a suggestion to try, `source-roots` (the source-root trial) and `hypothetical-catalog` (the trial of library names) when they ran, `contract-trial` when it tried a contract candidate (none when the block sets `src`, or when every candidate is past the places of its kind), `pattern-trial` when a block shown has a class pattern to try, and `verification` when the block adds rules or contracts and does not set `src` |
| `reports_now` | the counts of "Reports now", and `failing`: the reports shown (with a baseline, the regressions) that make `heki check` fail at the configuration's `fail-on` |
| `open_premises` | the counts of "What keeps reports heuristic": by code; by premise or condition and cause, with what the cause states, what closes it, the reports, the reports it is the only open cause of, and the first 50 reports; the sets of causes that reports leave open together |
| `blind_spots` | the counts of "What heki cannot see": the calls of library names without a catalog entry, by package and name, with what the trial run found; the names heki's catalog lacks in packages it covers; the calls heki does not resolve, by function and reason; the source-root candidates and their trials; the functions with an A1 hazard; the totals |
| `rules` | each rule of "Rules worth enabling here": its metadata, the reports it would add, its published measurement, whether the block enables it, and why |
| `contracts` | each block the configuration block declares, the first 3 of each kind (`--all`: every one): its kind, its targets (or the packages and modules of its scopes), the candidates it stands for, its entry, confidence, evidence, what the trial reported for its candidates, the class patterns tried with what the pattern trial reported and whether the block names them, and caveats |
| `contracts_not_shown` | per kind, the blocks past the first 3 and the candidates they stand for |
| `contract_blockers` | the sites of accesses heki cannot tie to a class that keep blocks at `unresolved = "ignore"`: how many, the first 5 (`--all`: 50) with the rule, path, line, function, the report as `heki check` writes it, and the candidates and blocks each holds back, and whether the list is cut |
| `suggestions` | the standard types the code already keeps (ADR-023): per kind, the exact and heuristic groups; the type checker the project configures (`found`, `config`, or `null`); the groups, the exact ones by rank, the first 50 (`--focus types`: every exact one; `--all`: every one, the heuristic ones after them), each with its `id` (kind, module, qualified name, parameter; no line), `certainty`, `message`, `items` (path, line, column, the byte span of the annotation's head, qualified name, parameter, the annotation now and as proposed), byte-span `edits` with a path each (applied together; spans are offsets in the file's text as UTF-8, the file's own bytes unless a PEP 263 declaration names Latin-1), `premises` and whether each is established, the `open` ones with their cause and place, `related` places, `guards`, `leverage` (the calls binding it, and those passing an attribute), and `labels` (`public`, `list[str]`, `family`); `truncated`; the groups the annotation trial withheld, by `reason` (`fact-would-change`, `report-would-change`, `trial-limit`), with what changed for the first 50; the parameters left out as test code, in generated files, or declared by a stub; per premise, the parameters it leaves out, the first 10 causes of those, and those it keeps heuristic; and where the project reads annotations at run time (`reader_sites`) |
| `rejected_contracts` | the candidates a run reported for, each alone, with the run and its reports |
| `contracts_not_tried` | per kind, the candidates past the trial's places (32 of each kind, the configuration's own `write-owners` contracts taking `write-owners` places), which no trial declared |
| `unmatched_entries` | each entry of "Contract entries that match nothing": the contracts' kind, the key, the entry, the contracts holding it (a name, or `#` and its position), what it names none of, the existing names like it, the names a `{...}` group of it lists that name nothing (`alternatives`, when it lists several), and `named_at_run_time` when its class family gets attributes named at run time (only with `unmatched-contract-entries = "error"`) |
| `notes` | the notes |
| `config`, `config_toml` | the keys to add or change, as keys and values and as TOML |
| `content` | the report as the text output prints it |

Exit codes: `0` the report was printed; `2` configuration, I/O, or syntax errors (the report
of the other files is still printed, as `heki check` does). It never exits with `1`: it checks
nothing.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/

# Coding Agents

heki gives coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and similar) the checks it gives people:
every diagnostic says what was proven, where the evidence is, and what blocks a fix. `heki
inspect` says what one function does, so an agent does not read its callees to find out. The
[Agent Skill](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#agent-skill-experimental) teaches an agent the routine of this page after an edit.
To make a project's architecture rules binding for agents, with CI, a Stop hook, and the skill,
follow [the whole setup, end to end](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#the-whole-setup-end-to-end).

## Analyze the project, not one file

heki follows calls across files, so it analyzes a project, never one file alone: `heki check
app/api.py` analyzes the project the file is in and shows the diagnostics that touch the file.
A directory below the project root is analyzed as given and misses what its callees elsewhere do
(heki notes the project modules its files import that it left out): run heki from the project
root.

A diagnostic sits where the problem shows, which is often not the file that was edited. In the
[first example](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/#a-bug-found-with-no-configuration) of the overview, adding
`requests.get` to `app/users.py` makes `EFF101` report at `app/api.py`, in the `async def` that
reaches it through two helpers. To see the diagnostics an edit can have caused, pass the edited
files to `--touched`, or name them as paths: heki still analyzes the project, and shows only the
diagnostics whose `path` or any `related[].path` is one of them, so the report in `app/api.py`
stays while `app/users.py` is the only edited file. The summary, the exit code, and every output
format follow the diagnostics shown. A change can also add a report in a file it left alone
without a call chain through it (a re-export, an annotation another module relied on): such a run
ends with a note on stderr counting the reports that would fail it and are not shown, also with
`--output-format json`, and with a baseline it shows every regression. Run the whole project
before finishing.

```console
$ heki check --touched app/users.py --output-format json
```

Or compare with the run before the edit: record the findings once in a baseline outside the
project, and each check with it reports only the new ones.

```console
$ heki check --baseline /tmp/heki-before.toml --update-baseline   # before the first edit
$ heki check --baseline /tmp/heki-before.toml --output-format json   # after each edit
```

## After an edit: `heki check`

A typical instruction for the agent:

> After changing Python files, run `heki check --touched <the files you changed> --output-format
> json` in the project: it shows the diagnostics whose `path` or a `related[].path` is a file you
> changed. For each, read its `help` and `heki rule <rule_code>`, follow `related` to the root
> cause, and fix it there. A diagnostic whose `certainty` is `heuristic` can be wrong about the
> code: confirm what its message says before changing anything. Apply `heki check --fix` for the
> safe rewrites. Never silence a diagnostic with `# heki: ignore` unless the rule's documentation
> describes the case as intended. When unsure, run `heki check --generate-prompt "<question>"`.
> Before you finish, run `heki check` on the whole project (with `--baseline` when it has one):
> `--touched` is for the loop while editing, and a change can cause a report in a file you did
> not touch.

```console
$ heki check --touched app/users.py app/api.py --output-format json
```

The configuration decides which rules run; `--heuristic` also runs the heuristic rules that are
off by default, whose reports can be wrong about the code.

Each diagnostic has:

| Field | Content |
| ----- | ------- |
| `path`, `line`, `column`, `span` | location (byte span in the file) |
| `rule_code`, `rule_slug`, `severity`, `message` | the finding: `message` is one sentence saying what happens |
| `certainty` | `exact`, or `heuristic` when a premise of the report's claim can be open, so that it can be wrong about the code ([Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/)) |
| `help` | what to do about it (`null` when the rule has no advice for the report) |
| `qualname`, `target` | the function and the object involved |
| `related` | every hop of the call chain behind the finding |
| `evidence` | what was established (for `OPT` rules: the proof obligations) |
| `blocker` | the obligation that blocks an automatic fix, if any |
| `fix` | byte-span edits for proven-safe rewrites |
| `sites` | the violation sites a contract report stands for, when more than one |
| `unresolved_sites` | for an effect boundary's `unresolved-calls` or `unresolved-writes` report, every site it stands for, with why heki cannot judge it ([Output Formats](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/output-formats/#what-an-effect-boundary-cannot-judge)) |
| `allowed_examples` | for a contract report, up to three public functions (`fqn`, `path`) that do the same from a place the contract allows, which `help` names |

A text run ends with one line per reported rule: `heki rule <CODE>` and the rule's page.

The run exits with 1 when it shows an exact `error`, a bug that can be critical, a report of a
contract with `fail = true`, a report of a rule `lint.fail` lists, or with `fail-on = "warning"` any report: a heuristic report counts
as a warning, whatever its `severity`.

When the run cannot check (exit code 2: a configuration, path, or file error), the error says
where the cause is, what to write instead, and which section of the documentation explains it.
With `--output-format json`, an error that stops the run (the configuration or a path) is an
object on stdout; a file that cannot be read or parsed is named on stderr, and stdout keeps the
diagnostics of the other files:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "message": "unknown key `select` in [tool.heki]",
    "path": "pyproject.toml",
    "line": 5,
    "column": 1,
    "help": [
      "`select` is a key of [tool.heki.lint]: move it there",
      "for example: `select = [\"EFF\", \"MUT101\"]`"
    ],
    "docs": "https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#rule-selection-toolhekilint",
    "candidates": []
  }
}
```

Apply what `help` says; `candidates` holds the names a misspelled one may have meant, the closest
first.

`heki rule <CODE>` prints a rule's documentation: what it does, why it matters, and what to do
instead, which makes a good prompt for the fix. `heki rule --all --output-format json` gives
every rule's metadata and documentation, the premises of its exact claim, and its published
precision: its certification and its latest measurement ([Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/)).

## Architecture rules with agents

Do not describe the architecture in the project's `AGENTS.md` or `CLAUDE.md`. Declare it as
[contracts](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#contracts) and let `heki check` enforce it. Three lines are enough:

> After editing Python, run `heki check`.
> A report that names a contract means the code crossed a wall the maintainers declared: change the
> code as the report's help says.
> Do not edit the contracts or the baseline, and do not add a suppression, unless the maintainer
> asks.

The `message` of a contract is what the agent reads as the fix, so write it as an instruction.
Contract reports are heuristic, so a run does not fail on them by default. Set `fail = true` on
each contract table, so that `heki check` exits with 1 on a crossed wall and every other warning
stays advisory.

```toml
# heki.toml
[[write-owners]]
name = "generation-store"
targets = ["pkg.model.DataModel.fields"]
allowed-writers = ["Store.*"]
message = "use GenerationStore.set_fields() instead"
fail = true
```

Put the contracts and the baseline path in `heki.toml`, and give that file an owner
(`CODEOWNERS`, or the host's rule for protected files). A change to a wall is then a reviewed
change, and an agent cannot move a wall to make a report go away.

CODEOWNERS protects the file, not the code around it. Run `heki check --report-suppressed <PATH>` in CI
to list every inline `# heki: ignore` and `# noqa` that silences a report, so an agent cannot quietly
go around a wall either ([review checklist](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#review-a-contract-change-from-an-agent)).

```text
# .github/CODEOWNERS
/heki.toml           @your-org/maintainers
/heki-baseline.toml  @your-org/maintainers
```

`fail-on = "warning"` makes every warning and heuristic report fail the run, not only the
contracts' reports; use it only when you want that, and record today's findings in the baseline
first, so that only new ones fail. The [starter recipe](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#walls-for-a-team-or-a-coding-agent) has the whole file.

### Keep the walls thin

Three layers carry the checks, and only the last one is written by hand:

1. The default rules report the bugs that need no declaration.
2. [`MUT103` snapshots](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#effect-snapshots-mut103) report a change of a public function's effects.
3. A dedicated `heki.toml` holds the core boundaries the team wants enforced, and nothing else.

A contract list nobody can review stops protecting anything. Declare a wall when breaking it is a
decision for the maintainers, not when the code happens to keep it today.

### Draft walls over legacy code

`heki recommend` lists the contracts the code already keeps. They are invariants of today, not
architectural intent, and an agent that copies every one of them, or every existing writer,
caller, or import into an `allowed-*` list, writes today's debt into the architecture. Declare the
wall the team wants, and record what already crosses it in a [Ratchet baseline](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#ratchet-baselines),
so that the old violations can only shrink and a new one fails at once.

1. The agent inspects the code with `heki recommend`, `heki inspect`, and `heki inspect
   --imports`.
2. It proposes a thin ideal wall in `heki.toml`, with `fail = true` on each table and a `message` that
   says what to write instead. The old and undesired writers, readers, callers, and imports stay
   out of `allowed-*`.
3. The maintainer approves the change to `heki.toml`, which is protected by `CODEOWNERS`.
4. The violations that exist today go to the baseline:
   `heki check --baseline heki-baseline.toml --update-baseline`.

The agent presents the change as a small diff: what each wall protects, why, and how many old
violations enter the baseline. It never widens an `allowed-*` list, loosens `forbid`, grows the
baseline, or adds a suppression without the maintainer's approval. The
[Agent Skill](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#agent-skill-experimental) carries this protocol in `references/contracts.md`, and
`heki check --generate-prompt` repeats it in its guidance.

### Review a contract change from an agent

Before approving a pull request that adds or changes contracts:

1. No `allowed-*` list holds a legacy workaround: every entry is a function or module that should
   write, read, call, or import the target.
2. Every `message` says what to write instead, so that an agent can act on it.
3. `heki.toml`, the baseline, and the CI configuration are protected by `CODEOWNERS`.
4. The baseline did not grow, and no new `# heki: ignore[...]` or `# noqa` hides a report: compare
   the `heki check --report-suppressed <PATH>` file of the pull request with the base branch's
   ([Auditing inline suppressions](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#auditing-inline-suppressions)).

### A Stop hook for Claude Code

A [Stop hook](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks) runs when Claude Code is about to end its turn.
The script below runs `heki check` and, when it exits with 1 (findings that fail the run), sends
the text to the agent and keeps it working. Exit code 2 of the hook means "block, and read
stderr". heki's own failure (exit code 2, or no `heki` on the path) lets the turn end, so a
configuration error does not loop. The hook input has `stop_hook_active`, which is `true` while
Claude Code is already continuing because of a stop hook; the script stops blocking then.

```sh
#!/bin/sh
input=$(cat)
case $input in
  *'"stop_hook_active":true'* | *'"stop_hook_active": true'*) exit 0 ;;
esac
report=$(heki check 2>&1)
status=$?
[ "$status" -eq 1 ] || exit 0
printf '%s\n' "$report" >&2
exit 2
```

Save it as `.claude/hooks/heki-stop.sh`, make it executable with `chmod +x .claude/hooks/heki-stop.sh`, and
register it in `.claude/settings.json`:

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "Stop": [{ "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": ".claude/hooks/heki-stop.sh" }] }]
  }
}
```

Run on a project with findings that are already known, it would block every turn: use
`heki check --baseline heki-baseline.toml` in the script so that only new findings count.

### The whole setup, end to end

One pull request adds the walls, and every later pull request, from a person or an agent, runs
against them. Replace `app` with your package.

1. Put the walls in a `heki.toml` of their own, with `fail = true` on each wall and the baseline path.
   heki reads the first of `heki.toml`, `.heki.toml`, and `pyproject.toml` it finds and does not
   merge them: a project that already has `[tool.heki]` in `pyproject.toml` must move every
   setting into `heki.toml` (without the `tool.heki` prefix), or they stop applying:

    ```toml
    # heki.toml
    baseline = "heki-baseline.toml"

    [[write-owners]]
    name = "order-store"
    targets = ["app.models.Order.items"]
    allowed-writers = ["app.store.*"]
    message = "change Order.items through app.store"
    fail = true   # contract reports are heuristic: this lets them fail the run
    ```

2. Record today's findings, the old crossings of the walls among them, so that only new ones
   fail:

    ```console
    $ uvx heki check --update-baseline
    ```

3. Give the files that decide the checks an owner. Branch protection must require a review from
   code owners for this to bind:

    ```text
    # .github/CODEOWNERS
    /heki.toml           @your-org/maintainers
    /heki-baseline.toml  @your-org/maintainers
    /.github/workflows/  @your-org/maintainers
    /.github/CODEOWNERS  @your-org/maintainers
    /.claude/            @your-org/maintainers
    /.agents/            @your-org/maintainers
    /AGENTS.md           @your-org/maintainers
    /CLAUDE.md           @your-org/maintainers
    ```

4. Run the checks on every pull request. The first step runs the walls with the baseline. The
   second compares the pull request with its protected base branch: no inline suppression that
   hides a report may be new ([Auditing inline suppressions](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#auditing-inline-suppressions)),
   and no public function may have gained an effect
   ([`MUT103` against the base](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#comparing-with-the-protected-base)):

    ```yaml
    # .github/workflows/heki.yml
    name: heki
    on: pull_request
    permissions:
      contents: read
    jobs:
      heki:
        runs-on: ubuntu-latest
        steps:
          - uses: actions/checkout@v7
            with:
              fetch-depth: 0   # the base branch is compared below
          - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@1db35dd8eee11c5894872e0b383ae6c406cf738d # v10.4.0
          - name: Walls
            run: uvx heki==0.11.0 check
          - name: Compare with the base branch
            shell: bash
            env:
              BASE: ${{ github.base_ref }}
              TARGET: py312   # your project's target version
            run: |
              git worktree add ../base "origin/$BASE"
              keys() { jq -r '.suppressed[] | [.file, .function, .code, .target] | @tsv' "$1" | sort; }
              uvx heki==0.11.0 check --report-suppressed "$RUNNER_TEMP/head.json" > /dev/null || test "$?" -eq 1
              (cd ../base && uvx heki==0.11.0 check --report-suppressed "$RUNNER_TEMP/base.json" > /dev/null || test "$?" -eq 1)
              new=$(diff <(keys "$RUNNER_TEMP/base.json") <(keys "$RUNNER_TEMP/head.json") | grep '^>' || true)
              test -z "$new" || { echo "New inline suppressions:"; echo "$new"; exit 1; }
              (cd ../base && uvx heki==0.11.0 snapshot --config "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE/heki.toml" --target-version "$TARGET" > "$RUNNER_TEMP/base-summary.json")
              uvx heki==0.11.0 check --select MUT103 --fail-on warning --target-version "$TARGET" --snapshot "$RUNNER_TEMP/base-summary.json" \
                --report-suppressed "$RUNNER_TEMP/mut103.json"
              hidden=$(keys "$RUNNER_TEMP/mut103.json")
              test -z "$hidden" || { echo "Effect changes hidden by inline suppressions:"; echo "$hidden"; exit 1; }
    ```

    The suppression audit runs the base branch with its own `heki.toml` and baseline, so the pull
    request cannot change what it is compared with. The `MUT103` comparison needs the same
    settings on both sides: the base snapshot is made with the pull request's `heki.toml`
    (`--config`) and the same `--target-version` as the check, so a pull request that changes
    the settings does not make unchanged code look different. The settings change itself is a
    change to a protected file. `MUT103` is opt-in, so the first audit does not see a
    `# heki: ignore[MUT103]`; the last run writes its own audit file, and any entry in it fails the
    step, since the base compared with its own snapshot has no `MUT103` report to hide.
    The base checkout sits next to the project (`../base`), not inside it, so that heki does not
    analyze it too.

5. For Claude Code, add the [Stop hook](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#a-stop-hook-for-claude-code) and register it in
   `.claude/settings.json`: the agent then sees a failing report before it ends its turn, not
   after CI. Its `heki check` reads the baseline `heki.toml` names, and it needs `heki` on the
   path (`uv tool install heki`).

6. Install the [skill](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#install-the-skill) (experimental) and commit it, so that every clone has it, and put the
   three lines of [Architecture rules with agents](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#architecture-rules-with-agents) in `AGENTS.md`
   or `CLAUDE.md`:

    ```console
    $ heki skill install --agent claude-code
    $ heki skill install --agent codex
    ```

What each layer catches: the hook gives the agent the report at once, the first CI step fails a
pull request that crosses a wall or adds a finding, and the comparison step fails one that hides
a report instead of fixing it or gives a public function a new effect. A change to the walls, the
baseline, the workflow, the hook, or the agent instructions is a change to a protected file, so a maintainer reads it.

## What a function does: `heki inspect` (experimental)

When a diagnostic or a question is about one function, `heki inspect` says what it reaches,
changes, keeps, and returns, with the call chains, without reading its callees. Run it when a
function's effects are in question, not before every edit.

The text form is the one to read in a terminal; it needs no configuration. A sample is in
[Getting Started](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/getting-started/#look-at-one-function).

```console
$ heki inspect app.users.load_user --output-format json
$ heki inspect app/users.py:42
$ heki inspect app/users.py::load_user --callers --depth 3
$ printf '%s\n' app.users.load_user 'app.orders.*' | heki inspect - --output-format json
```

| Field | Content |
| ----- | ------- |
| `version`, `heki`, `root`, `query`, `resolved_from` | the version of the object, the heki release, the project root, the symbol as given, and how it named the function (`name`, `glob`, `suffix`, or `line`; `null` for an exact full name) |
| `complete`, `errors` | `complete` is false when `errors` lists the files heki could not read or parse |
| `function` | the function: full name, module, kind, definition lines, `async`, `generator`, `abstract`, `stub`, class, decorators, parameters, the call that offloads it to a thread or process pool, and whether a caller drives it without an event loop |
| `effects` | the network, database, file, subprocess, sleep, and lock waits it reaches, and the clients and queries it creates, each with the shortest call chain |
| `changes` | the parameters, `self` attributes, other objects' attributes, module globals, and closure cells it changes, directly or through calls, with the call chain to the change |
| `retains` | the parameters it stores where they outlive the call |
| `only_reads` | its parameters annotated with a mutable container (`list`, `dict`, `set`), those it and every function it hands them to only read (no change, no store, every call resolved), those whose uses the read-only type (`Sequence`, `Mapping`, `AbstractSet`) allows, those whose name it binds once, and, by parameter it only reads, the kinds of read that reach the object here and in the functions it is handed to (`reads`). These are the function's facts: `heki recommend` also checks that no project subclass of the argument's class changes it in one of those reads, so a parameter listed here is no proof that every override only reads |
| `returns` | whether its result is a new object, a parameter, or state that outlives the call |
| `registered` | each registration that may reach it through a table of callbacks and a lookup by name (`getattr(self, <name>)`), with the parameter bound to the registering object and its class, the condition (`selector` equals the function's name; `others_open` when the name is not a constant), the sites on the way, and what it changes of that parameter under the context. Advisory: no other fact or report assumes it |
| `purity` | `pure`, `impure` with the reasons, or `unknown` with the reasons; whatever the verdict, the functions below it whose calls heki cannot resolve, nearest first, each with the call chain to it; and what the verdict assumes |
| `callers` | who calls it, whether in a loop; with `--callers`, transitively |
| `reports` | what `heki check` reports in it; with `--callers`, also above it |
| `contracts` | the contracts that name it, with its roles in them, and the contracts the reports above are of (role `reported`) |

- A name is a dotted name (`pkg.mod.Class.method`, or a suffix such as `Class.method`, or a
  glob), `path.py:line`, or `path.py::name`. An ambiguous or unknown name exits with 2: the error
  says what to do (in JSON, `error.help`; a misspelled name gets the functions whose names look
  like it) and lists the functions to choose from (`error.candidates`, `error.suggestions`,
  `error.methods`, or `error.functions`).
- With `-` for the name, the names are read from standard input, one per line, and heki analyzes
  the project once for all of them: the JSON output is an array of the objects, in the order of
  the names, and the text output one section per function. Here a glob names each function it
  matches, in the order of their full names (on the command line, a glob matching several is
  ambiguous). A name that names no single function takes its place in the array as the error
  object it prints alone, the others are still reported, and the exit code is 2. No names give
  an empty array.
- `pure` means heki found no effect and no change of an input or of shared state, and resolved
  every call below. Libraries the [catalog](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#ecosystem-knowledge-toolhekiecosystem)
  does not list count as having no effects.
- Constructing an object changes no existing one: `changes.class_attrs` marks the writes of an
  object under construction `fresh`, and the text form leaves them out. Such an object is one the
  function allocates and fills, or the `self` of a class's own initialization, written by the
  initializer or by a helper it passes `self` to (`Node(...)` running `_link(self)`).
- `purity.unknown_reach.entries` lists the functions heki cannot follow among the function and
  its callees (a call it cannot resolve, or a body only a stub declares), nearest first, at most
  100; `truncated` says there are more. `purity.unknown_at` is the first of them. Both are given
  for an `impure` function too: what it changes may then be incomplete.
- A field the configuration does not compute is `null`, with the setting that computes it.
- Exit code 0 when every function was inspected, 2 otherwise or when a file could not be
  analyzed (the reports are still printed, with `complete: false`).

To see what an edit changed in a function, inspect it before and after the edit and compare
