`fail = true` on a contract table makes the reports of that contract fail the run, and
`fail-on = "warning"` in `[tool.heki.lint]` (or `--fail-on warning`) makes every one of them fail it. A
code base with errors today records them in a [Ratchet baseline](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#ratchet-baselines) first, so
that the job fails only on new ones; [`heki recommend`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/recommend/) says how many reports fail
the run now.

=== "GitHub Actions annotations"

    ```yaml
    - run: uvx heki==0.11.0 check --output-format github
    ```

=== "Code scanning (SARIF)"

    ```yaml
    # The job needs `permissions: security-events: write`.
    - run: uvx heki==0.11.0 check --output-format sarif > heki.sarif || test "$?" -eq 1
    - uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v4
      with:
        sarif_file: heki.sarif
    ```

Each annotation is one workflow command at the reported location: its title names the rule
(`heki EFF101`, `heki EFF101 (heuristic)` for a heuristic report), and its body is the message followed by one
`related: <path>:<line>:<col>: <message>` line per related location (the hops of a call chain, in order).

The level of an annotation says whether its report fails the run. A report that fails it keeps
its severity, `error` or `warning`; one that does not is a `warning`, so an annotation reads as
a failure only when the step fails on it. Warnings and heuristic reports do not fail the step:
by default a heuristic report of an `error` rule is a `warning` annotation. `fail-on =
"warning"` in `[tool.heki.lint]` (or `--fail-on warning`) makes them fail it, as in pre-commit,
and the heuristic `error` is then an `error` annotation; so are the reports of a contract with
[`fail = true`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#failing-on-a-contract) and of a rule
[`lint.fail`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#rule-selection-toolhekilint) names. The JSON, SARIF, and text
formats give each report its severity.

In GitHub Actions (`GITHUB_ACTIONS=true`), `heki check` writes these annotations without
`--output-format github`. To keep the text output there, pass `--output-format full`, or set
`HEKI_OUTPUT_FORMAT` (any format) in the job's `env`: it applies whenever the option is not given.

One run is enough: the annotations step fails the job on what fails the run. A run prints one
output format, so a job that also keeps code-scanning alerts runs heki twice: the annotations
step is the one that fails the job, and the SARIF step, which keeps the step green on findings,
uploads them.

On a pull request, a project with old findings can report only what the change touches, as the
pre-commit hook does (the checkout needs `fetch-depth: 0` for the base branch):

```yaml
- run: git diff -z --name-only --diff-filter=d "origin/$BASE...HEAD" -- '*.py' '*.pyi' '*.toml' | xargs -0 -r uvx heki==0.11.0 check --touched
  env:
    BASE: ${{ github.base_ref }}
```

`'*.toml'` takes in every configuration file, also one listed in
[`include`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#several-configuration-files) under another name; heki passes over a
TOML file that is not part of its configuration. `--diff-filter=d` leaves out deleted files, and
`xargs -r` skips the run when no Python, stub, or TOML file changed. A path that names no
analyzed file (a typo, a file outside the analyzed directories, an excluded one) is named in a
warning, and the run goes on with the others. With `--unmatched-paths error` (or
[`unmatched-paths = "error"`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#rule-selection-toolhekilint) in `[tool.heki.lint]`),
it stops the run with exit code 2 instead, so a wrong path fails the job rather than passing it on
nothing.

A deleted path has nothing to touch: `--touched` names it in a warning and shows nothing for it,
though deleting a configuration file, a stub, or a module can change reports elsewhere. A pull
request that deletes one should run the whole project (`uvx heki==0.11.0 check`). With
`--no-renames`, a renamed file counts as the deletion of its old path, and the list is kept in a
variable before it is tested, so the test holds under `set -o pipefail` too:

```yaml
- run: |
    deleted=$(git diff --name-only --no-renames --diff-filter=D "origin/$BASE...HEAD" -- '*.py' '*.pyi' '*.toml')
    if [ -n "$deleted" ]; then
      uvx heki==0.11.0 check
    else
      git diff -z --name-only --diff-filter=d "origin/$BASE...HEAD" -- '*.py' '*.pyi' '*.toml' | xargs -0 -r uvx heki==0.11.0 check --touched
    fi
  env:
    BASE: ${{ github.base_ref }}
```

With SARIF:

- findings become code-scanning alerts, warnings included, and keep the step green (exit code
  `1` when one fails the run);
- a configuration, read, or syntax error (exit code `2`) still fails the step; a file heki could
  not read or parse is an `error` notification of the run
  (`invocations[0].toolExecutionNotifications`, with `executionSuccessful: false`), and the
  results of the other files are kept;
- results carry the message, the location, the call chain (`relatedLocations`), and the help
  (`properties.help`; SARIF's `rules[].help` is one text per rule, and a report's help can name
  the object it is about).

For custom tooling, `--output-format json` gives every field: see
[Coding Agents](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#after-an-edit-heki-check).

### Auditing inline suppressions

A baseline, `report-unused-suppressions`, and `require-suppression-codes` do not stop a new
`# heki: ignore[EFF101]`, `# noqa: EFF101`, or bare `# noqa` from hiding a report, and the run
still exits 0. `--report-suppressed <PATH>` writes the reports that inline suppressions hid to a
JSON file, next to any `--output-format`:

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "suppressed": [
    {
      "code": "EFF101",
      "file": "app/handlers.py",
      "function": "fetch",
      "target": "time.sleep",
      "line": 12,
      "column": 5,
      "directive": {"kind": "heki-ignore", "file": "app/handlers.py", "line": 12, "column": 20}
    }
  ]
}
```

- `file`, `function`, `code`, and `target` are the key of the report in a
  [baseline](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#ratchet-baselines), so a change of line numbers does not change what a CI job
  compares. Compare the entries as a multiset of those four fields: one removed entry does not
  offset an added one.
- `directive.kind` is `heki-ignore`, `heki-ignore-bare`, `noqa-code`, or `noqa-bare`. When several
  suppressions on a line hide the same report, the first one in the source is named.
- Only reports that a suppression hid are listed. A `# noqa: F401` that Ruff reads hides no heki
  report, and a suppression that hid nothing is not listed (`report-unused-suppressions`
  reports it).
- The file covers what the run shows: with `--touched` or a file in PATHS, the reports of those
  files, and a baseline changes nothing in it. It is the same bytes on every run of the same
  code, and the command exits with 2 when the file cannot be written.

A CI job can run the check on the base branch and on the change, and fail on an entry the change
adds. Check the base out from its protected ref, so that the change cannot alter the comparison:

```yaml
- run: |
    keys() { jq -r '.suppressed[] | [.file, .function, .code, .target] | @tsv' "$1" | sort; }
    uvx heki check --report-suppressed head.json || test "$?" -eq 1
    git worktree add ../base "origin/$BASE"
    (cd ../base && uvx heki check --report-suppressed "$GITHUB_WORKSPACE/base.json" || test "$?" -eq 1)
    # Sorted lines keep a repeated key apart, so one removed entry offsets no added one.
    new=$(diff <(keys base.json) <(keys head.json) | grep '^>' || true)
    test -z "$new" || { echo "New inline suppressions:"; echo "$new"; exit 1; }
  shell: bash
  env:
    BASE: ${{ github.base_ref }}
```

The configuration, the baseline, and the CI files that decide this (`pyproject.toml` or
`heki.toml`, the baseline file, and `.github/workflows/`) belong in `CODEOWNERS`:
the audit file shows what suppressions hide, and a weakened configuration or baseline is the
code owners' to review.

## Stability on the way to 1.0

On the way to 1.0, heki keeps these stable: the exit codes `0`, `1`, and `2`, the exact rules that
run by default, the format of the Ratchet baseline, the contract tables `write-owners`,
`read-owners`, `call-owners`, `readonly-returns`, `invalidation`, and `effect-boundaries` with
`fail = true` and `[lint] fail = [...]`, and the `json`, `sarif`, and `github` output formats. A
change to one of them is listed under "Breaking changes" in the release notes. The experimental
features can change in any release: `heki recommend`, `heki inspect`, `heki skill`,
`--generate-prompt`, and the rules marked experimental
([Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/) has the list).

## Rolling out rules

1. Run [`heki recommend`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/recommend/) (experimental): it says which rules would report on
   the project, what heki could not see, and the contracts the code already keeps, with the keys
   to add. It writes no file.
2. Start with the default rules and a baseline, or `--select` one family at a time. Only the
   exact rules that are not opt-in run by default; add the heuristic ones with
   `lint.heuristic = true` (or `--heuristic`), or name the ones you want in `extend-select`.
   Their reports can be wrong about the code, and every output labels them `heuristic`
   ([Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/)).
3. Declare [contracts](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#contracts) for the shared state and the operations you
   care about, and effect boundaries for the code that must stay pure. `MUT201`, `MUT203`,
   `MUT204`, `MUT208`, and `EFF201` report nothing until a contract exists.
4. Enable the opt-in rules where they matter:

    | Rule | Certainty | Turn it on for |
    | ---- | --------- | -------------- |
    | [`EFF105`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-blocking-fs/) | exact | async services |
    | [`EFF107`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unretained-async-task/) | heuristic | async services |
    | [`EFF106`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/lock-or-tx-held-across-io/) | heuristic | threaded code, and code that holds database transactions |
    | [`MUT103`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/summary-effect-regression/) | heuristic | library APIs (with [effect snapshots](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#effect-snapshots-mut103)) |
    | [`MUT106`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/iterator-double-consumption/) | heuristic | code that passes iterators and generators around |
    | [`MUT108`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-type-mutation/) | heuristic | code that relies on frozen dataclasses and `ReadOnly` fields |
    | `OPT103`, `OPT110`, `OPT111`, `OPT120`, `OPT121`, `OPT130` | exact | loops over large inputs; `--include-size-dependent` runs all of them except `OPT103` (which has no rewrite), and `--fix` then applies the rewrites |

5. Use `per-file-ignores` rather than broad `ignore` lists, so new code stays covered.

### From heki 0.1

heki 0.1 ran every rule that is not opt-in by default. Since rules have a certainty, only the
exact ones that are not opt-in do ([Getting Started](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/getting-started/#run-it) lists them).

- `lint.heuristic = true` restores the rules of 0.1, now labelled `heuristic` in every output,
  except the size-dependent `OPT` rules, which are opt-in since 0.3.0: name them in
  `extend-select` or `--select`, or pass `--include-size-dependent` for all but `OPT103` (`OPT103`, `OPT110`, `OPT111`, `OPT120`, `OPT121`, `OPT130`).
- A baseline keeps its entries: their keys (file, function, rule, target) do not change, with one
  exception. `MUT109` is now `MUT208` and the old code is no alias, so an entry with rule `MUT109`
  no longer matches: its report counts as a regression. Change `rule_code = "MUT109"` to
  `"MUT208"` in those entries, or record the baseline anew.
- `heki check --fix` applies the proven fixes of `OPT101` and `OPT102` by default, as in 0.1.

### From heki 0.2 and 0.3

`EFF111` and `EFF113` are no longer codes of their own: their reports are the heuristic reports
of `EFF101` and `EFF103`, labelled `heuristic` and shown, as before, with `lint.heuristic = true`
or where the code is named. The old codes and names are not kept.

- Write `EFF101` for `EFF111` (`async-possibly-blocking-call`) and `EFF103` for `EFF113`
  (`loop-possible-db-query`) in `select`, `extend-select`, `ignore`, `per-file-ignores`,
  `severity`, and suppression comments. In the configuration the old codes are unknown rules
  (exit code 2); a comment naming one suppresses nothing.
- A baseline entry with `rule_code = "EFF111"` or `"EFF113"` no longer matches: its reports count
  as regressions. Change the code to `"EFF101"` or `"EFF103"` (adding up the counts of two entries
  that then have the same file, function, and target), or record the baseline anew.

### From heki 0.5 and earlier

- `--update-baseline` writes `version = 3`, which heki 0.5.0 and earlier refuse: update heki
  everywhere the baseline is read (the pre-commit `rev`, CI) before committing a rewritten
  baseline. A file of version 2 is read as before, with a note ([What an entry
  allows](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#what-an-entry-allows)).
- Once rewritten, an entry recorded for a heuristic report no longer allows an exact one: a
  report that heki proves is a regression once.
- An exact `EFF101` or `EFF103` report is keyed by the last call of the shortest call chain, as a
  heuristic one is, in a file of version 3. A file of version 2 keeps the call the report names,
  so its entries still match, and `--update-baseline` rewrites them with the new key.

## Effect snapshots (`MUT103`)

For a library, a change in what a public function *does* is worth reviewing even when no rule
fires: it starts mutating an argument, or doing network I/O. Save the effect summaries of the
public functions and check against them:

```console
$ heki snapshot --write                        # writes .heki-summary-snapshot.json
$ heki check --extend-select MUT103            # reports functions that gained effects
```

1. Commit `.heki-summary-snapshot.json`.
2. When a new effect is intended, refresh the snapshot in the same pull request: the diff of the
   JSON file shows reviewers what changed.

A run that cannot analyze every file (a syntax error, an unreadable file) does not write the
snapshot: it reports the errors and exits with code 2, so the entries of those files are not
lost.

### Comparing with the protected base

Instead of committing the snapshot, a pull request can be compared with a snapshot of
its protected base branch. Generate `base.json` on the base with the same heki version, the same
knowledge bases, the same `--target-version`, and the same configuration as the check on the
pull request, then check the whole project against it:

```console
$ git switch --detach origin/main
$ heki snapshot > ../base.json
$ git switch --detach "$PR_HEAD"
$ heki check --select MUT103 --fail-on warning --snapshot ../base.json
```

`--snapshot PATH` replaces `.heki-summary-snapshot.json` at the project root. A path that does
not exist, a file that is not a snapshot, a snapshot of an unsupported version, and a run in
which `MUT103` is not enabled all exit with code 2: the check never passes without having
compared. A snapshot at the root is ignored while `--snapshot` is given. Run the whole project,
not `--touched` on the files of the pull request: a public function gains an effect through a
private helper in another module, and the report is on the public function.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/cli-reference/

# CLI Reference

Exit codes: `0` no diagnostic that fails the run (warnings and heuristic reports are reported without failing it), `1` an exact `error` diagnostic, or any diagnostic with `--fail-on warning` (`lint.fail-on`), among the Ratchet regressions when a baseline is used (or a refused `--update-baseline`, or pending `--diff` changes), `2` configuration / I/O / syntax errors.

A file that cannot be read or does not parse does not stop the run: `heki check` reports its error, checks and reports the other files, and exits with `2`, also when it reports diagnostics. A run over given files (file PATHS, or `--touched`) reports and fails on only the errors of those files, as it does with diagnostics, and names the other files it could not analyze in a note. A file that does not parse cannot run either, so nothing it would do is assumed; the names under its module resolve to nothing. SARIF output lists such files as `error` notifications of a run that did not execute successfully (`invocations[0].toolExecutionNotifications`, `executionSuccessful: false`); JSON output holds the diagnostics only.

## `heki`

```text
heki (壁, "wall") is a static checker for Python. It tracks side effects and mutations across function calls, and checks imports and the contracts you declare.

Usage: heki <COMMAND>

Commands:
  check        Check Python files or directories for blocking calls, mutations, imports, and broken contracts
  server       Start the incremental Language Server Protocol (LSP) server [alias: lsp]
  rule         Explain a rule, its Proof Obligations, and counterexamples (`ruff rule` style) [alias: explain]
  snapshot     Manage interprocedural effect summary snapshots (`MUT103`)
  assumptions  List Assumption A1 hazards (`eval`, `exec`, `locals()`, frame introspection, functions too large to model) in a project
  inspect      Experimental: what heki knows about one function (its effects, what it changes, keeps, and returns, whether it is pure, its callers, reports, and contracts)
  recommend    Experimental: advice on the configuration of a project, with counts from its analysis, and the keys to add (it writes no file)
  skill        Experimental: install heki's Agent Skill where a coding agent reads skills
  version      Print the version of this heki, and with `--changelog` what this release changed
  help         Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

  -V, --version
          Print version

Documentation:
  Documentation    https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/
  Getting started  https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/getting-started/
  Configuration    https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/
  Rules            https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/
  Coding agents    https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/
  llms.txt         https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/llms.txt
  Agent Skill      https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#agent-skill-experimental

Exit codes:
  0  no diagnostic fails the run
  1  a diagnostic at the `fail-on` severity (an exact `error` by default; a heuristic one counts as a `warning`), a report of a contract with `fail = true`, a refused `--update-baseline`, or pending `--diff` changes
  2  a configuration, path, read, or syntax error; the error says what to do and links the documentation

Examples:
  heki check
      check the project in the working directory
  heki check src tests --select EFF,MUT
      check two directories with two rule families
  heki check --fix
      apply the fixes heki proves safe
  heki rule EFF101
      the documentation of one rule
  heki skill install --agent claude-code
      install the Agent Skill for Claude Code (experimental)

Output for programs:
  heki check --output-format json
      the diagnostics; when the configuration or a path stops the run, {"error": {"message", "help", "docs", ...}}
  heki rule <CODE> --output-format json
      one rule's metadata
  heki inspect <SYMBOL> --output-format json
      what heki knows about one function (experimental)
```

## `heki check`

```text
Check Python files or directories for blocking calls, mutations, imports, and broken contracts

Usage: heki check [OPTIONS] [PATHS]...

Arguments:
  [PATHS]...
          Directories to analyze, and files to report on: a file is checked in its project, as `--touched` does from the project root (with directories, the directories are analyzed). A file outside any project is analyzed alone
          
          [default: .]

Options:
      --fix
          Apply `safe` + `unconditional` fixes (`OPT101`/`OPT102`)

      --include-size-dependent
          Also run the opt-in rules with a `size-dependent` rewrite (`OPT110`, `OPT111`, `OPT120`, `OPT121`, `OPT130`), as if `--extend-select` named them, and with `--fix` or `--diff` apply their proven-safe rewrites, in every function

      --unsafe-fixes
          With `--fix` or `--diff`, also apply the unsafe fixes, which change what the program does in a way the rule's page states (`MUT118`)

      --diff
          Preview fixes as a unified diff without writing files

      --touched <FILE>...
          Show and fail on only the diagnostics in one of these files or with a hop of their call chain (`related`) in one, such as the files a commit or a pull request changed, and let `--fix` and `--diff` rewrite only these files; the analysis still covers PATHS (put PATHS before the option). With a baseline, every Ratchet regression is shown, wherever it is; without one, a note counts the diagnostics that would fail the run and are not shown. A configuration file (`pyproject.toml`, `heki.toml`, a file its `include` lists, the baseline) shows every diagnostic. Another TOML file is passed over, and another path that is not an analyzed file is named in a warning (an error with `--unmatched-paths error`)

      --select <SELECT>
          Comma-separated rule codes, prefixes, or slugs to enable

      --extend-select <EXTEND_SELECT>
          Additional rules to enable on top of defaults/config

      --ignore <IGNORE>
          Comma-separated rule codes or slugs to ignore

      --heuristic
          Also run the heuristic rules, whose reports can be wrong about the code, by default and for every prefix and `ALL` (`lint.heuristic = true`)

      --no-heuristic
          Run a heuristic rule only when its code or name is selected (`lint.heuristic = false`)

      --config <CONFIG>
          Explicit configuration file: a `pyproject.toml` (its `[tool.heki]` table) or a file with the keys at its top level, like `heki.toml`

      --target-version <TARGET_VERSION>
          Target Python version (`py311`, `py312`, `py313`, `py314`, `py315`)

      --baseline <BASELINE>
          Ratchet baseline TOML file (line-number-independent)

      --snapshot <PATH>
          Summary snapshot (`heki snapshot` output) that `MUT103` compares with, in place of `.heki-summary-snapshot.json` at the project root. A file that is missing, unreadable, malformed or of an unsupported version is an error (exit code 2), and so is a run in which `MUT103` is not enabled

      --fail-on <FAIL_ON>
          Exit with code 1 on reports of this severity or higher: `error` (the default), or `warning` to fail on warnings too (`lint.fail-on`). A heuristic report counts as a warning. A report of a contract with `fail = true` fails the run at either
          
          [possible values: error, warning]

      --unmatched-paths <SEVERITY>
          What to do with a path given to report on (`--touched`, a file among PATHS) that names no analyzed file: `warning` (the default) names it and goes on, `error` stops the run with exit code 2 before it reports or rewrites anything (`lint.unmatched-paths`)
          
          [possible values: error, warning]

      --output-format <OUTPUT_FORMAT>
          Output format: `full`, or `github` in GitHub Actions (`GITHUB_ACTIONS=true`); `HEKI_OUTPUT_FORMAT` sets it when the option is not given
          
          [possible values: full, concise, json, github, sarif]

      --color <WHEN>
          When to color the `full` and `concise` output and `--diff`, as Ruff does: `auto` colors them on a terminal unless `NO_COLOR` is set (`FORCE_COLOR` or `CLICOLOR_FORCE` color them anywhere), `always`, or `never`
          
          [default: auto]
          [possible values: auto, always, never]

      --update-baseline
          Generate or shrink-update the Ratchet baseline file, from directories: the entries of files the paths leave out stay as they are

      --watch
          Watch the directories given for file changes and re-run incrementally

      --generate-prompt [<QUESTION>]
          Experimental: print a prompt for consulting a language model about this run instead of the report: the configuration, the rules that apply, the diagnostics, how to answer, and QUESTION when given (put PATHS before the option). `--output-format json` prints it as JSON. Writes no file and exits with 0

      --report-suppressed <PATH>
          Write the reports that inline suppressions hid (`# heki: ignore[...]`, `# noqa`) to this JSON file, next to any `--output-format`, so CI can compare it with the file of the protected base branch and find the suppressions a change adds. It lists the reports of the files the run shows (`--touched`, PATHS that are files); a baseline changes nothing in it. Each entry names the report (`code`, `file`, `function`, `target` as its baseline key, `line`, `column`) and the `directive` that hid it (`kind`, `file`, `line`, `column`); the entries are sorted, and the same project gives the same bytes. Exits with 2 when the file cannot be written

      --output-format-json-schema <TARGET>
          Print the JSON Schema of a JSON format heki writes and exit: `generate-prompt` (the object of `--generate-prompt --output-format json`), or a published schema by its name and version, such as `check-1` or `baseline-3` (docs/output-formats.md lists them)

          Possible values:
          - generate-prompt:     The object of `heki check --generate-prompt --output-format json`
          - check-1:             The array of `heki check --output-format json`
          - report-suppressed-1: The file `heki check --report-suppressed` writes
          - summary-snapshot-1:  The summary snapshot file `heki snapshot --write` writes
          - baseline-1:          A Ratchet baseline file, version 1 (counts diagnostics)
          - baseline-2:          A Ratchet baseline file, version 2 (counts violation sites)
          - baseline-3:          A Ratchet baseline file, version 3 (counts sites and the heuristic ones)
          - inspect-1:           The output of `heki inspect --output-format json`
          - inspect-imports-1:   The output of `heki inspect --imports --output-format json`
          - rule-1:              The output of `heki rule --output-format json`
          - assumptions-1:       The output of `heki assumptions --json`
          - error-1:             What a failed command writes to stdout with `--output-format json`

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

Documentation:
  This command     https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/cli-reference/#heki-check
  Documentation    https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/
  Getting started  https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/getting-started/
  Configuration    https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/
  Rules            https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/
  Coding agents    https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/
  llms.txt         https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/llms.txt
  Agent Skill      https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#agent-skill-experimental

Exit codes:
  0  no diagnostic fails the run
  1  a diagnostic at the `fail-on` severity (an exact `error` by default; a heuristic one counts as a `warning`), a report of a contract with `fail = true`, a refused `--update-baseline`, or pending `--diff` changes
  2  a configuration, path, read, or syntax error; the error says what to do and links the documentation

Examples:
  heki check src tests
      check two directories
  heki check app/api.py
      analyze the file's project, report only what touches the file
  heki check --select EFF,MUT101 --ignore OPT110
      choose the rules for one run
  heki check --touched app/users.py app/api.py
      analyze the project, report only what touches the two files (pre-commit, a pull request)
  heki check --diff
      show the fixes heki proves safe; `--fix` applies them
  heki check --baseline heki-baseline.toml --update-baseline
      record the current diagnostics; later runs report only new ones

Output for programs:
  heki check --output-format json
      the diagnostics; when the configuration or a path stops the run, {"error": {"message", "help", "docs", ...}}
  heki check --output-format sarif
      SARIF 2.1.0, with each rule's page as `helpUri`
  heki check --generate-prompt "<question>" --output-format json
      the project's diagnostics and configuration for a model (experimental)
```

## `heki inspect`

```text
Experimental: what heki knows about one function (its effects, what it changes, keeps, and returns, whether it is pure, its callers, reports, and contracts)

Usage: heki inspect [OPTIONS] <SYMBOL> [PATHS]...

Arguments:
  <SYMBOL>
          A dotted name (`pkg.mod.Class.method`, a dotted suffix such as `Class.method`, or a glob), `path.py:LINE`, or `path.py::NAME`. `-` reads such symbols from standard input, one per line, and reports on every function they name, a glob on each function it matches, from one analysis: a JSON array, or one text section per function

  [PATHS]...
          The project to analyze, as for `heki check`
          
          [default: .]

Options:
      --output-format <OUTPUT_FORMAT>
          `text`, or `json`
          
          [default: text]
          [possible values: text, json]

      --callers
          List the callers transitively, and the reports above the function

      --depth <DEPTH>
          How many caller levels `--callers` lists
          
          [default: 3]

      --imports
          Show the imports of the project modules SYMBOL names (a module name or a glob over module names): each import with when it runs and what it loads, and what loading the module loads while it loads

      --select <SELECT>
          Comma-separated rule codes, prefixes, or slugs to enable

      --extend-select <EXTEND_SELECT>
          Additional rules to enable on top of defaults/config

      --ignore <IGNORE>
          Comma-separated rule codes or slugs to ignore

      --heuristic
          Also run the heuristic rules, whose reports can be wrong about the code, by default and for every prefix and `ALL` (`lint.heuristic = true`)

      --no-heuristic
          Run a heuristic rule only when its code or name is selected (`lint.heuristic = false`)

      --config <CONFIG>
          Explicit configuration file: a `pyproject.toml` (its `[tool.heki]` table) or a file with the keys at its top level, like `heki.toml`

      --target-version <TARGET_VERSION>
          Target Python version (`py311`, `py312`, `py313`, `py314`, `py315`)

      --baseline <BASELINE>
          Ratchet baseline TOML file (line-number-independent)

      --snapshot <PATH>
          Summary snapshot (`heki snapshot` output) that `MUT103` compares with, in place of `.heki-summary-snapshot.json` at the project root. A file that is missing, unreadable, malformed or of an unsupported version is an error (exit code 2), and so is a run in which `MUT103` is not enabled

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

Documentation:
  This command     https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/cli-reference/#heki-inspect
  Documentation    https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/
  Getting started  https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/getting-started/
  Configuration    https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/
  Rules            https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/
  Coding agents    https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/
  llms.txt         https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/llms.txt
  Agent Skill      https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#agent-skill-experimental

Exit codes:
  0  the report of each function is printed
  2  a symbol names no single function (the error lists the candidates), or a file could not be analyzed

Examples:
  heki inspect pkg.users.fetch
      a function by its full name
  heki inspect src/pkg/users.py:42 --callers
      the function at a line, with its callers
  printf '%s\n' pkg.users.fetch 'pkg.orders.*' | heki inspect -
      every function the symbols name, from one analysis

Output for programs:
  heki inspect <SYMBOL> --output-format json
      the report as one object; on exit code 2, `error` with the candidates
  heki inspect - --output-format json
      an array: the object of each function the symbols on standard input name, in their order
```

## `heki recommend`

```text
Experimental: advice on the configuration of a project, with counts from its analysis, and the keys to add (it writes no file)

Usage: heki recommend [OPTIONS] [PATHS]...

Arguments:
  [PATHS]...
          The project to analyze, as for `heki check`
          
          [default: .]

Options:
      --output-format <OUTPUT_FORMAT>
          `text`, or `json` (one object, described by the JSON Schema its `$schema` names)
          
          [default: text]
          [possible values: text, json]

      --output-format-json-schema
          Print the JSON Schema of the object of `--output-format json` and exit

      --all
          Show every block of contracts (by default the first 3 of each kind) and up to 50 of the sites keeping them at `unresolved = "ignore"` (by default 5), in the report and in the keys to add, every suggestion group, the heuristic ones too (by default the text lists the first 3 exact ones), and every rule without reports by name

      --focus <FOCUS>
          Print one section in full, alone: `types`, the suggestions with every exact group (with `--all`, the heuristic ones too). The JSON object keeps every field
          
          [possible values: types]

      --diff
          With `--focus types`, print the exact suggestion groups as one unified diff that `git apply` or `patch -p1` applies, in place of the report: annotations and the imports they need, nothing else. Writes no file

      --select <SELECT>
          Comma-separated rule codes, prefixes, or slugs to enable

      --extend-select <EXTEND_SELECT>
          Additional rules to enable on top of defaults/config

      --ignore <IGNORE>
          Comma-separated rule codes or slugs to ignore

      --heuristic
          Also run the heuristic rules, whose reports can be wrong about the code, by default and for every prefix and `ALL` (`lint.heuristic = true`)

      --no-heuristic
          Run a heuristic rule only when its code or name is selected (`lint.heuristic = false`)

      --config <CONFIG>
          Explicit configuration file: a `pyproject.toml` (its `[tool.heki]` table) or a file with the keys at its top level, like `heki.toml`

      --target-version <TARGET_VERSION>
          Target Python version (`py311`, `py312`, `py313`, `py314`, `py315`)

      --baseline <BASELINE>
          Ratchet baseline TOML file (line-number-independent)

      --snapshot <PATH>
          Summary snapshot (`heki snapshot` output) that `MUT103` compares with, in place of `.heki-summary-snapshot.json` at the project root. A file that is missing, unreadable, malformed or of an unsupported version is an error (exit code 2), and so is a run in which `MUT103` is not enabled

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

Documentation:
  This command     https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/cli-reference/#heki-recommend
  Documentation    https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/
  Getting started  https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/getting-started/
  Configuration    https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/
  Rules            https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/
  Coding agents    https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/
  llms.txt         https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/llms.txt
  Agent Skill      https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#agent-skill-experimental

Exit codes:
  0  the advice is printed
  2  a configuration, path, read, or syntax error; the error says what to do and links the documentation

Examples:
  heki recommend
      advice for the project in the working directory
  heki recommend --focus types
      every standard type the code already keeps, as suggestions

Output for programs:
  heki recommend --output-format json
      the advice as one object
  heki recommend --focus types --diff | git apply
      the exact suggestions as one unified diff of annotations
  heki recommend --output-format-json-schema
      the JSON Schema of that object
```

# Output Formats

Every JSON format heki writes has a JSON Schema in the repository, so that CI, governance tools,
and coding agents can check what they read. The schemas are in
[`docs/schemas/`](https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki/tree/main/docs/schemas) and published at
`https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/schemas/<name>.json`, the `$id` of each. They follow JSON Schema draft
2020-12 and are derived from the types that write the output, so they cannot drift from it.
`heki check --output-format-json-schema <name>` prints the same schema.

| Format | Written by | Schema |
| ------ | ---------- | ------ |
| Diagnostics, an array | `heki check --output-format json` | [check-1](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/schemas/check-1.json) |
| Suppressed reports | `heki check --report-suppressed PATH` | [report-suppressed-1](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/schemas/report-suppressed-1.json) |
| Effect summary snapshot | `heki snapshot --write`, or `heki snapshot` on stdout | [summary-snapshot-1](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/schemas/summary-snapshot-1.json) |
| Ratchet baseline, version 1 | files written before baselines counted sites | [baseline-1](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/schemas/baseline-1.json) |
| Ratchet baseline, version 2 | files that count sites | [baseline-2](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/schemas/baseline-2.json) |
| Ratchet baseline, version 3 | `heki check --baseline FILE --update-baseline` | [baseline-3](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/schemas/baseline-3.json) |
| Function facts | `heki inspect SYMBOL --output-format json` | [inspect-1](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/schemas/inspect-1.json) |
| Import facts | `heki inspect --imports MODULE --output-format json` | [inspect-imports-1](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/schemas/inspect-imports-1.json) |
| Rule metadata | `heki rule [CODE] --output-format json` | [rule-1](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/schemas/rule-1.json) |
| Assumption A1 hazards | `heki assumptions --json` | [assumptions-1](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/schemas/assumptions-1.json) |
| Failure of a command | any command, with `--output-format json` | [error-1](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/schemas/error-1.json) |
| Configuration advice | `heki recommend --output-format json` | [recommend-3](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/schemas/recommend-3.json), and [version 1](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/schemas/recommend-1.json) and [2](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/schemas/recommend-2.json) |
| Prompt for a language model | `heki check --generate-prompt --output-format json` | `heki check --output-format-json-schema generate-prompt` |

The baseline and the snapshot are files you commit. A baseline is TOML: its schema describes its
values as JSON, which is what a TOML parser gives. Validate a baseline by parsing it first.
SARIF output (`--output-format sarif`) follows the public
[SARIF 2.1.0](https://docs.oasis-open.org/sarif/sarif/v2.1.0/sarif-v2.1.0.html) schema, which
heki does not copy.

## Where a contract report points

A report of a contract rule gives, in `contract_locations` of the JSON diagnostics, where the
configuration defines each contract it is of, then the entry of the contract the report is
about, when there is one. For `effect-boundaries` (`EFF201`), `invalidation` (`MUT208`), and
`import-boundaries` (`IMP201`), that is the entry the access matched, glob or module part
included: the `call-targets`, `read-targets`, `write-targets`, or `write-universe` entry, or the
`forbid` token, of a boundary; the `targets` entry of an invalidation contract; the
`forbidden-imports` pattern of a forbidden import, or the `relative-imports` one of a module
imported by its full name. A report of an access several entries match points at the first,
the one its `target` names. For the other contracts it is the entry whose text is the report's `target` (a
target of `write-owners`, `read-owners`, or `call-owners`, a producer of `readonly-returns`
written without a glob). Each has a `path`, a 1-based `line` and byte `column`, and a
`message` (``write-owners contract `fields` ``, ``` `targets` entry `pkg.m.Model.fields` ```,
with ``from group `name` `` for an entry a group holds). The places are where the file writes the table and the entry: in the main configuration
file, an included one, a defaults table, or a group. A table's
[`source` and `entry-sources`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#where-a-contract-is-defined) name other places,
which are given instead. SARIF output adds the same places to `relatedLocations`, after the
steps of the report's chain, and the [language server](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/lsp/) to its related information. The
places are no part of a baseline key.

## What an effect boundary cannot judge

An effect boundary with `unresolved = "report"` reports, under `EFF201`, the calls and writes it
cannot judge in a scope function's reach, one report per kind
(`<boundary>:unresolved-calls`, `<boundary>:unresolved-writes:<attribute>`) at the first one. In
the JSON diagnostics, `unresolved_sites` of such a report lists every site it stands for, ordered by
`path`, `line`, and `column`, with `function`, the function holding the site by its fully
qualified name. `sites` is the number of listed sites and is written only above one: a report
without `sites` stands for one site. A call has:

- `callee`: the method or value called (`get` of `table.get(...)`), `null` for a value computed in
  place (`make()(...)`), or for a body heki does not follow, that function's full name.
- `reason`: why heki does not follow it. For a call it resolves to no function, the reasons
  `heki recommend` gives: `unannotated-parameter`, `unresolved-annotation`, `any-value`,
  `callable-value`, `unbound-name`, `unlisted-protocol`, `call-result`, `attribute`,
  `computed-name`, `too-many-implementations`, `unknown-member`, or `untyped-value`. For a call
  of a function whose body heki does not model (`eval`, a body too large), `unmodeled-body`; for
  one only a stub declares, `stub-body`. A scope function whose own body is one of these is
  listed at its definition, as its own `function` and `callee`.
- `parameter`: the parameter a reason is about (`unannotated-parameter`, `unresolved-annotation`),
  else `null`.

A write has `attribute` (`null` for a name computed at run time, `setattr(obj, name, v)`) and
`kind`, as `heki inspect` names write kinds (`direct_attr`, `set_attr`, `container_mut`, ...).

```json
"unresolved_sites": [
  {"path": "pkg/m.py", "line": 7, "column": 9, "function": "pkg.m.run",
   "callee": "strip", "reason": "unannotated-parameter", "parameter": "text"},
  {"path": "pkg/m.py", "line": 9, "column": 5, "function": "pkg.m.run",
   "callee": "fn", "reason": "unannotated-parameter", "parameter": "fn"}
]
```

The list holds the sites the walk from the scope function records: the code behind a call heki
does not follow is not in it. A site several scope functions reach is listed in each of their
reports. Other diagnostics have no `unresolved_sites`, and the text output, SARIF, and the
language server do not show the list. A baseline entry keys such a report by its target, which
names no site, and counts its sites.

## Versions

The version of a format is part of its schema name. A format with a `version` or
`schema_version` field (the snapshot, the suppressed report, the baselines, `heki inspect`,
`heki recommend`) writes the number its schema is named by; the others (the diagnostics, the rule
metadata, the assumptions, the failure object) have no field and are known by the schema name.

- A change that breaks a reader, such as a field that is removed, renamed, or changes meaning,
  or a value a reader would not expect, makes the next version: a new schema file with the next
  number, and a new `version` where the format has the field. It is listed under Breaking
  changes in the release notes. The files of the earlier versions stay published.
- A field that is added is not breaking. The schema of the version gains the property, and the
  release notes list it. The schemas forbid properties they do not list, because they describe
  what this release writes; a reader should ignore fields it does not know.
- A baseline is read in every version. `heki check --update-baseline` writes version 3, and a
  file of an earlier version keeps its meaning until then.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/

# Rules

heki has 55 rules in four families. A rule is exact when it reports only what it established and was certified on the corpus, and heuristic (≈) when a report can be wrong about the code: [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/) says how a rule is certified and what each one measured. Each rule's page says what a report states.

- The exact rules run by default, and for a prefix such as `EFF` or `ALL`. A report of an exact rule that did not establish every premise (an `OPT` report whose rewrite is not proven) is shown where a heuristic rule would run.
- A heuristic rule runs when `select` / `extend-select` names its code or name. With `lint.heuristic = true` (`--heuristic`), the heuristic rules that are not opt-in also run by default and for a prefix or `ALL`.
- The opt-in rules marked 🔌 run only when `select` / `extend-select` names their exact code or name.
- The contract rules marked 📜 run when their contract is declared, whatever their certainty.

## Legend

- 🛠️ The fix is applied by `heki check --fix` when heki proves it safe.
- 🔧 A proven-safe rewrite applied only with `--fix --include-size-dependent` (it can be slower for tiny inputs).
- ≈ Heuristic rule: a report can be wrong about the code. Every output labels its reports `heuristic`.
- 🔌 Opt-in rule.
- 📜 Contract rule: it reports only what a declared contract asks for.
- 🧪 Experimental rule. Experimental features can still change in behavior or precision, or be removed, in any release, and each change is listed in the release notes. An opt-in rule that is not experimental is stable and only off by default. See [Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/).

## Mutation & State (MUT)

Shared state written behind its owner's back: stale caches, write-ownership contracts, shared return values, and effect regressions against a saved snapshot.

| Code | Name | Message | |
| ---- | ---- | ------- | ------: |
| MUT101 | [cached-property-stale-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-property-stale-mutation/) | Mutating an attribute read by `@cached_property` without invalidating the cache. | 🔌 🧪 |
| MUT103 | [summary-effect-regression](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/summary-effect-regression/) | Interprocedural mutation/escape/effect regression against saved summary snapshot. | ≈ 🔌 |
| MUT106 | [iterator-double-consumption](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/iterator-double-consumption/) | Opt-in: consuming a single-pass iterator or generator a second time (the second pass sees no items). | ≈ 🔌 |
| MUT107 | [hash-attr-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/hash-attr-mutation/) | Opt-in: a method other than the initializers rebinds or changes in place an attribute that the `__hash__` of its instances reads. | ≈ 🔌 |
| MUT108 | [readonly-type-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-type-mutation/) | Opt-in: changing in place a field that a standard type declares read-only (frozen dataclass / `NamedTuple` / `dataclass_transform` fields, `Final` / `ReadOnly` attributes, `ReadOnly` `TypedDict` keys), directly, through an alias, or in a helper. | ≈ 🔌 |
| MUT110 | [readonly-param-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-param-mutation/) | Handing a `Sequence` / `Mapping` / `AbstractSet` / `ReadOnly` parameter, as itself, to a function whose body (or a helper's) changes it in place at a named line. |  |
| MUT111 | [cached-property-stale-read](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-property-stale-read/) | Opt-in: reading a `@cached_property` that a method of its class family can leave stale (a write `MUT101` reports). | 🔌 🧪 |
| MUT112 | [conditional-ownership-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/conditional-ownership-mutation/) | Opt-in: changing in place a value that is a new object on one path and borrowed state (a parameter, an attribute, a global, or what a function returns of such state) on another. | ≈ 🔌 🧪 |
| MUT113 | [iterated-container-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/iterated-container-mutation/) | Opt-in: a dict, set, or deque of the instance changed while a method iterates it, by another method while a generator is suspended in the loop or by a function the loop's body calls (the next step raises `RuntimeError`). | ≈ 🔌 🧪 |
| MUT114 | [cached-result-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-result-mutation/) | Changing in place the list, dict, or set that a `functools.lru_cache` / `functools.cache` function returned (the cache hands the same object to later calls with the same arguments), directly or through the functions that return it. |  |
| MUT115 | [shallow-copy-nested-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/shallow-copy-nested-mutation/) | Opt-in: changing in place an object below a shallow copy the function made of state that outlives the call (`dict(x)`, `x.copy()`, `copy.copy(x)`, `model_copy()`): the copied value holds the same object, so the change is seen through it too. | ≈ 🔌 |
| MUT118 | [sentinel-lost-in-deepcopy](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/sentinel-lost-in-deepcopy/) | `copy.deepcopy` of an instance holding an `object()` sentinel in an attribute that a function tests against the sentinel by identity (the copy holds a new object, which the test does not match). | ≈ |
| MUT119 | [change-lost-on-new-object](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/change-lost-on-new-object/) | An in-place change of a builtin container applied to a new object that nothing else holds and no name keeps (`list(xs).sort()`, `env = os.environ.copy().update(...)`, `obj.settings[k] = v` with a getter returning a new dict): the change is lost when the statement ends. |  |
| MUT120 | [readonly-view-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-view-mutation/) | Opt-in: changing a value held through a read-only view (a protocol or class whose members are all properties without a setter) where a type checker does not see it: a helper that does not see the view's type rebinds one of its properties, or code changes in place the container a property returns. | ≈ 🔌 🧪 |
| MUT201 | [write-owner-violation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/write-owner-violation/) | Writing a guarded attribute/container (directly, via alias, or via helper) outside declared `write-owners`. | ≈ 📜 |
| MUT202 | [readonly-return-mutation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-return-mutation/) | Mutating a shared object returned by a declared `readonly-returns` producer, directly or through the functions that return it. | ≈ 📜 |
| MUT203 | [read-owner-violation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/read-owner-violation/) | Reading a guarded attribute (directly, via alias, `getattr`, or `__dict__`) outside declared `read-owners`. | ≈ 📜 |
| MUT204 | [call-owner-violation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/call-owner-violation/) | Calling a guarded function or method, or constructing a guarded class (directly, via a bound method, `getattr`, or a helper), outside declared `call-owners`. | ≈ 📜 |
| MUT205 | [unresolved-guarded-write](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-write/) | Strict mode of a `write-owners` contract (`unresolved = "report"`): writing an attribute named like a target on an object of unknown class, or a computed attribute name on a guarded class. | ≈ 📜 |
| MUT206 | [unresolved-guarded-read](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-read/) | Strict mode of a `read-owners` contract (`unresolved = "report"`): reading an attribute named like a target on an object of unknown class. | ≈ 📜 |
| MUT207 | [unresolved-guarded-call](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-call/) | Strict mode of a `call-owners` contract (`unresolved = "report"`): calling a method named like a target on an object of unknown class. | ≈ 📜 |
| MUT208 | [write-without-invalidation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/write-without-invalidation/) | Writing a declared `invalidation` target (directly, via alias, or via helper) without reaching one of its invalidators on every path to the function's return. | ≈ 📜 |

## Execution Effects (EFF)

Work that runs where it should not: blocking calls on the event loop, clients and queries inside loops.

| Code | Name | Message | |
| ---- | ---- | ------- | ------: |
| EFF101 | [async-blocking-call](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-blocking-call/) | A call in `async def` that always runs a network, database, subprocess, or sleep call that waits on the event loop; its heuristic reports, a call that can reach a blocking call. |  |
| EFF102 | [loop-unpooled-client](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-unpooled-client/) | A loop over data whose every iteration makes an unpooled HTTP/DB/RPC client or a sessionless request; its heuristic reports, a loop that can make one on every iteration. |  |
| EFF103 | [loop-db-query](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-db-query/) | A loop over data whose every iteration sends a database statement; its heuristic reports, a loop that can run a database query on every iteration. |  |
| EFF105 | [async-blocking-fs](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-blocking-fs/) | Opt-in: a call in `async def` that always runs blocking local filesystem I/O on the event loop; its heuristic reports, a call that can reach it. | 🔌 |
| EFF106 | [lock-or-tx-held-across-io](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/lock-or-tx-held-across-io/) | Opt-in: `await` or blocking network I/O while holding a `threading` lock or a DB transaction. | ≈ 🔌 |
| EFF107 | [unretained-async-task](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unretained-async-task/) | Opt-in: an `asyncio.create_task` result bound to a local variable but never awaited, returned, or stored. | ≈ 🔌 |
| EFF109 | [lock-reacquired-while-held](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/lock-reacquired-while-held/) | A non-reentrant lock (`threading.Lock`, `asyncio.Lock`) taken again, directly or through a call, while it is held (the thread or task waits for itself). |  |
| EFF110 | [exclusive-object-fanout](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/exclusive-object-fanout/) | Opt-in: an object allowing one operation at a time (`asyncio.StreamReader`, an asyncpg connection, a WebSocket) used by tasks started together (`asyncio.gather`, a task group). | ≈ 🔌 🧪 |
| EFF112 | [set-order-output](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/set-order-output/) | Opt-in: the iteration order of a set of strings, which changes between runs, reaches a file, a stream, a serializer, or a raised exception's message across a call. | ≈ 🔌 🧪 |
| EFF114 | [recursion-error-as-value](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/recursion-error-as-value/) | Opt-in: an `except` clause around a recursion (a call cycle reached from its `try` body) takes the `RecursionError` and goes on without raising, so the result depends on the stack depth. | ≈ 🔌 🧪 |
| EFF115 | [async-def-as-sync-callback](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-def-as-sync-callback/) | Opt-in: an `async def` handed to a library call that calls it without awaiting what it returns (a thread's target, an executor's function, an `atexit` or signal handler, a `filter` predicate), so the call only creates a coroutine and the body does not run. | ≈ 🔌 🧪 |
| EFF116 | [generator-never-iterated](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/generator-never-iterated/) | A call of a generator function whose generator nothing iterates (a statement, a value only tested for truth, a function handed to a thread, an `atexit` handler, or a `filter` predicate), so its body does not run. |  |
| EFF117 | [unlocked-write-of-guarded-state](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unlocked-write-of-guarded-state/) | State that another writer changes holding a thread lock (`threading.Lock`, `RLock`, `Condition`, `Semaphore`), changed here holding none, where a thread heki resolves can run one of the writes: an update can be lost. | ≈ |
| EFF118 | [unshielded-cleanup-checkpoint](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unshielded-cleanup-checkpoint/) | A cleanup (a `finally` body, an `except` taking the cancellation, an `__aexit__`) that awaits a call reaching an AnyIO or Trio cancellation checkpoint with no shield on the way: in a cancelled scope the cleanup stops there. | ≈ |
| EFF201 | [effect-boundary-violation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/effect-boundary-violation/) | Reaching a forbidden effect (directly or through calls) from a declared `effect-boundaries` scope. | ≈ 📜 |

## Data Pipelines (DATA)

Quadratic re-allocation of DataFrames and arrays across loop iterations.

| Code | Name | Message | |
| ---- | ---- | ------- | ------: |
| DATA101 | [loop-carried-concat](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-carried-concat/) | Loop-carried quadratic `pandas.concat` / `numpy.vstack` / `numpy.append` accumulation. |  |

## Complexity Rewrites (OPT)

Quadratic patterns heki can rewrite, each proven safe by the alias analysis before a fix is offered.

| Code | Name | Message | |
| ---- | ---- | ------- | ------: |
| OPT101 | [list-quadratic-concat](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/list-quadratic-concat/) | Unconditionally profitable `list` quadratic concatenation (`x = x + [e]` -> `x.append(e)`). | 🛠️ |
| OPT102 | [set-dict-quadratic-merge](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/set-dict-quadratic-merge/) | Unconditionally profitable `set`/`dict` quadratic merge (`{**d, ...}` with `d` first). | 🛠️ |
| OPT103 | [immutable-quadratic-concat](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/immutable-quadratic-concat/) | Opt-in: size-dependent immutable quadratic accumulation (`bytes`/`tuple`/attr `str`). | 🔌 |
| OPT110 | [loop-linear-membership](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-linear-membership/) | Opt-in: size-dependent `e in lst` inside a loop -> hoist `set` outside loop. | 🔧 🔌 |
| OPT111 | [loop-linear-dedup](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-linear-dedup/) | Opt-in: size-dependent `if v not in seen: seen.append(v)` -> auxiliary `set`. | 🔧 🔌 |
| OPT112 | [loop-linear-list-lookup](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-linear-list-lookup/) | Size-dependent `list.index` / `list.remove` / `list.count` inside a loop (repeated linear scans). | ≈ |
| OPT113 | [nested-loop-equijoin](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/nested-loop-equijoin/) | Size-dependent nested-loop equi-join (`for a in A: for b in B: if a.k == b.k`) -> `dict` index. |  |
| OPT120 | [list-front-pop](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/list-front-pop/) | Opt-in: size-dependent `q.pop(0)` / `del q[0]` / `q = q[1:]` -> `collections.deque`. | 🔧 🔌 |
| OPT121 | [list-front-insert](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/list-front-insert/) | Opt-in: size-dependent `q.insert(0, v)` -> `collections.deque`. | 🔧 🔌 |
| OPT130 | [loop-invariant-container-rebuild](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-invariant-container-rebuild/) | Opt-in: size-dependent loop-invariant container reconstruction (`e in set(keys)`). | 🔧 🔌 |

## Imports (IMP)

Imports a contract does not allow, modules importing each other, and code or dependencies the package loads that installing it does not provide, each counted as Python loads them.

| Code | Name | Message | |
| ---- | ---- | ------- | ------: |
| IMP101 | [import-cycle](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/import-cycle/) | Opt-in: project modules that import each other while they load (an import cycle), reported once per group at the import closing a shortest cycle. | ≈ 🔌 🧪 |
| IMP102 | [circular-import-failure](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/circular-import-failure/) | Opt-in: a `from M import name` that raises `ImportError` when a module of its import cycle is imported before the others, because `M` is still loading and has not bound `name`. | ≈ 🔌 🧪 |
| IMP104 | [development-code-import](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/development-code-import/) | Opt-in: a module of the package the project distributes imports test code, or a module outside the source roots of a src layout, by an import that runs. | ≈ 🔌 🧪 |
| IMP201 | [import-boundary-violation](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/import-boundary-violation/) | An import that an `import-boundaries` contract does not allow: a forbidden module, or one outside the allowed imports. | ≈ 📜 🧪 |
| IMP202 | [unresolved-guarded-import](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-import/) | Strict mode of an `import-boundaries` contract (`unresolved = "report"`): an import whose module heki cannot name, which may be one the contract does not allow. | ≈ 📜 🧪 |
| IMP301 | [development-dependency-at-import-time](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/development-dependency-at-import-time/) | Opt-in: a package module loads, while it loads, a module whose distribution the project declares only for development (a dependency group), not in its dependencies or extras. | ≈ 🔌 🧪 |
| IMP302 | [optional-dependency-at-import-time](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/optional-dependency-at-import-time/) | Opt-in: importing a top-level package or an entry point's module loads, while it loads, a module whose distribution the project declares only in extras, so the import fails without them. | ≈ 🔌 🧪 |
