Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/philosophy/

# Design Philosophy

heki asks nothing of your code and never runs it. This page says where heki comes from, the six
choices behind it, and what Python leaves open that heki checks.

| Question | Short answer |
| --- | --- |
| Does heki lock me in? | No. Your code imports nothing from it; remove it and the code runs as before ([1](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/philosophy/#1-a-linter-not-a-library)). |
| Does it run my code? | No. It reads the source, and never runs, imports, or instruments it ([3](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/philosophy/#3-static-only)). |
| How does it share the work with Ruff and type checkers? | Ruff keeps syntax and style, and mypy, Pyright, Pyrefly, and ty keep types. heki takes what needs the call graph: effects, changes to state, and aliases ([6](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/philosophy/#6-a-third-layer-gated-by-evidence)). |

## Why heki exists

heki grew out of
[datamodel-code-generator](https://github.com/datamodel-code-generator/datamodel-code-generator),
a tool that generates Python data models from schemas. The project started in 2019, long before
AI coding was common, and kept its quality mainly with end-to-end tests: a test runs the generator
on a schema and compares the code it writes with an expected file. As the project grew, so did the
tests, from 129 expected files at the start of 2021 to more than 21,000 in November 2026.

To keep test time down and make the code more robust, the maintainers added check scripts beside
the tests to guard invariants: which layers may import which, how many escape hatches the source
holds, and the patterns that reviews kept finding. The scripts and the CI grew too. During 2026
the `scripts/` folder went from 6 files to 100, and a scheduled run of the test workflow from 26
jobs and about half an hour of runner time to 203 jobs and about 13 hours. Each new invariant was
one more script to write, test, and keep running.

From that came the idea of heki: instead of one more script for each invariant, one fast, general
tool that checks state ownership, side effects, and architecture walls. datamodel-code-generator
now runs heki in its CI, and heki contracts have replaced its 929-line architecture checker.

Now that coding agents write much of the code, not only people, the same mechanism works as a
guardrail: a wall in `heki.toml` holds for an agent's change as it does for a person's.

## Design principles

### 1. A linter, not a library

heki is a program you run beside your code, not a package your code imports. There are no
decorators, contract types, or wrappers to add, and nothing runs with your program: the `heki`
package installs one executable and no Python dependencies. Remove heki and the code runs as
before; what stays behind is a configuration file and any `# heki: ignore[...]` comments.

A library of decorators would put each check next to the code it guards, but every module would
then import it, in tests and in production, and leaving it would mean editing that code again. A
tool you can drop at any time is cheap to try, and nothing in your code depends on it.

### 2. Standard Python, read as written

heki adds no syntax and asks for no new annotations. It reads what the code already says:

- a `Sequence`, `Mapping`, or `AbstractSet` parameter is one the function only reads (`MUT110`);
- a `frozen` dataclass, a `Final` attribute, or a `ReadOnly` key is not changed in place
  (`MUT108`);
- an `async def` must not wait on a blocking call, even several helpers below (`EFF101`);
- a lock that is not reentrant, held by a `with` block, is not taken again inside it, also
  through a call (`EFF109`);
- what an `lru_cache` or `cache` function returns is shared by every caller (`MUT114`).

Ownership or borrow markers would make some checks easier, but they would be a dialect only heki
understands. Type checkers, editors, and readers already know these types and statements, so the
promise is already written down; heki checks that the code keeps it.

### 3. Static only

heki never runs, imports, or instruments your program, and patches nothing at run time. It needs
no database, no environment variables, and no virtual environment with your dependencies: the
effects of the standard library and of installed packages come from a catalog, not from their
source ([Where heki's knowledge comes from](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/scope/#where-hekis-knowledge-comes-from)). That
makes it safe to run in CI on pull requests you do not trust. It is one Rust executable that
needs no Python interpreter, and it checks a 100,000-line project in a few seconds.

Tests see only the paths a run takes, and run-time checks cost time in production. heki follows
every path, including an error branch no test reaches, and adds nothing to the program.

### 4. Walls outside the code

Contracts live in a configuration file, best a `heki.toml` of its own, and today's findings in
`heki-baseline.toml`, not in the `.py` files. A wall written as a decorator or a marker would sit
in files that people and agents edit all day: deleting one line silences it, and `CODEOWNERS` can
protect that line only by protecting the whole file. A wall in its own file can have an owner, so
moving it is a change reviewed on its own
([Architecture rules with agents](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/coding-agents/#architecture-rules-with-agents)).

The only heki comment a `.py` file holds is an inline suppression (`# heki: ignore[...]`, or
Ruff's `# noqa`). `heki check --report-suppressed` writes them to a file, so CI can compare a pull
request with its base ([Auditing inline suppressions](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#auditing-inline-suppressions)).

### 5. Silent when unsure

heki does not report a guess as a fact. A report is exact only when every premise of its claim is
established, and the rules that run by default are exact: every report they made on 378 packages
and on a frozen holdout of 100 more was checked by hand, with no false claim. A report with an
open premise is labeled heuristic, and heuristic rules run only when you ask for them. When heki
cannot tell, it says nothing ([Rule precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/)).

The rewrites go further. `heki check --fix` uses a separate analysis that does not trust even
type annotations, because a subclass can override any method, and it applies a rewrite only when
it proves that the program behaves the same under CPython's semantics
([What a fix must prove](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/fixes/#what-a-fix-must-prove)). A checker that guesses gets ignored or
turned off; one that reports only what it can back can fail a build.

### 6. A third layer, gated by evidence

heki takes only what needs control flow, the call graph, or alias facts. What the syntax of one
file decides belongs to Ruff, and whether values match their types to mypy, Pyright, Pyrefly, and
ty. Where another tool covers part of a case, heki keeps the rest, and its configuration,
suppression comments, and output formats follow Ruff's ([Configuration](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/)).

A new rule is decided by evidence, not by feel. It is counted on a corpus of real projects (378
packages, 30.75 million lines), its reports are judged by hand for real harm, and it joins the
default set only when its census and a run on a frozen holdout show no false claim
([How a rule becomes exact](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/#how-a-rule-becomes-exact)). The shapes that failed are
listed with their counts in [Measured and not taken](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/scope/#measured-and-not-taken), and the
whole gate is [How a rule gets into heki](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/scope/#how-a-rule-gets-into-heki).

## What Python leaves open

Other languages enforce some of what heki checks when the code compiles. In Python nothing does,
so heki reports the code that breaks the expectation.

| What Python leaves open | What other languages enforce | What heki checks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Any code can change any object it reaches | ownership and borrowing (Rust; [each idea mapped to heki](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/ownership/#if-you-know-rust)), `const` / `readonly` | read-only parameters, fields, and views changed through helpers (`MUT110`, `MUT108`, `MUT120`); `write-owners` / `read-owners` contracts (`MUT201`, `MUT203`) |
| A signature does not say what a function does | effect types, `IO` in the type (Haskell) | blocking calls reached from `async def`, and clients and queries in loops (`EFF101`–`EFF103`); `effect-boundaries` (`EFF201`); effect snapshots (`MUT103`) |
| Shared mutable objects hide changes | value semantics, immutability by default | stale cached properties and hashes (`MUT101`, `MUT107`); changed shared return values (`MUT114`, `MUT202`); writes an `invalidation` contract must announce (`MUT208`) |
| Dynamic dispatch blocks optimizations | static types let a compiler prove a rewrite | quadratic patterns (`OPT`), rewritten only when proven under CPython's semantics |

The [Rust table](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/ownership/#if-you-know-rust) on State Ownership and Mutation maps each Rust
idea to the closest heki rule and says how Python differs.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/

# Rule Precision

## At a glance

heki reports a claim only when it can back it. What it can back decides the tier of a report, and
what it cannot decide gets no report.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    P["Python project"] --> S["heki static analysis<br/>(control flow, call graph, aliases, imports)"]
    S --> Q{"All premises of<br/>the claim established?"}
    Q -- "Yes" --> E["exact report<br/>on by default for certified rules;<br/>an error fails heki check"]
    Q -- "Some premise open" --> H["heuristic report<br/>shown with --heuristic or an explicit select;<br/>does not fail a default run"]
    Q -- "Cannot establish" --> N["no report<br/>heki stays quiet;<br/>heki recommend lists it under<br/>what heki cannot see"]
```

The same function-and-rule pair in three shapes. Each output below is from `heki check`.

**A, exact.** `handler` always reaches `requests.get` through `fetch`:

```python
async def handler(url):
    return fetch(url)  # fetch always calls requests.get(url)
```

```console
$ heki check .
app.py:9:12: EFF101 (async-blocking-call) [error] `app.fetch` always runs the waiting call `requests.get` on the event loop (1 call down, on every path)
Found 1 diagnostic(s) in 1 file(s).
$ echo $?
1
```

**B, heuristic.** `fetch` calls `requests.get` only `if refresh:`, so the premise "Every return"
(the function has made the next call on every path on which it returns) is open:

```python
def fetch(url, refresh):
    if refresh:
        return requests.get(url)
    return None
```

```console
$ heki check .
All checks passed (1 file(s)).
note: 5 heuristic rule(s) are off and 1 heuristic report(s) are not shown; enable them with `--heuristic` or `lint.heuristic = true`
$ heki check --heuristic .
app.py:11:12: EFF101 (async-blocking-call) [error, heuristic] `handler` reaches the blocking call `requests.get` on the event loop
Found 1 diagnostic(s) in 1 file(s).
$ echo $?
0
```

**C, no report.** `callback` is a parameter without an annotation, so heki does not follow the call:

```python
async def handler(url, callback):
    return callback(url)
```

```console
$ heki check --heuristic .
All checks passed (1 file(s)).
$ heki recommend .
  calls heki does not resolve: 1 call(s) in 1 function(s)
    function     calls  async  loops  why
    app.handler      1      1      0  parameter `callback` has no annotation (callback)
```

| Stage | Example | Default `heki check` | With `--heuristic` |
| ----- | ------- | -------------------- | ------------------ |
| exact | A | reported, exit code 1 | reported, exit code 1 |
| heuristic | B | not shown, exit code 0 | reported as `heuristic`, exit code 0 |
| no report | C | silent, exit code 0 | silent, exit code 0 |

The rest of this page defines the two tiers and says how a rule becomes exact.

Every heki report is **exact** or **heuristic**:

- An exact report is built only from facts heki established. Its claim, what its message states
  about the code, is a set of premises (its rule page lists them under "What a report states"),
  and each premise was established: where heki cannot tell, it does not report. A false exact
  report is a bug.
- A heuristic report states the same kind of claim, but some premise may be open: heki reported
  without ruling it out. It can be wrong about the code, and every output labels it `heuristic`.

A rule is exact once it is certified (below), and heuristic until then. An exact rule's report
is exact when it established every premise of the rule's exact claim, and heuristic when one is
open: an `OPT` rewrite heki could not prove safe, a size-dependent `OPT` rewrite over a loop whose
trip count the data does not decide (the code fixes or caps it, or the loop's items are not a
parameter, the rows of a query, the lines of a file, or the entries of a directory), an `OPT113`
join whose rule page premises do not all hold, or
an `EFF101`, `EFF102`, `EFF103`, `EFF105`, `EFF109`, `EFF116`, `DATA101`, `MUT110`, `MUT114`, or
`MUT119` report whose rule page premises are not all established. Only exact reports are shown by
default, and only those of the exact rules that are not opt-in.

- A heuristic rule runs when `select` or `extend-select` names its code or name. With
  `lint.heuristic = true` (`--heuristic`), the heuristic rules that are not opt-in also run by
  default and for their prefixes and `ALL`.
- The heuristic reports of an exact rule are shown under the same conditions: with
  `lint.heuristic = true`, or when its code or name is selected.
- A contract rule runs when its contract is declared, whatever its certainty.
- A run of `full` or `concise` output that leaves heuristic rules off, or heuristic reports out,
  ends with a note saying how many.
- Only an exact report fails a run by default: a heuristic report counts as a warning for
  [`fail-on`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#rule-selection-toolhekilint), whatever its rule's severity, and
  fails the run only with `fail-on = "warning"`, or when its contract table sets `fail = true`. A
  false heuristic report never stops a CI or a hook that keeps the default.

See [Rule selection](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#rule-selection-toolhekilint). `EFF101`, `EFF102`,
`EFF103`, `EFF105`, `EFF109`, `EFF116`, `DATA101`, `MUT101`, `MUT110`, `MUT111`, `MUT114`, `MUT119`, the proven tier of the eight `OPT`
rewrite rules, and the exact tier of `OPT113` are exact (certified below); the other rules are
heuristic. `MUT101`, `MUT111`, and the six size-dependent `OPT` rules (`OPT103`, `OPT110`,
`OPT111`, `OPT120`, `OPT121`, `OPT130`) are exact and opt-in, for their share of real harm
(below); `EFF105` is exact and opt-in, as local file I/O is usually fast.

## What a report states

A report states what its message says about the code, in the terms its rule page defines. It is
wrong when that statement is false. Whether the code does harm is a separate question, and so is
whether a rewrite of it would be valid:

- A query in a loop over three items has the shape the rule reports; the harm is small.
- A write the author meant, or a memo heki does not recognize, still changes the object.
- A rewrite that a fact heki cannot prove blocks is a question of [fix safety](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/fixes/).

The premises the rules use:

- **Resolves**: a call is to the function shown, through the calls heki resolves ([How a call is
  resolved](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/scope/#how-a-call-is-resolved)). Through a method call, every implementation the
  call can reach counts. A receiver typed by a `Protocol` is not resolved for an exact report:
  its implementers are never a complete set.
- **Reaches on every path**: whenever the reported call returns, the effect has run: each
  function on the chain reaches the next call on every path on which it returns. The claim is
  anchored at the reported call, so a branch around that call in its own function does not
  matter.
- **On every iteration**: the statement runs on every iteration of the loop that completes.
  It does not when every way on from it leaves the loop, or when a first-iteration flag, a flag
  set once, or a lazy initialization the loop tests guards it.
- **Steps through an input**: the loop iterates a named input, such as a parameter, an
  attribute of one, the rows of a query, or the lines of a file.
- **Data-sized** (heuristic reports only): the code does not fix the size or the number of
  iterations at 16 or fewer. heki counts a size it cannot bound as data-sized, so this premise
  is open whenever no bound is found. An exact report never claims a size: a bound of 16 or
  fewer only removes reports, and a larger fixed bound is no evidence either way.

Each exact rule's premises are rows of one table, `crates/heki_rules/src/premises.rs`: what each
states and where heki decides it, the one place every rule reading it goes through. A rule page
lists its claim's premises under "What a report states" by those names (the documentation build
checks it), `heki rule --output-format json` prints them, and a report is exact only when every
premise of its rule's row is established.

A heuristic report of an exact claim can also say which premises of its row it left open, each
with a cause from a closed list kept next to the premise in the same table (what the cause states,
and what closes it: an annotation, a change of the code, heki's catalog, or nothing today). The
causes come from the steps of the decision that made the report heuristic, each premise evaluated
on its own along the reported chain and loop, so they cannot disagree with its tier.
[`heki recommend`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/recommend/) counts the heuristic reports by these causes; no output format of
`heki check` and nothing in the language server shows them. The heuristic reports of `EFF101`,
`EFF103`, the eight `OPT` rewrite rules, `OPT113`, `DATA101`, `MUT110`, and `MUT114` record them. A proven size-dependent `OPT` rewrite, or an `OPT113` join whose premises all hold, over
a loop the data does not size is heuristic for a condition of the exact tier that is no premise,
"Trip count open" (the claim holds, but the change pays off only over a loop the data sizes): the
code fixes the loop at more than 16 trips or caps it, or, for a rewrite, the loop's items are not
the data's as `EFF103`'s Origin establishes them (a loop over an attribute of `self`, a project
function's result, `range` of a configured number, or a `while` loop runs as many times as the
program has parts). The report records that condition, with its cause, in the same list as the
premises it left open, if any.

An exact report's message states its claim and the witnesses of its premises, nothing else: no
cost estimate such as "(N+1)", and no advice (that goes into the help).

Exact claims hold in every run consistent with seven assumptions
([ARCHITECTURE.md, section 3.4](https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki/blob/main/ARCHITECTURE.md)):

- **R1**: the functions and classes on a call chain are not replaced at run time. A special
  method bound on a class after its body (`__setattr__`, `__delattr__`, `__getattribute__`,
  `__getattr__`, a copy hook) is bound under its own name: a store under a constant name (a
  string literal, or a module or class name bound once to one), or under a name the storing
  function builds with constant text that can still spell it, may bind it, and a store under a
  name of unknown value (a parameter, a loop variable over `dir()`, `vars()`, or a mapping's keys,
  a value read from data, a module name bound to a built string) is taken to bind none. This
  gives up `setattr(cls, name, hook)` binding `__setattr__` through such a `name`. Code heki
  does not read is taken to bind none either: a class decorator outside the project, and a call
  or a closure the class is handed to, bind on it only what the stores heki reads bind.
- **R2**: a value annotated `C` is an instance of `C` or of a project subclass. A premise that
  goes through a method call holds only when every implementation in such a subclass has it.
  A value annotated with a nominal container ABC (`Sequence`, `Mapping`, `Set`, and their mutable
  ABCs) is one of its family's builtins or another library class implementing it, taken to run
  what the builtin runs, or a project class implementing it (deriving from it or from a class of
  its family, or registered with it); a `register` heki cannot resolve or a `__subclasshook__`
  leaves such values open, as are those of a structural ABC (`Iterable`) or a protocol.
  Rewrites never rely on annotations.
- **R3**: the ecosystem catalog describes the library, an effect with its condition.
- **R4**: imports resolve as configured.
- **R5**: the checked files are the project.
- **R6**: a library call's argument is a value it waits on (a nonzero sleep, a host name to look
  up) unless heki establishes otherwise, and so are the arguments that opened the connection it
  runs on (a SQLAlchemy engine or another DB-API connection opened from a URL heki does not
  know waits). `sqlite3.connect` is the one exception, as its in-memory form is common: a SQLite
  connection waits only when heki establishes that it was opened on a file. In the same way, an
  argument selects none of the cases of its call's catalog entry unless heki establishes
  otherwise, so the call has the entry's own effects: `open(name)` opens a path, not a file
  descriptor, and `openai.OpenAI(http_client=client)` makes a client of its own.
- **R7**: no asynchronous or resource-exhaustion exception (`MemoryError`, `KeyboardInterrupt`, a
  signal) is raised. Under it, loading a local, a module name bound once, a builtin, or a member
  of an imported module, and building a `list` or `tuple` display, do not raise; other attribute
  loads, subscripts, `set` and `dict` displays, calls, awaits, and operators may.

"A branch heki cannot decide can go both ways" is not an assumption: a report that needs it is
heuristic. Neither is a context manager heki does not resolve: it may suppress exceptions, so an
exact report claims nothing that runs in its body after a statement that may raise.

Each checked report gets one class:

| Class | Meaning |
| ----- | ------- |
| C (confirmed) | The problem is real and observable from the code. |
| P (plausible) | The report is right, and the code does harm at realistic sizes. |
| B (benign) | The report is right, but the code is deliberate or harmless at realistic sizes. |
| F (false) | The report is wrong about the code. |

"Right about the code" is C, P, and B together; "real harm" is C and P. Real harm is published
for each rule. It decides only whether an exact rule runs by default: it does when its share of
real harm is worth the line it prints, and is opt-in otherwise. For the `OPT` rules the share is
that of their exact reports in their certification runs ([Harm of the exact
reports](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/#harm-of-the-exact-reports)):

- The six size-dependent rules are opt-in: their rewrites are proven, but of their exact reports
  only 2 of the 203 the census classified, and 1 of the 233 of the holdout run, were of real
  harm.
- `OPT101` and `OPT102` run by default although none of their exact reports was: their rewrite
  is faster for every input and the default `heki check --fix` applies it
  ([Fixes and Safety](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/fixes/)), so a report is a fix, not only a line to read.
- `OPT113` runs by default on its own share: 2 of its 8 census reports, and none of its 6
  holdout reports.
- A rule with fewer than 10 exact reports in its certification runs by default on the real bugs
  it found instead: [Rare failures](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/#rare-failures).

## How a rule becomes exact

A rule is certified exact when all four hold:

1. **Premise stripping**: for each premise of its claim, the tests hold a counterexample that
   the rule reports once that premise is taken as established, and does not report otherwise.
2. **Census**: every report the rule has on the development corpus (the 378 packages of Stage
   0-A, 30.75 million lines, and the packages added for the rules with few reports) is checked
   by hand by two reviewers. A false claim needs a minimal reproduction, and is fixed as a
   defect of a premise's fact, never by a list of exclusions.
3. **Holdout**: one run on a frozen holdout corpus of 100 packages, never looked at while the
   rule was designed or fixed, finds no false claim outside a violation of R1-R7.
4. **Run-time oracle**: the claimed events (the call that runs, the statement executed on each
   iteration) happen where the code ran, checked with `sys.monitoring` on the differential test
   suite and on datamodel-code-generator and, for a rule whose sites those do not have, on
   programs its premise table generates: each base program fails as claimed, and no program with
   a premise stripped does.

Every release then runs the corpus with the release candidate and checks every report it adds
or changes in an exact rule. A false claim found later is a bug: it is fixed before the next
release, or the rule becomes heuristic in that release and needs a new certification.

## Rare failures

Some rules report a failure that mature code has already fixed: an import that raises, a lock
that waits for itself, a function body that never runs. heki reports them where the code is
written, in the editor and in hooks, so the corpus has few of them, and a share of real harm
cannot be read from a handful of reports. Such a rule is certified as any other, and runs by
default when all of these hold:

1. Its consequence is `Bug`, and its claim is a failure a run shows: an exception, a wait that
   never ends, a body that does not run, or a test that gives the opposite answer.
2. Its census and its holdout run have fewer than 10 exact reports together, and no false claim.
   A census or a holdout run without a report counts; packages added for the rule are not
   required.
3. The run-time oracle shows both sides on programs its premise table generates: every base
   program reports and fails as claimed where it runs, and no program with one premise stripped
   reports or fails.
4. It found at least two real bugs, in two projects: exact reports that two reviewers class as
   confirmed, at the parent commit of a merged pull request that fixes the failure (the report
   is gone at the fix), or in the young repositories of the development corpus.

A false claim found later demotes the rule as for any exact rule. A rule that reaches 10 exact
reports is judged on its share of real harm. Below 10, one report moves the share by more than 10
points, so the 10 % bar decides nothing.

The certifications table records the real bugs of such a rule, and `build_docs.py` fails when a
rule in the default set with fewer than 10 exact reports has none recorded. It exempts the rules
of consequence `MinorBug` and the rules certified before this section existed (`OPT101`,
`OPT102`, `OPT103`, `OPT110`, `OPT111`, `OPT120`, `OPT121`, `OPT130`, `OPT113`, `EFF101`,
`EFF103`, `DATA101`, `MUT110`, `MUT114`, `MUT101`, `MUT111`, `MUT119`); a rule certified after it
is not exempt.

## Certifications

A certified rule has a row here: the release that certified it, and the reports of its census
and of its holdout run with the false claims among them. The census of the proven `OPT` tier
checked by hand every exact report on the Stage 0-A corpus with the build of 2026-11-21 (one
report, whose rewrite needed the set-order obligation, left the tier); the holdout run checked
every exact report of one run on the 100 packages of the frozen holdout corpus. `OPT113`'s
census reports are those of its exact tier with the plain-key premise, all among the reports
the census of the earlier tier checked by hand. The census of `EFF101` counts its boundaries
before reports reaching one waiting call are folded together.

# Scope and Limitations

This page says what heki checks, what it leaves to other tools, where its knowledge comes from,
and what it does when it cannot tell.

## What heki covers

1. The core is what a program does across functions and modules: effects, changes to state,
   aliasing, purity, and async and resource behavior. One file or one type cannot decide these.
2. Walls are contracts you write, or that [`heki recommend`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/recommend/) proposes, on who may
   write, read, call, reach an effect, and import what. Which modules may import which, and
   import cycles, are walls
   ([ADR-022](https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki/blob/main/docs/DESIGN_HISTORY_AND_ADR.md#adr-022)).
   heki's import rules ship as experimental: the `import-boundaries` contracts, and opt-in rules for
   import cycles, circular imports that fail, and imports of test code or of dependencies
   declared only for development or in an extra. Reading tach's and import-linter's contracts is
   planned.
3. Patterns and style that one file decides belong to linters such as Ruff and isort, and type
   correctness to type checkers.
4. An idea from another language's tools is taken when it fits the core or the walls and passes
   the evidence gate: counts on a corpus, real harm, and no false exact claim
   ([How a rule gets into heki](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/scope/#how-a-rule-gets-into-heki)).
5. Framework knowledge enters as catalog data
   ([`[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#ecosystem-knowledge-toolhekiecosystem)). heki has
   no rules written for one framework.

## Where heki fits

| Tool | Looks at | Example |
| ---- | -------- | ------- |
| A linter such as [Ruff](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/) | Syntax and style, one file at a time | `time.sleep()` written directly in an `async def`; a discarded `asyncio.create_task(...)` |
| A type checker such as mypy, Pyright, Pyrefly, or ty | Whether values match their declared types | a `str` passed where an `int` is expected |
| An import-graph checker such as [tach](https://github.com/gauge-sh/tach) or [import-linter](https://github.com/seddonym/import-linter) | Which modules may import which | `app.api` importing `app.db` when the declared layers forbid it; planned in heki: these tools' contracts read as heki contracts, and which imports run while a module loads |
| heki | What code does, not what types it has: effects and aliases, through any number of calls | an `async def` that reaches `requests.get` three helpers away; a model field written outside the store that owns it; an attribute `__hash__` reads changing after the object went into a `set` |

heki differs from these tools in what it models: effects and aliases. It leaves syntax and types
to the tools that model them, also as they grow. Where another tool covers part of a case, heki
keeps the rest: Ruff's `RUF006` reports discarded tasks, so `EFF107` reports only the tasks bound
to a variable. An `await` written directly in a `finally` body or an `__aexit__` with no shielded
scope around it is a single-file linter's check (flake8-async's `ASYNC102`); `EFF118` adds what
needs the call graph: which awaits reach a cancellation checkpoint through helpers, and which
helpers and callers shield them.

[Design Philosophy](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/philosophy/) says why heki is built this way and what Python leaves open.

### Clean for Ruff, mypy, Pyright, Pyrefly, ty, and tach; broken all the same

```python
# app/clients.py
import requests


def fetch_json(url: str) -> dict:
    return requests.get(url, timeout=5).json()


# app/users.py
from app.clients import fetch_json


def load_profile(user_id: int) -> dict:
    return fetch_json(f"https://api.example.com/users/{user_id}")


def load_user(user_id: int) -> dict:
    return {"id": user_id, **load_profile(user_id)}


# app/api.py
from app.users import load_user


async def handler(user_id: int) -> dict:
    return load_user(user_id)  # blocks the event loop three calls down
```

```python
# app/models.py: only `Store.*` may write `Model.fields` (a write-owners contract)
class Model:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.fields: list[str] = []


class Store:
    def add_field(self, model: Model, name: str) -> None:
        model.fields.append(name)


def add_default(fields: list[str]) -> None:
    fields.append("id")


def parse(model: Model) -> None:
    fields = model.fields
    add_default(fields)  # changes `Model.fields` behind the store's back
```

```toml
[[tool.heki.write-owners]]
name = "model-store"
targets = ["Model.fields"]
allowed-writers = ["Store.*"]
```

Each of these passes, because each tool sees one step:

| Command | Sees | Does not see |
| ------- | ---- | ------------ |
| `ruff check --select ASYNC,B,RUF,PERF,PL,SIM,FURB,S` | `requests.get` only when it is written in the `async def` itself | the call three helpers down |
| your type checker (`mypy app`, `pyright`, `pyrefly check`, `ty check`) | a `list[str]` passed where a `list[str]` is expected | that `add_default` changes `Model.fields` |
| `tach check` (with `app.api` → `app.users` → `app.clients` declared) | `app.api` importing `app.users`, which is allowed | what `load_user` does |

heki follows the call into `load_user` and the alias into `add_default`:

```console
$ heki check --output-format concise
app/api.py:5:12: EFF101 `app.users.load_user` always runs the waiting call `requests.get` on the event loop (3 calls down, on every path)
app/models.py:17:5: MUT201 [heuristic] `parse` writes `Model.fields` (through a helper) via `app.models.add_default` outside the write owners of `model-store`
Found 2 diagnostic(s) in 4 file(s).
note: 5 heuristic rule(s) are off; enable them with `--heuristic` or `lint.heuristic = true`
```

## Where heki pays off

| Code | What heki finds |
| ---- | --------------- |
| Async services, and web or database code written in layers of helpers | blocking calls that reach the event loop, clients and queries created inside loops (N+1), I/O while a lock or a transaction is held |
| Large code bases that protect shared state by convention, review, or their own checkers | contract violations, followed through aliases, helpers, and subclasses |
| Loops over growing collections | proven-safe rewrites and suggestions for quadratic patterns |

In small scripts, or code that is mostly synchronous and self-contained, a linter and a type
checker cover most of what matters, and heki reports little.

## What heki does not do

| Check | Use instead |
| ----- | ----------- |
| Style, formatting, and syntax | a linter such as Ruff |
| Type errors | a type checker such as mypy, Pyright, Pyrefly, or ty |
| Import order, required imports, import conventions, relative-import style, and the `lazy` policy of one file | a linter such as Ruff (`I`, `ICN`, `TID252`, `TID254`, `TID255`), or isort for the order |
| Dead code and duplicated code | Ruff or [vulture](https://github.com/jendrikseipp/vulture) |
| Constant-factor micro-optimizations, such as hoisting `re.compile` | no heki rule |

- heki does not change your code's shape: it adds no decorators, contract types, or runtime
  checks, and it does not compile or rewrite code at build time.
- heki never runs or instruments your program, and reads no profile of it.

## Where heki's knowledge comes from

| Source | What it tells heki | Extend it with |
| ------ | ------------------ | -------------- |
| Its own analysis | an SSA form of every function; aliases (copies, attributes, and the iterators and views derived from an object); what each function mutates and which effects it reaches, propagated over the project's call graph until nothing changes | - |
| A catalog of library behavior | `requests.get` blocks on the network; `asyncio.to_thread(fn)` and `@sync_to_async` run a function on another thread; `logging` calls are never reported; `sqlite3.connect()` returns a `Connection`; `threading.Lock` is a synchronous lock | [`[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#ecosystem-knowledge-toolhekiecosystem) |
| Contracts you declare | who may write, read, or call (`write-owners`, `read-owners`, `call-owners`); which returned objects are shared (`readonly-returns`); which changes must be announced (`invalidation`); which functions must not reach I/O or writes (`effect-boundaries`); which modules a module may import (`import-boundaries`) | [contracts](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#contracts) in the configuration |
| Type annotations, as hints only | which class an object has and which method a call reaches: `session: Session` makes `session.execute(...)` a database call | annotations in your code |

- heki does not analyze the source of the standard library or of installed packages: the
  catalog declares their effects.
- Contracts need no decorators, no special types, and nothing at run time.
- The checking rules (`MUT`, `EFF`, `DATA`, `OPT112`, `OPT113`) use annotations. The rewriting
  rules never read them, because a subclass can override any method (see
  [Fixes and Safety](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/fixes/#what-a-fix-must-prove)).

### How a call is resolved

heki looks for the callee in this order:

1. local constructors and imports;
2. annotations;
3. attributes `__init__` or `__post_init__` assigns and globals the module body assigns: the
   join of what every store of each binds;
4. the class hierarchy, up to eight overriding methods.

It also follows container item types (`list[Model]`), return annotations along the MRO,
`isinstance` narrowing, unions (up to eight classes an annotation declares, also through a type
alias, and up to three that different assignments join), and project `Protocol`s.

A call on what a builtin or standard-library call returns resolves too, so `text.strip().lower()`,
`shlex.split(line)[0].upper()`, and `datetime.now().date().isoformat()` are followed to the end.
The result types come from typeshed's stubs, read when heki is built, so a run needs no stubs.
heki infers:

- the result of a method or function (`str.strip` returns `str`, `shlex.split` a `list[str]`),
  with `Self` as the receiver's class and a type argument of a container (`deque[str].popleft`
  returns `str`);
- a standard-library attribute, property, or named-tuple field (`datetime.year`,
  `shutil.disk_usage(path).free`), and a method a base class declares (`bool.bit_length`, from
  `int`; `asyncio.Task.done`, from `asyncio.Future`);
- `bytes[0]` as an `int`, a member of a project enumeration as an instance of it, and its `value`
  as the data type the enumeration mixes in (`class Version(str, Enum)`), unless a class along
  its MRO binds `__new__`;
- the subject of a `match` class pattern as that class inside the case.

Its limits: a method with several overloads gets the join of their results, and no result when
one is `Any`, `object`, or a type variable of the function itself, so `d.get(key).upper()` on a
`dict` stays unresolved, as does `json.loads(text).get(...)`. Module-level variables of the
standard library are not typed yet, and neither is anything from a package outside the standard
library. An instance of a project class keeps the project's own facts; only library classes read
the stubs.

## When heki cannot tell

A rewrite and an exact report make the same choice when information is missing, in opposite
directions; a heuristic report makes it only for some premises:

| | A rewrite (`OPT` fix) | An exact report | A heuristic report |
| - | --------------------- | --------------- | ------------------ |
| Needs | a proof | every premise of its claim established | evidence, with some premises open |
| What heki cannot see | counts as shared and blocks the fix | stops the report | stops it for an unresolved call; does not stop it for the premises its rule page marks open |
| What you get | the diagnostic names the failed obligation: `[not auto-fixable: ...]` | no report: a missed finding, never a guess | a report labelled `heuristic`, which can be wrong about the code |

[Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/#at-a-glance) shows the three outcomes (exact, heuristic, no report) with a run of each.

Each rule page lists the premises of its claim under "What a report states", and which of them
a heuristic report may not have established ([Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/)).

A report that crosses functions shows its call chain as related locations. A call heki cannot
resolve is not followed:

- a value of type `Any`, or an unannotated parameter;
- a method name computed at run time;
- a call with more than eight possible overrides;
- a method no project class along a class's MRO defines, when a base of the class is a value
  heki cannot name where its class statement runs (`class Derived(base)` with `base` a
  parameter, a local, or a call's result), which may define it; such a class is no subclass of
  any project class either;
- a function outside the checked files that the catalog does not list.

Two more cases stay quiet by design:

- A branch the caller's arguments switch off is not followed: `load(name, cache=False)` does not
  reach the request under `if cache:`.
- A client or query created only while an attribute is unset counts once per object, not once
  per loop iteration, and so does a `functools.cached_property` getter; one created only while
  a module global or a local variable the loop carries is unset (or a first-iteration flag
  holds), or right before the loop ends (`break`, `return`, `raise`), counts once per loop.
- A blocking wait on a `concurrent.futures.Future` known to be done (`if f.done():`, after
  `await asyncio.wrap_future(f)`) returns at once.
- `queue.Queue.put` waits only on a queue known to be bounded: a positive `maxsize` on some
  path, every path known. A `put` on a queue heki cannot follow to where it is built is not
  reported.

A file that cannot be read or does not parse is reported (exit code 2), and every other file is
checked as usual. A file that does not parse cannot run either, so heki assumes nothing it would
do: it calls nothing, defines no subclass, and patches no `builtins`. Its module still owns its
name: `import requests` reaches a project's own `requests.py`, and while that file does not
parse, the names under it resolve to nothing, never to the `requests` of the catalog.

A function whose model would pass its size budget (4 units per byte of its source, at most
50,000; real code stays below one unit per byte) is left unmodeled: heki rewrites nothing in it
and treats its body as one call it cannot resolve. `heki assumptions` lists it with the hazard
`unmodeled`. A function whose proof state (a fact per variable per block) would pass 8 cells per
byte of its source, at most 250,000, gets no `OPT` finding: heki does not try to prove a rewrite
in it. A function whose lazy initializations (the blocks each covers, and the walks that find
them) would take more than 8 cells per byte of its source, at most 250,000, has none of them
recognized: in a heuristic report its clients and queries count as made on every iteration,
and an exact report stops there.

A heuristic report goes the other way for the premises its rule page marks open: a branch heki
cannot decide counts as taken, a loop in which heki cannot show that a call runs once counts as
running it on every iteration, and a size heki cannot bound counts as data-sized (the code does
not fix it at 16 items or fewer). A loop over a list that is small by its nature (the columns of
a table, a handful of options) is reported: the report states a loop whose size the code does
not bound, and whether the loop is slow is the harm, which the rule cannot see. When an open
premise is false (a bound the code states that heki does not read, a call that cannot run on
every iteration), the report is wrong about the code, which is why it is heuristic. An exact
report never claims a size: it names the input a loop steps through.

Missed findings close as heki learns more:

| heki lacks | Add |
| ---------- | --- |
| the class of a value | an annotation |
| your blocking or offloading APIs | an entry in [`[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#ecosystem-knowledge-toolhekiecosystem) |
| the rules of your shared state | a [contract](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#contracts) |

## Known limitations

### Dynamic names

`setattr(obj, "fields", v)`, `getattr(obj, "fields")`, `getattr(obj, "method")(...)`, and
`obj.__dict__["fields"]`:

- **Followed** when the name is a constant: a literal, a module-level `Final` string
  (`KEY: Final = "_key"`), also when imported, re-exported, or bound to another `Final` name, a
  module-level string bound once in its module, or a class constant declared `ClassVar` or
  `Final` and bound once (`Model.KEY`, `self.KEY`, `cls.KEY`).
- **Not followed** for a module-level name without `Final` that another module rebinds or deletes,
  one bound in a loop, or before a star import that may rebind it or on only some of the paths
  after it (`if flag: from m import *` / `else: KEY = "x"`), a class constant stored on its
  class or an instance outside the class body (`Model.KEY = "x"`; from another module, only one
  without `Final`), a class constant a subclass defines again, is given its own value
  (`Child.KEY = "x"`), or inherits first from another base it lists before the class
  (`class Child(Other, Model)`; read on that subclass, or on an instance or `cls` that may be one),
  a `Final` field of a dataclass or of a class a `dataclass_transform` builds read on an instance
  (`Keys("x").KEY` is `"x"`), or on a class object whose default a class with `slots=True` or built
  by a transform replaces, or a computed name.
- `setattr` and `object.__setattr__` are followed through a module-level name bound once to them
  (`_set = object.__setattr__`) and called on their module (`builtins.setattr`), and `getattr(obj, "fields")` is `obj.fields` itself: changing
  what it returns changes the attribute's object.
- `vars(obj)` (the builtin, not a name shadowing it) is `obj.__dict__`: an entry stored, deleted,
  set by a container method, or updated in place (`vars(obj) |= other`, also on
  `obj.__dict__`) through either is a write of the attribute it names. Where reading it runs no
  code of the instance's classes, the namespace is a builtin `dict`, so its methods resolve
  (`obj.__dict__.get(KEY)` is no call heki cannot resolve); a class object's namespace is a
  read-only proxy and has no class.
- A name a loop takes from the keys of a `TypedDict` (`for name, value in td.items():
  setattr(obj, name, value)`, `for name in td`, `vars(obj).update(td)`) is one of the keys the
  class and its bases declare. A `TypedDict` passing a class keyword (`total=False`, `closed=`,
  `extra_items=`) or binding a method in its body, and a plain `dict`, may hold any key: the
  name is computed.
- A write-owners contract sees a container change through what a method or a property returns
  when it returns the attribute itself on every `return` (`node.members().append(x)` with
  `return self.items`) and every class the object may be runs it. A `cached_property` hands out
  nothing: what the instance keeps can be replaced.
- A `write-owners` contract with `unresolved = "report"` reports the writes heki cannot tie to a
  class ([`MUT205`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-write/)).
- A private helper hands its accesses to the callers heki sees. A helper some code also hands on
  as a value (a table, a class attribute, an argument) has callers heki does not see: an owner
  contract with `unresolved = "report"` judges it as if it had no callers, and one without lets
  its callers decide.
- An effect boundary is silent where heki cannot see: a call it cannot resolve, or a write on an
  object of unknown class, in a scope's reach. With `unresolved = "report"` it reports them
  (`EFF201`).

### Objects without a known class

- Reads and writes through `Any` or unannotated parameters are not tied to a class, so contracts
  on that class do not see them. A contract with `unresolved = "report"` reports them by name:
  writes under [`MUT205`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-write/), reads under
  [`MUT206`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-read/), and method calls under
  [`MUT207`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-call/).
- A write in an unannotated helper is still found where a caller passes it an object of a known
  class. A read is not.
- Typed: builtin classes, the builtin exception and warning classes among them
  (`error: ValueError`; not `IOError` or `EnvironmentError`, and not a name the module or the
  function binds itself), what a standard library call the catalog types gives, by its declared
  return type (`importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)` and `importlib.import_module(name)` are a
  `types.ModuleType`, though a custom loader's `create_module` may return another object and a
  module may put another object in `sys.modules`), or by the kind of path or URL it is passed
  (`os.path.abspath(path)`, `urllib.parse.urlparse(url)`), an annotation of a local that names an
  import of its own function (not a name the function binds more than once or otherwise), a
  call of a value declared `type[C]` wherever the value is held (a parameter, a local, or an
  attribute annotated in `__init__` or the class body, read in a subclass too), and, in a
  `finally` body, what the annotations say before the `try`.
- Not typed: values declared `Any` or `types.ModuleType`, generics substituted through
  unbounded `TypeVar`s (a bounded or constrained one gives its bound or constraints), names a
  module binds to a type expression more than once or with type parameters (a type alias bound
  once names its value), calls of a subscripted class other than a builtin or `collections`
  container (`Box[int]()`), and calls of a `type[A | B]`.
- A module-level table of functions (`HANDLERS = {"create": create}`) gives the value of a key
  a string constant gives, and one of its values for any other key, only while no code changes
  it in place; a change through a call it is handed to (`register(HANDLERS)`) is not seen.
  Changing a dict, set, or list a global or an attribute holds in place joins what the change
  adds to its items when heki types it (`append(x)` with `x: Field`, `extend` or `+=` of a list
  of known items, `d[k] = v` with `v` of a known class), and leaves its items untyped otherwise.
  A change of an item it holds (`d[k].append(x)`) is not seen.
- A function a value holds is known where the code that makes the value shows it: a field of a
  `NamedTuple` or a frozen dataclass whose generated constructor the code calls (also through a
  table of such instances bound once), the function a factory returns when every `return` gives
  one, and a class attribute bound to `functools.partial` of a function, read through the class
  or wrapped in `staticmethod`. A call through a field of a dataclass that is not frozen, one with
  a `__post_init__`, or a class a `dataclass_transform` decorator builds, through a value handed
  in as a parameter (a view or a callback a caller passes), through a plain `partial` attribute
  read on an instance (Python 3.14 binds the instance to it, older versions do not), and through
  a `partial` holding a positional argument is a call heki cannot resolve.
- The type of a module global or an instance attribute joins every store of it through a
  receiver whose type heki knows: `self`, an instance of the class (a parameter `obj: Helper`,
  `cls()` in a class method, one the storing module keeps in its own attribute or global, as
  in `self.base.client = ...`), the module (also imported in a function, or through `setattr` or
  `vars`). A store through a receiver without a known type (`def configure(obj): obj.client =
  ...`, a parameter whose default is the module) is not joined, nor is one through a `Protocol`
  value, so the join of the other stores may be wrong for values it stores. The same holds
  for a receiver read from an attribute or a global of another module (`def swap(app: App):
  app.state.client = ...`, where `App`'s module types `state`), and a receiver kept in an
  attribute or a global of the storing module has the type that module's stores give it: when
  yet another module stores an instance of another class there (`owner.base = Other()`), a store
  through it is not joined into that class.
- The items of a container an attribute or a global holds are those of the values its stores
  bind (`self.clients = [httpx.Client()]`): what another function adds to the container
  (`self.clients.append(client)`, `self.clients += [client]`) is not joined, so a loop over it
  takes every item to be of the classes the stores give.
- `__setstate__` restoring an instance's namespace from its state keeps the attributes' types when
  the class's `__getstate__` builds the state from the instance's own attributes. One putting an
  attribute's value under another attribute's name (`return {"client": self.other}`) is not seen.
- A store into an instance's namespace through a method called with a `*` argument
  (`self.__dict__.setdefault(*pair)`) is not seen.
- Two shapes of module-level names that no linted code writes are taken wrongly. After a
  `global` statement at the module level (where it does nothing), a store of the name in a `try`
  body counts as run even when a call before it in the body raises, and a list bound to
  `__all__` counts as unchanged when the module body appends to it. A `TYPE_CHECKING` that a
  branch binds to the flag after the module bound it to something else (`TYPE_CHECKING = True`,
  then `if cond: from typing import TYPE_CHECKING`) counts as the flag on every path, so imports
  under a later `if TYPE_CHECKING:` count as not running.

### Names the catalog does not list

Catalog lookups are exact. These contribute no effect until you add them with
[`[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#ecosystem-knowledge-toolhekiecosystem):

- a class reached through another public name: `from sqlalchemy import Engine` for
  `sqlalchemy.engine.Engine`, `redis.StrictRedis` for `redis.Redis`;
- a method the catalog does not list;
- objects reached through subscripts or framework attributes, which have no known class:
  `client["app"]["users"]`, Django's related managers (`question.choice_set`, a many-to-many
  field read on an instance).

Django's `Model.objects` is a `Manager` (a `[[class_attributes]]` row of the catalog): reading
it on a model class, or on `cls` or `type(self)`, gives the manager Django adds to a model that
declares none, and a name the model's body binds to a manager it declares (`objects =
StreamManager()`, a project subclass of `models.Manager`) gives that manager's class. Its query
methods (`get`, `count`, `get_or_create`, ...) send a statement on every call, and its lazy ones
(`filter`, `exclude`, `all`) give a `QuerySet`. A manager that binds a name those methods use
(`get_queryset`, `_queryset_class`, `__init__`: the catalog's `delegates_to` of `Manager`) runs
its own code under them, which the rows do not describe: a query through it is heuristic, and so
is one through a `Manager` while the project defines such a manager (R2). The same holds for a
project `QuerySet` subclass binding a name a query method of `QuerySet` looks up (each row's
`delegates_to`: `get` looks up `filter` and `_fetch_all`) and for a project model binding `save`
behind `create` without calling `super().save(...)` on every path (`effect_through`); which
model a manager or queryset is for is not tracked, so one such model opens every `create`. A model whose body may
bind another manager (a call of a project function, `QuerySet.as_manager()`) has no `objects` to
heki, nor does one whose `objects` a module stores outside the class body, or is a manager of a
class outside the project or of one `Manager.from_queryset()` builds. A manager of a library
class bound under another name (`tree = TreeManager()`) is not seen: heki takes the model to
have the default `objects`, which Django does not add. An abstract model has no `objects`
either, which heki does not tell from its `Meta`.

### Properties

- **Followed:** reading a `@property` or `functools.cached_property` of a project class runs its
  getter. Its effects, writes, and the attributes it reads count for the reader, also through
  base classes, overriding subclasses, and `super()`. The getter's return annotation types the
  value read.
- **Not followed:** a property that also defines a setter or deleter (`@x.setter`), and
  `x = property(get_x)`.

### Read-only types

- `MUT110` follows `Sequence` / `Mapping` / `AbstractSet` / `ReadOnly` parameters into the
  helpers they are handed to, any number of calls deep. A helper parameter annotated with a mutable type is left
  to the type checker, and a container inside the argument does not count.
- `MUT108` (opt-in) follows frozen dataclasses, `NamedTuple`s, classes that a
  `dataclass_transform(frozen_default=True)` in the checked files builds, `Final` / `ReadOnly`
  attributes, and `ReadOnly` `TypedDict` keys. It does not see the transforms of installed
  packages (attrs, Pydantic), and an instance the function constructs itself counts as under
  construction.
- `MUT120` (opt-in) follows read-only views, classes and protocols of properties without a
  setter: a helper that does not see the view's type and rebinds one of its properties, and the
  container a property returns changed in place. A write through the view itself is left to the
  type checker.

### Generators and coroutines

A generator's body runs where it is iterated:

| Followed | Not followed |
| -------- | ------------ |
| a `for` loop or a comprehension | a generator handed to anything else: `StreamingResponse(rows())`, a container |
| unpacking, `yield from` | a generator only stepped with `next()` |
| a consuming call: `list(...)`, `"".join(...)`, `items.extend(...)` | a generator unpacked into a call: `f(*rows())` |
| a lazy wrapper iterated there: `enumerate(...)` | |
| a project function iterating it | |

- A generator a function returns runs where its caller iterates it.
- A generator nothing iterates (a call as a statement, a value only tested for truth) never runs
  its body; `EFF116` reports such calls.
- A generator expression counts where it is written.
- A coroutine runs where it is awaited; one only scheduled (`asyncio.create_task`) is checked on
  its own.
- Iterating an object runs its class's `__iter__` only for classes the catalog lists (a
  SQLAlchemy `Query`). The `__iter__` methods of project classes are not followed.

### Guards

- **Followed:** a test of the function's own input: truthiness, `is None`, `isinstance` with
  builtin classes, the `io` classes, or `os.PathLike`, or `hasattr` with a string literal, also
  after the function rebinds the input on some paths (`if buf is None: buf = StringIO()`).
- **Decided by:** constants, displays and comprehensions, `io.StringIO` / `io.BytesIO` objects
  the caller constructs, and the literal defaults of omitted parameters (`hasattr` only for the
  methods of the file protocol: `read`, `write`, `close`, ...); not by an f-string, the result of
  another call, or an instance of a subclass.
- **Not followed:** `a or b` (no guard on either value), and `isinstance` with project classes or
  annotated types.
- A lazy initialization needs a direct test and the store in the function itself: a test in a
  caller of the method that stores, a test combined with `or` / `and`, and memos keyed by an
  argument (`@lru_cache`, a dict) are not followed.
- A future is known to be done only through `f.done()` and `await asyncio.wrap_future(f)`, not
  through an event or another future its done callback sets.
- A queue is known to be bounded through local variables, the attributes its class family's own
  bodies and methods store, module globals, and parameters whose project callers decide (a
  helper's at each call, an `async def`'s by the join of every caller). Not followed: stores into
  an attribute from outside the class family, a `maxsize` checked to be positive but not known,
  an integer constant imported from another module or passed on through a parameter other than
  a literal default, and a queue whose function has no project caller.
- `EFF201` does not use guards.
- An object a factory function returns counts as obtained once, like a pooled connection.

### Separate scopes

- Generator expressions and lambdas are analyzed as functions of their own:
  `next(b for b in bs if b.id == a.id)` inside a loop is not reported as a nested-loop join.
- Two lambdas in one function share the qualified name `f.<locals>.<lambda>`, so heki may
  attribute one lambda's effects to a call of the other:

```python
import requests


async def handler(url: str) -> int:
    fetch = lambda: requests.get(url, timeout=5)
    size = lambda: len(url)
    return size()  # reported as reaching `requests.get` (EFF101)
```

### Metaprogramming and frameworks

`__getattr__` proxies, metaclasses, classes created at run time, and framework machinery
(validators, ORM lazy loading, dependency injection) are not modeled. heki has no
framework-specific rules.

### The target Python version

Results follow [`target-version`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#top-level-settings), which defaults to the
oldest version `requires-python` admits.

- From Python 3.12, list, set, and dict comprehensions run in the enclosing function (PEP 709): a
  comprehension inside a loop can be reported for `py312` and not for `py311`.
- From Python 3.14, annotations are evaluated lazily in `__annotate__` scopes (PEP 649).
- From Python 3.15, `sentinel` is a builtin (PEP 661): a `MUT118` report recommends it, and
  has a fix that uses it; for an older version it names `typing_extensions.sentinel`.
- The parser reads Python 3.15 syntax for every target version: `lazy import` (PEP 810) is a lazy
  import also in code for an older version.
- Syntax newer than the target version is analyzed, not reported: that is Ruff's check.

### Source encodings

heki reads the encoding a PEP 263 declaration names: UTF-8 (with or without a BOM), Latin-1, and
ASCII. A file declaring any other encoding is reported as an error and not checked. Unlike a file
that does not parse, such a file runs: what it defines and does stays unknown to the analysis of
the other files.

### Sizes known only at run time

Whether a collection is small is decided from the code: a list whose size depends on the
input counts as large, even when it always holds three items. The rules this affects are marked size-dependent;
[Fixes and Safety](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/fixes/#when-the-size-is-fixed) lists what counts as a fixed size.

### Callers outside the checked files

Contracts reason about the callers heki sees: a private helper hands its reports to its callers,
and a function called only from allowed writers is not reported. Code outside the run, such as
tests left out of it, is not known.

## Measured and not taken

These shapes were measured on the Stage 0-A corpus (378 packages, 30.75 million lines) and not built.
Each failed the bar for a default rule: at least 10 % of the judged sample harmful, and no false exact
claim.

- Late binding of loop variables: 132 closures in 38 packages beyond the 3,865 names Ruff B023
  reports; every harmful one is already a B023 report, and heki found none that B023 misses.
- Resource use after close: 289 sites in 80 packages, 8 % harmful, with false exact claims. Left to
  runtime and review.
- Resource leaks across calls: 1,848 sites in 162 packages, 4 % harmful; about half are direct
  constructors that Ruff `SIM115` and Pylint `R1732` flag.
- Command-query separation (a `get_*`, `is_*`, or property that changes state): 11,558 sites in 254
  packages, 4 % harmful; most are caches heki does not see as caches.
- Dropped results of pure calls: 59,083 sites in 327 packages, no harm in the sample; the real bugs
  are `str` methods on `str` values, which pyright `reportUnusedCallResult` covers.
- Stale caches: 199 sites in 54 packages, 5 % harmful; Ruff B019 and Pylint W1518 flag the cache on
  a method.
- `asyncio.run` under a running loop: 71 sites in 12 packages, 1 of 25 judged right; nearly all are
  guarded by a test heki does not model.
- Writes lost in a child process: 62 sites in 27 packages, 4 % harmful.
- `Popen` pipes left unread: 22 sites in 13 packages, 5 % harmful.
- `CancelledError` swallowed: 466 sites in 62 packages, none harmful as judged; flake8-async
  `ASYNC103` and `ASYNC104` cover the shape.
- `BytesIO` read without a seek: 69 sites in 7 packages, 57 of them one test suite; too rare.
- Opposite lock orders: 106 ordered pairs of named locks in 31 packages, no pair in opposite order.
- An `except` clause that nothing in its `try` body raises, through its calls: 2,730 clauses in 157 packages
  for project exceptions and 3,597 in 153 for library ones; of 60 judged, one was harmful, and that one is a
  one-statement shape. Which exceptions a function can raise is planned as a `heki inspect` fact instead.

## How a rule gets into heki

heki only takes checks that need what it can prove. A proposed rule goes through four questions,
in order:

1. **Can the syntax of one file decide it?** Then it belongs in a linter such as Ruff.
2. **Is it a type error, or can an annotation express it?** Then it belongs in a type checker
   such as mypy, Pyright, Pyrefly, or ty. heki's part is to say where the code already keeps
   what such an annotation would state, so that the annotation can be written and the type
   checker checks it from then on (planned in [`heki recommend`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/recommend/),
   [ADR-023](https://github.com/koxudaxi/heki/blob/main/docs/DESIGN_HISTORY_AND_ADR.md#adr-023)).
3. **Can one import statement decide it?** Its order, its form, or a banned name: then it
   belongs in a linter such as Ruff.
4. **Does it need at least one of the proofs below?** Only then is it a heki rule.

A heki rule is measured on a corpus and reviewed by hand before it is enabled by default. Where
another tool covers part of it, heki keeps only the rest (`EFF107` and Ruff's `RUF006`). An idea
from another language's tools goes through the same questions, and joins with counts on a corpus,
real harm in the reports, and no false exact claim.

The proofs heki can make, on five axes:

| Axis | What heki establishes | Used by |
| ---- | --------------------- | ------- |
| Control flow | which statements can run after which: CFG paths, loops and their bounds, exception edges | `MUT106`, `MUT113`, `MUT208`, `EFF102`, `EFF103`, `EFF106`, `EFF109`, `EFF110`, `EFF114`, `DATA101`, `OPT` |
| Calls | which functions a call reaches across modules, and what they do (summaries propagated over the call graph) | `EFF101`, `EFF109`, `EFF110`, `EFF112`, `EFF114`, `EFF115`, `EFF116`, `EFF117`, `EFF118`, `EFF201`, `MUT103`, `MUT108`, `MUT110`, `MUT120`, `MUT112`, `MUT113`, `MUT119`, `MUT201`–`MUT204`, `MUT208` |
| Aliases | which names, iterators, and views refer to one object; whether it is unique to its frame and of an exact builtin type | `MUT202`, `MUT201`, `MUT204`, `MUT108`, `MUT110`, `MUT120`, `MUT112`, `MUT119`, `EFF107`, `EFF109`, `EFF110`, `EFF112`, `OPT101`–`OPT130` |
| Effects | which blocking, network, file, or database work runs, from the catalog of library behavior | `EFF101`–`EFF106`, `EFF201`, `DATA101` |
| State | which attributes and containers a function reads, writes, or mutates, and who may do so | `MUT101`, `MUT107`, `MUT108`, `MUT110`, `MUT120`, `MUT111`, `MUT112`, `MUT113`, `MUT201`–`MUT204`, `MUT208` |


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/

# Experimental Features

Experimental features can still change in behavior or precision, or be removed, in any release, and each change is listed in the release notes. An opt-in rule that is not experimental is stable and only off by default. A feature leaves this page when it becomes stable.

An experimental rule is never enabled by default: it runs only when `select` or `extend-select` names its code or name, and `heki check` then reports it like any other rule. `heki rule <CODE>` and the rule's page say that it is experimental.

On the way to 1.0, heki keeps these stable: the exit codes `0`, `1`, and `2`, the exact rules that run by default, the format of the Ratchet baseline, the contract tables `write-owners`, `read-owners`, `call-owners`, `readonly-returns`, `invalidation`, and `effect-boundaries` with `fail = true` and `[lint] fail = [...]`, and the `json`, `sarif`, and `github` output formats. A change to one of them is listed under "Breaking changes" in the release notes. See [Adopting heki](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#stability-on-the-way-to-10).

| ID | Kind | Target | Since | Tracking |
| -- | ---- | ------ | ----- | -------- |
| `cli-option.generate-prompt` | cli-option | `heki check --generate-prompt` | 0.2.2 | - |
| `command.inspect` | command | `heki inspect` | 0.2.1 | - |
| `command.recommend` | command | `heki recommend` | 0.2.2 | - |

## `cli-option.generate-prompt`

- **Kind:** cli-option
- **Target:** `heki check --generate-prompt`
- **Since:** 0.2.2

What the prompt holds and how it says it can still change as it is tried with models, and so can its JSON object, whose schema `heki check --output-format-json-schema generate-prompt` prints; the object's `version` changes when a field is removed or changes meaning.

## `command.inspect`

- **Kind:** command
- **Target:** `heki inspect`
- **Since:** 0.2.1

The facts it shows, its purity verdict, and its JSON object can still change as heki's summaries close gaps; the object's `version` changes when a field is removed or changes meaning.

## `command.recommend`

- **Kind:** command
- **Target:** `heki recommend`
- **Since:** 0.2.2

The sections, their policies, the candidates it infers, and its JSON object can still change as the policies are calibrated; the object's `version` changes when a field is removed or changes meaning.

## `command.skill`

- **Kind:** command
- **Target:** `heki skill`
- **Since:** 0.2.5

Where coding agents read skills, and so where `heki skill install` writes, can change as the agents evolve; the skill's wording changes with heki's commands.

## `rule.EFF110`

- **Kind:** rule
- **Target:** [`EFF110`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/exclusive-object-fanout/)
- **Since:** 0.2.1

Its precision is measured on a small sample of reports only.

## `rule.EFF112`

- **Kind:** rule
- **Target:** [`EFF112`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/set-order-output/)
- **Since:** 0.2.4

Its precision is measured on a sample of reports of one corpus only, and its premises are not yet certified.

## `rule.EFF114`

- **Kind:** rule
- **Target:** [`EFF114`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/recursion-error-as-value/)
- **Since:** 0.2.4

Its precision is measured on a sample of reports of one corpus only, and its premises are not yet certified.

## `rule.EFF115`

- **Kind:** rule
- **Target:** [`EFF115`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-def-as-sync-callback/)
- **Since:** 0.2.5

The development corpus has no report of it, so its precision is not measured, and its premises are not yet certified.

## `rule.IMP101`

- **Kind:** rule
- **Target:** [`IMP101`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/import-cycle/)
- **Since:** 0.2.7

It is new: its reports are heuristic until a review of its reports on real code bases certifies its claim, and which imports count can still change.

## `rule.IMP102`

- **Kind:** rule
- **Target:** [`IMP102`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/circular-import-failure/)
- **Since:** 0.3.0

It is new: every report rests on established premises only, but its reports are heuristic until a review of its reports on real code bases certifies its claim, and which imports and code stop a run can still change.

## `rule.IMP104`

- **Kind:** rule
- **Target:** [`IMP104`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/development-code-import/)
- **Since:** 0.3.0

It is new: every report rests on established premises only, but its reports are heuristic until a review of its reports on real code bases certifies its claim, and which modules count as package and development code can still change.

## `rule.IMP201`

- **Kind:** rule
- **Target:** [`IMP201`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/import-boundary-violation/)
- **Since:** 0.2.7

It is new: its reports are heuristic until a review of its reports on real code bases certifies its claim.

## `rule.IMP202`

- **Kind:** rule
- **Target:** [`IMP202`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-import/)
- **Since:** 0.2.7

It is the strict mode of `IMP201`, which is experimental.

## `rule.IMP301`

- **Kind:** rule
- **Target:** [`IMP301`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/development-dependency-at-import-time/)
- **Since:** 0.3.0

It is new: every report rests on established premises only, but its reports are heuristic until a review of its reports on real code bases certifies its claim, and which distributions provide a module can still change.

## `rule.IMP302`

- **Kind:** rule
- **Target:** [`IMP302`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/optional-dependency-at-import-time/)
- **Since:** 0.3.0

It is new: every report rests on established premises only, but its reports are heuristic until a review of its reports on real code bases certifies its claim, and which distributions provide a module and which modules are base modules can still change.

## `rule.MUT101`

- **Kind:** rule
- **Target:** [`MUT101`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-property-stale-mutation/)
- **Since:** 0.1.0

Its precision outside a few code bases is still low.

## `rule.MUT111`

- **Kind:** rule
- **Target:** [`MUT111`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-property-stale-read/)
- **Since:** 0.1.1

It reports the readers of the stale writes `MUT101` finds, so it shares `MUT101`'s precision.

## `rule.MUT112`

- **Kind:** rule
- **Target:** [`MUT112`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/conditional-ownership-mutation/)
- **Since:** 0.2.0

Its precision on real code bases is still low: much of what it reports is code that changes a borrowed container on purpose.

## `rule.MUT113`

- **Kind:** rule
- **Target:** [`MUT113`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/iterated-container-mutation/)
- **Since:** 0.2.0

It has few reports, and most of them are still false.

## `rule.MUT120`

- **Kind:** rule
- **Target:** [`MUT120`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-view-mutation/)
- **Since:** 0.2.7

It is new: its reports are heuristic until a review of its reports on real code bases certifies its claim.

# Editors (LSP)

`heki server` (alias `heki lsp`) is a Language Server Protocol server on stdin / stdout: it shows
heki's diagnostics and fixes while you edit, with the results `heki check` reports. It checks no
types, so run it beside the language server of your type checker, whether that is mypy, Pyright,
Pyrefly, or ty; the Helix example pairs it with Pyright, and the others work the same way.

## Set up your editor

=== "VS Code"

    heki ships no extension of its own: `heki server` speaks LSP, so any generic LSP client
    extension that starts a command for a language runs it. Configure it to run `heki server`
    for `python` documents, for example:

    ```json
    {
      "command": "heki",
      "args": ["server"],
      "languages": ["python"]
    }
    ```

=== "Neovim"

    ```lua
    vim.lsp.config("heki", {
      cmd = { "heki", "server" },
      filetypes = { "python" },
      root_markers = { "pyproject.toml", "heki.toml", ".git" },
    })
    vim.lsp.enable("heki")
    ```

=== "Helix"

    ```toml
    # languages.toml
    [language-server.heki]
    command = "heki"
    args = ["server"]

    [[language]]
    name = "python"
    language-servers = ["pyright", "heki"]
    ```

=== "Zed"

    ```json
    {
      "lsp": {
        "heki": {
          "binary": { "path": "heki", "arguments": ["server"] }
        }
      },
      "languages": {
        "Python": { "language_servers": ["...", "heki"] }
      }
    }
    ```

## What the server provides

- Diagnostics for open files, with every hop of a call chain (for example the path from an
  `async def` to `time.sleep`) as related information you can jump to, and a contract report's
  [contract and entry](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/output-formats/#where-a-contract-report-points) after them. The message is the
  report's one sentence; its help, what to do about it, is the last related-information entry
  (`help: ...`) at the diagnostic's own range, the way rust-analyzer shows a `help:` note.
- The message of a [heuristic](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/) report ends in `[heuristic]`, and every diagnostic's
  `data.certainty` is `"exact"` or `"heuristic"`. The rule code links to the rule's page
  (`codeDescription`).
- `heki server --heuristic` (or `--no-heuristic`) overrides `lint.heuristic` of the
  configuration, as on the command line.
- Quick fixes for the safe `OPT101` / `OPT102` rewrites, and a quick fix that is not preferred
  for the unsafe `MUT118` fix (`heki check --fix --unsafe-fixes`).
- `refactor.rewrite.heki` code actions for the proven-safe size-dependent rewrites. A fix whose
  result would not parse is never offered, as `heki check --fix` refuses it.
- A quick fix that appends `# heki: ignore[CODE]` to the line of any diagnostic, unless a comment
  cannot go there (the line ends inside a string or with a `\` continuation).
- With [`report-unused-suppressions`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#unused-suppressions), a quick fix that
  removes the codes of a suppression comment that suppressed nothing, or the whole comment when
  none is left.

Code actions edit the version of the document their diagnostics were computed on:

- while an edit waits for its analysis, none are offered;
- a client that applies versioned workspace edits (`workspaceEdit.documentChanges`) gets them
  with that version, so it rejects them if the document changed meanwhile.

## The same results as `heki check`

- The server reads the same [configuration](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/), including the Ratchet baseline:
  with `baseline` configured, a file shows what `heki check` reports against it (every finding of
  an entry that grew).
- A file belongs to the project when `heki check` would find it. A file that an ignore file, a
  hidden directory, or `exclude` leaves out is not analyzed, also when it is created or opened.
- A file that does not parse is a module heki knows nothing about until it parses again, as in
  `heki check`: the names under it resolve to nothing in the other files.
- A configuration `heki check` rejects (an unknown rule, a contract target that is not
  `Class.attr`, an invalid pattern) is logged as a warning, and the server analyzes nothing until
  it is fixed.

One difference is deliberate. When more than ten `async def` boundaries reach the same blocking
call, `heki check` reports them once, with a count; the server groups them per file, so the file
you edit always shows its own boundary.

## When the server re-analyzes

The server indexes the workspace in the background, then keeps only the per-function effect
summaries in memory. It runs the analyses one at a time, in the order of the editor's messages
(an edit's analysis takes its place when its debounce ends), so the diagnostics do not depend on
which analysis happens to start first: of documents opened together, each is analyzed with the
ones opened before it already indexed. When the editor closes the server's input or goes away
