Opt-in: a call in `async def` that always runs blocking local filesystem I/O on the event loop; its heuristic reports, a call that can reach it.

## What it does
Checks `async def` functions that reach blocking local filesystem I/O: `open(...)`,
`pathlib.Path.read_text` / `write_text` / `read_bytes` / `write_bytes` / `open`, `os.listdir`,
`os.scandir`, iterating `os.walk(...)`, `shutil` copies and removals, file metadata (`os.stat`,
`os.path.exists` / `isfile` / `isdir` / `realpath`, `pathlib.Path.exists` / `stat` / `is_file` /
`is_dir` / `resolve`, Starlette's `StaticFiles.lookup_path`), and the pandas file readers
(`pd.read_csv(path)`; one given a URL literal downloads it and is `EFF101`, one given an
`io.StringIO` / `io.BytesIO` buffer does no I/O). It follows the same boundary,
offload, and guard rules as `EFF101`, generators and offloading decorators included: `await
in_thread(self.open) if isinstance(self._input, PathLike) else self.open()` is not reported
when `open` only opens a file under `isinstance(self._input, PathLike)`, and neither is
`save(text, io.StringIO())` when `save` opens its argument only where `hasattr(buf, "write")`
is false, or `save(text)` when it opens it only where `isinstance(buf, str)` holds after
`if buf is None: buf = io.StringIO()`.

This rule is opt-in: enable it with `--extend-select EFF105` or `extend-select = ["EFF105"]`.
Selecting the `EFF` prefix does not enable it.

## What a report states

A report states that whenever the reported call returns, the blocking filesystem call at the end
of the chain has run on the event loop's thread. A heuristic report states that the `async def`
can reach the blocking filesystem call at the end of the chain: some premise below may be open.

Its premises:

- **Every return**: each function on the chain has made the next call on every path on which it
  returns normally, exception edges into handlers included; the last call counts as made also
  when it raised. Open in a heuristic report: one path that reaches the next call is enough, and
  a branch heki cannot decide counts as taken; only the branches the caller's arguments switch
  off, and the cases listed above, are left out.
- **Every implementation**: each call on the chain has as its targets every implementation it
  can run (assumptions R1, R2, and R5), each a synchronous function run as written, and each
  has the fact. Open in a heuristic report: through a method call, one candidate implementation
  that leads on is enough.
- **Touches the file system**: the last call reads or changes the local file system on every
  call, as the ecosystem catalog describes it (R3), for every argument heki cannot evaluate (R6:
  `open(name)` opens a path, not a file descriptor). Open in a heuristic report: a call the
  catalog marks as one that can do its work without the file system (`emits =
  "may-avoid-the-file-system"`): a member of a file object (`f.read()`, `f.write()`, iterating
  `f`), which its buffer or the memory it wraps can answer; `Path.iterdir()`, which before Python
  3.13 lists the directory only when its result is iterated; `os.path.isjunction`, which does no
  I/O on POSIX; psutil, which reads `/proc` on Linux only; fsspec, whose file system may be memory
  or the network; and a pandas or polars reader whose source may be a URL. A call whose case an
  argument from the caller can select counts too.

Not part of the claim: how long the call blocks, and how often the reported call runs.

## Why is this bad?
Local file I/O is usually fast, which is why it is opt-in, but on network file systems, large
files, or busy disks it blocks the event loop like any other blocking call.

## Example
```python
async def read_config(path: str) -> str:
    with open(path) as f:  # EFF105
        return f.read()
```

Use instead:
```python
import asyncio
from pathlib import Path


async def read_config(path: str) -> str:
    return await asyncio.to_thread(Path(path).read_text)
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `lint.extend-select = ["EFF105"]` enables the rule.
- `lint.relax-async-in-tests` applies as for `EFF101`.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/async-def-as-sync-callback/

# async-def-as-sync-callback (EFF115)

Family: Execution Effects (EFF) · Heuristic · Opt-in · Experimental · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Opt-in: an `async def` handed to a library call that calls it without awaiting what it returns (a thread's target, an executor's function, an `atexit` or signal handler, a `filter` predicate), so the call only creates a coroutine and the body does not run.

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs only when `select` or `extend-select` names its code or name. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

!!! warning "Experimental"

    The development corpus has no report of it, so its precision is not measured, and its premises are not yet certified. Experimental features can still change in behavior or precision, or be removed, in any release, and each change is listed in the release notes. An opt-in rule that is not experimental is stable and only off by default. See [Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/).

## What it does
Checks for an `async def` handed to a library call that calls it as a plain function and never
awaits what it returns. Calling an `async def` only creates a coroutine: the call returns at
once, the body does not run, and Python warns `coroutine ... was never awaited` when the
coroutine is collected, if anyone sees the warning. A few of the calls test for a coroutine
function and raise `TypeError` instead (`sync_to_async`, `trio.to_thread.run_sync`, and the
event loop's scheduling methods in debug mode); the body does not run there either.

The library calls are the ecosystem catalog's (`calls_unawaited`), and the offloading APIs that
run a callable on a worker thread (`offloads_blocking_arg`):

- run the callable on another thread or process, or later: `threading.Thread(target=f)`,
  `threading.Timer(t, f)`, `multiprocessing.Process(target=f)`, `executor.submit(f)`,
  `executor.map(f, xs)`, `loop.run_in_executor(None, f)`, `asyncio.to_thread(f)`,
  `anyio.to_thread.run_sync(f)`, `trio.to_thread.run_sync(f)`, `run_in_threadpool(f)`,
  `sync_to_async(f)`, `loop.call_soon(f)` (with `call_soon_threadsafe`, `call_later`, and
  `call_at`), `atexit.register(f)`, `signal.signal(sig, f)`, `stack.callback(f)` of an
  `ExitStack` or `AsyncExitStack`, and `weakref.finalize(obj, f)`;
- test what the callable returns for truth: `filter(f, xs)`, `itertools.filterfalse`,
  `itertools.takewhile`, and `itertools.dropwhile`. A coroutine is always true, so every item
  passes the test (or none, for `filterfalse`).

The callable is the function itself, a bound method (`self.flush`), or a `functools.partial` of
either. A report is worded as certain when every function the value calls is an `async def`
without decorators other than `staticmethod`, `classmethod`, `abstractmethod`, `override`, or
`final`; when a decorator replaces one, or another implementation of the method is a plain
function, the report says the function may not create a coroutine.

It does not report:

- `map`, `itertools.starmap`, or `functools.reduce`: they hand the coroutines on, and a caller
  may await them (`await asyncio.gather(*map(fetch, urls))`);
- a sort key (`sorted`, `min`, `max`, `list.sort`): the coroutines are no comparable values,
  which the type checkers report;
- a project function that takes a callable, whatever it does with it: a runner of the project
  may test `inspect.iscoroutinefunction` and drive the coroutine itself; so may a project
  subclass of `threading.Thread`, whose construction is the project's;
- an async generator function, a class, or a lambda.

## What a report states

A report states that the library call never awaits what the named function returns (the function
itself, or what the value handed to it calls), and that the function is an `async def`: calling
it only creates a coroutine, and the body of the function does not run there.

Its premises:

- **Unawaited call**: the call is one the catalog says never awaits what the argument at the
  position or keyword it names returns. Established from the catalog.
- **Coroutine function**: every function the handed value calls is an `async def` that no
  decorator replaces. Open when a decorator may replace it, or when another implementation of
  the method is a plain function.

Not part of the claim: whether a caller awaits the coroutine that an offloading API or an
executor hands back (`await (await asyncio.to_thread(f))`), which runs the body on the event
loop instead.

## Why is this bad?
The work never happens, and nothing fails: a thread starts and ends at once, a cleanup handler
does nothing, a signal handler ignores the signal, a filter keeps every item. Turning a
function into an `async def` breaks every such caller of it without an error at the call.

## Example
```python
import atexit
import threading


async def flush_metrics() -> None:
    await client.flush()


def start() -> None:
    threading.Thread(target=flush_metrics, daemon=True).start()  # EFF115
    atexit.register(flush_metrics)  # EFF115
```

Use instead:
```python
import asyncio
import atexit
import threading


async def flush_metrics() -> None:
    await client.flush()


def flush_now() -> None:
    asyncio.run(flush_metrics())


def start() -> None:
    threading.Thread(target=flush_now, daemon=True).start()
    atexit.register(flush_now)
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `lint.extend-select = ["EFF115"]` (or `--extend-select EFF115`) enables the rule. It is
  opt-in: selecting the `EFF` prefix does not enable it.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-property-stale-mutation/

# cached-property-stale-mutation (MUT101)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Exact · Opt-in · Experimental · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Mutating an attribute read by `@cached_property` without invalidating the cache.

!!! warning "Experimental"

    Its precision outside a few code bases is still low. Experimental features can still change in behavior or precision, or be removed, in any release, and each change is listed in the release notes. An opt-in rule that is not experimental is stable and only off by default. See [Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/).

## What it does
Opt-in: enable it with `extend-select = ["MUT101"]`. Its exact reports are true claims (census
on the Stage 0-A corpus: 26 exact reports, none false; holdout: 1, none false), but few show real
harm (1 of the 26 by majority of three reviewers), below the 10% share a default rule needs: most are writes that run before the property
is first read, keep the value's meaning, or run on objects whose cached value nothing reads
again.

Checks for methods that rebind or mutate an attribute that a `@functools.cached_property`
of the same class (or of a subclass) reads, without invalidating the cached value. A method the
class inherits from a project base class and does not override runs on its instances too, so it
is checked against the class's cached properties (reported in the base class).
A decorator is known by what its name is bound to in the module: an import alias counts
(`from functools import cached_property as cached`), a decorator the module defines itself does
not (a `def cache(fn)` of its own), and a name bound by neither counts by its spelling.

## What a report states

An exact report states that whenever the method runs on an instance of any class that runs it,
and that instance holds a value of the cached property when the write runs, the getter computed
that value from the attribute the write rebinds or changes, and the instance still holds it when
the method returns normally: the next read of the property returns a value computed from the
attribute's state before the write. An instance that holds no value when the write runs makes
the claim hold vacuously, whatever a later read keeps.

Its premises:

- **Cached property**: every class the instance may be (R2, R5) that names the property gets it
  from a synchronous getter, the first definition along its MRO with no base heki does not know
  before it, decorated by a cached-property decorator the ecosystem catalog lists as keeping the
  value in the instance `__dict__` (`[[cached_properties]]`: `functools.cached_property` and
  Django's, Werkzeug's, propcache's, and kombu's, R3; with Werkzeug's, which keeps it in a slot on
  an instance without a `__dict__`, no class along the MRO defines `__slots__`), and none has a
  metaclass other than `type` or `abc.ABCMeta`. An instance of a class that names nothing under
  the property's name holds no value of it, so the claim says nothing of it. Established.
- **Reads on every path**: the getter reads the written attribute, with the written constant key
  or as a whole, on every path on which it returns normally, itself or through `self` methods and
  property reads it makes on every such path. Each of those runs its body at every call (no cache
  decorator) and has the fact. Established.
- **Every implementation**: each of those calls has as its targets every implementation it can
  run (R2, R5). Established.
- **Plain write**: the write is one of two kinds. It may rebind or delete the attribute with a
  plain store: no property, descriptor, `__setattr__`, `__delattr__`, or metaclass heki does not
  know in a class the instance may be, no `__setattr__` or `__delattr__` bound on one after its
  body by a store heki reads (through a value that may be a class object, under that name or a
  name built at run time that may be it, also in a class decorator or an `__init_subclass__`,
  as for `MUT115`; a name of unknown value and code heki does not read binding none under R1),
  and every base a project class or a plain one. Or it may change in place the builtin list,
  dict, or set the attribute holds by its type, through a changing method or an item store that
  no project subclass of the container replaces.
  Established.
- **Kept to the return**: no point from the write to the method's normal return may remove or
  replace the kept value, exception edges into handlers included. The write's own instruction
  counts: an in-place change runs code while it changes the attribute (it iterates its argument
  or hashes a key). That rules out a store or a deletion of the property's name, or of an item of
  a `__dict__` under it, through any reference
  (`self`, a parameter, a closure, a global, an item of a container, `*args`, `setattr`,
  `vars()`), except one heki establishes as an object that keeps no value under the name: a
  value the method builds, or an instance of classes none of which (R2) binds a property getter
  of that name. A store or a deletion of a `__dict__` or a `__class__`, an `await` (also the
  implicit ones of `async for` and `async with`), and a `yield` count as removing every value.
  It also rules out every call except two kinds: a project call whose targets are every
  implementation it can run and remove nothing, and a call of a library the catalog covers that
  runs no project code by its `[[invokes]]` entry, or, without one, is handed no callable, no
  instance of a project class, and no value of unknown type (R3). Implicit calls count the same.
  A special method an instruction runs on an operand's class (an operator, a comparison, `in`, a
  conversion or format, a subscript and its key, an unpacking, a call's `*` and `**` arguments,
  a key a set or dict display hashes, a truth test, `with`) runs no code of the project only
  where heki establishes what implements it on every class the operand may be (R2): `object`'s;
  a builtin type's, with what it runs on the items it holds (a container's comparison, hash, or
  `repr()` runs its items', and a dict or set compares a key with each key it holds under an
  equal hash, the names of attributes, strings, in an object's `__dict__`); or a library class's, as a call of that library (R3). A value of a nominal
  container ABC (`Sequence`, `Mapping`, `collections.abc.Set`, and their mutable ABCs, which
  accept only the classes deriving from them or registered with them) is one of its family's
  builtins or of another class outside the project, taken to run what they run, or of a project
  class implementing it: one deriving, through project classes, from the ABC or from a class of
  its family (`list`, `tuple`, `dict`, `OrderedDict`, `UserDict`, `ChainMap`, ...), or one
  registered with them (`Mapping.register(C)`, `@Mapping.register`), and the method it runs is
  established as on those classes (a method of the ABC as the builtin's, unless such a class
  binds it or inherits it from a class outside the project). A `register` heki cannot resolve,
  or a `__subclasshook__` of such a class (which may accept any class), leaves the family's
  values established by none. A value of any other abstract class (`Iterable`, `Collection`) or
  of a protocol, one annotated `object`, and one of a class heki does not know establish none,
  and a comparison's or a conversion's result is a builtin `bool` or `str` only where
  those methods are `object`'s or a builtin type's. No attribute access may run a `__getattr__`,
  `__setattr__`, property, or other descriptor of the project that heki does not resolve (an
  access on a library object counts as a call of that attribute), no `raise` may construct a
  value that may be a class of the project, and no class statement or import of a project module
  runs there. Established.

Besides R1-R7, the claim assumes that no finalizer (`__del__`, which reference counting or the
garbage collector runs when it frees an object) and no other thread runs code between the write
and the method's return: either may remove the value at any instruction, and no premise rules
them out.

Not part of the claim: whether the method runs after the property was first read. A write that
runs only during two-phase setup makes the claim hold vacuously, so a setup step stays heuristic
(**After setup** is open): a finalizer (`__del__`), a method that an `__init__` along the MRO of a
class the instance may be calls on the instance or stores through (a property setter), and lazy
setup through a second cached property (the writer is a listed cached-property getter that no
function of the project invalidates by name, and the property's getter reads it on every path).

A heuristic report states that a method that can run after initialization rebinds or changes an
attribute that a `@cached_property` of the class family reads, and that a path after the write
leaves the cached value in place. Open: the property may read the attribute on some paths only
(through a call, one path of the callee is enough), initialization hooks are recognized by their
names, a `cached_property` of a library the catalog does not list counts by its name, and calls
after the write may remove the value.

## Why is this bad?
A `cached_property` computes its value once and stores it in the instance `__dict__`. Once the
attribute it was computed from changes, the property keeps returning the old value until the
cache entry is deleted. The stale value is usually noticed far away from the write.

The rule follows `self.helper()` calls in both directions (a property that reads through a
helper, a method that writes through a helper) and the getters of the properties the cached
property reads (`self.key` where the `@property` `key` reads `self.name`), and reports the write
itself, once per property. A property that also defines a setter or deleter is not followed.
It does not report:

- two-phase initialization: `__init__`, `__post_init__`, `model_post_init`, `__setstate__`,
  `__enter__`, `setup`, `setup_*` / `_setup_*` / `_init_*` / `_configure_*` methods, and private helpers called from
  `__init__`;
- classes with a metaclass other than `type` / `abc.ABCMeta` along their MRO (also one heki
  cannot resolve): the metaclass may turn attribute writes into descriptor calls (a generated
  property whose setter invalidates the cached value), which heki does not see;
- memo / cache dictionaries (`self._cache[key] = value`, `setdefault`, the
  `if key not in self._memo:` pattern): in-place changes of an attribute with a `cache` or
  `memo` word in its name; rebinding it (`self.cache_size = n`) and names such as
  `memory_limit` are no memo operation;
- constant dictionary keys the property never reads (`self.params["proxy"]` while the property
  reads `self.params["outtmpl"]`);
- writes after which every path invalidates the property (`del self.prop`,
  `self.__dict__.pop("prop", None)` or `vars(self).pop("prop", None)`, also with the key in a
  string constant as `MUT201` follows it, a `self` method that does), or before which every path
  already did and nothing read it
  since; an invalidation under a condition, such as
  `if clear:`, leaves the other path stale and is reported;
- private helpers whose every caller invalidates the property;
- lazy initialization: a write where a `None` / falsy test of the attribute found it unset
  (`if self._conn is None: self._conn = connect()`, also in a `@property` getter; the test may
  be of `getattr(self, "_conn", None)` or `hasattr(self, "_conn")`, or the write in the
  `except AttributeError:` clause of a `try` that reads it), when the
  cached property reads the attribute only through such initializations
  (`return self._connect().db`): computing the cached value set the attribute, so the test
  cannot find it unset again. A cached property that reads it directly
  (`return self._conn is not None`) may have cached its unset value and is reported;
- changes made in place (`clear()`, `append()`, item assignment) to an attribute whose object
  the cached value holds itself, when the getter reads it for nothing else: it returns
  `self.items`, or puts it as itself into a display or a container it returns
  (`{"items": self.items}`, `ctx["k"] = (x, self.items)`). The cached value sees those changes;
  rebinding the attribute (`self.items = []`) is still reported. A getter that also computes
  from it (`len(self.items)`), copies it (`list(self.items)`, `(*self.items,)`), reads it through
  a `self` method or property, or hands `self` to other code is reported as before. A `self`
  call whose result the getter discards (`self.finalize()` before `return self.items`) counts
  only when it writes an attribute the getter reads, itself or through a call whose result it
  uses.

## Example
```python
from functools import cached_property


class Settings:
    def __init__(self, raw: dict[str, str]) -> None:
        self.raw = raw

    @cached_property
    def keys(self) -> tuple[str, ...]:
        return tuple(self.raw)

    def replace(self, raw: dict[str, str]) -> None:
        self.raw = raw  # `self.keys` still returns the old keys
```

Use instead:
```python
    def replace(self, raw: dict[str, str]) -> None:
        self.raw = raw
        self.__dict__.pop("keys", None)  # or `del self.keys` when it was computed
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix: whether to invalidate, recompute, or make the attribute read-only is a design
decision.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-property-stale-read/

# cached-property-stale-read (MUT111)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Exact · Opt-in · Experimental · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Opt-in: reading a `@cached_property` that a method of its class family can leave stale (a write `MUT101` reports).

!!! warning "Experimental"

    It reports the readers of the stale writes `MUT101` finds, so it shares `MUT101`'s precision. Experimental features can still change in behavior or precision, or be removed, in any release, and each change is listed in the release notes. An opt-in rule that is not experimental is stable and only off by default. See [Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/).

## What it does
Checks for functions that read a `@functools.cached_property` that a method can leave stale: a
method that changes an attribute the property reads without invalidating the cached value, as
`MUT101` reports it. The rule is opt-in: enable it with `--extend-select MUT111` or
`extend-select = ["MUT111"]`. Its exact reports are true claims (census on the Stage 0-A corpus:
60 exact reports, none false; holdout: 2, none false), but at most 2 of the 60 show real harm,
below the 10% share a default rule needs: they read values that the writers behind them leave
stale only in setup or on objects nothing reads again.

A read is one in the function's own body, on any object of the class: `self.prop`, `obj.prop`
on a parameter, attribute, or value whose class heki knows (as for `MUT203`),
`getattr(obj, "prop")`, and `obj.__dict__["prop"]` / `obj.__dict__.get("prop")` (also on
`vars(obj)`). The object may be an instance of the read's class or of any project subclass of
it. The read is reported when
an instance of one of those classes runs both the cached property and the method that leaves it
stale: the first definition of each along its MRO, or one that the definitions before it call
through `super()` without invalidating the property themselves. A method of a sibling class, or
one that a subclass replaces without calling it, does not count for that subclass's instances.

A `@property` getter or a helper that reads the cached property is the function reported; the
functions calling it are not. One new reader of a stale value is one new diagnostic under a
Ratchet baseline. The rule reports one diagnostic per function and property name, at the first
read, and lists every method that can leave the value stale as related locations.

The writes count whatever is selected: `MUT101` need not be enabled, and a `MUT101` diagnostic
suppressed at the write still counts. It does not report what `MUT101` does not: a property
whose writers invalidate it on every path, whose inputs are set only during two-phase
initialization, or that no method changes.

## What a report states

An exact report states that the function's own body reads the cached property on an object every
class of which runs a write that `MUT101` reports exact: the value read may have been computed
before that write and kept after it.

The first five premises are those of that `MUT101` report, as its page states them: a value of
a container ABC that the writer uses after its write, for one, counts as one of the classes of its
family (**Kept to the return**).

Its premises:

- **Cached property**: the getter's decorator is one the catalog lists, the first definition along
  each class's MRO. Established.
- **Reads on every path**: the getter reads the written attribute on every path on which it
  returns normally. Established.
- **Every implementation**: each call on the getter's chain has every implementation as its
  targets. Established.
- **Plain write**: the write is a plain store or an in-place change of a builtin container no
  project subclass replaces. Established.
- **Kept to the return**: nothing from the write, its own instruction included, to the writer's
  normal return may remove the kept value. Established.
- **Reads the property**: the function's own body reads the property on the object (`obj.prop`, a
  constant `getattr`, an item of `obj.__dict__`). Established.
- **Runs the writer**: every class the object may be (R2) gets the property from a
  `@cached_property` getter and runs a write of it whose `MUT101` report is exact: the first
  definition of the writing method along its MRO, or one that the definitions before it reach
  through `super()` without invalidating the property. Established.

Besides R1-R7, the claim assumes what that `MUT101` report assumes: no finalizer (`__del__`,
which reference counting or the garbage collector runs when it frees an object) and no other
thread runs code between the write and the writer's return.

A heuristic report states that the function reads a `@cached_property` that a write `MUT101`
reports can leave stale on the instances the object may be. Open: the premises of the `MUT101`
report behind it, which are open where its page says so.

## Why is this bad?
A `cached_property` computes its value once and keeps it in the instance `__dict__`. After a
method changes what the value was computed from, every later read returns the old value. A
function that reads the property depends on whether it runs before or after that method, which
nothing at the read shows.

## Example
```python
from functools import cached_property


class Parser:
    def __init__(self, raw: dict[str, str]) -> None:
        self.raw = raw

    @cached_property
    def dialect(self) -> str:
        return self.raw.get("$schema", "")

    def parse_all(self, docs: list[dict[str, str]]) -> None:
        for doc in docs:
            self.raw = doc  # MUT101: `dialect` keeps the first document's value
            self.parse_one()

    def parse_one(self) -> bool:
        return self.dialect == "draft-07"  # MUT111
```

Use instead:
```python
    def parse_all(self, docs: list[dict[str, str]]) -> None:
        for doc in docs:
            self.raw = doc
            self.__dict__.pop("dialect", None)
            self.parse_one()
```

## How to fix
Invalidate the cached value where it goes stale (`self.__dict__.pop("dialect", None)`, or
`del self.dialect` once it was computed), compute the value without caching it where its inputs
change, or make sure the reading function only runs before the method that changes them.

## Fix safety
No automatic fix: whether to invalidate, recompute, or reorder is a design decision.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/cached-result-mutation/

# cached-result-mutation (MUT114)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Exact · Enabled by default · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Changing in place the list, dict, or set that a `functools.lru_cache` / `functools.cache` function returned (the cache hands the same object to later calls with the same arguments), directly or through the functions that return it.

## What it does
Checks in-place changes of an object that a function cached by `functools.lru_cache` /
`functools.cache` returned. The cache hands the same object to every later call with the same
arguments, so the change is seen by all of them.

A report is exact when the function changes in place, at the reported line, the list, dict, or
set that a cached function returned:

- the cached function is decorated with `functools.cache`, or with `functools.lru_cache` whose
  `maxsize` is left out, `None`, or a literal number above `0` (a name holding `0` would keep
  nothing), known by what its name is bound to (`from functools import lru_cache as _lru_cache`
  counts, a `cache` decorator the module defines itself does not), and
  otherwise only with `staticmethod`, `classmethod`, `typing.override`, or `typing.final` (also
  of `typing_extensions`);
- it takes a parameter besides a method's `self` / `cls`, so the cache keys its results;
- every return a run can reach hands out a builtin container of one kind: its return annotation
  names `list`, `dict`, or `set` as a whole (`dict[str, Any]`, not `dict | None`), or each
  returned value is built as one (a display, a comprehension, `list(...)`, `dict(...)`,
  `set(...)`, `sorted(...)`, `str.split(...)`);
- the changed object is the result of a direct call of that one function on every path to the
  line, through assignments, with no copy;
- that function is every implementation the call can run: the receiver is not typed by a
  protocol, no base class heki knows nothing of may define the method, every member of a union
  resolves, and the project binds no name the call goes through to another object;
- the line is an in-place change of a container of that kind: an item store or delete on a list
  or dict, a method that changes it (`append`, `update`, `pop`, `add`, ...), or an augmented
  assignment that changes it in place (`+=` on a list, `|=` on a dict or set), and no project
  subclass of that container overrides the method or operator.

The other changes of a cached function's result are heuristic reports: an object below the
result (`cached(k)["rows"].append(x)`), an instance of a class, a value handed out through
other functions that return it on some path, a change made by a helper the value is passed to,
a function that returns its cached value on some paths only, and a call that may run a function
heki does not see, such as a method called on a value typed by a protocol whose one implementer
in the project is cached.

Mutations through attributes, subscripts, container methods, in-place operators, and helpers
that mutate their argument are followed for the heuristic reports, with the same copies and
memo fills as `MUT202` (`readonly-return-mutation`).

## What a report states

An exact report states that the function changes in place, at the reported line, the list,
dict, or set that a function cached by `functools.lru_cache` / `functools.cache` returned.

Its premises:

- **Cached**: the decorator is `functools.cache`, or `functools.lru_cache` with `maxsize` left
  out, `None`, or a literal number above `0`, known by what its name is bound to. Established.
- **Keyed**: the cached function takes a parameter besides `self` / `cls`. Established.
- **Container kind**: every return a run can reach hands out a builtin container of the named
  kind, by its return annotation (R2) or by construction. Established.
- **Same object**: the changed object is that call's result on every path, with no copy.
  Established.
- **Every implementation**: the call has as its targets every implementation it can run
  (assumptions R1, R2, and R5, as for `EFF101`): the receiver is no protocol, no base class heki
  knows nothing of may define the method, every member of a union resolves, and the project
  binds no name the call goes through to another object. Established.
- **Changed in place**: the line is an in-place change of a container of that kind. When only
  the return annotation names the kind, no project subclass of that container overrides the
  method or operator, has a metaclass that may install it, or, for a method called by name,
  defines `__getattribute__` (under R2 the result may be an instance of one, whose `sort` or
  `__ior__` may change nothing). Established.

A heuristic report states that the function changes an object that a cached function returned,
or an object below it. Open: the value may be the cached one on some paths only, the call may
run another implementation that caches nothing, and the object may be a class instance whose
change heki cannot tell from a memo fill.

## Why is this bad?
A cached return value is shared by every caller with the same arguments. Changing it in place
corrupts the cache for every later caller, usually long after the change happened.

## Example
```python
from functools import lru_cache


@lru_cache(maxsize=32)
def fields(name: str) -> list[str]:
    return [name, "id"]


def extended(name: str) -> list[str]:
    result = fields(name)
    result.append("extra")  # changes the list the cache keeps
    return result
```

Use instead:
```python
def extended(name: str) -> list[str]:
    result = list(fields(name))
    result.append("extra")
    return result
```

## Known limitations
- A cached value stored in an attribute (`self.kept = fields(...)`) and changed in another
  method is not followed.
- A generator's values and a coroutine's result (`await`) are not followed.

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/call-owner-violation/

# call-owner-violation (MUT204)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Heuristic · Runs when its contract is declared · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Calling a guarded function or method, or constructing a guarded class (directly, via a bound method, `getattr`, or a helper), outside declared `call-owners`.

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs when its contract is declared. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

## What it does
Checks calls of functions and methods, and constructions of classes, that a
`[[tool.heki.call-owners]]` contract reserves for a set of allowed callers: the call side of
`MUT201` (who may write) and `MUT203` (who may read). A call is reported when it happens outside
the allowed callers and resolves to a target:

- a method called on an instance of the target's class or of a subclass, including an override of
  the method in a subclass (`data_type.replace_reference(ref)`);
- the same method through a bound-method alias (`replace = data_type.replace_reference`, then
  `replace(ref)`) or `getattr(data_type, "replace_reference")(...)` with a constant name;
- a module-level function (`pkg.util.reset_cache()`);
- a class: constructing it or a subclass (`FinalFacts(...)`, `pkg.facts.FinalFacts(...)`,
  `cls(...)` in a class method, a value typed `type[FinalFacts]` or `typing.Type[FinalFacts]`,
  `type(facts)(...)`), also for a dataclass or another class without an `__init__` of its own,
  through a `functools.partial` object holding the class (`make = partial(FinalFacts)`, then
  `make()`, reported at `make()`), and through a library method building an instance of its
  receiver's class without its `__init__` (a pydantic model's `FinalFacts.model_construct(...)`,
  `FinalFacts.model_validate({...})` of a dict, `facts.model_copy(...)`); with
  `subclasses = false`, constructing exactly the class;
- what a property returns, called (`self.data_type(is_dict=True)` with a property `data_type`
  returning `type[DataType]` constructs `DataType`): the value the getter's return annotation
  names is called, and the getter runs as reading the property does;
- what a name bound to the target holds, called: a class attribute bound once to it
  (`factory = FinalFacts` or `run = staticmethod(reset_cache)`, then `self.factory()`,
  `cls.factory()`, or `Parser.factory()`), an entry of a module-level table of functions
  (`HANDLERS["reset"]()`), and a module a function returns (`_ops().reset_cache()` of a function
  returning the module it imports);
- a private method by the name Python's name mangling gives it (`parser._Parser__run()` with
  `parser: Parser`, `Parser._Parser__run(p)`, `self._Parser__run()` in a subclass): a target
  names it `Parser.__run` or `Parser._Parser__run`. A subclass's own `__run` is another method
  (`_JsonParser__run`), no override of the target;
- a function or class outside the project a target names by its full dotted name
  (`sys._getframe`), or every private member outside the project (`<external>._*`, leaving out
  the names that are public API though they start with an underscore: dunder and sunder names
  and the `collections.namedtuple` API): a call heki resolves to the symbol, also through
  `from sys import _getframe`, an alias, or a project module re-exporting it
  ([configuration](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#symbols-outside-the-project)). A reference handing such a
  symbol on is no call of it; a `read-owners` target counts it as a read.

A target ending in an argument list names only the calls passing those constants:
`DataType(is_dict=True)` is `DataType(is_dict=True)`, not `DataType(is_list=True)`, and
`container_flags(kind="dict")` is `container_flags(dt, "dict")`, not `container_flags(dt, "list")`.
A call passes a constant when heki establishes it: the argument is a literal, a string constant
bound once (a module's `Final` name), or a module's number or boolean bound once (`LIMIT = 0`),
read by name, through an import (also a function's own), or as an attribute of the module
(`settings.LIMIT`), and unless the importing module binds the name again (a `global` store or
`del` in a function, another module-level store, a star import); passed by keyword, by position
where every function the call may run binds that position to the parameter, or left out where
every such function's default is `True`, `False`, `None`, `0`, or `""` and the value. A keyword
binds as Python binds it: never a positional-only parameter, and one naming no parameter passes its
value under its name into `**kwargs`; the receiver is the first position. A `**` operand that is a
mapping the function builds, which nothing changes (a name holding it is only unpacked with `**`,
merged into another mapping, bound to another name, tested, or returned), passes its entries as
keywords: a dict display with string constant keys (`DataType(**{"is_dict": True})`,
`flags = {"is_dict": True}` then `DataType(**flags)`); a merge (`{**a, **b}`, `dict(a, k=v)`,
`a | b` of two mappings the function builds), which passes the last entry of each key, a mapping
heki does not build (a parameter) replacing every key before it; and one built on several paths
(`flags = a if c else b`), which passes a key where every path passes the same constant for it.
Calling a `functools.partial` object the function makes passes what the object holds first (its
positions, and its keywords, which a keyword of the call replaces), then the call's arguments; a
call unpacking a mapping over keywords the object holds is not followed. A pydantic model's
`model_construct` passes its keywords to the fields, `model_validate` the entries of the dict it
is passed, and `model_copy` those of `update`. A call that
raises `TypeError` instead of running the function (two keywords of one name, a parameter bound by a
position, or the receiver, and a keyword, a keyword without `**kwargs` to land in, a position past
the parameters without `*args`, a parameter without a default left unbound where no `*` unpacking or
`**` unpacking of another mapping may bind it) passes nothing. A variable, a call result, `*`
unpacking, `**` unpacking of another mapping, or a position of a class without a project `__init__`
establishes nothing, and the call is not reported. A reference passes nothing, so it never matches
such a target.

With `references = "calls"` (or `"calls-and-bases"` or `"reads"`), a reference handing a target on to be
called later counts as a call of it, reported where the target is named ("`f` hands on `pkg.core.decide`"; a name an import or
the module body binds is read in the scope binding it without a position of its own, so it is
reported there at the statement handing it on): passed to a call
(`partial(decide)`, `register(self.decide)`, `field(default_factory=Rule)`), stored in an
attribute, an item, or a global, returned, yielded, raised, or held by a display that is
(`[decide]`, `{"a": decide}`), also through an import alias (`from pkg.core import decide as
chosen`), a module alias (`run = core.decide`), or a module attribute (`core.decide`). A use that
only names a class is no reference: an argument of `isinstance`, `issubclass`, another builtin that
only inspects its arguments (`print`, `getattr`, `type`), `super`, `typing.TypeVar`,
`typing.NewType`, or `contextlib.suppress`, and the type a `typing.cast` names (the value it hands
back is the value itself: `register(cast(Callable[[int], int], decide))` hands `decide` on); an `except` clause, a class's bases and keywords, a
function's defaults and annotations; a subscript (`Optional[Rule]`), a comparison (`f is decide`), a
receiver (`Rule.of(...)`), and a module binding another name to it. A callable a builtin calls once
per item (`sorted(xs, key=decide)`, `map(decide, xs)`) is a call already, and so is the
`functools.partial` object handed to one. A call or a reference in a class body (a class
attribute's value, a method's decorator or default argument) counts for the function running the
class statement (`<module>` for a class at module level, a nested class's included); a method's own
body is the method's. A class body, a function, a
lambda, or a comprehension nested in a function names what the function binds to a name it reads
(a local import), at the name.

With `references = "calls-and-bases"`, a class statement naming a class target among its bases
counts too ("`<module>` subclasses `pkg.core.Base`"): the class it makes holds the base, and
constructing it runs the base's initialization unless it overrides it. A base is a positional
argument of the class statement whose value is the class where the statement runs (`Base`,
`core.Base`, `Base[int]`, also through an import alias, a local alias, or a closure cell holding
it; a parameter, a local, or a class-body name of the imported class's name is another value),
matched as a construction is, so a base that is a subclass of the target counts unless
`subclasses = false`; a keyword (`metaclass=Base`) is no base. It is reported at the base where
the statement loads it, and at the class statement for a name an import or the module body
binds, for the function running the class statement (a nested class: the function running the
outer one).

With `references = "reads"`, everything `"calls-and-bases"` counts is reported as before, and every
other use of a target's value counts too ("`build` reads `pkg.core.Keys`"), reported where it is
named as a hand-on is: the object of an attribute access and a method's receiver
(`Keys.of(names)`, `Keys.__annotations__`, `Code.OK`), an argument of a call that only names it
(`isinstance(value, Keys)`, `cast(Keys, x)`), a subscript or its index (`tuple[Keys, int]`), an
operand (`f is decide`), a tested condition, an iterated, awaited, formatted, or `with` value, a
dict display's key, the class of a class pattern (`case Keys():`), the types of an `except` clause
an exception may reach, a decorator, a default of a function or lambda, a keyword of a class
statement, and the cause of `raise ... from`, also through copies and the displays holding it.
A class body or a module binding a name to the target (`model_type = Keys`, `Alias = Keys`) is a
read too: the uses of a class attribute or a global are not all followed back to the target. No
read: a call, an annotation, evaluated or not (`list[Keys]`), the values Python evaluates only
when asked (a `type` statement's value, the bounds and defaults of type parameters), an import, a
name bound to the target by itself in a function (a local), whose own uses count, and a value
nothing uses. A load handing a target on is reported as a hand-on only, and a read is matched as a
construction is.

A call through a value typed with a project `Protocol` that declares the method is judged by the
protocol's declaration (`h._helper()` with `h: Host` calls `Host._helper`), and what an
implementation's private method calls inside stays with it (also when other callers call the
method through the class and take its calls over). The call is one of a target `Model._helper`
too when heki lists the classes implementing the protocol, there is at least one, each is
`Model` or a subclass of it, and every method the call may run is a target, as for a call
through a base class; a protocol that another class implements too, or that no project class
implements, calls no target of `Model`'s. A static or class method the protocol declares, called
through such a value, is judged the same way.

A target's last segment names the function, method, or class: a glob there matches within that
name only (`pkg.*._*` is every private member in `pkg`, not every function of a private module,
and `pkg.api_*` is `pkg.api_commit`, not `pkg.api_helpers.api_reset`), and the report names the
function the call reaches.

A call is reported only when every function it may call is a target: when the receiver's class
hierarchy also offers a method that is no target (a receiver typed with a base class whose own
`replace_reference` is not guarded), the call is not reported. The functions it may call can be
targets of different entries of one contract: with `A.reset` and `B.reset` both listed, `obj.reset()`
on `obj: Base`, whose subclasses `A` and `B` implement `reset`, is one report for
`A.reset|B.reset`. A call every function of which several targets of one contract name
(`A.reset` and `reset` for `a.reset()` on `a: A`) is one report too, under the target configured
first, naming the others (`(also `reset`)`). A call on a receiver whose class heki does not know (an unannotated
parameter, `Any`) is not seen; with `unresolved = "report"`,
`MUT207` reports it.

A private helper (`_name`, or a comprehension, generator expression, or lambda scope) with project
callers hands its calls to its callers (with `unresolved = "report"`, not one that some code also
hands on as a value, which has callers heki does not see): the call is reported at the call sites of the first
non-private callers, with the chain of calls down to the call as related information. A call runs
where the body holding it runs, as for `MUT201`: a generator's calls where it is iterated (a
generator an allowed caller creates and returns calls outside it when its caller iterates it), a
coroutine's where it is awaited. Not reported either:

- a function that only runs inside allowed callers: it has project callers, and every path of
  callers above it starts in an allowed caller, an exempt method, or a class's own
  initialization (as for `MUT201`);
- a class's own initialization: an initializer (`__init__`, `__post_init__`, ...) of a class of
  the target's family calling a guarded method on its own `self`, or handing it on with
  `references = "calls"`, directly or through a private helper (for a target naming no class,
  `reset`, the family is the classes defining the methods it names and their subclasses);
- a target calling a target of the same contract (`remove_reference` calling
  `self.replace_reference(None)`, an override calling `super().replace_reference(...)`): the
  guarded operation is checked where it is called, so what it does inside is part of it. With
  `targets-call-each-other = "report"` a target is allowed to call itself only, and a call of
  another target is judged as a one-target contract would judge it.

With `attribution = "lexical"`, a call is judged in the function whose code holds it instead: a
private helper reports its calls itself, and a function that only runs inside allowed callers
is reported too. A lambda, comprehension, or generator expression is part of the function it is
written in (`any(decide() for x in xs)` in an allowed function is allowed), and a nested `def`
is a function of its own. A class's own initialization, through the helpers it passes `self` to
too (a helper whose every path of project callers starts in an initializer handing it its own
`self`), and the targets calling each other stay allowed.

With `own-receiver = "allow"`, a call through the receiver of the method it is judged in is
allowed: the function reported (with `attribution = "lexical"`, the function holding the call) is
a method that is no static method, and the object the called method is looked up on may be its
first parameter (`self._label()`, `cls._kind()`, `super()._label()`, `self._norm(x)` of a static
method, `Resolver._label(self)`), also for a method the class inherits. A static method called
through its class (`Resolver._norm(x)`), a call on another parameter, and a nested `def`, lambda,
or comprehension calling through the enclosing method's `self` stay reported.

With `allowed-protocols`, a call through a value typed with a project protocol the key names that
declares the method, itself or through its protocol bases, is allowed wherever it is judged, and so
is a reference handing the method on through such a value (`return h._helper` with `references`);
a call through another protocol or the implementation's class stays reported. A pattern names the
subprotocols of the protocols it matches too, unless `protocol-subclasses = false`.

The help starts with the contract's `message` and then names up to three allowed callers that
make the call the report names themselves: public functions and methods an `allowed-callers`
pattern names (with `forbidden-callers`, every function outside them), by fully qualified name
(``allowed callers of `DataType.replace_reference`: `pkg.store.GenerationStore.replace_ref` ``).
A reference handing a target on, the targets calling each other, private functions (`_name`),
special methods, and the exempt methods do not count. JSON output gives them with their files as
`allowed_examples` (`fqn`, `path`).

## What a report states

A report states that the function calls a function or method, or constructs a class, that a
`call-owners` contract reserves, outside the contract's call owners; with `references = "calls"`,
that it hands one on; with `references = "calls-and-bases"`, also that it subclasses one; with
`references = "reads"`, also that it reads one.

Its premises:

- **Target**: the receiver or the callee is an instance of a class the contract names, or of a
  subclass, or the class object of one, by construction or annotation (assumption R2). A subclass
  derives from the class through bases named where their class statements run: a parameter, a
  local, or a closure cell of the class's name is another class. Open: an alias bound on one path
  is enough.
- **Outside the owners**: the function is not in the allowed modules and classes, nor runs only
  inside allowed contexts (with `attribution = "lexical"`: the function holding the call is not
  allowed, nor runs only inside a class's own initialization; with `own-receiver = "allow"`, the
  receiver is not the one of the method judging it). Established from the contract.
- **Through helpers**: a helper's write, read, or call counts at its caller (never with
  `attribution = "lexical"`). Open: one path of the helper is enough.
- **Hands on** (`references = "calls"`): the value named is the target, and it reaches, through
  copies and displays, an argument, a store, a `return`, a `yield`, or a `raise`. Open: a value
  merged from several paths is enough. Whether the code it is handed to calls it is not part of
  the claim.
- **Subclasses** (`references = "calls-and-bases"`): the value the class statement passes as a
  base is the target class, typed where the statement runs. Established: a base heki cannot type
  (a parameter, a call's result, a value merged from paths that disagree) is no match. Whether
  the subclass is constructed is not part of the claim.
- **Reads** (`references = "reads"`): the value named is the target, and it reaches, through
  copies and displays, a use other than a call, a hand-on, a binding of another name, or an
  annotation. Open: a value merged from several paths is enough. What the use does with the
  target (whether a test of a display holding it looks at it) is not part of the claim.
- **Arguments** (a target with an argument list): the call binds each parameter the list names to
  its constant, as Python binds the call. Established: an argument heki cannot tell is no match,
  a mapping built on several paths passes a key only where every path passes the same constant
  (as every function the call may run must agree), and a call that raises `TypeError` instead of
  running the function binds nothing. Not followed: a mapping or a `functools.partial` object
  the function does not build itself through copies (a parameter, an attribute, a call's result,
  one chosen on several paths), a mapping something changes in place, a key computed at run time,
  and a pydantic model's `model_validate` of a value not established to be a dict.

## Why is this bad?
Some operations keep invariants only when one component runs them: a store that updates its
indexes after redirecting a reference, a factory that builds a sealed object exactly once. A
direct call from elsewhere skips the bookkeeping, and nothing fails until an input exercises the
stale state. A linter cannot tell `data_type.replace_reference(ref)` from `text.replace("a", "b")`
without the receiver's class, and an import rule cannot forbid a method of an object the caller
legitimately imports. The contract states the ownership once in configuration.

## Example
```toml
[[tool.heki.call-owners]]
name = "reference-mutators"
targets = ["DataType.replace_reference", "FinalFacts"]
allowed-callers = ["pkg.store.GenerationStore.*"]
message = "use a GenerationStore operation instead"
```

```python
# pkg/store.py
class GenerationStore:
    def replace_data_type_ref(self, data_type: DataType, ref: Reference) -> None:
        data_type.replace_reference(ref)  # allowed caller


def swap(data_type: DataType, ref: Reference) -> None:
    data_type.replace_reference(ref)  # MUT204: outside `pkg.store.GenerationStore.*`


def rename(text: str) -> str:
    return text.replace("a", "b")  # not reported: a `str`, not a `DataType`
```

Use instead:
```python
def swap(store: GenerationStore, data_type: DataType, ref: Reference) -> None:
    store.replace_data_type_ref(data_type, ref)
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `[[tool.heki.call-owners]]`:
  - `name`: the contract name, shown in messages.
  - `targets`: functions, methods, or classes, as dotted names or globs matched against the fully
    qualified name and any dotted suffix (`DataType.replace_reference`, `pkg.util.reset_cache`,
    `FinalFacts`, `Parser._*`). A `Class.method` target covers the method's overrides in
    subclasses; a class target covers constructing the class and its subclasses; a target
    naming no class (`reset`) covers every project function and method of that name. A target
    may end in an argument list of `parameter=value` entries (`DataType(is_dict=True)`), each
    value `True`, `False`, `None`, an integer, or a quoted string (a glob when it holds `*`, `?`,
    `[`, or `{`: `module="pkg.backend.*"`). `*` with an argument list names every call passing
    its constants, whatever it calls (`*(module="pkg.backend.*")`). A target with a module part
    (`pkg:Kind`, `pkg:*`) also names the names the module imports, read or called through the
    module object (`pkg.Kind.A`), judged at the access. A target can also name
    functions and classes outside the project by their full name (`sys._getframe`, `os._*`), or
    `<external>.<name>` for the members of every module and class outside the project.
  - `allowed-callers`: functions allowed to call the targets, as dotted names or globs matched
    against the function's qualified name and its `Class.method` qualname (`pkg.store.*`). A
    module part names one module without its submodules: `pkg:*` allows what `pkg/__init__.py`
    defines, not `pkg.sub.user.sub_user`.
  - `forbidden-callers`: when set, only calls by these functions are reported (matched like
    `allowed-callers`); `allowed-callers` and `exempt-methods` stay exceptions inside them. A
    call is in scope when the reporting function or one of the private helpers it hands the call
    through is forbidden (`forbidden-callers = ["pkg.parser.*"]`: the parser layer must not call
    the targets).
  - `exempt-methods`: methods allowed to call the targets (`__deepcopy__`); a plain name matches
    any function or method of that name, an entry with a dot or a glob is matched like
    `allowed-callers`.
  - `message`: the help of every report of the contract.
  - `fail`: `true` makes every report of the contract fail `heki check` (exit code 1), whatever its tier and severity (default `false`).
  - `unresolved`: `"ignore"` (default) or `"report"`: also report the calls the contract cannot
    tie to a class, under `MUT207`. A function some code hands
    on as a value (a display, a class attribute, an argument, a return: `HANDLERS = [helper]`,
    `REQUIRE = staticmethod(helper)`) has callers heki does not see: with `"report"`, it judges
    its calls itself, as if it had no callers.
  - `references`: `"ignore"` (default), `"calls"`, `"calls-and-bases"`, or `"reads"`: a
    reference handing a target on to be called later counts as a call of it, with
    `"calls-and-bases"` a class statement naming a class target among its bases too, and with
    `"reads"` every other use of a target's value as well.
  - `attribution`: `"call-graph"` (default) or `"lexical"`: whether a private helper hands its
    calls to its callers and a function that only runs inside allowed callers is allowed, or
    each call is judged in the function holding it.
  - `own-receiver`: `"report"` (default) or `"allow"`: whether a call through the receiver of the
    method it is judged in (`self`, `cls`, `super()`) is allowed.
  - `targets-call-each-other`: `"allow"` (default) or `"report"`: whether a target may call the
    other targets of the contract. With `"report"`, each target is judged like the one target of a
    contract with the same keys, so a contract listing independent targets reports what one
    contract per target reports for every call whose candidates all belong to one target. A call
    that may reach several targets (`obj.reset()` on `obj: Base` with `A.reset` and `B.reset`
    listed) is judged once for each target it may reach, with only that target guarded, and is
    reported when any of those judgements reports it.
  - `allowed-protocols`: project protocols (class patterns, their subclasses included): a call
    through a value typed with one that declares the method, itself or through its protocol
    bases, is allowed, also through a class object typed `type[P]` of one (`MUT207`).
  - `protocol-subclasses`: `true` (default) or `false`: whether an `allowed-protocols` pattern
    names the subprotocols of the protocols it matches, or those protocols only.
  - `include-overrides`: `true` or `false` (default): whether an entry naming a method
    (`Class.method`, `module:Class.method`) in `allowed-callers`, `forbidden-callers`, and the `exempt-methods`
    patterns also names the methods of that name in the
    project subclasses of `Class` (a private name overrides nothing).


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/change-lost-on-new-object/

# change-lost-on-new-object (MUT119)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Exact · Enabled by default · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

An in-place change of a builtin container applied to a new object that nothing else holds and no name keeps (`list(xs).sort()`, `env = os.environ.copy().update(...)`, `obj.settings[k] = v` with a getter returning a new dict): the change is lost when the statement ends.

## What it does
Checks in-place changes of a builtin container (`list`, `dict`, `set`, `bytearray`,
`collections.deque`) applied to a new object that nothing else holds and that the code never
names: `list(xs).sort()`, `env = os.environ.copy().update(HOME=home)`,
`task.environment["KEY"] = value` when the `environment` getter returns a new dict. Nothing can
read the object after the statement, so the change is lost.

The object is the value of the expression the change is applied to, and it is new when it is:

- built as the builtin itself: a display, a comprehension, a call of `list`, `dict`, `set`,
  `bytearray`, `collections.deque`, or `sorted`;
- a copy the ecosystem catalog describes (`x.copy()` of a builtin container, `copy.copy(x)`,
  `os.environ.copy()`) of a value whose builtin container type heki knows, called with nothing
  but the value it copies (`copy.deepcopy(x, memo)` keeps the copy in `memo`), or a slice of a
  list or `bytearray`;
- what a call of a project function, or a read of a property, returns, when every return of each
  function the call can run is such an object and the function keeps it nowhere: not stored,
  captured, yielded, raised, handed to a call that may keep it (a builtin that only inspects its
  argument, such as `len`, keeps nothing), handed to a method whose result may hold it (a view
  such as `d.values()` or an iterator holds it, unless only a loop or a test reads it), used as
  a key (`del registry[items]` hands it to the registry's `__delitem__`), or read through an
  attribute (a bound method holds its object). A function returning the result of another such
  function qualifies too.

The change is a changing method of the object's own type (`append`, `extend`, `insert`, `sort`,
`reverse`, `update`, `pop`, `clear`, `setdefault`, `add`, `discard`, `remove`, ...), an item
assignment, an augmented item assignment (`d()[k] += 1`), or an item deletion. A method returning
`None` is reported when its result is unused, or bound to a name or stored
(`opts[k] = list(v).extend(w)`); `pop`, `popitem`, `popleft`, and `setdefault` only when their
result is unused.

It does not report:

- a method of a project class, even one named like a container's (`Inventory.remove` returning
  a filtered copy);
- an object bound to a name first (`items = list(xs)`, then `items.sort()`): whether a later
  statement reads it is a question of flow;
- a result the code reads (`top = list(heap).pop()`, `return list(xs).sort() or xs`);
- what a function returns when it may return state that outlives the call, keeps the new object
  somewhere, returns `None` on some path, is a generator or `async def`, or is decorated with a
  cache (`functools.cache`, `cached_property`): the change is then seen elsewhere.

A test that changes a returned copy on purpose to check that it is a copy is reported; suppress
it there.

Type checkers report one of these shapes: mypy reports a `None` result stored into an item or an
attribute (`opts[k] = list(v).extend(w)`) as `func-returns-value`, in the functions it checks,
but not one bound to a name, and none of the other shapes; pyright and ty report none of them.

## What a report states

A report states that the object the change is applied to is new, that nothing else holds it and
no name keeps it, and that the change is one its builtin type makes in place, so the change is
lost when the statement ends.

Its premises:

- **New object**: the object is built as the builtin itself where it is changed, copied there by
  a copy the catalog describes from a value of a builtin container type no project subclass
  copies otherwise (R2), or returned by project functions whose every return is such an object
  that they keep nowhere, and the call or property read, and each one whose result those
  functions return, resolves to every function it can run.
  Open for a copy whose class only comes from the copied value's type (R2) when a project
  subclass may replace the copy or the change, for the result of a function returning such a
  copy, and when the call may run functions heki does not resolve.
- **Unnamed**: the object is only the value of the changed expression; nothing reads it but the
  change and, for an augmented item assignment, the item load it starts with.
- **Changed in place**: the change is a changing method of the object's builtin type, an item
  assignment, or an item deletion, and its result is unused or a `None` bound to a name or
  stored. Open for an augmented item assignment, whose item's own in-place operator runs first
  and may change an item other code holds.

## Why is this bad?
The statement reads like an update, but it changes an object that disappears when the statement
ends: the sort, the override, or the new item never reaches the code that reads the value. A
`None` bound or stored in its place (`environ = os.environ.copy().update(...)`) fails later and
far from the cause.

## Example
```python
import os


class Task:
    @property
    def environment(self):
        return {}

    def run(self):
        self.environment["PYTHONPATH"] = "/app"  # the dict is gone after this line


def child_env(home):
    env = os.environ.copy().update(HOME=home)  # `env` is None
    return env
```

Use instead:
```python
import os


class Task:
    def __init__(self):
        self.environment = {}

    def run(self):
        self.environment["PYTHONPATH"] = "/app"


def child_env(home):
    env = os.environ.copy()
    env.update(HOME=home)
    return env
```

## Known limitations
- A comprehension changed in the same expression (`[x for x in xs].append(y)`) is not reported:
  its own appends read the new list too.
- A new object bound to a name and never read again is out of scope.
- Library functions returning new containers (`str.split`, `json.loads`) are not followed unless
  the catalog describes them as copies.
- A function that compares the new object (`items == other`, `items in seen`) or tests it with
  `isinstance` is taken to keep nothing: a project `__eq__`, `__contains__`, or metaclass
  `__instancecheck__` that stored the operand it is handed would keep it. These hooks answer a
  test, and code that stores their operand is not known.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/circular-import-failure/

# circular-import-failure (IMP102)

Family: Imports (IMP) · Heuristic · Opt-in · Experimental · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Opt-in: a `from M import name` that raises `ImportError` when a module of its import cycle is imported before the others, because `M` is still loading and has not bound `name`.

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs only when `select` or `extend-select` names its code or name. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

!!! warning "Experimental"

    It is new: every report rests on established premises only, but its reports are heuristic until a review of its reports on real code bases certifies its claim, and which imports and code stop a run can still change. Experimental features can still change in behavior or precision, or be removed, in any release, and each change is listed in the release notes. An opt-in rule that is not experimental is stable and only off by default. See [Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/).

## What it does
Reports a `from M import name` that raises `ImportError` when a module of its import cycle is
imported before the other modules of the cycle have loaded. Importing that module runs its body,
and the imports in module bodies lead from it to the statement while `M` is still loading: `M`
is paused at the import that started the chain, and has not bound `name` yet. Python then raises
`ImportError: cannot import name 'name' from partially initialized module 'M' (most likely due to
a circular import)`.

heki finds it without configuration. For each group of the project's modules that import each
other while they load, it imports each module of the group first in turn, and each package
holding one whose `__init__.py` imports the group: the module's parent packages load first, then
the module bodies run in order through their imports, and each import of a module that has not
loaded yet runs that module's body before the import goes on. One report is given per failing
statement, naming the modules whose import fails there, with the imports of the chain from the
first of them as related locations.

Only `from M import name` fails this way. `import M` and `import M as m` take the module while
it is still loading and do not fail there, and neither does `from pkg import sub` of a submodule
`pkg.sub`, which Python finds in `sys.modules`.

## What a report states

A report states that importing one of the modules it names, while no module of the import cycle
has been imported in the process, does not complete: unless code that runs before raises first,
the chain of imports shown reaches the reported statement while `M` is loading and has not bound
`name`, and the statement raises `ImportError`.

Its premises, each established or no report:

- **Chain**: each import of the chain is in a module body (or a class body it runs, or a constant
  by-name import there), runs on every path through the body, is no lazy import, and loads the
  module shown: its name resolved against the project's modules, a `from` import split between a
  submodule and an attribute as Python splits it, and the parent packages of a module loading
  first. The reported statement is such an import too, and takes the name from `M` itself.
- **Not loaded before**: each module the chain enters has not loaded yet. A module of the cycle
  has not, by the claim; a module outside it has not when its import imports a module of the
  cycle whenever it runs, and every way from its imports to the cycle is an import in a module
  body that heki names. Otherwise an import of a module outside the cycle that may load one of
  the cycle stops the run.
- **No handler**: no handler takes the `ImportError` on the way, a plain one: no `except` clause
  naming `ImportError`, `Exception`, `BaseException`, a type heki cannot tell is another builtin
  exception, or a bare `except`, whose body may end without raising, no `with` block, and no
  `finally` body that may leave without raising it again, around an import of the chain or the
  statement. `except ModuleNotFoundError:` does not take it (a subclass does not take its base),
  a clause whose body raises on every path (`raise`) takes nothing, and a clause that certainly
  matches hides the clauses after it. A handler taking the `ModuleNotFoundError` of a module a
  project package lacks lets the module body go on past that import.
- **Not a submodule**: the project has no module `M.name` (Python falls back to a submodule of
  that name once it is loaded), and `name` is not a dunder the import system sets
  (`__name__`, `__path__`).
- **Not bound yet**: before the import `M` is paused at, `M`'s body has no statement that may
  bind `name` (an assignment, a definition, an import, also on a branch), binds no
  `__getattr__`, which a `from` import falls back to, and runs no star import; `M` has no
  `exec`, no change through `globals()`, no `vars()` or `locals()` in its body, and no function
  or class body binding `name` under `global`.
- **Not bound elsewhere**: no other module of the project stores into or deletes `M.name`, by
  name or with `setattr` under a name heki cannot read.
- **Nothing else loads the cycle**: nothing that runs before the statement may load a module of
  the cycle out of the order shown. An import heki cannot place there (on a branch, behind a
  handler, lazy) of a module of the cycle that has not loaded yet, an import of a module heki
  cannot name, and a module outside the cycle whose own load may load one of the cycle stop the
  run. When some function or lazy import of the project may load a module of the cycle, so does
  any code that runs before the statement other than imports and stores of names (a call, a
  class statement, a decorator, an operator, an attribute or item access): it may call that
  function.

A report says which module, imported first, fails: importing another module of the cycle first
may load them in an order that works.

## Why is this bad?
A package whose modules import names from each other works only while it is imported through
the module that loads them in a working order. Importing another of its modules first, as a
test, a script, a plugin loader, or a user of the library may do, fails with an `ImportError`
that names a module that exists and a name it defines. The failure depends on the order modules
are imported in, so it can appear only in one environment or one test run. A type checker, which
reads the names a module defines but not the order statements run in, does not see it.

## Example
```python
# pkg/a.py
from pkg.b import helper_b  # IMP102 when `pkg.b` is imported first


def helper_a() -> int:
    return helper_b() + 1
```

```python
# pkg/b.py
from pkg.a import helper_a  # IMP102 when `pkg.a` is imported first


def helper_b() -> int:
    return 1


def uses_a() -> int:
    return helper_a()
```

Importing `pkg.a` first runs `pkg/a.py`, which imports `pkg.b` before it defines `helper_a`;
`pkg/b.py` then asks `pkg.a` for `helper_a`, which it has not bound yet.

Use instead:
```python
# pkg/b.py
def helper_b() -> int:
    return 1


def uses_a() -> int:
    from pkg.a import helper_a

    return helper_a()
```

## How to fix
When one import is on every cycle of the failure's group (the modules importing each other
while they load), the help names it: moved into the functions that use it, or made `lazy` on
Python 3.15 and later, it leaves the group with no cycle, so no import of the group fails.
heki names it only after one search of the group's other imports finds no cycle without it, and
names no import whose name code running while its module loads may read, or another module
takes while that module loads, as `IMP101` says; a read of another module in a function rules
out the move into functions only, leaving `lazy`. It
is the failing import itself when that one is such an import, else one of the imports the related
locations show. Without such an import, the help lists the ways out of this failure: import the
name inside the function that uses it, import the module and read the name where it is used, or
bind the name before the import of the cycle.

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- Its reports are errors: `lint.severity = { IMP102 = "warning" }` makes them warnings.

## Known limitations
- Imports heki does not see (`exec`, `runpy`, a module loaded from a file path, an import a
  library function makes, such as a plugin manager loading entry points) are not followed, and
  neither is a write to `sys.modules` or a module object given another class.
- A run stops, and reports nothing from that point on, at the first code that may load a module
  of the cycle out of order. An import under `if __name__ == "__main__":`, which never runs when
  the module is imported, counts as an import on a branch.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/conditional-ownership-mutation/

# conditional-ownership-mutation (MUT112)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Heuristic · Opt-in · Experimental · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Opt-in: changing in place a value that is a new object on one path and borrowed state (a parameter, an attribute, a global, or what a function returns of such state) on another.

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs only when `select` or `extend-select` names its code or name. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

!!! warning "Experimental"

    Its precision on real code bases is still low: much of what it reports is code that changes a borrowed container on purpose. Experimental features can still change in behavior or precision, or be removed, in any release, and each change is listed in the release notes. An opt-in rule that is not experimental is stable and only off by default. See [Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/).

## What it does
Checks for a container that is a new object on one path and borrowed state on another, and that
is then changed in place. The rule is opt-in: enable it with `--extend-select MUT112` or
`extend-select = ["MUT112"]`.

A value is a new object where the function makes it: a display (`[]`, `{}`), a comprehension, a
copy (`list(x)`, `dict(x)`, `x.copy()`, `copy.copy`), a constructor call, an operator's result
(`a + b`), or a call of a project function that returns a new object. It is borrowed where it
comes from state that outlives the call: a parameter, an attribute, a global, a variable of an
enclosing function, an element of one of these, or a call of a project function that returns
such state. An attribute of an object the function makes itself (`visitor = Visitor()`, then
