  ([configuration](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#imports-toolhekiimports)).
- Its reports are heuristic warnings: `lint.fail-on = "warning"` makes a cycle fail the run.
- A [Ratchet baseline](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/adoption/#import-cycle-groups) records each group by its modules,
  not by the import its report sits at: an entry covers a group when it holds all of the
  group's modules.

## Known limitations
- Imports heki does not see (`exec`, `runpy`, a module loaded from a file path, a write to
  `sys.modules`) are no steps, and neither is a cycle through a module outside the project.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/iterated-container-mutation/

# iterated-container-mutation (MUT113)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Heuristic · Opt-in · Experimental · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Opt-in: a dict, set, or deque of the instance changed while a method iterates it, by another method while a generator is suspended in the loop or by a function the loop's body calls (the next step raises `RuntimeError`).

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs only when `select` or `extend-select` names its code or name. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

!!! warning "Experimental"

    It has few reports, and most of them are still false. Experimental features can still change in behavior or precision, or be removed, in any release, and each change is listed in the release notes. An opt-in rule that is not experimental is stable and only off by default. See [Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/).

## What it does
Checks for a `dict`, `set`, or `collections.deque` held in an attribute of `self` that is
changed in place while a method of the class iterates it, by code outside the loop:

- a method of the class that runs while a generator method is suspended inside the iteration (at
  a `yield` from which the loop goes on, or inside a `yield from`);
- a function or method that the loop's body calls.

The rule is opt-in: enable it with `--extend-select MUT113` or `extend-select = ["MUT113"]`.

An iteration is a `for` loop or a `yield from` over the container, over its `keys()`,
`values()`, or `items()` view, or over a lazy wrapper of either (`iter`, `enumerate`, `zip`,
`map`, `filter`, `reversed`, `itertools.chain`, a generator expression, ...). A snapshot
(`list(...)`, `tuple(...)`, `sorted(...)`, `.copy()`) is a container of its own. The
container's class comes from its annotation or its assignment in `__init__` (`OrderedDict`,
`defaultdict`, and `Counter` are mappings).

A change is an in-place change of the attribute's container, made by the method itself, by the
methods and properties it calls on `self`, or by a helper it hands the container to (the
helper's change counts as the same change made in the method):

- inserting, removing, or moving items: `append`, `add`, `update`, `setdefault`, `pop`,
  `popleft`, `discard`, `clear`, `del self.items[k]`, `rotate`, `move_to_end`, `|=`, ...;
- storing an item (`self.items[k] = v`), which counts for a mapping (the key may be new) but not
  for a deque, whose iterators allow it;
- reading a missing key of a `defaultdict` (`self.groups[k].append(v)`).

A store or a `defaultdict` read under a key the container holds adds no key, and does not count:
inside `if k in self.items:`, past `if k not in self.items: return` or
`if self.items.get(k) is None: raise KeyError(k)`, or after a read of `self.items[k]` in the same
block (not for a `Counter`, whose read of a missing key inserts nothing).

Rebinding the attribute (`self.items = {}`) changes no container, and the changes a function makes
after it binds a new container to the attribute on every path (`self.items = {}`, then
`self.items[k] = v`) are that new container's, not the one an iteration steps. Changes that a
method it calls after the rebinding makes (`self.items = {}`, then `self.add(k)`) still count.

What runs while a generator is suspended depends on where its generator object goes:

- A private generator (`_name`) runs only where the project iterates it. Between its steps, the
  body of the loop iterating it runs: the methods of the class that this body calls on the
  generator's instance count, on the same `self`, variable, or attribute (`self.registry`) the
  generator was called on, also through the functions that hand the generator on. A call that
  consumes it (`list(...)`, `sorted(...)`) runs nothing in between, and a generator that
  suspends inside such a loop is followed in turn.
- When the generator object outlives one use of it, any public method of the class, its project
  subclasses, and the bases it inherits from can run in between: it is stored (on the instance,
  in a list), yielded, or handed to code heki does not follow, or a step that leaves it suspended
  (`next()`, `send()`, a loop that leaves early or over a wrapper that stops first, `any()`,
  `islice()`) is followed by another use of it. Initialization does not count: `__init__`,
  `__post_init__`, `__new__`, `__setstate__`, `__enter__`, `setup`, and the other two-phase
  initialization methods `MUT101` names run before any iteration. A private method counts
  through the methods calling it.
- A public generator, `__iter__` included, is an iteration the class offers its callers, as
  `dict.items()` is: its public methods that change the container are the rest of that
  interface, and changing a container while iterating it is the caller's mistake, as for a
  builtin container. Only the changes made by reads count: property getters and the read dunder
  methods (`__getitem__`, `__len__`, `__contains__`, ...). The project's own loops over it count
  as for a private generator.

A change written in the loop's body itself is the linters' check (Ruff's `B909` and
`PLE4703`), and not reported. The rule reports one diagnostic per iteration of a suspended
generator, at the iteration, naming one changing method and listing each one as a related
location, and one per call in a loop's body that changes the container, at the call.

## What a report states

A report states that a `dict`, `set`, or `deque` held in `self.<attr>` is changed in place by code
that can run while a method iterates it, so the next step of the iteration raises `RuntimeError`.

Its premises:

- **Container**: the attribute holds one of these containers, by its assignment in `__init__` or
  its annotation (assumption R2).
- **Iterated**: a `for` loop or `yield from` steps through it, or through a view or lazy wrapper of
  it. Established.
- **Can run meanwhile**: the change is in a function the loop's body calls, or in a method that can
  run while a generator is suspended in the loop. Open: what can run while a generator is suspended
  follows where its object goes, as described above, not the calls the program makes.

## Why is this bad?
A dict or set iterator raises `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration` (or
`Set changed size during iteration`) at its next step after its container gained or lost an
item, and a deque iterator raises `RuntimeError: deque mutated during iteration` after any
change but an item store. A generator suspended inside such an iteration fails when it resumes
after another method ran, which may be far from both and only for some orders of calls.

## Example
```python
class Subscriptions:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.by_node: dict[str, object] = {}
        self._cursor = self._cycle()

    def _cycle(self):
        while True:
            yield from self.by_node.values()  # MUT113

    def next_subscriber(self) -> object:
        return next(self._cursor)

    def drop(self, node: str) -> None:
        self.by_node.pop(node, None)
```

Use instead:
```python
    def _cycle(self):
        while True:
            yield from list(self.by_node.values())
```

## How to fix
Iterate over a snapshot taken before the loop (`list(self.by_node.values())`), or collect the
changes and apply them after the loop has finished.

## Fix safety
No automatic fix: a snapshot no longer sees the items added during the iteration, which can be
what the code wants.

## Known limitations
- A `list` does not count: a list iterator sees the items appended during the iteration and
  skips or repeats items when others move, without an error.
- A container of an abstract class (`MutableMapping`, `MutableSet`) or of a class heki does not
  know does not count. A `deque()` or `defaultdict(...)` assigned without an annotation has no
  class for heki: annotate the attribute (`self.queue: deque[int] = deque()`).
- An `await` inside a loop, and threads, are not suspensions the rule follows.
- A loop's call on another object than the generator's instance does not count, even on another
  parameter that may be the same object at run time (`for k in source._walk():
  destination.remove(k)` called as `copy_over(r, r)`).
- A method returning an iterator or a view instead of being a generator
  (`return iter(self.items)`) is not followed, and neither is a generator passed to a project
  function that iterates it.
- A generator handed to code heki does not follow counts as outliving the call, also when that
  code consumes it at once (`self.assertCountEqual(gen(), [...])`).
- The tests on the paths to a change are not followed across calls: a change only a lazy
  initialization makes (`if not self.loaded: self._load()`) counts although the iterating method
  ran it first, and so does a change that a constant argument of the call turns off
  (`add(item, check=False)` where `add` changes the container only `if check:`).


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/iterator-double-consumption/

# iterator-double-consumption (MUT106)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Heuristic · Opt-in · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Opt-in: consuming a single-pass iterator or generator a second time (the second pass sees no items).

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs only when `select` or `extend-select` names its code or name. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

## What it does
Checks for a single-pass iterator or generator that is consumed a second time. Once an
iterator is exhausted, every further pass over it sees no items, silently.

Single-pass values are:

- generator expressions (`(x for x in xs)`);
- `iter`, `zip`, `map`, `filter`, `enumerate`, `reversed`, `heapq.merge`, and the single-pass
  `itertools` functions (`chain`, `islice`, `starmap`, `takewhile`, `dropwhile`, `filterfalse`,
  `compress`, `accumulate`, `groupby`, `pairwise`, `batched`, `zip_longest`, `product`,
  `permutations`, `combinations`, `combinations_with_replacement`), resolved through imports
  so a shadowed name is never matched;
- calls of project generator functions (from any module);
- parameters and locals annotated `Iterator`, `Generator`, `AsyncIterator`, or
  `AsyncGenerator` (`typing` or `collections.abc`; `Iterable`, `Sequence`, and `Collection`
  may be re-iterable and are not tracked).

A value is consumed by a `for` loop or comprehension over it, unpacking (`a, *rest = it`),
`yield from`, a call that materializes it (`list`, `tuple`, `set`, `frozenset`, `dict`, `bytes`,
`bytearray`, `sum`, `min`, `max`, `sorted`, `str.join`, `bytes.join`,
`dict.fromkeys`, `list.extend`, `set.update` / `union` / `intersection` / `difference`,
`dict.update`, `collections.deque` / `Counter` / `OrderedDict` / `defaultdict`,
`heapq.nlargest` / `nsmallest`, `functools.reduce`, `math.prod` / `fsum`), a wrapper that is
itself consumed (`enumerate(it)`, `map(f, it)`, `chain(it, other)`, `heapq.merge(it, other)`,
`zip(it, it)`, a generator expression over it, ...), or a project function that iterates the
parameter it is passed to exhaustion (for a method, every implementation the call may run must;
an `@abstractmethod` never runs). `next(it)` and `len` are not consumptions, and neither are
`zip` / `map` over several iterables, `islice`, or `takewhile`: they stop at the shortest one or
early (`zip(range(n), it)` takes `n` items). The same table decides where a generator's body
runs for the effect and contract rules.

The rule reports the second pass when the first one runs to exhaustion and the second is
reachable from it, without rebinding the variable in between. It also reports a value created
outside a loop and consumed to exhaustion inside it: the next iteration sees nothing.

It does not report:

- a first pass that may stop early: a `for` loop with `break`, `return`, or `raise` inside
  (`it = iter(lines)`, then `for line in it: ... break`, then `for line in it:` is the
  idiomatic way to resume), and `any(it)` / `all(it)`, which stop at the first item that decides
  the result (they still run a generator's body where they are called);
- passes on exclusive branches (`if c: list(it) else: sorted(it)`);
- a variable rebound to a fresh iterator in between;
- `itertools.tee` results, `repeat`, `cycle`, and `count`;
- loops that run at most once (`for _ in range(1)`), and a consumption followed by leaving the
  loop (`data = list(it)` then `break`);
- consuming the rest of an iterator inside a loop over that iterator itself.

## What a report states

A report states that a single-pass iterator is consumed a second time after a full first pass, so
the second pass sees no items.

Its premises:

- **Single-pass**: the value is one of the iterators listed above. Established from its construction
  or annotation.
- **Full first pass**: the first consumption exhausts it. Established: partial passes (`break`,
  `any` / `all`, `next()`) do not count.
- **Second pass after it**: the second consumption is reachable from the first. Open: reachable
  means some path of the control flow, which the code may never take.

## Why is this bad?
The second pass silently gets an empty iterator: totals become zero, a second report is empty,
and a retry processes nothing. Nothing fails, so the bug is noticed far away from its cause.

## Example
```python
def summarize(lines: list[str]) -> tuple[int, list[str]]:
    rows = (line.strip() for line in lines)
    count = sum(1 for _ in rows)
    kept = [r for r in rows if r]  # MUT106: `rows` was consumed by `sum`
    return count, kept
```

Use instead:
```python
def summarize(lines: list[str]) -> tuple[int, list[str]]:
    rows = [line.strip() for line in lines]  # a list can be iterated any number of times
    count = len(rows)
    kept = [r for r in rows if r]
    return count, kept
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `lint.extend-select = ["MUT106"]` (or `--extend-select MUT106`) enables the rule. It is
  opt-in: selecting the `MUT` prefix does not enable it.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/list-front-insert/

# list-front-insert (OPT121)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Exact · Opt-in · Severity `warning` (slower code) · Proven-safe suggestion (`--fix --include-size-dependent`)

Opt-in: size-dependent `q.insert(0, v)` -> `collections.deque`.

## What it does
Checks loops that insert at the front of a list, `q.insert(0, v)`, and suggests a
`collections.deque` with `appendleft(v)`.

Opt-in and size-dependent: it runs when `extend-select` names it or with
`--include-size-dependent`, which also applies its proven rewrites with `--fix`. A list rebuilt
in every iteration of the loop is not reported: its front insert costs no more than building it.

## What a report states

A report states that inserting at the front of the list (`lst.insert(0, x)`), in a loop, moves
every element each time it runs.

Its premises:

- **Builtin type by construction**: the value is a builtin `list` by its construction (a display, a comprehension,
  `list(...)`). Established: the Soundness lane takes types from constructions only, never from
  annotations.
- **In a loop**: the statement is in the body of a loop. Established by the IR.
- **Rewrite proven safe**: the help says `[safe fix: ...]`, `[proven-safe suggestion: ...]`, or
  `[proven safe; ...]`. A report whose help names a blocking obligation instead (`[not auto-fixable:
  ...]`) lacks this premise and is heuristic whatever the rule's certainty; the proven reports are
  the rule's exact tier.

Not part of the claim: how many times the statement runs (one under a branch inside the loop
counts), and how large the loop or the list is. The message claims no size and no cost estimate. A
loop or a list that the code fixes at 16 or fewer items is not reported, since the rewrite would not
pay off. The exact tier also asks that the data decide how many times the loop runs: the loop steps
through a parameter (`*args` included) or a part of one, the rows of a query, the lines of a file,
or the entries of a directory, as `EFF103`'s Origin establishes them, and the code does not fix or
cap their number. A proven report over any other loop is heuristic, for example over a loop whose
trip count the code fixes at more than 16 or caps with a length test every path to the loop passes,
over the program's structure (an attribute of `self`, a project function's result, `range` of a
configured number, a class's MRO, a module-level list), or in a `while` loop. Such a report is true,
but its loop usually runs a few times, however large the input.

## Why is this bad?
Inserting at the front shifts every element, so building a list this way is quadratic.

## Example
```python
def reverse(items: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    out = []
    for i in items:
        out.insert(0, i)
    return list(out)
```

Use instead:
```python
import collections


def reverse(items: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    out = collections.deque()
    for i in items:
        out.appendleft(i)
    return list(out)
```

## Fix safety
The same obligations as `OPT120`, and the same rewrite of annotations and imports.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/list-front-pop/

# list-front-pop (OPT120)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Exact · Opt-in · Severity `warning` (slower code) · Proven-safe suggestion (`--fix --include-size-dependent`)

Opt-in: size-dependent `q.pop(0)` / `del q[0]` / `q = q[1:]` -> `collections.deque`.

## What it does
Checks loops that remove the first element of a list: `q.pop(0)`, `del q[0]`, and
`q = q[1:]`, and suggests a `collections.deque` with `popleft()`.

Opt-in and size-dependent: it runs when `extend-select` names it or with
`--include-size-dependent`, which also applies its proven rewrites with `--fix`.

The rewrite changes the list's creation to `collections.deque(...)`, rewrites the variable's
`list[...]` annotation to `collections.deque[...]`, and adds `import collections` when needed: in
sorted position among the module's standard-library imports, or after the docstring and
`__future__` imports of a module without other imports.

Not reported: a small display that the loop only drains (`expected = [b"a", b""]` and
`expected.pop(0)` in the loop: it never holds more than its items), and a list rebuilt in every
iteration of the loop.

## What a report states

A report states that removing the first element of the list (`lst.pop(0)`, `del lst[0]`, `lst =
lst[1:]`), in a loop, moves or copies every remaining element each time it runs.

Its premises:

- **Builtin type by construction**: the value is a builtin `list` by its construction (a display, a comprehension,
  `list(...)`). Established: the Soundness lane takes types from constructions only, never from
  annotations.
- **In a loop**: the statement is in the body of a loop. Established by the IR.
- **Rewrite proven safe**: the help says `[safe fix: ...]`, `[proven-safe suggestion: ...]`, or
  `[proven safe; ...]`. A report whose help names a blocking obligation instead (`[not auto-fixable:
  ...]`) lacks this premise and is heuristic whatever the rule's certainty; the proven reports are
  the rule's exact tier.

Not part of the claim: how many times the statement runs (one under a branch inside the loop
counts), and how large the loop or the list is. The message claims no size and no cost estimate. A
loop or a list that the code fixes at 16 or fewer items is not reported, since the rewrite would not
pay off. The exact tier also asks that the data decide how many times the loop runs: the loop steps
through a parameter (`*args` included) or a part of one, the rows of a query, the lines of a file,
or the entries of a directory, as `EFF103`'s Origin establishes them, and the code does not fix or
cap their number. A proven report over any other loop is heuristic, for example over a loop whose
trip count the code fixes at more than 16 or caps with a length test every path to the loop passes,
over the program's structure (an attribute of `self`, a project function's result, `range` of a
configured number, a class's MRO, a module-level list), or in a `while` loop. Such a report is true,
but its loop usually runs a few times, however large the input.

## Why is this bad?
Removing the first element shifts every remaining element, so a queue drained this way is
quadratic. `deque.popleft()` is constant time.

## Example
```python
def bfs(graph: dict[int, list[int]], start: int) -> list[int]:
    queue = [start]
    seen = {start}
    order = []
    while queue:
        node = queue.pop(0)
        order.append(node)
        for child in graph[node]:
            if child not in seen:
                seen.add(child)
                queue.append(child)
    return order
```

Use instead:
```python
import collections


def bfs(graph: dict[int, list[int]], start: int) -> list[int]:
    queue = collections.deque([start])
    seen = {start}
    order = []
    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()
        order.append(node)
        for child in graph[node]:
            if child not in seen:
                seen.add(child)
                queue.append(child)
    return order
```

## Fix safety
Proven safe only when the list is created in the function, never leaves it (not returned,
stored, or passed to other code except read-only builtins such as `len`), and every use has a
`deque` equivalent: no sorting, no slicing, no indexes other than `0` and `-1`, no `==`
against lists, and no text of it (a replacement field of an f-string, `str()`), which differs
for a `deque`. An annotation the rewrite cannot turn into a `deque` one (`Sequence[str]`, a
union) or another annotated declaration of the variable blocks the fix, so that a type checker
accepts the fixed file. So does any other binding of a variable the list reaches, since a type
checker gives the variable one type: `s = [...]` before `s = q`, a later `q = [...]` the loop
never sees, a `for s in ...`, or a parameter `s`.

A `deque` iterator raises `RuntimeError` when the deque changes under it and is another type
than a list iterator: no iterator of the list may be live at a change, consumed by the changing
call (`q.extend(reversed(q))`), or used for more than its elements (`type(iter(q))`). `list(xs)`
of a value that is not a builtin container becomes `deque(list(xs))`, which keeps the length
query `list` makes; `list(**kw)` and `list(*args)` block the fix (`deque` reads a second
argument as `maxlen`), and so does a list a starred target or pattern makes (`first, *q =
items`), which has no display to rewrite. Only `q = q[1:]` is a front pop: `q[1:n]` and
`q[1::2]` are not.

`q.extend(x)` and `q += x` make the same length query of `x` (`__len__`, else
`__length_hint__`), and their `deque` forms do not, so the fix needs an `x` whose query runs no
code: a builtin container, a string, or a `range` (a display, `list(...)`, `range(n)`). Any
other `x` blocks it, a generator expression and the result of a project function among them, and
so does `q.extend(*parts)`.

An operation that raises on the list raises the same exception type on the `deque`, with the
`deque`'s message: `q[0]` of an empty queue raises `IndexError` with `deque index out of range`
instead of `list index out of range`, and `q.remove(x)` of a missing item a `ValueError` that
names a deque. A fix keeps the types of builtin exceptions, not their messages
([what a fix keeps](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/fixes/#safety)).


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/list-quadratic-concat/

# list-quadratic-concat (OPT101)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Exact · Enabled by default · Severity `warning` (slower code) · Safe fix (`--fix`)

Unconditionally profitable `list` quadratic concatenation (`x = x + [e]` -> `x.append(e)`).

## What it does
Checks loops that grow a list by building a new one every iteration, `x = x + [e]`, and
rewrites it to `x.append(e)` (`x.extend([...])` for several elements).

## What a report states

A report states that `x = x + [e]`, in a loop, builds a new list from the whole accumulated list
each time it runs, where appending would change it in place.

Its premises:

- **Builtin type by construction**: the value is a builtin `list` by its construction (a display, a comprehension,
  `list(...)`). Established: the Soundness lane takes types from constructions only, never from
  annotations.
- **Loop-carried**: the result is the value the next iteration starts from. Established by the IR.
- **In a loop**: the statement is in the body of a loop. Established by the IR.
- **Rewrite proven safe**: the help says `[safe fix: ...]`, `[proven-safe suggestion: ...]`, or
  `[proven safe; ...]`. A report whose help names a blocking obligation instead (`[not auto-fixable:
  ...]`) lacks this premise and is heuristic whatever the rule's certainty; the proven reports are
  the rule's exact tier.

Not part of the claim: how many times the statement runs (one under a branch inside the loop
counts), and how large the loop or the list is. The message claims no size and no cost estimate. The
rewrite never makes the code slower, so a loop the code fixes at a few items is reported too.

## Why is this bad?
`x + [e]` copies the whole list, so the loop is quadratic. `append` is amortized constant time
and is never slower, even for one iteration.

## Example
```python
def squares(n: int) -> list[int]:
    out = []
    for i in range(n):
        out = out + [i * i]
    return out
```

Use instead:
```python
def squares(n: int) -> list[int]:
    out = []
    for i in range(n):
        out.append(i * i)
    return out
```

## Fix safety
The fix is applied by `heki check --fix` only when heki proves it safe:

- the list is an exact builtin `list` created in the function, not shared (not a parameter,
  not stored in another object, not captured by a closure, not passed to unknown code);
- no other reference to the old list is live after the statement: no alias, no `for` loop
  iterating it, no `iter(x)` or view;
- evaluating the right-hand side does not rebind or mutate the list;
- no exception handler can observe an older binding of another name aliasing it.

Otherwise the diagnostic explains which proof obligation blocks the fix, and nothing is
rewritten. A disproved candidate is not reported at all: `for v in x: x = x + [v]` terminates,
but `x.append(v)` would loop forever, so heki says nothing there and never touches it. Type
annotations are never trusted.

The fix rewrites a plain `x = x + [...]` statement. For other shapes of the same update (a
parenthesized `x = (x + [i])` or `x = (x) + [i]`, an annotated `x: list = x + [i]`), the
diagnostic says that the rewrite is proven safe and leaves it to be made by hand.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/lock-or-tx-held-across-io/

# lock-or-tx-held-across-io (EFF106)

Family: Execution Effects (EFF) · Heuristic · Opt-in · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Opt-in: `await` or blocking network I/O while holding a `threading` lock or a DB transaction.

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs only when `select` or `extend-select` names its code or name. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

## What it does
Checks for an `await` (also the implicit ones of `async for` and `async with`), or a call
reaching blocking network I/O (directly or through project helpers, including the getter of a
property read), while a `with` block holds a synchronous lock or a database transaction.

The held resource must be type-certain:

- an instance of `threading.Lock`, `RLock`, `Semaphore`, `BoundedSemaphore`, or `Condition`,
  created in `__init__` (`self._lock = threading.Lock()`), at module level, locally, or given
  by an annotated parameter;
- a transaction started by `sqlalchemy.orm.Session.begin()` / `begin_nested()`,
  `Connection.begin()` / `begin_nested()`, `Engine.begin()`, `sqlmodel.Session.begin()`,
  `django.db.transaction.atomic()`, or `psycopg.Connection.transaction()`.

The rule reports the `await` or the call while the resource is certainly held (on every path),
with the call chain to the network I/O as related information. Leaving the `with` block
releases what that block acquired: a re-entrant lock entered again by a nested `with` stays held
until the outer block exits.

It does not report:

- `async with` and async locks (`asyncio.Lock`, `anyio.Lock`, ...);
- objects whose type is not known, or not a registered lock or transaction;
- work after the `with` block, and handlers reached only after the block exited;
- calls offloaded to a thread (`asyncio.to_thread`, `loop.run_in_executor`, ...);
- database queries inside a transaction, local file I/O, or `time.sleep`;
- CLI commands, ASGI lifespan handlers, and tests, as for `EFF101`.

## What a report states

A report states that, while a `with` block holds a synchronous lock or a database transaction, the
statement awaits or reaches blocking network I/O.

Its premises:

- **Holds**: the resource is a `threading` lock or a transaction of the kinds listed above.
  Established: its type is certain (constructed, or an annotated parameter).
- **Inside the block**: the `await` or the call is in the body of the `with` block. Established.
- **Resolves**: each call on the chain is to the function shown, through the calls heki resolves.
  Open through a method call: one candidate implementation that leads on is enough.
- **Reaches**: each function on the chain reaches the next call. Open: one path is enough, and a
  branch heki cannot decide counts as taken; only the branches the caller's arguments switch off,
  and the cases listed above, are left out.

## Why is this bad?
A synchronous lock held across an `await` blocks every thread that wants it until the coroutine
resumes, and a second coroutine acquiring it on the event loop thread deadlocks the loop. Held
across a network request, the lock serializes every waiting thread behind that request. A
transaction held across a request or an `await` keeps its pooled connection checked out and its
row locks taken, which exhausts the pool under load.

## Example
```python
import asyncio
import threading


class Cache:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        self._data: dict[str, bytes] = {}

    async def refresh(self, key: str) -> None:
        with self._lock:
            self._data[key] = await fetch(key)  # EFF106
```

Use instead:
```python
    async def refresh(self, key: str) -> None:
        value = await fetch(key)
        with self._lock:  # hold the lock only for the update
            self._data[key] = value
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `lint.extend-select = ["EFF106"]` (or `--extend-select EFF106`) enables the rule. It is
  opt-in: selecting the `EFF` prefix does not enable it.
- `lint.relax-async-in-tests` applies as for `EFF101`.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/lock-reacquired-while-held/

# lock-reacquired-while-held (EFF109)

Family: Execution Effects (EFF) · Exact · Enabled by default · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

A non-reentrant lock (`threading.Lock`, `asyncio.Lock`) taken again, directly or through a call, while it is held (the thread or task waits for itself).

## What it does
Checks for a non-reentrant lock taken again while it is held: by the function holding it, or by
a function it calls, any number of calls deep.

A lock is non-reentrant when the catalog says so: `threading.Lock`, `asyncio.Lock`,
`asyncio.Condition`, and `multiprocessing.Lock` (`threading.RLock` is reentrant; a
`threading.Condition` uses an `RLock` unless it is given another lock; a semaphore's class does
not say its count). Add your own with `non-reentrant-lock = true` in
`[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]`. `anyio.Lock` is not one of them: taken again by the task holding it,
it raises `RuntimeError` instead of waiting, so the error shows where it happens.

A function holds a lock from a `with` or `async with` over it to the end of that statement, and
from an `acquire()` to a `release()`, on every path. An `acquire()` counts when it is awaited,
or when it blocks without a timeout (`lock.acquire()`, `lock.acquire(True)`). The lock is the
same object on both sides when both name it the same way, through the calls between them:

- an attribute of `self`, or of another parameter (`self._lock`, passed on as `self` or as the
  lock itself);
- a module global, also imported from another module or read on its module (`_LOCK`,
  `locks._LOCK`);
- a variable of an enclosing function that a closure it calls captures.

The calls followed are those that run there, on the same thread or task: plain calls, awaited
coroutines, property getters, generators iterated there, and functions builtins call there
(`sorted(xs, key=self._rank)`). The rule reports the inner acquisition, or the call that leads
to it, with the call chain as related locations.

It does not report:

- a call that only creates a coroutine or a generator (`asyncio.create_task(self.refresh())`),
  a function run on another thread (`asyncio.to_thread`, `loop.run_in_executor`, a
  `threading.Thread` target), and a callable stored or handed to code heki does not follow;
- an acquisition a branch switches off for the call's arguments (`self._close(notify=False)`
  where only `notify` leads to the lock);
- an acquisition behind a test of state the holder changes: an attribute of the lock's owner
  that the holder, or what it calls, changes (`if self._closed: return`,
  `if self._in_own_start(): raise`, in the acquiring function or in one on the way to it), or a
  module global the holder sets (`if _LIB is not None: return _LIB` in a lazy initialization
  under the lock): such code keeps a flag to know whether it holds the lock, which heki does not
  evaluate;
- a lock the code gives back before taking it again, also inside the `with` that took it
  (`self._lock.release()`, then `self._lock.acquire()`), or in a function it calls (a helper
  releasing its caller's lock);
- a lock whose name may be bound to another object before it is taken again
  (`self._lock = threading.Lock()`, `global _LOCK`, `del self._lock`): by the holder, by a
  function the holder calls first, or by the function taking the lock or one on the way to it;
  the name then reaches another lock;
- a lock some function of the module releases without holding it: another thread gives it back
  as a signal, so taking it again waits for that thread, by design;
- `acquire(blocking=False)` and `acquire(timeout=...)`, which return;
- locks whose class is not known, a lock in a local variable handed to a helper, and the same
  lock reached under two different names.

## What a report states

A report states that a function holding a non-reentrant lock attempts to take the same lock
again whenever the reported call or acquisition returns, itself or through the calls it makes on
its thread or task, so the thread or task waits for itself there. A heuristic report states that
the function holding the lock can reach an acquisition of it: some premise below may be open.

Its premises:

- **Non-reentrant**: the lock is an instance of a class the catalog or the configuration flags,
  by the value inferred or an annotation (assumptions R2, R3), and no project class a value of it
  may be binds how it is taken or given back (`acquire`, `release`, `__enter__`, `__exit__`,
  `__aenter__`, `__aexit__`). Open in a heuristic report: a project subclass of the lock class
  binds one of them.
- **Held**: a `with` over it, or an awaited or blocking `acquire()`, holds it on every path to
  the reported call or inner acquisition, and nothing the holder runs on the way gives it back or
  binds its name: neither the holder nor a function it calls, nor the code iterating the holder
  when it is a generator. Open in a heuristic report: the holder is a generator that suspends on
  the way, at a `yield` or `yield from`, so the code iterating it may give the lock back before
  it resumes; in an async generator every `await` counts as such a suspension.
- **Same lock**: both sides name the lock the same way, through the arguments of each call, and
  no function on the way may bind that name or give a lock back under it. Established for every
  report.
- **Every implementation**: each call on the chain has as its targets every implementation it
  can run (assumptions R1, R2, and R5), each run as written at the call (no decorator that may
  replace it, its name bound to one definition), and each has the fact below. Open in a
  heuristic report: through a method call, one candidate implementation that takes the lock is
  enough.
- **Every return**: each function on the chain attempts the next call, or the acquisition, on
  every path on which it returns normally, exception edges into handlers included. Open in a
  heuristic report: one path is enough, and a branch heki cannot decide counts as taken; only
  the branches the caller's arguments switch off, and those behind a test of state the holder
  changes, are left out.

Not part of the claim: what another thread or task does with the lock's name while it is held,
and whether the call is reached at all (the claim is anchored at it, so a branch around it in the
holder does not matter).

## Why is this bad?
A thread that takes a `threading.Lock` it already holds waits for itself forever, and so does an
`asyncio` task taking an `asyncio.Lock` it holds: the lock never becomes free, and every other
thread or task that needs it stops behind it. The retake is usually hidden in a helper that
takes the lock for its own callers, called from a method that already holds it, often only on
an error path.

## Example
```python
import threading


class Registry:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        self._items: dict[str, int] = {}

    def size(self) -> int:
        with self._lock:
            return len(self._items)

    def add(self, key: str) -> int:
        with self._lock:
            self._items[key] = 1
            return self.size()  # EFF109
```

Use instead:
```python
    def _size_locked(self) -> int:
        return len(self._items)

    def size(self) -> int:
        with self._lock:
            return self._size_locked()

    def add(self, key: str) -> int:
        with self._lock:
            self._items[key] = 1
            return self._size_locked()
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]` entries with `non-reentrant-lock = true` add lock classes.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-carried-concat/

# loop-carried-concat (DATA101)

Family: Data Pipelines (DATA) · Exact · Enabled by default · Severity `warning` (slower code) · No automatic fix

Loop-carried quadratic `pandas.concat` / `numpy.vstack` / `numpy.append` accumulation.

## What it does
Checks loops that grow a DataFrame or array by re-concatenating it on every iteration:
`df = pd.concat([df, chunk])`, `arr = np.vstack([arr, row])`, `arr = np.append(arr, x)`,
`arr = np.r_[arr, x]` (and `np.c_`), and the other quadratic reallocations of the ecosystem knowledge base. Only loop-carried
accumulation is reported: the result feeds the next iteration and is computed from the previous
value, also when it grows on some iterations only. An update through a project function counts
when that function returns a reallocation of the argument carrying the previous value, directly
or through further helpers (`acc = grow(acc)` where `grow` returns `np.append(acc, x)`), also
when an `isinstance` test picks the method (`if isinstance(g, Grower): acc = g.grow(acc)`) or an
offloading API runs it (`acc = await asyncio.to_thread(grow, acc)`); a helper that reallocates
something else and returns its argument unchanged does not. One-off
concatenations inside a loop are not reported, also on a branch that leaves the variable
unchanged otherwise (`if step: x = np.append(edges, last)`), nor is writing into a buffer passed
as `out=` (`out = np.concatenate(([a], [b]), out=out)` reuses the same buffer): the previous
value must be among the data that is combined. A list holding it counts (`pd.concat([df] +
parts)`), arithmetic on it does not (`x = np.concatenate((x - np.outer(u, v), [a]))`,
`q = np.concatenate([[w * q[0]], w * q[1:]])`): every entry of the new value changed, so each
iteration already works in proportion to the value's size, and there are no unchanged parts to
collect and combine once. A loop whose trip count the code fixes is not reported either
(`for is_p_wave in [False, True]`, `for _ in range(steps)` with `steps = 8`): it copies a fixed
number of times, whatever the input.

## What a report states

A report states that the value is rebuilt from its previous value by the reallocating call on every
iteration of the loop that completes, so each such iteration copies all of it. Its exact reports
(those the rule shows by default once it is certified) also name what the loop steps through: a
parameter, a part of one, the rows of a query, the lines of a file, or the entries of a directory.

Its premises:

- **Loop-carried on every path**: every path around the back edge carries the new value, computed from the
  previous one (no path resets the variable). Open in a heuristic report: one path that updates
  it is enough.
- **Every iteration**: the reallocating call returns on every iteration that completes,
  exception edges into handlers included. Open in a heuristic report: one that runs on some
  iterations only counts.
- **Origin**: the loop steps through items the data decides (as for `EFF103`), and the code does
  not fix its trip count. Open in a heuristic report: a trip count heki cannot bound counts as
  data-sized.
- **Reallocates**: the call copies all of its inputs into a new value on every call, as the
  ecosystem catalog describes it. Open in a heuristic report: a project function that
  reallocates the value it is handed may return another value on some path.

Not part of the claim: how large the value grows. An exact report gives no advice: collecting
the parts first does not fit a loop that reads the value on every iteration.

## Why is this bad?
Every concatenation copies everything accumulated so far, so the loop is quadratic in the total
size.

## Example
```python
import pandas as pd


def load(chunks: list[pd.DataFrame]) -> pd.DataFrame:
    df = pd.DataFrame()
    for chunk in chunks:
        df = pd.concat([df, chunk])  # DATA101
    return df
```

Use instead:
```python
def load(chunks: list[pd.DataFrame]) -> pd.DataFrame:
    return pd.concat(chunks) if chunks else pd.DataFrame()  # `pd.concat([])` raises
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-db-query/

# loop-db-query (EFF103)

Family: Execution Effects (EFF) · Exact · Enabled by default · Severity `warning` (slower code) · No automatic fix

A loop over data whose every iteration sends a database statement; its heuristic reports, a loop that can run a database query on every iteration.

## What it does
Checks loops that run a database query on every iteration:
`cursor.execute(...)`, `session.execute(...)` (awaited ones on async sessions and connections
too), the SQLAlchemy `Query` methods that run the query (`all`, `first`, `one`, `count`, ...)
and iterating a `Query` (`for row in session.query(User):` in an outer loop, a comprehension,
`list(query)`),
the Django `QuerySet` methods that run the query (`get`, `first`, `count`, ... and their `a*`
variants), `pymongo`, `redis`, and DynamoDB commands, the `execute()` of a supabase-py / postgrest
query, `pandas.read_sql`, and project functions
that reach them, also when an offloading API runs them on a worker thread per item (`await
asyncio.to_thread(load, i)`, a function decorated with `@sync_to_async`, a `concurrent.futures`
pool's `executor.submit(load, i)` in a loop and `executor.map(load, ids)`), including the getter of a property read in the loop and a generator iterated in
the loop (its body runs where it is iterated, as for `EFF101`). A function a builtin calls once
per item runs in a loop as long as the items (`sorted(users, key=lambda u: score(conn, u))`,
`list(map(load, ids))`; see `EFF102` for the builtins and the items whose number the code fixes).

It does not report reading the rows of a statement already executed (`cursor.fetchone()`),
calls that only build a query (`session.query(User).filter(...)`, `QuerySet.filter(...)`,
`Redis.pipeline()`), the bulk APIs, which send many rows in one statement and are called per
batch by design (`QuerySet.bulk_create`, `in_bulk`, pymongo's `insert_many`, `bulk_write`), DDL
statements (SQL starting with `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, or `PRAGMA` run by a DB-API
`execute` / `executemany` / `executescript` or SQLAlchemy's `exec_driver_sql`, also inside a
helper the loop calls: a literal, an f-string, `%`, or `.format()` whose literal start is one,
SQLAlchemy's `text()` of one, and the statements of a module's string constants: the items of a
tuple, the pieces `.split(";")` / `.splitlines()` cut a schema into), migration code
(`upgrade` / `downgrade` functions, files under `migrations/` or `alembic/`), the ORM packages'
own implementation, or loops whose size the code fixes when no data-sized loop is around them
(`for ident in enumerate((1, 2), 1)`, `zip(order, ["m1", "m2"])`, a name bound to a small
display; see `EFF102`).

As for `EFF102`, a query that only runs while an attribute is unset, which the code then sets
(`if self._columns is None: self._columns = cursor.execute(...)`), runs once per object and is
not reported when the loop does not construct the object; so does one in a
`functools.cached_property` getter, and one behind a module global runs once per process. A
query that only runs while a local variable the loop carries is unset or a first-iteration flag
holds (`if first: cursor.execute(...); first = False`), or that every way on from leaves the
loop (`cursor.execute(...)` followed by `return`, `break`, or `raise`), runs once per run of the
loop. A call whose arguments switch off the branch with the query (a constant, a literal
default, a test the caller has made) is not followed into it.

A report is exact when the loop sends a database statement on every iteration that completes,
over items whose number the data decides: a parameter (or an attribute or element of one), the
rows of a query, the lines of a file, or the entries of a directory. The statement is sent by the
call in the loop itself, or at the end of a chain of functions each of which makes the next call
on every path on which it returns.

Each step is established, not assumed:

- the loop steps through items of such an origin, through wrappers that keep them (`sorted`,
  `list`, `filter`, slices, dict views, the components of `enumerate` and `zip`); through `map`
  or a comprehension's element only their number carries. The items a project function returns
  are those every `return` of it gives, read from its module's own code: the rows of a query it
  runs (also on a parameter annotated with the connection's class) or of another function of
  the module it returns, whether the loop calls it directly, awaits it, calls it through a
  `functools.partial` object, or awaits an API that hands back what it returns (`await
  asyncio.to_thread(load_rows, conn)`). A loop whose number of iterations the code fixes gives no
  exact report, whatever the number: a constant range, a display, or rows whose number the query
  fixes (a `LIMIT` with a literal count at the end of its text, `fetchmany` of a constant, a
  `SELECT` of aggregates only without `GROUP BY`), in the loop or in the function returning
  them;
- the call runs on every iteration that completes, exception edges included: an `except`
  handler that `continue`s before it is an iteration without it;
- every implementation each call on the chain can run is followed and makes the next call on
  every path on which it returns, as for `EFF101`;
- the last call sends a statement on every call, as the ecosystem catalog describes it: not a
  `Session.get` the identity map may answer, a `flush()` / `commit()` that sends only pending
  changes, or a Django query set's `count()` that may read its cache; DDL, bulk APIs, and calls
  that only build a query are left out.

Every other report the rule finds is heuristic: items whose origin heki does not establish, a
path heki cannot decide, a call it cannot resolve to every implementation, a database call that
sends a statement only in some state, a function an API runs for the call (a worker of
`asyncio.to_thread` or of a pool, which may run it after the call returns, or a builtin calling
it per item).

## What a report states

A report states that every iteration of the loop that completes sends a database statement: the
one named, or, when the implementations a call can run reach different ones, each with its
implementation. A heuristic report states that every iteration of the loop can run a database
query (or a command of a database client) through the call shown: some premise below may be
open.

Its premises:

- **Origin**: the loop steps through items of a parameter, the rows of a query, the lines of a
  file, or the entries of a directory, also as a project function returns them, and the code does
  not fix their number. Open in a heuristic report: a loop whose size the code does not fix at 16
  or fewer counts, and a size heki cannot bound counts as data-sized. Not followed, so open: the
  rows a module global holds (`ROWS = conn.execute(...).fetchall()`), the rows a function returns
  of a value another module gives it or of a parameter without an annotation, a function calling
  itself, and a chain of more than eight functions each returning what the next returns.
- **Every iteration**: the call runs on every iteration that completes, exception edges into
  handlers included. Open in a heuristic report: the call counts as running on every iteration
  unless heki shows that it runs once per object, per process, or per run of the loop (the cases
  above).
- **Every return**: each function on the chain has made the next call on every path on which it
  returns normally. Open in a heuristic report: one path that reaches the next call is enough,
  and a branch heki cannot decide counts as taken; only the branches the caller's arguments
  switch off, and the cases listed above, are left out.
- **Every implementation**: each call on the chain has as its targets every implementation it
  can run (assumptions R1, R2, and R5), each with the fact. Open in a heuristic report: through a
  method call, one candidate implementation that leads on is enough.
- **Sends**: the last call sends a statement on every call, as the ecosystem catalog describes it
  (R3). Open in a heuristic report: a call that sends one only in some state of its session
  (`emits` in the catalog: `Session.get` answered by the identity map, `Session.flush` without
  pending changes).

Not part of the claim: how many items the loop has, how slow the statement is, and whether the
statements could be batched.

## Why is this bad?
One round trip per item makes the run time grow with the number of rows and with the network
latency to the database. A single batched query is usually orders of magnitude faster.

## Example
```python
import sqlite3


def names(cursor: sqlite3.Cursor, ids: list[int]) -> list[str]:
    out = []
    for i in ids:
        cursor.execute("SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = ?", (i,))  # EFF103
        out.append(cursor.fetchone()[0])
    return out
```

The same query under `if i > 0:` is a heuristic report: it runs on some iterations only.

Use instead:
```python
import sqlite3


def names(cursor: sqlite3.Cursor, ids: list[int]) -> list[str]:
    if not ids:
        return []
    marks = ",".join("?" * len(ids))
    cursor.execute(f"SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE id IN ({marks})", ids)
    name_of = dict(cursor.fetchall())
    return [name_of[i] for i in ids]  # `KeyError` for an unknown ID (the loop: `TypeError`)
```

The query returns each matching row once and in no particular order, so the result is rebuilt
from the IDs: in their order, with repeated IDs repeated. A database caps the number of
parameters in one statement; split a long list of IDs into chunks.

## Known limitations
A call through a name the project binds to another object in a way `EFF101` lists among its
known limitations (`mock.patch` outside tests, `sys.modules`) still counts as running its
definition here too.

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-invariant-container-rebuild/

# loop-invariant-container-rebuild (OPT130)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Exact · Opt-in · Severity `warning` (slower code) · Proven-safe suggestion (`--fix --include-size-dependent`)

Opt-in: size-dependent loop-invariant container reconstruction (`e in set(keys)`).

## What it does
Checks loops that rebuild the same container on every iteration just to test membership,
`e in set(keys)` (also `list(...)`, `tuple(...)`, `dict(...)`), and suggests building it once
before the loop.

Opt-in and size-dependent: it runs when `extend-select` names it or with
`--include-size-dependent`, which also applies its proven rewrites with `--fix`.

## What a report states

A report states that a builtin constructor (`set(keys)`, `list(...)`, `tuple(...)`, `dict(...)`),
in a loop, builds a new container for a membership test each time it runs.

Its premises:

- **Builtin type by construction**: the constructor builds a builtin container of a known type.
  Established: heki reports only a call of the builtin constructor. What it builds the container
  from may be of an unknown type, which blocks the rewrite (`ZeroTripExceptionSafe`): "Rewrite
  proven safe" is then open.
- **In a loop**: the statement is in the body of a loop. Established by the IR.
- **Rewrite proven safe**: the help says `[safe fix: ...]`, `[proven-safe suggestion: ...]`, or
  `[proven safe; ...]`. A report whose help names a blocking obligation instead (`[not auto-fixable:
  ...]`) lacks this premise and is heuristic whatever the rule's certainty; the proven reports are
  the rule's exact tier.

Not part of the claim: how many times the statement runs (one under a branch inside the loop
counts), and how large the loop or the container is. The message claims no size and no cost
estimate. A loop or a container that the code fixes at 16 or fewer items is not reported, since the
rewrite would not pay off. The exact tier also asks that the data decide how many times the loop
runs: the loop steps through a parameter (`*args` included) or a part of one, the rows of a query,
the lines of a file, or the entries of a directory, as `EFF103`'s Origin establishes them, and the
code does not fix or cap their number. A proven report over any other loop is heuristic, for example
over a loop whose trip count the code fixes at more than 16 or caps with a length test every path to
the loop passes, over the program's structure (an attribute of `self`, a project function's result,
`range` of a configured number, a class's MRO, a module-level list), or in a `while` loop. Such a
report is true, but its loop usually runs a few times, however large the input.

The rewrite also needs what the container is built from to stay the same during the loop
(`ValueLoopInvariant`), which only a proven report establishes.

## Why is this bad?
The container is rebuilt from scratch on every iteration, which costs as much as the scan it
was meant to avoid.

## Example
```python
def matches(items: list[int], keys: list[int]) -> int:
    hits = 0
    for i in items:
        if i in set(keys):
            hits += 1
    return hits
```

Use instead:
```python
def matches(items: list[int], keys: list[int]) -> int:
    keys_set = set(keys)
    hits = 0
    for i in items:
        if i in keys_set:
            hits += 1
    return hits
```

## Fix safety
Proven safe only when the rebuilt expression is a builtin constructor without side effects,
every value it reads is bound outside the loop and not changed inside it, and building it before
the loop cannot raise even when the loop runs zero times (hashable builtin elements). The
container must be used by the membership test only: `(tmp := list(keys))` followed by
`tmp.clear()` would clear the one shared container. Calls with `*` arguments (`list(*args)`
passes the elements of `args`) and method calls with arguments are not hoisted.

Not reported when the loop runs a fixed small number of times, when the rebuilt container is
small whatever the input (`set(paths[:2])`, `tuple(".;:")`), or when nothing is rebuilt:
`tuple(t)` of a tuple returns `t` itself.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-linear-dedup/

# loop-linear-dedup (OPT111)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Exact · Opt-in · Severity `warning` (slower code) · Proven-safe suggestion (`--fix --include-size-dependent`)

Opt-in: size-dependent `if v not in seen: seen.append(v)` -> auxiliary `set`.

## What it does
Checks the de-duplication idiom `if v not in seen: seen.append(v)` inside a loop and suggests
keeping an auxiliary `set` next to the list.

Opt-in and size-dependent: it runs when `extend-select` names it or with
`--include-size-dependent`, which also applies its proven rewrites with `--fix`.

## What a report states

A report states that `if v not in seen: seen.append(v)`, in a loop, scans the list each time it
runs.

Its premises:

- **Builtin type by construction**: the value is a builtin `list` by its construction (a display, a comprehension,
  `list(...)`). Established: the Soundness lane takes types from constructions only, never from
  annotations.
- **In a loop**: the statement is in the body of a loop. Established by the IR.
- **Rewrite proven safe**: the help says `[safe fix: ...]`, `[proven-safe suggestion: ...]`, or
  `[proven safe; ...]`. A report whose help names a blocking obligation instead (`[not auto-fixable:
  ...]`) lacks this premise and is heuristic whatever the rule's certainty; the proven reports are
  the rule's exact tier.

Not part of the claim: how many times the statement runs (one under a branch inside the loop
counts), and how large the loop or the list is. The message claims no size and no cost estimate. A
loop or a list that the code fixes at 16 or fewer items is not reported, since the rewrite would not
pay off. The exact tier also asks that the data decide how many times the loop runs: the loop steps
through a parameter (`*args` included) or a part of one, the rows of a query, the lines of a file,
or the entries of a directory, as `EFF103`'s Origin establishes them, and the code does not fix or
cap their number. A proven report over any other loop is heuristic, for example over a loop whose
trip count the code fixes at more than 16 or caps with a length test every path to the loop passes,
over the program's structure (an attribute of `self`, a project function's result, `range` of a
configured number, a class's MRO, a module-level list), or in a `while` loop. Such a report is true,
but its loop usually runs a few times, however large the input.

## Why is this bad?
The membership test scans the list, so de-duplicating `n` items costs `n²` comparisons.

## Example
```python
def unique(values: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    seen = []
    for v in values:
        if v not in seen:
            seen.append(v)
    return seen
```

Use instead:
```python
def unique(values: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    seen = []
    seen_set = set()
    for v in values:
        if v not in seen_set:
            seen.append(v)
            seen_set.add(v)
    return seen
```

## Fix safety
Proven safe only when the list is an exact builtin list owned by the function, the paired
`append` is its only change inside the loop (a removal would make the set stale), no other live
reference could change it, and every element and probe is a hashable builtin scalar.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-linear-list-lookup/

# loop-linear-list-lookup (OPT112)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Heuristic · Off by default · Severity `warning` (slower code) · No automatic fix

Size-dependent `list.index` / `list.remove` / `list.count` inside a loop (repeated linear scans).

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs when `select` or `extend-select` names its code or name, and with `lint.heuristic = true` (`--heuristic`) also by default and for its prefixes and `ALL`. Of 50 sampled reports (round 3, 2026-11-21), 90% were right about the code. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

## What it does
Checks `list.index()`, `list.remove()`, and `list.count()` calls that run on every iteration
of a loop, on a list that outlives the iteration.

The receiver must certainly be a builtin `list`: a list display or comprehension, `list(...)`,
or a `list[...]` / `List[...]` annotation on a parameter, a local, or a class attribute
(`self.items`). Calls on a `set`, a `str`, a project class, or a receiver of unknown type are
not reported. Neither are:

- loops whose size does not depend on the data: small constant ranges and displays
  (`for i in range(3)`, `for s in SUFFIXES` with `SUFFIXES = (".py", ".pyi")`, also through
  `enumerate` / `zip` / `reversed` / `sorted` / `.items()` and `range(ATTEMPTS - 1)` with a
  constant `ATTEMPTS`), retry loops, and daemon polling loops; the iterable of a `for` loop,
  which runs once;
- lists built in the iteration (`parts = [...]` inside the loop) and lists of the loop element
  (`row.cells.index(x)`);
- small lists: a display of at most 16 items that nothing grows (the loop may shrink it with
  `remove()` / `pop()` or replace its items), in the function, as a module global (also of
  another module: `LEVELS = ["low", "mid", "high"]`), or as an attribute its class and
  subclasses only ever assign such a display (`self.preferred = [",", ";"]`, a class
  attribute); also a list the code builds from a fixed iterable (`list(range(7))`, `[c for c
  in LABELS if overflow.get(c)]`) or fills a fixed number of times (`ids.append(card["id"])`
  for each of at most 6 cards a test allowed). A display handed to code that may grow it (any
  call but read-only builtins; a `*items` argument passes the items only) is not small;
- calls after which the loop always ends (`return items.index(x)`, a `break` on every path);
- `index(x, start)`, which scans from a position that usually moves forward.

## What a report states

A report states that `xs.index(...)`, `xs.remove(...)`, or `xs.count(...)`, in a loop, scans the
list each time it runs (`count` scans all of it; `index` and `remove` scan up to the first match).

Its premises:

- **List**: the receiver is a `list`, by construction or annotation (assumption R2).
- **In a loop**: the call is in the body of a loop that can run it again on the same list.
  Established. How many times it runs is not part of the claim: a call under a branch counts.
- **Data-sized**: the code does not fix the sizes the cost depends on (the loop's and the
  container's) at 16 or fewer. Open: a size heki cannot bound counts as data-sized.

## Why is this bad?
Each call scans the list from the start (and `remove()` also shifts the elements after the
removed one), so the loop costs the product of the loop size and the list size: O(n²) when both
grow with the input. A `dict` or `set` built once before the loop answers each lookup in
constant time, and `collections.Counter` counts every value in one pass.

## Example
```python
def ranks(names: list[str], winners: list[str]) -> list[int]:
    return [names.index(w) for w in winners]


def drop(items: list[int], unwanted: list[int]) -> None:
    for x in unwanted:
        items.remove(x)
```

Use instead:
```python
def ranks(names: list[str], winners: list[str]) -> list[int]:
    position = {}
    for i, name in enumerate(names):
        position.setdefault(name, i)  # the first index, as `list.index`
    return [position[w] for w in winners]  # `KeyError` where `index` raised `ValueError`


def drop(items: list[int], unwanted: list[int]) -> None:
    gone = set(unwanted)
    items[:] = [x for x in items if x not in gone]
```

The rewrites are not drop-in replacements: `remove()` drops only the first occurrence of each
value and raises `ValueError` for a missing one, and the values must be hashable.

The advice follows what the loop does with the list. Removals can wait for one rebuild after
the loop only when the loop reads the list nowhere else (a membership test guarding the removal,
`if x in items: items.remove(x)`, aside); when it iterates, tests, indexes, or passes on the list
after a removal (a greedy match over the remaining values), the help advises a `set` or a
`dict` with constant-time deletion instead. An index or a count built once before the loop stays
right only while the loop does not change the list, in place or through a project function it
hands the list to (`change(names)` where `change` calls `names.reverse()`); otherwise the
help advises keeping it up to date with each change.

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-linear-membership/

# loop-linear-membership (OPT110)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Exact · Opt-in · Severity `warning` (slower code) · Proven-safe suggestion (`--fix --include-size-dependent`)

Opt-in: size-dependent `e in lst` inside a loop -> hoist `set` outside loop.

## What it does
Checks membership tests against a list or tuple inside a loop, `e in lst`, where the list does
not change during the loop, and suggests building a `set` once before the loop.

This is a size-dependent rewrite, and the rule is opt-in: it runs when `extend-select` names it
or with `heki check --include-size-dependent`, which also applies its proven rewrites with
`--fix`. Not reported:

- small containers: at most 16 items that nothing grows, whatever the items are
  (`x in ("a", "b")`, `x in [b"1", b"2"]`, also through a name bound to one, a comprehension
  over one, or `list(range(5))`);
- lists whose elements are dicts, lists, or sets: no `set` can hold them.

## What a report states

A report states that the membership test `e in lst`, in a loop, scans the list (or tuple) each
time it runs.

Its premises:

- **Builtin type by construction**: the value is a builtin `list` or `tuple` by its construction (a display, a
  comprehension, `list(...)`). Established: the Soundness lane takes types from constructions only,
  never from annotations.
- **In a loop**: the statement is in the body of a loop. Established by the IR.
- **Rewrite proven safe**: the help says `[safe fix: ...]`, `[proven-safe suggestion: ...]`, or
  `[proven safe; ...]`. A report whose help names a blocking obligation instead (`[not auto-fixable:
  ...]`) lacks this premise and is heuristic whatever the rule's certainty; the proven reports are
  the rule's exact tier.

Not part of the claim: how many times the statement runs (one under a branch inside the loop
counts), and how large the loop or the list is. The message claims no size and no cost estimate. A
loop or a list that the code fixes at 16 or fewer items is not reported, since the rewrite would not
pay off. The exact tier also asks that the data decide how many times the loop runs: the loop steps
through a parameter (`*args` included) or a part of one, the rows of a query, the lines of a file,
or the entries of a directory, as `EFF103`'s Origin establishes them, and the code does not fix or
cap their number. A proven report over any other loop is heuristic, for example over a loop whose
trip count the code fixes at more than 16 or caps with a length test every path to the loop passes,
over the program's structure (an attribute of `self`, a project function's result, `range` of a
configured number, a class's MRO, a module-level list), or in a `while` loop. Such a report is true,
but its loop usually runs a few times, however large the input. Whether a `set` can replace the list
is not part of the claim either: elements that cannot be hashed, or a list that changes during the
loop, block the rewrite (the help names the obligation); the scan happens either way.

## Why is this bad?
`e in lst` scans the list, so the loop costs the product of both sizes. A set lookup is
constant time once the set exists.

## Example
```python
def allowed(items: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    ok = list(range(0, 1000, 3))
    return [i for i in items if i in ok]
```

Use instead:
```python
def allowed(items: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    ok = set(range(0, 1000, 3))
    return [i for i in items if i in ok]
```

## Fix safety
Proven safe only when:

- the container is an exact `list` / `tuple` bound outside the loop and not changed inside it
  (a list mutated in the loop would make the hoisted set stale);
- every element is an `int`, `str`, `bytes`, `bool`, or `float`: building the set cannot raise
  even when the loop runs zero times, and hashing agrees with `==`;
- the probe value is of those types too (an object with a custom `__eq__` could match list
  elements a set lookup never compares with).

A `list[int]` annotation is never trusted: a list subclass can override `__contains__`.

Not reported when the container is small whatever the input, or when the loop runs a fixed
small number of times (`for i in range(3):`): building the set costs about as much as the scans
it saves.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/loop-unpooled-client/

# loop-unpooled-client (EFF102)

Family: Execution Effects (EFF) · Exact · Enabled by default · Severity `warning` (slower code) · No automatic fix

A loop over data whose every iteration makes an unpooled HTTP/DB/RPC client or a sessionless request; its heuristic reports, a loop that can make one on every iteration.

## What it does
Checks loops that allocate a network or database client on every iteration: module-level
request helpers that open a new connection per call (`requests.get`, `httpx.get`), client
constructors, sync and async (`requests.Session()`, `httpx.AsyncClient()`,
`aiohttp.ClientSession()`, `boto3.client(...)`), connection factories (`sqlite3.connect`,
`redis.Redis`, `create_async_engine`, ...), and connection pools (`psycopg_pool.ConnectionPool`),
directly or through project functions,
including the getter of a property read in the loop (`self.client.get(url)` where the `client`
getter builds a new client).

A function a builtin calls once per item runs in a loop too: the function handed to `map`,
`filter`, `itertools.starmap`, `itertools.filterfalse`, and `functools.reduce`, and the `key` of
`sorted`, `list.sort`, `min`, `max`, and `itertools.groupby` (`list(map(fetch, urls))`), whether
it is a lambda, a project function, a bound method, or a `functools.partial` of one. The loop is
as long as the items, which are sized as a `for` loop's iterable: `map(fetch, ("a", "b"))` is
not reported, nor is `max(a, b, key=fetch)`, which compares two values. A lambda written in the
same function as another lambda is not followed: every lambda of a function has the same name
(`f.<locals>.<lambda>`), and heki keeps one summary per name.

A function a `concurrent.futures` pool runs counts the same way, on a `ThreadPoolExecutor`, a
`ProcessPoolExecutor`, or a value typed with their `Executor` base: `executor.submit(fetch, url)`
in a loop is a call of `fetch` on every iteration, and `executor.map(fetch, urls)` calls it once
per item of its iterables, also through a `functools.partial`. So does
`loop.run_in_executor(executor, fetch, url)` in a loop. An executor whose class heki does not
know runs nothing heki follows.

The iterable of a `for` loop is evaluated once and is not reported; neither are calls in
loops whose size the code fixes, when no data-sized loop is around them: displays of at most 16
items (also through a name or a module constant bound to one that nothing in the project
grows, a tuple whatever other code does with it short of rebinding it, and through
`enumerate` / `zip` / `reversed` / `sorted` / `.items()`), `range` of integer constants with at
most 16 steps (`range(ATTEMPTS - 1)`), what a builtin constructor, a comprehension, or a fixed
loop of `append`s makes of those (`list(range(7))`, `[n.upper() for n in ("a", "b")]`), slices
with a constant bound (`for case in cases[:3]`), iterables a length test on every path to the
loop caps (`if len(cases) > 3: raise ...`), a `while` loop over a counter the code starts,
steps, and limits with constants (`i = 1` ... `while i < 6:` ... `i += 1`, at most 16 times),
retry loops, and daemon polling loops.

A retry loop repeats one attempt: its body leaves the loop on success or sleeps in an exception
handler, and it runs over a small constant range or a target named like `attempt` / `retry`
(also one name of a tuple target: `for attempt, proxy in enumerate(proxies)`). A loop that
waits on every path back to its test is paced by time, as polls and retries are: a `while` loop,
or a `for` loop whose body never reads its target (`for _ in range(30):`), in which every
iteration sleeps or waits with a timeout (`time.sleep(5)`, `stop.wait(1)`, in a coroutine
`await asyncio.sleep(5)`; `sleep(0)` only yields, and a sleep an exception can skip or a
coroutine does not await does not count). A daemon polling loop runs until a
flag or an event says to stop (`while self._running:`, `while not self._stopped:`, `while not
stop_event.is_set():`), or is a `while True:` loop that waits on every iteration. A `for` loop
reading its target steps through items, also when it sleeps per item.

A client that is only created while an attribute is unset, which the code then sets (lazy
initialization: `if not self._sock: self._sock = connect()`, `if self._sock: return` before
connecting, `if not hasattr(self, "_sock"):`, a `None` test of `getattr(self, "_sock", None)`,
or the `except AttributeError:` clause of a `try` reading `self._sock`; the store may be
`setattr` or `object.__setattr__`), is created once per object, not on every iteration: the call is not
reported unless a data-sized loop around it constructs the object in each iteration
(`Connection().send(cmd)`); `conn.send(cmd)` on a connection made before the loop, taken from
a pool, or held by the receiver is not reported. The receiver of a bound method, the arguments a
`functools.partial` holds, and the items a builtin passes are no new objects either:
`map(self.fetch, urls)`, where `fetch` sets `self._session` once, is not reported. A
`functools.cached_property` getter (also imported through a module that re-exports it, such as
`kombu.utils.cached_property`) runs once per instance in the same way, and a lazy
initialization of a module global (`global _session`) once per process.

A client created only while a local variable the loop carries is unset (`if conn is None: conn
= connect()`, `conn = conn or connect()`), or only while a first-iteration flag holds (`if
first: ...; first = False`), is created once per run of the loop, and so is one created where
every way on leaves the loop (`return s.get(url)`, `connect(); break`, `raise` after it). Still
reported: a variable or flag set back in the loop (also by an `except` handler), or set there to
a value the branch does not compute (`prev = row`, which may be `None`), a global the function
also sets back to `None` (before the test, or after the initialization), a branch that does not always set it, a loop around that starts it unset again in each iteration, and a `break` out of
an inner loop, which runs again in each iteration of the outer one.

A call whose arguments switch off the branch that creates the client is not followed into
it: `load(name, cache=False)` does not reach the `urlopen` under `if cache:` in `load`. This
covers constant arguments and the literal defaults of omitted ones (`False`, `None`, `0`, `""`,
empty displays), tests the caller has already made on the same value (`isinstance`, `is None`,
truthiness), and wrappers that pass the value on.

## What a report states

A report states that every iteration of the loop that completes makes a new client, session,
connection, or pool through the call shown: the allocating call named, or, when the
implementations a call can run reach different ones, or a function makes the client with
different calls, each with the function that makes it. A heuristic
report states that every iteration of the loop can allocate a new client (or open a new
connection) through the call shown: some premise below may be open.

Its premises:

- **Origin**: the loop steps through items of a parameter, the rows of a query, the lines of a
  file, or the entries of a directory, also as a project function returns them, and the code does
  not fix their number. Open in a heuristic report: a loop whose size the code does not fix at 16
  or fewer counts, and a size heki cannot bound counts as data-sized.
- **Every iteration**: the call returns on every iteration that completes, exception edges into
  handlers included. Open in a heuristic report: the call counts as running on every iteration
  unless heki shows that it runs once per object, per process, or per run of the loop (the cases
  above), and a builtin's call once per item (`map(fetch, urls)`) counts.
- **Every return**: each function on the chain has made the next call on every path on which it
  returns normally, and the last call returned there: a constructor that raised into a handler
  that then returns may have made no client. A function whose catalog calls make a client on
  every path on which it returns normally, one returning on each (a handler that makes the
  client another way when the first call raised), has the fact. Open in a heuristic report: one
  path that reaches the next call is enough, and a branch heki cannot decide counts as taken;
  only the branches the caller's arguments switch off, and the cases listed above, are left out.
- **Every implementation**: each call on the chain has as its targets every implementation it
  can run (assumptions R1, R2, and R5), each with the fact. Open in a heuristic report: through a
  method call, one candidate implementation that leads on is enough.
- **Allocates**: the last call makes a new client, session, connection, or pool on every call
  that returns, as the ecosystem catalog describes it (R3), for every argument heki cannot
  evaluate (R6). Open in a heuristic report: a call whose case an argument from the caller can
  select (`openai.OpenAI(http_client=client)` with the client handed in reuses it).

Not part of the claim: how many items the loop has, and what a client costs.

## Why is this bad?
