Each new client pays for DNS, TCP, and TLS setup again and throws its connection pool away.
In a loop this dominates the run time and exhausts sockets.

## Example
```python
import requests


def fetch_all(urls: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    out = []
    for url in urls:
        out.append(requests.get(url).text)  # EFF102: a new connection per iteration
    return out
```

Use instead:
```python
def fetch_all(urls: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    with requests.Session() as session:
        return [session.get(url).text for url in urls]
```

A reused client keeps state from one request to the next. A `requests.Session` persists the
cookies that responses set across all requests made from it, and sends the `auth` and `headers`
set on it with each of them
([Session Objects](https://requests.readthedocs.io/en/latest/user/advanced/#session-objects)).
An `httpx.Client` also persists cookies across requests, and applies the headers and auth passed
to its constructor to every request
([Clients](https://www.python-httpx.org/advanced/clients/#why-use-a-client)). When the loop
makes requests for unrelated parties (other sites, other users), keep one client per party:
clearing the cookies (`client.cookies.clear()` in both libraries) leaves the `auth` and the
headers set on the client, so the next party's requests still carry the first party's
credentials. A client shared across parties needs all three reset before each party's requests.

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/nested-loop-equijoin/

# nested-loop-equijoin (OPT113)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Exact · Enabled by default · Severity `warning` (slower code) · No automatic fix

Size-dependent nested-loop equi-join (`for a in A: for b in B: if a.k == b.k`) -> `dict` index.

## What it does
Checks nested loops that join two collections by comparing a key of each with `==`:
`for a in A: for b in B: if a.k == b.k:`, including a comprehension as the inner loop
(`[b for b in B if b.k == a.k]`).

The keys are the loop elements themselves, their unpacked components (`for k, v in pairs`),
attributes (`a.k`, `a.x.y`), and constant subscripts (`a["k"]`, `a[0]`). Both loops must be
`for` loops whose size depends on the data. The rule reports one diagnostic per inner loop, at
its first matching comparison. It does not report:

- traversals, where the inner iterable is computed from the outer element
  (`for b in a.children`, `for b in index[a.k]`, `for b in f(a)`, `for b in xs[i + 1:]`);
- comparisons that do not select pairs: `!=`, a negated `==`, one alternative of an `or`
  (`a.k == b.k or match(a, b)`), a result that is stored instead of tested, a value picked for
  every pair (`1 if a.k == b.k else 0`), a match that only skips to the next iteration
  (`if a == b: continue` in an all-pairs loop), or a comparison whose false side does work:
  an `else` / `elif` body, the failure of an `assert a == b`, a `break` / `return` on a
  mismatch, or statements that only the mismatches run because a match `break`s. They run for
  the pairs an index would skip, so every pair is needed. Statements after the `if` that every
  pair runs do not stop a report, but it is then heuristic (below);
- joins where the code fixes the size of either loop, so that the cost grows with one side
  only: a display of at most 16 items (`for b in ("x", "y")`, also through a name or a module
  constant of this or another module (`NAME`, `module.NAME`, also read in a module body) when
  nothing grows it, a comprehension over one (`[r for r in ("a", "b") if r in seen]`), and
  through `enumerate` / `zip` / `sorted` / `.items()` ...), `range` of integer constants with
  at most 16 steps (`range(10)`, `range(LIMIT)`), and an iterable a length test on every path
  caps (`if len(groups) > 8: raise ...`).

## What a report states

A report of the rule's exact tier states that, for each item of the outer loop, the inner loop
compares a key of the outer item with a key of the inner item and does nothing else for an inner
item that does not match. Its message says so: "for each item of `orders`, the loop over
`customers` compares `order.customer_id == customer.id` and does nothing else for an item that
does not match".

Its premises:

- **Equality of keys**: the comparison is `==` between keys of the two items (the items, their
  components, attributes, or constant subscripts). Established. Each key that the inner loop loads
  runs no code of the project: an attribute is a plain one of an item whose class heki knows (a
  dataclass, `attrs`, or `NamedTuple` field, a slot, or what the class body or a method stores, with
  no property, method, other descriptor, `__getattr__`, or `__getattribute__` of that name along the
  class's MRO or in a project subclass, every base a project class, and no metaclass heki does not
  know), and a subscript reads a builtin container or a component of a tuple the inner loop's
  builtin step makes. An attribute of an item of unknown class may be a property, so the report is
  then heuristic.
- **Steps through inputs**: each loop steps through items of the function's inputs: every source
  of its items is a parameter, or an attribute or an item of one (`orders`, `req.rows`,
  `sorted(customers)`), also through a list the function fills only by appending items of such a
  source (`for row in rows: results.append((key, row))`). A call's result, a method's receiver
  (`self.rows`), a module constant, or a display leaves it open.
- **Idle on a mismatch**: an inner item whose key differs runs only the loads of the two keys and
  the comparison: no statement before the test or after the `if`, no `else` or `elif`, no earlier
  `and` operand (`b.active and a.k == b.k`), and no code of the project to advance the inner loop.
  The inner iterable is a builtin container by its type (`customers: list[Customer]`; an annotation
  counts, assumption R2, unless a project subclass of the container defines its own `__iter__`), a
  display, `sorted(...)` or another builtin that builds a container, a view of a `dict`, or the
  pieces of a `str` (with the same condition on `items` and `split`). A value of unknown type may be
  a generator, and a generator, `map`, `filter`, or another call runs code for each item.
- **Same collection, same keys**: the inner loop steps through the same collection on every
  iteration of the outer loop: its iterable is bound before the outer loop, or computed inside it
  only from values bound before it, and the outer loop does not change those values through their
  names, every name a copy binds to them (`rows = ys` makes `ys` one): no changing method, store,
  `del`, call that receives one (a builtin counts too when it is handed a function, as `sorted(ys,
  key=f)` is; a method of a builtin container only stores or reads its arguments), closure that
  captures one, `yield`, or `await`. Nor does it change the compared key of an inner item: no store
  into or deletion of what the key loads (`b.k = ...` for the key `b.k`), and no such call or
  closure that reaches the item or the key's object.

Not part of the claim: any count or size. A loop whose trip count the code fixes or caps (a
constant `range`, a constant slice, a display, or a length test every path to the loop passes,
`if len(rows) > 100: raise ...`) has no report in the exact tier: one of 16 or fewer is not
reported at all, and a larger one is no evidence either way.

A report without one of these premises is heuristic, and its message says only "nested loops
join `orders` and `customers` on `order.customer_id == customer.id`". It rests on the open
premise that both loops are data-sized: the code does not fix the size of either loop at 16 or
fewer, and a size heki cannot bound counts as data-sized.

No message claims a size or a cost. The help names a `set` or a `dict` only for keys known to be
hashable, and an index built before the outer loop only for an inner collection that is the same,
with the same keys, on every outer iteration; otherwise it states the condition ("if the keys are
hashable, ..."). For a mapping the inner loop steps through by its own keys (`for k, v in
d.items()` with the key `k`), it says to look each outer key up in the mapping instead.

## Why is this bad?
The inner loop runs completely for every outer element, so the join costs O(n·m) comparisons.
Indexing the inner collection by its key once (a `dict` from key to elements, or a `set` of the
keys) makes it O(n + m). A `break` after the first match does not help much: a missing key
still scans the whole inner collection.

## Example
```python
def attach(orders, customers):
    for order in orders:
        for customer in customers:
            if order.customer_id == customer.id:
                order.customer = customer
                break
```

Use instead:
```python
def attach(orders, customers):
    by_id = {}
    for customer in customers:
        by_id.setdefault(customer.id, customer)  # the first match, as the `break`
    for order in orders:
        customer = by_id.get(order.customer_id)
        if customer is not None:
            order.customer = customer
```

The advice follows how the matches are used. When a match leaves the inner loop (`break`,
`return`, `raise`), one element per key is enough: a `set` of the elements, or a `dict` from the
key to its first element, as above. When every match is used (`out.append((a, b))` for each
equal pair), a `set` or a one-element `dict` would drop the repeated matches, so the help
advises a `dict` from each key (or value) to the list of its elements. Each outer key then reads
its list with `.get(key, [])`: a loop over the index instead would drop the outer keys that
match no element, which the nested loops give an empty list.

The keys must be hashable, and `==` must agree with their hash. When a key is known to be a
`list`, `dict`, `set`, or `bytearray` (from its annotation, or as an element of a display of
such displays), the help advises indexing a hashable form of it instead (a `tuple` or
`frozenset` of its items).

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/optional-dependency-at-import-time/

# optional-dependency-at-import-time (IMP302)

Family: Imports (IMP) · Heuristic · Opt-in · Experimental · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Opt-in: importing a top-level package or an entry point's module loads, while it loads, a module whose distribution the project declares only in extras, so the import fails without them.

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs only when `select` or `extend-select` names its code or name. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

!!! warning "Experimental"

    It is new: every report rests on established premises only, but its reports are heuristic until a review of its reports on real code bases certifies its claim, and which distributions provide a module and which modules are base modules can still change. Experimental features can still change in behavior or precision, or be removed, in any release, and each change is listed in the release notes. An opt-in rule that is not experimental is stable and only off by default. See [Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/).

## What it does
Reports an import, run while a base module of the project loads, of a module whose distribution
the project declares only in extras (`[project.optional-dependencies]`, `[tool.poetry.extras]`).
A base module is a top-level package of the package the project distributes, or a module an entry
point names (`[project.scripts]`, `[project.gui-scripts]`, `[project.entry-points.<group>]`,
`[tool.poetry.scripts]`) with the packages holding it. Installing the package without the extra
leaves the distribution out, and importing the base module raises `ImportError`.

The import is in the base module's body, or in the body of a project module it loads while it loads.
One report is given per module and module imported, at its first import (the names of one `from`
statement are one import), naming the base module whose import fails, with the imports leading there
as related locations. A module that only some other module loads, such as `acme.backends.redis` for
the extra `redis`, is not reported.

## What a report states

A report states that importing the base module it names runs the reported import whenever it
loads, and that the project declares every distribution that may provide the imported module only
in extras: importing the base module needs them. Unless something else installs them, the import
raises `ImportError` in an installation without the extras.

Its premises, each established or no report:

- **Base module**: the module whose load runs the import is a top-level package module of the
  package code ([`IMP104`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/development-code-import/) says which code that is), or a module an
  entry point names, or a package holding one.
- **Chain**: the reported import, and each import leading to it from that module, is in a module
  body (or a class body it runs, or a constant by-name import there), runs on every path through
  the body, is no lazy import, and loads the module shown, its parent packages first.
- **No handler**: no handler may take the `ModuleNotFoundError` of any of them, which a module
  that is not installed raises: no `except` clause naming `ModuleNotFoundError`, `ImportError`,
  `Exception`, `BaseException`, a type heki cannot tell is another builtin exception, or a bare
  `except`, whose body may end without raising, no `with` block around one, and no `finally`
  body that may leave without raising the error again. A clause whose body raises on every path
  (`raise`, `raise RuntimeError(...) from e`) takes nothing, and a clause that certainly matches
  hides the clauses after it.
- **Distribution**: the distributions that may provide the imported module are found as for
  [`IMP301`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/development-dependency-at-import-time/), with its premise that the project holds no
  copy of the module. The project declares at least one of them, and each one it declares is in
  an extra and in no dependency.
- **Known dependencies**: the project's `pyproject.toml` has a `[project]` or `[tool.poetry]`
  table, and `[project] dynamic` lists neither `dependencies` nor `optional-dependencies`.

## Why is this bad?
An extra is what users opt into: `pip install acme` installs the package without it, and
`pip install "acme[redis]"` with it. When `import acme` loads the extra's distribution, the plain
install is broken, and the error names a module the user never imported. A command an entry point
installs fails the same way before it can say which extra it needs.

## Example
```toml
[project]
name = "acme"
dependencies = ["httpx"]

[project.optional-dependencies]
redis = ["redis"]
```

```python
# acme/__init__.py
from acme.cache import Cache
```

```python
# acme/cache.py
import redis  # IMP302


class Cache:
    def __init__(self, url: str) -> None:
        self.client = redis.Redis.from_url(url)
```

Use instead:
```python
# acme/cache.py
class Cache:
    def __init__(self, url: str) -> None:
        try:
            import redis
        except ImportError as e:
            raise ImportError("install acme[redis] to use Cache") from e
        self.client = redis.Redis.from_url(url)
```

## How to fix
Import the module only inside the functions that use it, where a handler of its `ImportError` can
name the extra to install, as in the example; give it a fallback under `except ImportError:` that
lets the module load; or declare the distribution in `[project] dependencies`. A handler at the
module's import that only raises again leaves the report. When the import is in a module a base
module loads, and one import carries every chain from a base module to it, the help names that
import instead, the one nearest the reported import: moved into the functions that use it, or made
`lazy` on Python 3.15 and later, it takes the report away. heki names it only after one search of
what the base modules load without it no longer reaches the module, and names no import whose name
code running while its module loads may read, or another module takes while that module loads, as
`IMP101` says; a read of another module in a function rules out the move into functions only,
leaving `lazy`.

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `[tool.heki.imports] module-distributions` names the distributions that may provide a module
  (see [`IMP301`](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/development-dependency-at-import-time/)).
- Its reports are errors: `lint.severity = { IMP302 = "warning" }` makes them warnings.

## Known limitations
- An entry point of a plugin group (`[project.entry-points."pytest11"]`) is loaded by the program
  that defines the group, which may itself be the extra's distribution; such a report is right
  about the import and harmless in practice.
- A distribution a dependency installs is still reported: the report is about what the project
  declares.
- Imports inside functions, lazy imports, and imports on a branch of the module body are not
  judged, and neither are the modules of a distribution named neither like them nor by the
  catalog or `module-distributions`.
- Dependencies declared outside `pyproject.toml` are not known.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/read-owner-violation/

# read-owner-violation (MUT203)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Heuristic · Runs when its contract is declared · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Reading a guarded attribute (directly, via alias, `getattr`, or `__dict__`) outside declared `read-owners`.

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs when its contract is declared. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

## What it does
Checks reads of attributes that a `[[tool.heki.read-owners]]` contract reserves for a set of
allowed reader functions: the read side of `MUT201`. A read is reported when it happens outside
the allowed readers:

- directly (`ref.children`), also on `self` and through local aliases;
- through a class object, which reads the class attribute: the class itself
  (`Reference.children`), `cls` in a class method, `type(ref)`, or a value typed
  `type[Reference]` / `typing.Type[Reference]`;
- through `getattr(ref, "children"[, default])`, `object.__getattribute__(ref, "children")`, or
  `hasattr(ref, "children")` (which evaluates the attribute) with a constant name: a string
  literal or a string constant, as for `MUT201`;
- through `ref.__dict__["children"]` or `ref.__dict__.get("children")` (also on `vars(ref)`),
  also with a string constant for the key.

A target can also name an attribute of a module outside the project by its full dotted name
(`sys._getframe`), or every private member outside the project (`<external>._*`, which leaves
out the names that are public API though they start with an underscore: dunder and sunder names
and the `collections.namedtuple` API). Every load of the symbol heki resolves is a read of it
(`return sys._getframe`, `getframe = sys._getframe`, `from sys import _getframe` at the import),
also through a project module re-exporting it, except a name loaded only to be called there,
which is a call (`MUT204`)
([configuration](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#symbols-outside-the-project)).

A target names a class and an attribute; it covers the class's subclasses too. A private
attribute (`self.__secret` in class `Vault`) is the member `_Vault__secret`, which a target names
`Vault.__secret` or `Vault._Vault__secret`, read inside the class as `self.__secret` and outside
as `vault._Vault__secret`. A container
entry (`Class.attr["key"]`) is a write target only: reading an entry reads the attribute, so a
read target names `Class.attr` (an entry is a configuration error).

The read object's class is the one heki infers for it, with annotations as hints: a
parameter, local, attribute, or return annotation, including the items of `list[...]`,
`Sequence[...]`, `Iterable[...]`, `Iterator[...]`, `Generator[...]`, `dict[...]`,
`Mapping[...]`, `tuple[...]`, and `set[...]`, and a type alias naming one (`Models: TypeAlias =
list[Model]`); a constructor call; and what the object comes
from: a loop over such a container (`for model in models`), a subscript (`models[0]`,
`by_name["a"]`), unpacking (`model, _ = pair`), `dict` views and `get` / `pop`, `enumerate`,
`zip`, `reversed`, `sorted`, `iter`, `next`, `list` / `tuple` / `set`, `itertools.chain`, a
display, the items appended to a local list, or a comprehension or generator expression. A
method call or a `@property` / `cached_property` read has the return annotation of the
definition the receiver's class finds first along its MRO, as for a type checker (`typing.Self`
is the receiver's class, and a class method returning `Self`, such as pydantic's
`Model.model_construct(...)`, gives the class it is called on); an attribute annotated with a
type parameter of its class (`obj: T` in `class Site(Generic[T])` or `class Site[T]:`) holds
the argument the instance's annotation gives (`site: Site[Schema]`, also through a type alias);
a name another module binds only under `if TYPE_CHECKING:` (serving it from a module
`__getattr__`) is the class that import names, also as a base class, and a name a module
serves only from its `__getattr__` is what the hook returns for it where heki follows the hook
(a branch testing the name against the literal, a factory read from a module-level dict by the
name and called, also through a function of the module calling what it is handed, and the hook
a project factory returns, `__getattr__, __dir__ = make_hooks(__name__, _EXPORTS)`), as an import
of it would be, and a class object a factory annotated `-> type[C]`
returns is `C` as a `TYPE_CHECKING` import is; a copy (`copy.copy`,
`copy.deepcopy`, `dataclasses.replace`, `model_copy`) has its original's class, calling a `functools.partial` object returns what the
wrapped function returns, and `typing.cast` names the class of its value, its type read as
an annotation (`cast(list[Model], x)` as `cast("list[Model]", x)`): a cast to a subclass narrows
a value known as its base, and a cast to `Any` or to a base class keeps the class the value is
known to have, as an annotated local does. A variable rebound in a loop
(`node = node.parent`) or assigned on some paths only (a walrus inside `and` / `or`) has the
classes of the values reaching it; a value of several classes (`Model | Node`: up to eight an
annotation declares, up to three from different assignments) is each of them, and an
`isinstance` check narrows it
in the code it guards (`if isinstance(x, Model): ...`, `if not isinstance(x, Model): return`,
also inside `and` / `or`), whatever class it had before and under each of its names
(`isinstance(v := x.source, Model)` narrows `v`). An assignment expression in a comprehension binds
the enclosing function's variable with the class of its value, in the items built from it and after
the comprehension, when the comprehension's body runs. A generator expression runs its body only as
it advances, so an unadvanced generator binds nothing. A nested scope that rebinds the variable with
`nonlocal` makes its type unknown. A value typed with a project `Protocol` is an instance of the project
classes that implement it structurally (having every member it defines; at most eight, counting
a class and not its subclasses), but a read of a member the protocol declares is judged by the
protocol, the type the code reads it through: it reads the protocol's member
(`def f(h: Host): h._m` reads `Host._m` when `Host` declares `_m`), and a private method of an
implementation called through the protocol keeps its own reads instead of handing them to the
caller (also when other callers call it through the class and take them over). The read is one
of a target `Model._m` too when heki lists the classes implementing the protocol, there is at
least one, and each is `Model` or a subclass of it; a protocol that another class implements
too, or that no project class implements, reads no target of `Model`'s. An object whose class
heki cannot see (an unannotated parameter or return, `Any`, a value of more classes than those,
a protocol implemented by more than eight) is not tied to the target.

A private helper (`_name`, or a comprehension, generator expression, or lambda scope) with
project callers hands the responsibility to its callers: the read is reported at every call
site of the first non-private callers above it, with the chain of calls as related
information. Reading a `@property` or `functools.cached_property` attribute calls its getter,
so a private getter (`ref._kids` returning `self.children`) hands its read to the functions
reading it. Reads in a class's own initializer on its own `self` are allowed, and so are reads
in a function that only runs inside allowed contexts (every path of callers above it starts in
an allowed reader or an exempt method), as for `MUT201`. One report stands for every read behind
its call (`sites` in JSON), as for `MUT201`, and a read matching several targets of one contract
is one report, under the target configured first, naming the others. A read runs where the body holding it runs, as for
`MUT201`: a generator's reads where it is iterated, a coroutine's where it is awaited.

With `attribution = "lexical"`, a read is judged in the function whose code holds it instead: a
private helper reports its reads itself, and a function that only runs inside allowed readers is
reported too. A lambda, comprehension, or generator expression is part of the function it is
written in. A class's own initialization still allows a read, through the helpers it passes
`self` to too (a helper whose every path of project callers starts in an initializer handing it
its own `self`).

With `own-receiver = "allow"`, a read through the receiver of the method it is judged in is
allowed: the function reported (with `attribution = "lexical"`, the function holding the read)
is a method that is no static method, and the object the member is looked up on may be its first
parameter (`self._seen`, `cls._kind`, `obj._seen` with `obj = self if flag else peer`), also for
a member the class inherits. Another parameter, an attribute of the receiver, and a nested
`def`, lambda, or comprehension using the enclosing method's `self` stay reported.

With `allowed-protocols`, a read through a value typed with a project protocol the key names that
declares the attribute, itself or through its protocol bases, is allowed wherever it is judged; a
read through another protocol or the implementation's class stays reported. A pattern names the
subprotocols of the protocols it matches too, unless `protocol-subclasses = false`.

The help starts with the contract's `message` and then names up to three allowed readers that
read the member the report names themselves: public functions and methods an `allowed-readers`
pattern names (with `forbidden-readers`, every function outside them), by fully qualified name
(``allowed readers of `Reference.children`: `pkg.index.GenerationIndex.children_of` ``). Private
functions (`_name`), special methods, and the exempt methods do not count. JSON output gives them
with their files as `allowed_examples` (`fqn`, `path`).

## What a report states

A report states that the function reads a target of a `read-owners` contract outside the contract's
read owners, directly, through an alias, `getattr`, `hasattr`, or `__dict__`, or through the helpers shown.

Its premises:

- **Target**: the object is an instance of a class the contract names, or of a subclass, or the
  class object of one, by construction or annotation (assumption R2). Open: an alias bound on
  one path is enough.
- **Outside the owners**: the function is not in the allowed modules and classes, nor runs only
  inside allowed contexts (with `attribution = "lexical"`: the function holding the read is not
  allowed, nor runs only inside a class's own initialization; with `own-receiver = "allow"`, the
  read object is not the receiver of the method judging it). Established from the contract.
- **Through helpers**: a helper's write, read, or call counts at its caller (never with
  `attribution = "lexical"`). Open: one path of the helper is enough.

## Why is this bad?
Some state is only meaningful through the component that maintains it: an index that keeps a
derived view consistent, a store that resolves references lazily. Reading the raw attribute
elsewhere sees stale or partial data, and the bug only shows up for some inputs. The contract
states which functions may read it once in configuration, with no runtime cost.

## Example
```toml
[[tool.heki.read-owners]]
name = "reference-children"
targets = ["Reference.children"]
allowed-readers = ["*GenerationIndex*"]
message = "read children through GenerationIndex instead"
```

```python
class Reference:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.children: list["Reference"] = []


class GenerationIndex:
    def children_of(self, ref: Reference) -> list[Reference]:
        return list(ref.children)  # allowed reader


def _kids(ref: Reference) -> list[Reference]:
    return ref.children


def render(ref: Reference) -> str:
    return ", ".join(map(str, _kids(ref)))  # MUT203: reads `Reference.children` via `_kids`
```

Use instead:
```python
def render(ref: Reference, index: GenerationIndex) -> str:
    return ", ".join(map(str, index.children_of(ref)))
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `[[tool.heki.read-owners]]`:
  - `name`: the contract name, shown in messages.
  - `targets`: `Class.attr` entries; globs and dotted suffixes match. An entry can also name
    attributes of modules outside the project by their full name (`sys._getframe`), or
    `<external>.<name>` for the members of every module and class outside the project.
  - `allowed-readers`: functions allowed to read the targets, as dotted names or globs matched
    against the function's qualified name and its `Class.method` qualname.
  - `forbidden-readers`: when set, only reads by these functions are reported (matched like
    `allowed-readers`; `forbidden-readers = ["pkg.parser.*"]`: the parser layer must not read the
    targets); `allowed-readers` and `exempt-methods` stay exceptions inside them. A read is in
    scope when the reporting function or a private helper it hands the read through is
    forbidden.
  - `exempt-methods`: methods allowed to read the targets (`__repr__`, `__deepcopy__`); a plain
    name matches any function or method of that name, an entry with a dot or a glob is matched
    like `allowed-readers`.
  - `message`: the help of every report of the contract.
  - `fail`: `true` makes every report of the contract fail `heki check` (exit code 1), whatever its tier and severity (default `false`).
  - `unresolved`: `"ignore"` (default) or `"report"`: also report the reads the contract cannot
    tie to a class, under `MUT206`. A function some code hands
    on as a value (a display, a class attribute, an argument, a return: `HANDLERS = [helper]`,
    `REQUIRE = staticmethod(helper)`) has callers heki does not see: with `"report"`, it judges
    its reads itself, as if it had no callers.
  - `attribution`: `"call-graph"` (default) or `"lexical"`: whether a private helper hands its
    reads to its callers and a function that only runs inside allowed readers is allowed, or
    each read is judged in the function holding it.
  - `own-receiver`: `"report"` (default) or `"allow"`: whether a read through the receiver of the
    method it is judged in (`self`, `cls`, `super()`) is allowed.
  - `allowed-protocols`: project protocols (class patterns, their subclasses included): a read
    through a value typed with one that declares the attribute, itself or through its protocol
    bases, is allowed, also through a class object typed `type[P]` of one (`MUT206`).
  - `protocol-subclasses`: `true` (default) or `false`: whether an `allowed-protocols` pattern
    names the subprotocols of the protocols it matches, or those protocols only.
  - `include-overrides`: `true` or `false` (default): whether an entry naming a method
    (`Class.method`, `module:Class.method`) in `allowed-readers`, `forbidden-readers`, and the `exempt-methods`
    patterns also names the methods of that name in the
    project subclasses of `Class` (a private name overrides nothing).

Known limitation: a read through a parameter without a project-class annotation
(`def helper(ref): return ref.children`) is not seen, since the read object's class is unknown
there; unlike a write, a read is not handed to the caller that knows it. With
`unresolved = "report"`, `MUT206` reports it.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-param-mutation/

# readonly-param-mutation (MUT110)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Exact · Enabled by default · Severity `warning` (a bug that is rarely harmful) · No automatic fix

Handing a `Sequence` / `Mapping` / `AbstractSet` / `ReadOnly` parameter, as itself, to a function whose body (or a helper's) changes it in place at a named line.

## What it does
Checks functions that hand a parameter annotated as a read-only container to code that changes
it in place: a parameter annotated `Sequence[...]`, `Mapping[...]`, `AbstractSet[...]`
(`typing.AbstractSet` or `collections.abc.Set`, not `typing.Set`, which is `set`), or
`ReadOnly[...]` (also inside `Optional`, `| None`, `Annotated`, and quotes), passed as itself,
through a local alias (`alias = items`), or through a call that hands it back as itself
(`typing.cast(list[int], items)`, a project function returning its parameter on every path,
itself or through calls of other such functions) to
a function that changes its argument in place
(`items.sort()`, `items.append(...)`, `table[key] = ...`, `tags.add(...)`), itself or through
further helpers, any number of calls deep.

The rule reports the call that hands the parameter over, and names the line where the change
happens, with the calls down to it and the line itself as related locations. A generator function changes what it is handed where its generator is
iterated (`for`, `list(...)`, a function iterating it), and is reported there; one that is
created and never iterated changes nothing.

It does not report:

- a change in the function itself (`items.append(1)`, `alias = items; alias.append(1)`): type
  checkers report it on the read-only type. A change through a value a call hands back as
  itself is reported, at the change: `cast(list, items).append(1)` and
  `same(items).append(1)` hide the read-only type from the type checker;
- a container inside the argument (`values["a"].append(1)` with
  `values: Mapping[str, list[int]]`): only the argument itself counts;
- a call that hands over a copy (`helper(list(items))`, `helper(dict(table))`,
  `helper(set(tags))`), also one that hands it to a worker in another process, which gets a
  copy made by pickling (`ProcessPoolExecutor.submit`, `anyio.to_process.run_sync`,
  `loop.run_in_executor` with a process pool);
- a helper parameter annotated with a mutable type (`list[int]`, `dict[str, int]`,
  `set[int]`, `MutableSequence[int]`, `deque[int]`, ...): the type checker reports the argument,
  unless a call handed it back (`fill(cast(list[int], items))`), which the type checker accepts;
- a helper parameter annotated read-only: that helper is checked in turn (its own handing over is
  reported, a change in its own body is a type error); a change reached only through such a
  helper, or through one whose parameter is annotated with a mutable type, further down the
  calls, is no report of the outer call either;
- variadic parameters (`*items: Sequence[int]`).

## What a report states

A report states that the function hands its parameter annotated `Sequence`, `Mapping`,
`AbstractSet`, or `ReadOnly`, as itself, to a function, and that whenever the named line runs
during that call, it changes the caller's object in place. A report at a change in the function
itself states that the line changes the object bound to the parameter in place, through a value a
call handed back as itself. It does not say that every call
reaches the line: the change often sits under a test of the argument's type
(`if isinstance(values, list):`), and the claim is anchored there.

Its premises:

- **Read-only parameter**: the parameter's annotation. Established.
- **Passed as itself**: on every path to the call (or to the change in the function itself),
  the value is the parameter, a local alias of it, or what a call hands back of it as itself:
  `typing.cast`, or a call binding only project functions that return that parameter on every
  path, directly or as what a call of another such function returns of it (`return same(x)`,
  any number of calls deep). Not a copy or another value. Established. A call handing it to an
  executor that heki cannot tell a thread pool from a process pool (a value typed
  `concurrent.futures.Executor`, or one of a class heki does not know given to
  `run_in_executor`) is open: a process pool hands the function a copy. A function returning
  the result of any other call (a class, a method, a function outside the project, a function
  the project may bind again, `f = other` or `module.f = other`), or one that may return it
  only by calling itself again (`a(x)` returning `b(x)`, which returns `a(x)`), is open, and
  its call hands nothing back; so is a call of a function the project may bind again.
- **Changed at the line**: the named line changes in place the object bound to the parameter of
  the function it is in, on every path to the line, a builtin container there (`list`, `dict`,
  `set`, `bytearray`, `deque`, ... by annotation, construction, or an `isinstance` test), and
  that parameter receives the argument through the calls shown, each handing it on as itself,
  none of them annotated. No project subclass of that container overrides the changing method
  (`reverse`, `__setitem__`, `__iadd__`, ...), has a metaclass that may install it, or, for a
  method called by name, defines `__getattribute__`: under R2 the value may be an instance of
  one.
  Established. Open: a change of a value of another class (a `Sequence` whose `append` returns a
  new one), a change by a method a project subclass overrides, and one made where a generator
  that another function returns is iterated; such a report names no line and is heuristic.

## Why is this bad?
A `Sequence`, `Mapping`, or `AbstractSet` annotation promises the caller that the function only
reads its argument, so callers pass their own lists, dictionaries, and sets, shared values, or
tuples and frozensets. A helper that changes the argument in place breaks the promise: the
caller's object changes behind its back, or the call fails on a tuple or a frozenset. Type
checkers trust the helper's signature, so an unannotated or `Any` helper accepts the `Sequence`
and hides the change.

## Example
```python
from collections.abc import Sequence


def sort_values(values):
    values.sort()


def median(values: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    sort_values(values)  # MUT110: reorders the caller's list
    return values[len(values) // 2]
```

Use instead:
```python
from collections.abc import Sequence


def median(values: Sequence[float]) -> float:
    ordered = sorted(values)
    return ordered[len(ordered) // 2]
```

If the helper is meant to change its argument, annotate its parameter with a mutable type
(`def sort_values(values: list[float]) -> None`): the type checker then shows the mismatch at
the call.

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
No configuration: the rule reads standard `typing` declarations only.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-return-mutation/

# readonly-return-mutation (MUT202)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Heuristic · Runs when its contract is declared · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Mutating a shared object returned by a declared `readonly-returns` producer, directly or through the functions that return it.

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs when its contract is declared. Of 20 sampled reports (round 3, 2026-11-21), 70% were right about the code. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

## What it does
Checks mutations of objects returned by a shared producer declared in
`[[tool.heki.readonly-returns]]`, and by the functions that return a producer's value, or a part
of it, on some path: a wrapper is a producer itself, without configuration, through any number
of wrappers, property getters, and recursion. The rule runs when such a contract is declared.
The results of `functools.lru_cache` / `functools.cache` functions are checked without
configuration by `MUT114` (`cached-result-mutation`).

Mutations through attributes, subscripts, container methods, in-place operators, and helpers
that mutate their argument (also run on a worker thread: `asyncio.to_thread(clear, shared)`; not
a worker in another process, which changes a copy made by pickling: `ProcessPoolExecutor`,
`anyio.to_process.run_sync`) are followed, also on the call result itself
(`schema_of(raw).items.append(x)`); a generator function mutates its argument only where the
generator that call returns is iterated. Copies end the protection: `copy.deepcopy(...)`,
`model.model_copy(deep=True)` (without `update=`, whose values Pydantic assigns to the copy by
reference), and the deep copy sanitizers of the ecosystem knowledge base clear it, shallow copies
(`copy.copy`, `.copy()`, `dataclasses.replace(...)`, `dict(...)`, `list(...)`, `tuple(...)`,
`set(...)`, `frozenset(...)`, displays that only unpack the value (`{**shared}`, `[*rows]`), a
sanitizer declared `copy-sanitizer = "shallow"`, and slices of builtin lists, other builtin
sequences, and values whose class heki cannot infer, `rows()[:]`) free the top level only: the
values below stay shared, so a helper rebinding an attribute of the copy (`b.name = "new"`)
changes nothing shared, and one changing the object an attribute or an item holds
(`b.tags.append(x)`, `b["tags"].append(x)`, `for row in b: row.clear()`, also on its own
shallow copy of the argument) does, unless it gave that item a new object first. A producer
that is not `deep` shares only the object itself: a helper changing what it holds as items does
not change it. A slice of an object of another known class may
be a view of it (`numpy`) and stays shared. A `copy()` method of a project class copies as
deeply as its body does: its result is shared only when the method returns a shared value. A
wrapper that returns a copy on one path and the shared value on another still returns a shared
value.

Filling a memo of the shared object, directly or in a method or helper it is handed to, is no
mutation: an in-place change of an attribute named as a cache or memo (`self._style_cache[k] =
v`, also through the methods of a cache object held there), a store under a test finding the
key missing (`if k not in self._decoders:`, the `else` of `if k in ...:`, a `None` or falsy
`self._index.get(k)`, the key computed again by the same expression, `id(raw)`) or through
`setdefault`, a fill of a container a helper has as its default (`def fill(key, _seen={})`), and
a lazy initialization leave what the object computes as it was. A lazy initialization stores
an attribute (`self._x = v`, `setattr`, `object.__setattr__`) where a test found it unset: `if
self._runtime is None:`, `if not hasattr(self, "_runtime"):`, a `None` test of `getattr(self,
"_runtime", None)`, or the `except AttributeError:` clause of a `try` that reads it.

## What a report states

A report states that the function changes in place an object that a shared producer returned: a
producer declared in `readonly-returns`, or a function returning a producer's value.

Its premises:

- **Producer**: the declaration. Established.
- **Returned through wrappers**: a function returning a producer's value on some path is a producer.
  Open: one path is enough.
- **Same object**: the changed object is the returned one, or an object below it, not a copy. Open:
  a value that is the shared one on one path counts.
- **Changed in place**: a store, a mutator, an in-place operator, or a helper changing its argument.
  The memo fills listed above are left out; a memo fill heki does not recognize does change the
  object.

## Why is this bad?
A shared return value is seen by every caller. Mutating it corrupts it for everyone else,
usually long after the mutation happened.

## Example
```toml
[[tool.heki.readonly-returns]]
name = "schemas"
producers = ["registry.schema"]
deep = true
```

```python
from registry import schema


def schema_of(name: str) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
    return schema(name)


def extend(name: str) -> None:
    s = schema_of(name)
    s["fields"].append("extra")  # MUT202: mutates the shared object
```

Use instead:
```python
import copy


def extend(name: str) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
    s = copy.deepcopy(schema_of(name))
    s["fields"].append("extra")
    return s
```

## Known limitations
- A shared value stored in an attribute (`self.kept = schema(...)`) and changed in another
  method is not followed.
- A generator's values and a coroutine's result (`await`) are not followed.
- A method call on a shared value whose class heki cannot resolve (a producer returning a type
  variable) is not followed; a wrapper with a concrete return annotation resolves it.
- A dict that also holds values of its own (`{**shared, "extra": []}`,
  `dict(shared, extra=[])`) or unpacks another mapping (`{**shared, **overrides}`) is not
  followed.
- A project method returning a part of a shared receiver (`return self._items[key]`) is not
  followed, nor is a `copy()` method of a project class that shares the receiver's values
  (`return Post(self.tags)`).

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `[[tool.heki.readonly-returns]]`: `name`, `producers` (function names or globs), `deep`
  (protect nested values too).


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-type-mutation/

# readonly-type-mutation (MUT108)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Heuristic · Opt-in · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Opt-in: changing in place a field that a standard type declares read-only (frozen dataclass / `NamedTuple` / `dataclass_transform` fields, `Final` / `ReadOnly` attributes, `ReadOnly` `TypedDict` keys), directly, through an alias, or in a helper.

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs only when `select` or `extend-select` names its code or name. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

## What it does
Checks in-place changes of containers held in fields that a standard type declares read-only,
which type checkers let through because they only stop rebinding:

- a field that holds a container in a `@dataclass(frozen=True)`, a `NamedTuple`, or a class that a
  PEP 681 `dataclass_transform(frozen_default=True)` builds (a decorator function, base class, or
  metaclass carrying it, unless the class passes `frozen=False`), also on an instance of a
  subclass: `config.tags.append(...)`;
- an attribute declared `Final[...]` (`self.items: Final[list[int]] = []` in `__init__`, or a
  `Final` field of a dataclass or `NamedTuple`) or `ReadOnly[...]`, and a `ReadOnly` key of a
  `TypedDict` (`movie["names"].append(...)`).

A `Sequence` / `Mapping` / `AbstractSet` parameter handed to a helper that changes it is
`MUT110` (`readonly-param-mutation`), which shares this analysis.

Changes are followed through local aliases (`tags = config.tags; tags.append(...)`) and through
helpers, annotated or not and any number of calls deep, that change what they are handed: the
attribute itself (`add_default(config.tags)`) or the object holding it (`reset(config)`). Such a
change is reported at the call that hands the attribute or the object over, with the calls down
to the change as related locations. A helper that sees the object's type reports its own change
instead. A generator function changes what it is handed where its generator is iterated, and is
reported there; one that is created and never iterated changes nothing.

The rule does not report:

- rebinding or deleting the attribute (`config.tags = []`, `del config.tags`): type checkers
  report it;
- `object.__setattr__(...)`, `setattr(...)`, and `__dict__` writes: the deliberate way to set up a
  frozen instance, caches included;
- the class's own initialization: `__init__`, `__post_init__`, `__new__`, `model_post_init`,
  `__setstate__` changing their own instance, also through helpers that only run inside them;
- an instance the function constructs itself and fills before anyone else holds it
  (`index = Index({}, {}); index.names["a"] = 1`), directly or through a helper;
- fields declared `field(compare=False)` (state outside the instance's value, such as a cache);
  fields and attributes whose annotation is no container type (an object of a project class
  changes through its own methods); class variables (`ClassVar`); class-level constants of other
  classes; and module-level constants;
- a container inside the read-only one (`config.tables["a"].append(1)` with a frozen
  `tables: dict[str, list[int]]`): only the container in the read-only field counts;
- a field of a frozen dataclass or `NamedTuple` that holds an object rejecting every change,
  wherever the project makes an instance of the class or of a subclass: every construction
  (`Segment(MappingProxyType(meta))`, `cls(...)` in a class method) and every copy replacing the
  field (`dataclasses.replace(segment, meta=...)`, `segment._replace(meta=...)`) stores a
  `tuple`, `frozenset`, `str`, `bytes`, `range`, `frozendict`, or `types.MappingProxyType`
  there. Changing it in place raises (`TypeError`, `AttributeError`) and changes nothing. A
  dict stored by one construction, a value of a class heki does not know (a parameter
  annotated `Mapping`), a default, an unpacked argument, a copy of an object of unknown class
  that may replace a field of that name (`replace(obj, meta={})` with `obj` unannotated), or a
  class without a construction heki sees keeps the report.

Out of scope: `dataclass_transform`s defined outside the checked files, such as the frozen models
of `attrs` and Pydantic (heki does not analyze installed packages, so it cannot see the
transform); properties with a setter; `TypedDict` values read through `.get()`
(`movie.get("names")`); objects whose class heki cannot see (an `Any` or unannotated
receiver); and what one instance holds: a field that may hold a dict somewhere is reported
also where the instance at hand holds a read-only view (`snapshot.meta` of a snapshot that
another function built with `MappingProxyType`). Instances made where heki does not see the
call (a class handed on as a callable, `map(Segment, rows)`) are not among the constructions
the rule reads.

## What a report states

A report states that the code changes in place a container held in a field that a standard type
declares read-only, directly, through an alias, or through the helpers shown.

Its premises:

- **Read-only field**: the class declares the field read-only (frozen dataclass, `NamedTuple`,
  `dataclass_transform`, `Final`, `ReadOnly`). Established from the declarations.
- **Instance**: the object is an instance of the class or of a subclass, by construction or
  annotation (assumption R2).
- **Changed in place**: an item store, a mutator method, or a helper changing its argument. Open
  through a helper: a change on one of its paths is enough.
- **Changeable object**: the field may hold an object that a change does not reject: some
  construction or copy stores a mutable container or a value of a class heki does not know
  there, or heki does not see what every instance holds. Established from the constructions
  the project makes.

## Why is this bad?
A frozen dataclass or a `NamedTuple` promises immutable instances, so code shares them freely: as
module-level defaults, in caches, or by handing the same value to several owners. An in-place
change of a container inside one is seen by every holder and changes the results of `==`. A
`Final` or `ReadOnly` declaration makes the same promise to the readers of the value. Type
checkers stop the rebinding, but not a change of the container inside, directly, through an
alias, or in a helper that receives a plain `list` or an unannotated value.

## Example
```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field


def add_default(tags):
    tags.append("default")


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Config:
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)


def configure(config: Config) -> None:
    add_default(config.tags)  # MUT108: changes the frozen `Config.tags` in place
```

Use instead:
```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, replace


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Config:
    tags: tuple[str, ...] = ()


def configure(config: Config) -> Config:
    return replace(config, tags=(*config.tags, "default"))
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `lint.extend-select = ["MUT108"]` (or `--extend-select MUT108`) enables the rule. It is
  opt-in: selecting the `MUT` prefix does not enable it.
- No other configuration: the rule reads standard `typing` and `dataclasses` declarations only.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/readonly-view-mutation/

# readonly-view-mutation (MUT120)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Heuristic · Opt-in · Experimental · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Opt-in: changing a value held through a read-only view (a protocol or class whose members are all properties without a setter) where a type checker does not see it: a helper that does not see the view's type rebinds one of its properties, or code changes in place the container a property returns.

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs only when `select` or `extend-select` names its code or name. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

!!! warning "Experimental"

    It is new: its reports are heuristic until a review of its reports on real code bases certifies its claim. Experimental features can still change in behavior or precision, or be removed, in any release, and each change is listed in the release notes. An opt-in rule that is not experimental is stable and only off by default. See [Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/).

## What it does
Checks changes of a value that the code holds through a read-only view, where a type checker
does not see them. A read-only view is a class, a `typing.Protocol` or not, whose members are all
properties without a setter or deleter: no plain attribute, no method, no `__setattr__`, along
its bases in the project, and no other base than `object`, `abc.ABC`, `Generic`, or `Protocol`.
A value is held through the view when its type is the view by annotation, as for `MUT108`: a
parameter, a variable, an element of a `Sequence[View]` another view returns.

A type checker reports a write of a view's property made through the view
(`view.required = True`), but not two other ways to change the value:

- handing the view to a helper that does not see its type (an unannotated or `Any` parameter),
  which rebinds or deletes one of the view's properties (`p.required = ...`, `del p.required`,
  `setattr(p, "required", ...)`), itself or through further helpers. The call that hands the
  view over is reported, with the calls down to the write as related locations;
- changing in place the container a property returns, when the property's annotation is a
  mutable container type (`view.extras["k"] = v`, `view.items.append(x)`), directly, through a
  local alias, or through helpers (`fill(view.extras)`, `reset(view)` changing `p.extras`), as
  `MUT108` does for frozen fields. Through a helper, a property annotated with a read-only type
  (`Sequence`, `Mapping`, `AbstractSet`) counts too.

The rule does not report:

- a write of a property through the view itself, or through a helper whose parameter is
  annotated with the view: the type checker reports it there. A helper that sees the view and
  hands it on to one that does not is reported at its own call;
- a change made through a value of a class that implements the view (`field: Field`, not
  `field: FieldView`);
- a direct change of a container a property annotated `Sequence` / `Mapping` / `AbstractSet`
  returns: the type checker reports it;
- a copy (`extras = dict(view.extras)`, `fill(list(view.items))`), and a container inside the one
  the property returns (`view.tables["a"].append(1)`);
- a class with a setter or deleter, a plain attribute (`required: bool` in a protocol), a
  method, or a `functools.cached_property`: it is no read-only view;
- an attribute the view does not declare (`p.cache = {}` in a helper).

Out of scope, both for a protocol that classes in the project implement: a property whose
getter returns one attribute of their own in every implementation (`return self._extras`), which
heki follows to that attribute, one the view does not declare; and the container of a property
handed to a helper (`fill(view.extras)`), which heki does not tie to one class. Such changes are
not reported.

## What a report states

A report states that a value the code holds through a read-only view is changed: a helper that
does not see the view's type rebinds or deletes one of its properties, or the container a
property returns is changed in place.

Its premises:

- **Read-only view**: every member of the class and of its bases in the project is a property
  without a setter or deleter. Established from the declarations.
- **Held through the view**: the value's type is the view, by annotation (assumption R2).
- **Changed**: an attribute store or deletion in a helper whose parameter has no type a checker
  reads, or an item store or mutator method on the container a property returns. Open through a
  helper: a change on one of its paths is enough.

## Why is this bad?
A read-only view hands code the facts it may read and nothing it may change: callers pass their
live objects through it, often while other code relies on them being final. A type checker keeps
the promise only as far as it sees the view's type. A helper without annotations, or a container
a property returns, lets a change through, and the change reaches every other holder of the
object.

## Example
```python
from typing import Protocol


class FieldView(Protocol):
    @property
    def required(self) -> bool: ...

    @property
    def extras(self) -> dict[str, object]: ...


def _flip(field):
    field.required = not field.required


def decide(field: FieldView) -> None:
    _flip(field)  # MUT120: `_flip` rebinds the view's property `required`
    field.extras["init"] = False  # MUT120: changes the container `extras` returns
```

Use instead:
```python
from collections.abc import Mapping
from typing import Protocol


class FieldView(Protocol):
    @property
    def required(self) -> bool: ...

    @property
    def extras(self) -> Mapping[str, object]: ...


def decide(field: FieldView) -> dict[str, object]:
    return {**field.extras, "init": False, "required": not field.required}
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `lint.extend-select = ["MUT120"]` (or `--extend-select MUT120`) enables the rule. It is
  opt-in: selecting the `MUT` prefix does not enable it.
- No other configuration: the rule reads standard `typing` and `abc` declarations only.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/recursion-error-as-value/

# recursion-error-as-value (EFF114)

Family: Execution Effects (EFF) · Heuristic · Opt-in · Experimental · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Opt-in: an `except` clause around a recursion (a call cycle reached from its `try` body) takes the `RecursionError` and goes on without raising, so the result depends on the stack depth.

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs only when `select` or `extend-select` names its code or name. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

!!! warning "Experimental"

    Its precision is measured on a sample of reports of one corpus only, and its premises are not yet certified. Experimental features can still change in behavior or precision, or be removed, in any release, and each change is listed in the release notes. An opt-in rule that is not experimental is stable and only off by default. See [Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/).

## What it does
Checks for an `except` clause that takes the `RecursionError` a recursion can raise and goes on
without raising: its `try` body calls a function on a call cycle, directly or through other
calls, across modules, and every path through the clause falls through, returns, breaks, or
continues. The rule is opt-in: enable it with `--extend-select EFF114` or
`extend-select = ["EFF114"]`.

A function is on a call cycle when it can call itself again through calls whose bodies run on
the caller's stack: plain calls, awaited coroutines, property getters, generators iterated
there, generator expressions where they are written, and functions builtins call there
(`list(map(self.depth, children))`, where the `map` is consumed in the `try`). Each call of the
cycle has as its targets every implementation it can run: a call heki resolves, or a method of
a class it knows whose overrides it has all. A method found only by its name, such as a member
of a protocol a receiver is typed with, closes no cycle: a getter that reads the same attribute
of another object (`self._backend.max_bits` in a property `max_bits`) does not call itself. The
way down from the `try` body to the cycle may go through such a call. A clause takes a `RecursionError` when it names
`RecursionError`, `RuntimeError`, `Exception`, or `BaseException` (also in a tuple, or imported
from `builtins`), or is a bare `except`, and no earlier clause of the same `try` takes it. The
rule reports the clause, with the call in the `try` body as a related location, and, when the
function on the cycle is further down, the first eight calls on the way to it.

A `RecursionError` raised in a `with` body inside the `try` counts (the context manager is taken
to let it through), and so does one raised in an inner `try` none of whose clauses takes it.

It does not report:

- a clause after one that takes `RecursionError` first (`except RecursionError: raise`), or after
  one whose classes heki cannot tell: a name bound to a tuple of classes, or a class that is
  neither a builtin nor a class statement of the project (one of a dependency or of the standard
  library may be `RuntimeError` itself, as `threading.ThreadError` is);
- a clause that raises on some path (`if isinstance(error, RecursionError): raise`), or calls
  `sys.exit`, `os._exit`, `os.abort`, `exit`, `quit`, or a project function that returns on no
  path (it raises on every path);
- a CLI boundary: a clause that reports the error (`print(..., file=sys.stderr)`,
  `sys.stderr.write`, `traceback.print_exc()`, or a `logging` call with the exception:
  `logger.exception(...)`, `exc_info=...`, or the exception as an argument) and returns an
  integer constant, an exit status, on every `return` (a literal, or a module-level name bound
  once to an integer);
- a `try` body whose calls reach no call cycle, or reach one only through a call heki cannot
  resolve, a coroutine only created, or a function run on another thread
  (`asyncio.to_thread`, `loop.run_in_executor`), and a cycle closed only through a method found
  by its name;
- `except*` clauses, and a `RecursionError` that reaches the clause only through a `finally`
  body.

## What a report states

A report states that the clause takes the `RecursionError` that a call cycle its `try` body
reaches can raise, and that no path through it raises, so the function goes on with a value
that depends on the depth of the stack instead of the error.

Its premises:

- **Call cycle**: a call in the `try` body runs, through calls whose bodies run on its stack, a
  function that can call itself again through such calls, each of them a call whose targets are
  every implementation it can run. Open through a method call on the way down: one candidate
  implementation of it is enough. Open as well where state or an argument stops the
  recursion after one more level (a flag set before the recursive call, a retry with an argument
  that no longer recurses): the recursion may stop there and never raise.
- **Catches RecursionError**: the clause's classes include `RecursionError`, as the builtins the
  module does not rebind (assumption R1), and no earlier clause of the same `try` takes it.
  Established.
- **Completes normally**: every path through the clause's body ends in a fall-through, a
  `return`, a `break`, or a `continue`, none in a `raise`, a call that ends the process, or a
  call of project functions that return on no path. Open: an instruction in the body that may
  raise is not counted.

## Why is this bad?
How deep a recursion may go before Python raises `RecursionError` depends on the recursion limit
and on how much of the stack the caller already uses, not on the data. A broad clause around a
recursion turns that limit into an answer: a long chain of references reads as circular, a deep
tree as unreadable, and the result changes with the caller, the platform, or
`sys.setrecursionlimit`. The error the code meant to catch (a missing key, a bad value) and the
stack running out look the same to it.

## Example
```python
class RefWalker:
    def __init__(self, graph: dict[str, list[str]]) -> None:
        self.graph = graph

    def is_circular(self, ref: str) -> bool:
        try:
            return self._reaches(ref, ref, set())
        except Exception:  # EFF114
            return True

    def _reaches(self, target: str, ref: str, seen: set[str]) -> bool:
        for following in self.graph.get(ref, []):
            if following == target:
                return True
            if following not in seen:
                seen.add(following)
                if self._reaches(target, following, seen):
                    return True
        return False
```

Use instead:
```python
    def is_circular(self, ref: str) -> bool:
        try:
            return self._reaches(ref, ref, set())
        except RecursionError:
            raise
        except Exception:
            return True
```

Or walk the graph with an explicit stack, so that its depth is limited by memory, not by the
recursion limit.

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `lint.extend-select = ["EFF114"]` (or `--extend-select EFF114`) enables the rule. It is
  opt-in: selecting the `EFF` prefix does not enable it.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/sentinel-lost-in-deepcopy/

# sentinel-lost-in-deepcopy (MUT118)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Heuristic · Off by default · Severity `error` (a bug) · Unsafe fix (`--fix --unsafe-fixes`)

`copy.deepcopy` of an instance holding an `object()` sentinel in an attribute that a function tests against the sentinel by identity (the copy holds a new object, which the test does not match).

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs when `select` or `extend-select` names its code or name, and with `lint.heuristic = true` (`--heuristic`) also by default and for its prefixes and `ALL`. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

## What it does
Checks `copy.deepcopy` calls that copy an instance holding an `object()` sentinel in an
attribute that a function tests against that sentinel by identity (`item.default is
MISSING`). The copy holds a new object in the attribute, so the test gives the opposite answer
on the copy.

A sentinel is a module-level name bound once to `object()` (`MISSING = object()`) that no module
binds again. A class holds it in an attribute when its own code puts it there:

- the default of a field of a stdlib `@dataclass` whose generated `__init__` stores it (`init`
  left on, no `__init__` of the class's own, and the field not declared `init=False`):
  `default: object = MISSING`, `default: object = field(default=MISSING)`;
- a store in a method: `self.default = MISSING`, or `self.default = default` of a parameter
  declared `default=MISSING`;
- the default of a public field of a class whose base the catalog describes as keeping a
  hashable default as the object itself (`pydantic.BaseModel`), when nothing may validate the
  default (no `validate_default` in the field's annotation, and no `model_config` or `Config`
  in the class or a project base, which may turn it on): a validated default is what the
  validation returns.

The test is a comparison with `is` or `is not` in any function of the project, on an object
whose class heki knows (as for `MUT203`). The deep copy is a call of `copy.deepcopy` with one
argument, of an object of the class or of a subclass; the report is at that call, with the tests
as related locations, so one new deep copy is one new diagnostic under a Ratchet baseline.

A deep copy also copies what the object holds in its attributes. An instance of the class held
there or below, by the attributes' types (an optional attribute, the items of a list or dict,
the classes implementing a protocol), is a heuristic report naming the copied object's attribute
it is in or below (`reference`): what the attributes hold when the program runs may be other
objects. A class that copies its instances itself (a copy hook, a `copyreg` registration) is not
followed.

It does not report:

- a sentinel that copies as itself (`sentinel("MISSING")`: the builtin from Python 3.15, or
  `typing_extensions.sentinel`, also through `import typing_extensions as te`; an instance of a
  class with `__deepcopy__`), or any other value bound to the name;
- a sentinel only used as a parameter default or a `dict.get` default, never stored on an
  instance;
- a class whose own code (or a base's) decides how it is copied: `__deepcopy__`, `__reduce__`,
  `__reduce_ex__`, `__getstate__`, `__setstate__`, or a `copyreg` registration;
- a `copy.deepcopy` call given a `memo` (a `__deepcopy__` passing its memo on);
- comparisons with `==`, and `pickle`, whose copy is made where it is loaded.

## What a report states

A report states that the `object()` sentinel `S` is a value that class `C` stores in attribute
`a` of its instances, that a function tests `a` against `S` by identity, and that
`copy.deepcopy` receives an instance of `C` at the reported call: whenever the instance holds `S`
in `a`, the copy holds a new object there, which the test does not match.

Its premises:

- **Object sentinel**: `S` is a module-level name bound once to the builtin `object()`, which no
  module binds again. Established.
- **Held by the class**: `S` is the default of a field that the `__init__` a stdlib dataclass
  generates stores, a method of `C` stores `S` in `self.a` (or a parameter whose default is
  `S`), or `S` is the default of a public field and a base of `C` keeps hashable defaults as
  they are (R3) with nothing that may validate the default; the store runs no property,
  `__setattr__`, or metaclass of the project.
  Open for the default of a field under another base outside the project, or of a dataclass
  with an `__init__` of its own, which may or may not store it.
- **Tested by identity**: a function compares `x.a` with `S` by `is` or `is not`, where `x` is an
  instance of `C` or of a project subclass (by construction, or by annotation under R2), and
  reading `a` runs no code: no property, `__getattr__`, `__getattribute__`, or metaclass in a
  class it may be, and every base outside the project is `object`, `typing.Generic`,
  `NamedTuple`, or one whose `__setattr__` the catalog describes as storing on the instance
  (R3: `pydantic.BaseModel`). Open when `x` may be of a base class of `C`, a union, or a
  protocol.
- **Deep-copied**: `copy.deepcopy` receives, as its only argument, an instance of `C` (by
  construction, or by annotation under R2), reading `a` on it runs no code, and no class it may
  be defines `__deepcopy__`, `__reduce__`, `__reduce_ex__`, `__getstate__`, `__setstate__`,
  `__getattr__`, or `__getattribute__`, has a metaclass other than `type` / `abc.ABCMeta`, is
  registered with `copyreg`, or derives from a class outside the project other than `object`,
  `typing.Generic`, `abc.ABC`, or one whose `__deepcopy__` the catalog describes as copying the
  attributes deeply (R3). Open when the argument may be of a subclass of its class that holds
  the sentinel, when it may hold such an instance below its attributes (by their types), or
  when a subclass, a base, or a metaclass may decide the copy.

## Why is this bad?
`copy.deepcopy` copies every attribute of the instance, the sentinel included: an `object()`
copies as a new `object()`. Code that asks whether a value was given (`item.default is not
MISSING`) then answers yes for the copy, and treats the new object as a real value: it may
write `<object object at 0x...>` into output, or skip a default it should apply.

## Example
```python
import copy
from dataclasses import dataclass

MISSING = object()


@dataclass
class Field:
    name: str
    default: object = MISSING


def has_default(field: Field) -> bool:
    return field.default is not MISSING


def isolated(field: Field) -> Field:
    return copy.deepcopy(field)  # `has_default(isolated(f))` is True for every field
```

Use instead:
```python
MISSING = sentinel("MISSING")  # copies as itself
```

`sentinel` (PEP 661) is a builtin from Python 3.15; for an older target, import it from
`typing_extensions` 4.16.0 or later (`from typing_extensions import sentinel`). The help of a
report names the one the [target version](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/scope/#the-target-python-version) has.
`typing_extensions` 4.14 and 4.15 spell it `Sentinel`, and `copy.deepcopy` of one of those raises
`TypeError`. A sentinel's repr is its name, and `pickle` finds it by that name in its module, so
give it the name it is bound to.

## Known limitations
- A deep copy of a container (`copy.deepcopy([field])`) is not followed, and an instance below
  the copied object's attributes is found only by their types.
- A sentinel bound in a class body, or under another name (`MISSING = UNDEFINED`), is not
  recognized.
- A deep copy or a test in the body of a class defined at module level (`class Defaults:
  SPEC = copy.deepcopy(...)`) is not seen; one in a class defined in a function is.

## Fix safety
When the target version is Python 3.15 or later and the file of the report binds the sentinel,
the report has an unsafe fix: it replaces the `object()` call with `sentinel("NAME")`, `NAME`
being the name the sentinel is bound to, and needs no import. `heki check --fix` alone never
applies it; `--fix --unsafe-fixes` does (`--diff --unsafe-fixes` shows it), and the language
server offers it as a quick fix. It is unsafe because the object changes: its type is `sentinel`
instead of `object`, its repr is `NAME` instead of `<object object at 0x...>`, and `pickle` of an
object holding it stores the sentinel by its name and loads it as the same object, where it made
a new `object()` before. heki assumes that the module-level name is how `pickle` finds it. The
fix is not offered when the module binds the name `sentinel` (an import of
`unittest.mock.sentinel`, a function, an assignment), or below Python 3.15.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/set-dict-quadratic-merge/

# set-dict-quadratic-merge (OPT102)

Family: Complexity Rewrites (OPT) · Exact · Enabled by default · Severity `warning` (slower code) · Safe fix (`--fix`)

Unconditionally profitable `set`/`dict` quadratic merge (`{**d, ...}` with `d` first).

## What it does
Checks loops that rebuild a dict or set every iteration and rewrites them in place:

- `d = {**d, k: v}` → `d[k] = v`, or `d.update({...})` when the remaining entries have side
  effects;
- `d = {**d, **other}` → `d.update(other)`;
- `s = s | {e}` → `s |= {e}` (also `d = d | other` for dicts).

## What a report states

A report states that the merge (`{**d, ...}` with the accumulator first, `s = s | t`, `d = d |
other`), in a loop, builds a new set or dict from the whole accumulated one each time it runs, where
updating it would change it in place.

Its premises:

- **Builtin type by construction**: the value is a builtin `set` or `dict` by its construction. Established:
  the Soundness lane takes types from constructions only.
- **Loop-carried**: the result is the value the next iteration starts from. Established by the IR.
- **In a loop**: the statement is in the body of a loop. Established by the IR.
- **Rewrite proven safe**: the help says `[safe fix: ...]`, `[proven-safe suggestion: ...]`, or
  `[proven safe; ...]`. A report whose help names a blocking obligation instead (`[not auto-fixable:
  ...]`) lacks this premise and is heuristic whatever the rule's certainty; the proven reports are
  the rule's exact tier.

Not part of the claim: how many times the statement runs (one under a branch inside the loop
counts), and how large the loop or the set or dict is. The message claims no size and no cost
estimate. The rewrite never makes the code slower, so a loop the code fixes at a few items is
reported too.

## Why is this bad?
Each rebuild copies the whole container, so the loop is quadratic. The in-place update is never
slower.

## Example
```python
def index(items: list[tuple[str, int]]) -> dict[str, int]:
    d = {}
    for k, v in items:
        d = {**d, k: v}
    return d
```

Use instead:
```python
def index(items: list[tuple[str, int]]) -> dict[str, int]:
    d = {}
    for k, v in items:
        d[k] = v
    return d
```

## Fix safety
Applied by `heki check --fix` only when proven safe, with the same obligations as `OPT101`
(exact builtin, unique, no live alias / iterator / view, evaluation order preserved), plus:

- the accumulator must be the leading `**` entry. `found = {**site, **found}` keeps the keys
  already in `found`, while `found.update(site)` would overwrite them, so it is never rewritten;
- for `|`, the right operand must be an exact `set` / `dict` (a subclass could make
  `__ror__` and `__ior__` disagree);
- the display inserts each entry before it evaluates the next one, and an insertion can run a
  key's `__eq__` (on a hash collision) or a mapping's `keys()` / `__getitem__`. Gathering
  several entries into one `d.update({...})` is applied only when the keys are `int` / `str` /
  `bytes` / `bool` / `float` values and the later entries are constants or local names;
  `d = {**d, **other}` with an unknown mapping `other` is not rewritten;
- an update that inserts several keys stops halfway when an insertion raises, where the display
