  left `d` unchanged: it is not applied when an exception handler reads `d`;
- `s |= t` grows the set's table in place, while `s = s | t` copies it into a new one, and the
  two can iterate the same elements in different orders (an `int` set in the same order in every
  run). The set form is applied only when every later use of the set just tests it (`x in s`,
  `len(s)`, truthiness, `==` / `!=` with a builtin value); a set that is iterated, converted
  (`sorted(s)`, `list(s)`), formatted, returned, stored, yielded, or passed to other code keeps
  `s = s | t`. A dict keeps its insertion order either way.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/set-order-output/

# set-order-output (EFF112)

Family: Execution Effects (EFF) · Heuristic · Opt-in · Experimental · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Opt-in: the iteration order of a set of strings, which changes between runs, reaches a file, a stream, a serializer, or a raised exception's message across a call.

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs only when `select` or `extend-select` names its code or name. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

!!! warning "Experimental"

    Its precision is measured on a sample of reports of one corpus only, and its premises are not yet certified. Experimental features can still change in behavior or precision, or be removed, in any release, and each change is listed in the release notes. An opt-in rule that is not experimental is stable and only off by default. See [Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/).

## What it does
Checks for the iteration order of a set of strings reaching an output across a call: a
function builds a value in the order it iterates a set (or picks an element of one) and returns
it, and its caller writes it; or a function hands such a value to a call that writes it. The
rule is opt-in: enable it with `--extend-select EFF112` or `extend-select = ["EFF112"]`.

The set is a `set` or `frozenset` of `str` or `bytes` values (or tuples of them), by
construction (a display, a comprehension, `set()`, `frozenset()`, a set operator such as
`a & b.keys()`, a module constant bound once to one) or by annotation (`set[str]`, a callee's
declared return type). Python randomizes the hashes of strings per process, so such a set
iterates in a different order from run to run.

The order is taken where the code iterates the set (a loop, a comprehension, a generator
expression), copies it into a sequence or text (`list()`, `tuple()`, `str.join()`, formatting),
or picks an element of it (`set.pop()`, `next(iter(...))`, the first element a loop returns). It
follows the value through assignments, displays, formatting, string concatenation (text built
element by element in a loop included), the containers it is appended to or stored in, returns,
and the calls of the project.

The outputs are:

- files and streams: `pathlib.Path.write_text` / `write_bytes`, `print`, `sys.stdout.write`,
  and `write` on a file the function opens;
- serializers: `json.dumps` / `json.dump` unless `sort_keys=True`, `yaml.dump` /
  `yaml.safe_dump` with `sort_keys=False`, `pprint.pprint` / `pprint.pformat` with
  `sort_dicts=False`, and `pprint.pp`;
- the message of a raised builtin exception built from the whole value
  (`ValueError("unknown: " + ", ".join(names))`).

Add your own writers with `writes-in-order` in `[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]`. The report is placed
where the ordered value meets the output: the call whose result is written, or the place the
order is taken when it is handed to a call that writes it. The place the order is taken and the
calls on the way are related locations.

It does not report:

- a flow inside one function (`", ".join(names)` written in the same function): one expression
  and its type decide it, which is a linter's check;
- a set of other values (`set[int]` iterates in the same order in every run), or of values whose
  type heki does not know;
- a value sorted on the way (`sorted(...)`), turned back into a set, measured (`len`), compared,
  or only tested for membership;
- a set holding at most one element on every path to where its order is taken
  (`if len(s) > 1: return None`, then `s.pop()`, also as one operand of `or` / `and`:
  `if len(s) != 1 or not ok: return None`), or a sequence copied from it holding at most one
  where an item is read from it (`if len(rest) > 1: ...`, then `rest[0]`);
- one element at a time written to its own file (`(root / name).write_text(...)` in a loop
  over the set): only an output that appends, such as a stream, writes the set's order;
- an exception raised for one element at a time (`for name in names: check(f"pkg.{name}")`,
  raising with its argument): it names the first element that fails, which depends on the order
  only when two fail;
- a mapping read back by key (`summary[path]` for each `path` of `sorted(summary)`), and a key
  read from the mapping before and stored again (`fields[k] = fields[k].strip()`), which keeps
  its place;
- a set filled with the elements (`seen.update(...)`): a set has an order of its own, and
  iterating it is a take of its own; `insert`, `update`, and `setdefault` on a value heki does
  not know as a list or a mapping;
- a writer whose sorting switch heki cannot evaluate (`json.dumps(data, sort_keys=flag)`), and
  `logging` and `warnings.warn`;
- a value passed through code heki does not follow: a template engine, a call it cannot
  resolve.

## What a report states

A report states that a value whose order (or whose element, for a pick) comes from iterating a
set of strings reaches the output call shown in that order, across a call, so the written text
changes from run to run.

Its premises:

- **Set order**: the iterated value is a `set` or `frozenset`, by construction or annotation
  (assumption R2). Open through an annotation.
- **Run-dependent hashes**: its elements are `str` or `bytes`, or tuples of them, by
  construction or annotation. Open through an annotation.
- **Order taken**: the code iterates, copies, formats, or picks from the set, with no `sorted()`
  after it on the way, and the set may hold two elements there. Established.
- **Reaches output**: the value, or a value built from it in order, is the argument of the
  output call, through assignments, returns, and calls. Open: one path is enough.
- **Writes in order**: the output call writes its argument in the value's order, as the catalog
  describes it (assumption R3), with its sorting switch established off. Established.

## Why is this bad?
A program whose output depends on the iteration order of a set of strings writes different
files on different runs: generated code and configuration change without a change to their
input, `--check` modes fail at random, caches and snapshots miss, and two runs of a test
disagree. The order is fixed only within one process, so the difference shows on another
machine or in CI, rarely where the code was written.

## Example
```python
import json
from pathlib import Path


def referenced(schema: dict[str, dict]) -> set[str]:
    return {value["$ref"] for value in schema.values() if "$ref" in value}


def components(schema: dict[str, dict], schemas: dict[str, dict]) -> dict[str, dict]:
    return {name: schemas[name] for name in referenced(schema)}


def write_components(schema: dict[str, dict], schemas: dict[str, dict], path: Path) -> None:
    path.write_text(json.dumps(components(schema, schemas)))  # EFF112
```

Use instead:
```python
def components(schema: dict[str, dict], schemas: dict[str, dict]) -> dict[str, dict]:
    return {name: schemas[name] for name in sorted(referenced(schema))}
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `lint.extend-select = ["EFF112"]` (or `--extend-select EFF112`) enables the rule. It is
  opt-in: selecting the `EFF` prefix does not enable it.
- `[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]` entries with `writes-in-order` add writers.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/shallow-copy-nested-mutation/

# shallow-copy-nested-mutation (MUT115)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Heuristic · Opt-in · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Opt-in: changing in place an object below a shallow copy the function made of state that outlives the call (`dict(x)`, `x.copy()`, `copy.copy(x)`, `model_copy()`): the copied value holds the same object, so the change is seen through it too.

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs only when `select` or `extend-select` names its code or name. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

## What it does
Checks in-place changes of an object that the function reaches below a shallow copy it made
itself of state that outlives the call: a parameter, a global, a variable of an enclosing
function, or an attribute or item read from such state. A shallow copy is a new object holding the same objects as the copied
value, so changing one of those objects changes it for the copied value too.
The rule is opt-in: enable it with `--extend-select MUT115` or `extend-select = ["MUT115"]`.

The copies are those `MUT202` follows: a builtin container's `copy()`, `dict(x)`, `list(x)`,
`set(x)`, a display that only unpacks the value (`{**x}`, `[*x]`), a slice of a builtin list,
`copy.copy`, `copy.replace`, `dataclasses.replace`, a pydantic model's `model_copy()` without
`deep=True`, and the shallow copy sanitizers of the ecosystem catalog. The change is an item
store or delete, a changing method (`append`, `update`, `pop`, ...), an in-place operator, or an
attribute store or delete, on an object read from the copy (`copied["tags"]`,
`copied.children`, `copied.data_type.type = "int"`), directly or through a helper the object is
handed to.

It does not report:

- a change of the copy itself (`copied["k"] = v`, `copied.name = v`): the copy is the
  function's own;
- an object the copy was given a value of its own for: rebound before the change on every path
  (`copied.tags = [*tags]`, then `copied.tags.append(x)`), passed to `replace(x, tags=...)`, or
  named by `model_copy(update={"tags": ...})`;
- a deep copy (`copy.deepcopy`, `model_copy(deep=True)`);
- a store into the copy's own `__dict__` (`copied.__dict__["_k"] = v`);
- the elements of an iteration over the copy (`for task in list(tasks): task.x = 1`): iterating
  a copy is how code changes a container while looping over it;
- a copy of a value the function made itself;
- filling a memo of the shared object, or initializing one of its attributes lazily (as for
  `MUT202`).

## What a report states

A report states that the function changes in place, at the reported line, an object that it
reaches below a shallow copy it made of a value it did not make (a parameter, a global, a
variable of an enclosing function, or an attribute or item read from one), and that the copied
value held that object at that place when the function copied it.

Its premises:

- **Shallow copy**: the value is the result of a copy that shares what is below its top level: a
  builtin container's `copy()`, its constructor (`dict(x)`, `list(x)`, `set(x)`), `{**x}`,
  `[*x]`, or a slice, of a builtin container (by annotation, R2) whose copying methods no
  project subclass replaces; `copy.copy` of an instance of a project class no class of which
  (R2) defines `__copy__`, `__reduce__`, `__reduce_ex__`, `__getstate__`, or `__setstate__`, or
  has a metaclass or a base heki does not know; or `model_copy()` without `deep=True` of a
  pydantic model (R3) whose classes define no `__copy__` or `model_copy`. A class defines a
  name also when a store heki reads binds it on the class after its body: a store through a
  value that may be a class object (any value heki does not establish as an instance: `self`,
  what a class call makes, a parameter annotated with a class other than `type`) under the
  name, or under a name built at run time whose constant text at its ends may be the name's
  (`Node.__copy__ = f`, `setattr(cls, "__copy__", f)` in a class decorator, an
  `__init_subclass__`, or another function handed the class; `f"_cached_{name}"` is never
  `__copy__`). A store under a name of unknown value (a parameter, a key of `vars()` or of a
  mapping, a value read from data) binds none, and so does code heki does not read: a class
  decorator outside the project, and a call or a closure the class is handed to, bind only what
  the stores heki reads bind (R1). Open for the other copies (`dataclasses.replace`,
  `copy.replace`, the catalog's other sanitizers).
- **Borrowed original**: on every path the copied value is state that outlives the call: a
  parameter, a global, a variable of an enclosing function, or what a plain attribute or item
  load reads from such state. Open: one path is enough. What a call returns is not followed.
- **Still shared**: on every path to the line, the changed object is what the copy holds at one
  of its levels, read from the copy by a plain item or attribute load (an item of a builtin list
  or dict, a plain attribute of an instance), and nothing gives that level a value of its own:
  no store or delete of it into the copy, no keyword of the copy call or `update=` key naming
  it, no method changing a copied container's items, and the copy reaches no other code. Open:
  a value that is below the copy on one path counts, and so does an object further below
  (`copied["a"]["b"]`): it lives in an object the copied value shares, which any code reaching
  that object may have given a new one since the copy.
- **Changed below the copy**: the line changes that object in place: an item store or delete, a
  changing method, or an in-place operator on a builtin `list`, `dict`, or `set` (by
  annotation, R2) that no project subclass replaces, or a plain attribute store or delete on an
  instance of a project class (no property, descriptor, `__setattr__`, or metaclass in a class it
  may be, also none bound on the class after its body as for **Shallow copy**; pydantic's
  `BaseModel.__setattr__` stores on the instance, R3). Open: a change made by a helper the
  object is handed to.

## Why is this bad?
The copy suggests the original stays as it was, but the objects below the copy are the
original's. Changing one through the copy changes the original, usually far from where the copy
was made: a default shared by every model, an option dictionary of the caller, a node of a tree
another part of the program still reads.

## Example
```python
def with_base(options: dict[str, list[str]], base: str) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
    result = options.copy()
    result["bases"].append(base)  # changes the list `options["bases"]` holds
    return result
```

Use instead:
```python
def with_base(options: dict[str, list[str]], base: str) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
    result = options.copy()
    result["bases"] = [*result["bases"], base]
    return result
```

## Known limitations
- A copy made by a project function (`copy_deep()` that copies one level and shares the next)
  is not followed: a project copy method copies as deeply as its body does, which its summary
  does not state level by level.
- A copy stored in an attribute and changed in another method is not followed.

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/summary-effect-regression/

# summary-effect-regression (MUT103)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Heuristic · Opt-in · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Interprocedural mutation/escape/effect regression against saved summary snapshot.

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs only when `select` or `extend-select` names its code or name. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

## What it does
Compares the interprocedural side effects of every public function with the summary snapshot
saved by `heki snapshot --write` (`.heki-summary-snapshot.json` at the project root), and reports
functions that gained one of:

- a mutated parameter (the function now changes an argument it receives);
- an escaping parameter (an argument is now stored in an attribute, a container, a global, or a
  variable of an enclosing function);
- a mutated `self` attribute;
- an execution effect (blocking network / database / subprocess / filesystem I/O, sleeping,
  client allocation, database queries), including effects reached through callees.

This rule is opt-in: enable it with `--extend-select MUT103` or `extend-select = ["MUT103"]`.

## What a report states

A report states that a public function now has a side effect (a changed or escaping parameter, a
changed `self` attribute, or an execution effect) that its summary in the saved snapshot does not
have.

Its premises:

- **Has the effect**: the function's current summary has it. Open: a summary counts an effect on any
  path, and of any candidate implementation of a call.
- **New**: the snapshot's summary of the function lacks it. Established.

## Why is this bad?
A pull request that makes a widely used helper start mutating its argument, or start doing
network I/O, often looks harmless in the diff of the helper and breaks callers far away. The
snapshot makes such effect regressions visible in review, the way a lock file makes dependency
changes visible.

## Example
```python
# snapshot taken while `add` was pure
def add(items: list[int], x: int) -> list[int]:
    return items + [x]
```

After an edit:
```python
def add(items: list[int], x: int) -> list[int]:  # MUT103: `add` now mutates parameter `items`
    items.append(x)
    return items
```

The report is on the function's `def` line, which is also where a suppression comment goes.

If the new effect is intended, refresh the snapshot with `heki snapshot --write` and commit it.
The refresh writes nothing while a file of the project cannot be read or parsed (it exits with
2): the snapshot would lose that module's entries. A module with a `.pyi` stub is recorded and
compared with the parameter names of its `.py` file.

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `lint.extend-select = ["MUT103"]` enables the rule.
- The snapshot lives at `.heki-summary-snapshot.json`; `heki snapshot` prints it without writing.
- `heki check --snapshot PATH` compares with the snapshot at `PATH` instead, for example one
  generated on the protected base branch. The file must exist and be a snapshot of the supported
  version, and the rule must be enabled, or the run exits with 2.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unlocked-write-of-guarded-state/

# unlocked-write-of-guarded-state (EFF117)

Family: Execution Effects (EFF) · Heuristic · Off by default · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

State that another writer changes holding a thread lock (`threading.Lock`, `RLock`, `Condition`, `Semaphore`), changed here holding none, where a thread heki resolves can run one of the writes: an update can be lost.

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs when `select` or `extend-select` names its code or name, and with `lint.heuristic = true` (`--heuristic`) also by default and for its prefixes and `ALL`. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

## What it does
Checks for shared state that one function changes while it holds a thread lock and another
changes holding none, where a thread heki resolves can run one of the two writes. The rule is
heuristic: it runs when `select` or `extend-select` names it, and with `--heuristic`
(`lint.heuristic = true`).

A thread lock is a value whose class the catalog flags `sync-lock-or-tx`: `threading.Lock`,
`threading.RLock`, `threading.Condition`, `threading.Semaphore`, and
`threading.BoundedSemaphore`. A function holds one:

- from a `with` over it to the end of that statement, and from an `acquire()` (with or without a
  timeout) to a `release()`, on every path;
- after a call of a helper that returns holding it (`def _acquire(self): self._lock.acquire()`),
  a lock of `self` when the call passes the caller's own `self`;
- before a `release()` that comes on every path from there: code that gives back a lock it did
  not take itself took it through a helper or was called holding it;
- in a function every call of which is made holding a lock, up to two calls above it: a
  generator expression made, or a lambda called (`sorted(xs, key=lambda x: self._rank(x))`),
  inside `with self._lock:` runs holding the lock, and so does a private method only such code
  calls, until it gives that lock back with a `release()`.

The shared state is an attribute of the instance a method runs on (`self.count`), a module
global (`global _cache`), or an attribute of a class or module (`Registry.items`), assigned or
deleted, or changed in place where heki knows it holds a builtin container: an item store or
delete (`self.failures[key] = n`) or a method of the container's class that changes it
(`self.pending.append(item)`). Attributes of a `threading.local` are not shared.

The threads heki resolves are the project functions handed to `threading.Thread(target=...)`,
`threading.Timer`, `asyncio.to_thread`, `loop.run_in_executor`, the `submit` and `map` of a
thread pool (or of an executor of unknown kind), `anyio.to_thread.run_sync`,
`trio.to_thread.run_sync`, and `run_in_threadpool`, and the `run` method of a
`threading.Thread` subclass, with every function they reach over project calls. A coroutine
function or a generator function handed to a thread is no entry (the thread only creates the
object), nor is a function `loop.run_in_executor` hands to a process pool. A function a thread
runs is not taken for one that only construction runs, even when a constructor calls it too.

The rule reports the first such write of each state in a function, with a write made holding
the lock in another function as a related location.

It does not report:

- a write in a constructor (`__init__`, `__new__`, `__post_init__`, `__init_subclass__`), in an
  `os.register_at_fork(after_in_child=...)` handler, or in a function only those call (up to two
  calls above): the object or the child process is not shared yet; nor does a write there make
  the state one a lock guards;
- a write in test code;
- state no writer changes holding a lock, and a write where heki finds any thread lock held,
  whether or not it is the one the other writer holds;
- a method call heki cannot tie to a builtin container (`self.client.add(...)`).

## What a report states

A report states that two writes of the same state can run at once on two threads, one holding a
lock and one holding none, so the lock does not keep them apart and one can lose the other's
update.

Its premises:

- **Same state**: both writes reach the same attribute of the same instance, or the same global
  (assumption R1 for the methods). Open: two instances of the class are not told apart, and the
  methods of a base class and its subclasses write the same attribute.
- **Guarded**: the other writer holds the lock at its write. Open: a timed `acquire()` that
  failed is not told apart from one that succeeded.
- **Not held**: no thread lock is held at the write in the function, through the helpers it
  calls, or in its callers up to two calls above. Open: a caller further up, a caller heki does
  not see (a public method called from outside the project), a helper taking the lock through
  another helper, and a project context manager taking it in `__enter__` may hold one.
- **Shared**: the write runs after the object or the state is shared. Open: a function that runs
  before any thread starts, or only on one thread, is not told apart.
- **Threaded**: a thread entry heki resolves reaches one of the two writes. Open: one path is
  enough, and that two threads touch the same instance at once is not established.

An exact tier, with the same lock object on both sides, every caller known (a private method or
a module-private function), and every thread entry and helper followed, is future work.

## Why is this bad?
A lock only keeps apart the code that takes it. A write made without it can run in the middle
of a locked update: a counter incremented under the lock and reset without it loses the reset or
the increments, an invalidation (`cache["mtime"] = 0`) made without the lock is lost when a
locked rebuild stores the old value back, and a dictionary changed without the lock while a
locked reader iterates it raises `RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration`. Under
free-threaded CPython, single operations that the GIL kept whole can interleave too.

## Example
```python
import threading


class Stats:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        self.received = 0

    def start(self) -> None:
        threading.Thread(target=self._read).start()

    def _read(self) -> None:
        with self._lock:
            self.received += 1

    def reset(self) -> None:
        self.received = 0  # EFF117
```

Use instead:
```python
    def reset(self) -> None:
        with self._lock:
            self.received = 0
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `lint.heuristic = true` (or `--heuristic`) runs the rule by default; `--select EFF117` runs
  it alone.
- `[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]` entries with `sync-lock-or-tx = true` add lock classes.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-call/

# unresolved-guarded-call (MUT207)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Heuristic · Runs when its contract is declared · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Strict mode of a `call-owners` contract (`unresolved = "report"`): calling a method named like a target on an object of unknown class.

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs when its contract is declared. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

## What it does
The strict mode of a `[[tool.heki.call-owners]]` contract that sets `unresolved = "report"`:
reports the calls outside the call owners that `MUT204` cannot tie to a target, so a clean
`MUT204` run says how much it did not check. A call of a method named like a target (the last
name of the target: `replace_reference` for `DataType.replace_reference`, also for a function or
class target; for a glob, `Parser._*`, a name `Parser`, a project subclass, or a project base
gives its instances in project code, not one only a base outside the project gives them:
`_replace` of a `NamedTuple` is none,
[configuration](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#globs-on-objects-of-unknown-class)) is reported once, at
the call, when its receiver is of unknown class: an
unannotated parameter, a loop variable, the result of a call heki does not resolve, a value
annotated `Any` or `object` (unless an `isinstance` test around the call narrows it to a class),
a protocol whose implementations heki cannot list (one without members, or implemented by more
than eight classes), or a variable of an enclosing function that a nested scope rebinds
(`nonlocal`). `obj.replace_reference(...)`, a bound-method alias of it
(`replace = obj.replace_reference`), and `getattr(obj, "replace_reference")(...)` with a
constant name count. A call of a value of unknown origin (`callback()`) names nothing and is not
reported.

The rules of `MUT204` for what is allowed apply: allowed callers, exempt methods, the targets
themselves (they may call each other), functions that only run inside allowed callers,
`forbidden-callers` (the calling function must be one), and `allowed-protocols`, also for a
receiver heki cannot tie to a class that is typed with a named protocol declaring the method: a
class object typed `type[P]` (`cls._items_constraints(obj)` with `cls: type[KeywordsHost]`), or
an instance of a protocol whose implementations heki cannot list. `MUT204` does not follow a call into a
parameter that its function does not type, so the callers decide for such a receiver: the call is
reported unless every caller path binds to it an instance of a project class whose method of that
name is no target: a class outside the target's family (`DataType` and its subclasses for
`DataType.replace_reference`) whose MRO finds no method the target names either (for the target
`reset`, any project class's `reset`; a `reset` inherited from a library base is none). With
`attribution = "lexical"`, a function that only runs inside allowed callers is not allowed, and a
caller path through an allowed caller counts like any other: the call is the function's own, and
its callers only tell the receiver's class.

The help names up to three allowed callers that call a target of the method's name
themselves, as for `MUT204`, after the contract's `message`:
``allowed callers of `replace_reference`: ...``.

## What a report states

A report states that, outside the call owners, the function calls a method named like a target of
the `call-owners` contract on an object whose class heki does not know.

Its premises:

- **Named like a target**: the method's name matches a target's (for a target with an argument
  list, its name before the list: heki does not bind the arguments of a call on an object of
  unknown class). Established.
- **Unknown class**: heki did not resolve the class of the object. Established: the claim is about
  heki's own resolution.
- **Outside the owners**: the function is not in the allowed modules and classes, nor runs only
  inside allowed contexts (with `attribution = "lexical"`: the function holding the access is not
  allowed). Established from the contract.

## Why is this bad?
`MUT204` reports a call only when every function it may call is a target, which needs the
receiver's class: a call on an object it cannot type is not seen, so a contract that passes says
nothing about those calls. Name-based checkers report them all; heki reports them separately,
under their own code, so they can be counted, ratcheted with a baseline, and reduced by
annotating the receivers, without mixing them with the violations `MUT204` proves.

## Example
```toml
[[tool.heki.call-owners]]
name = "reference-mutators"
targets = ["DataType.replace_reference"]
allowed-callers = ["pkg.store.GenerationStore.*"]
unresolved = "report"
```

```python
def swap(data_type, ref) -> None:  # no annotation: heki cannot tell what `data_type` is
    data_type.replace_reference(ref)  # MUT207


def rename(text: str) -> str:
    return text.replace("a", "b")  # not reported: a `str`
```

Use instead:
```python
def swap(store: GenerationStore, data_type: DataType, ref: Reference) -> None:
    store.replace_data_type_ref(data_type, ref)
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `[[tool.heki.call-owners]]`:
  - `unresolved`: `"ignore"` (default) or `"report"`.
  - `targets`, `allowed-callers`, `forbidden-callers`, `exempt-methods`, `attribution`,
    `message`: as for `MUT204`.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-import/

# unresolved-guarded-import (IMP202)

Family: Imports (IMP) · Heuristic · Runs when its contract is declared · Experimental · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Strict mode of an `import-boundaries` contract (`unresolved = "report"`): an import whose module heki cannot name, which may be one the contract does not allow.

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs when its contract is declared. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

!!! warning "Experimental"

    It is the strict mode of `IMP201`, which is experimental. Experimental features can still change in behavior or precision, or be removed, in any release, and each change is listed in the release notes. An opt-in rule that is not experimental is stable and only off by default. See [Experimental Features](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/experimental/).

## What it does
The strict mode of a `[[tool.heki.import-boundaries]]` contract that sets `unresolved = "report"`:
reports the imports of the judged modules that `IMP201` cannot judge because heki cannot name
the module they load, when that module may be one the contract does not allow:

- a by-name import (`importlib.import_module`, `__import__`) of a name the code does not fix;
- a by-name import of a name built from a known start (`f"pkg.plugins.{name}"`), unless no
  forbidden pattern can match a module under it, or an allowed glob covers every one
  (`pkg.plugins.*`); a full name may also be one of a module `relative-imports` allows only
  through a relative import;
- a call that may be a by-name import: a method named `import_module` or `__import__` on an
  object of unknown class (`loader.import_module("pkg.backend")`), or a call of a name that may be
  bound to one of them on some path (`load = importlib.import_module if flag else print`). The
  call may be another function, so its modules are not read and the report says it may be one;
- a relative import that climbs past the top-level package (`from ... import x` in
  `pkg/sub/use.py`): it names no module and raises `ImportError` when it runs;
- a by-name import of one of several names, some breaking the contract and some not;
  the report gives every reason one of them may break it for;
- `from a import c` where heki cannot tell whether `c` is the submodule `a.c`: a package outside
  the project, one whose `__init__.py` binds `c` before the submodule may be imported, one that
  binds `c` to an object of the submodule after importing it (`from .c import c`), which the
  import takes the submodule instead of while the package is still loading, or one that binds no
  `c` while the project has no module `a.c`, which Python then looks for outside the project's
  files (a compiled extension module). The package `a` loads either way, and `IMP201` judges it.
  A forbidden name (`forbidden-imports = ["xml:etree"]`) is exact only where heki knows `c` is
  not a submodule; otherwise `from xml import etree` is reported here, as it may be the submodule.
  A by-name import takes no forbidden name, but it is still reported for the rest of the contract
  (`relative-imports`).

With `reach`, the sites of the modules a walk reaches are judged too, and reported at the import
of the importer that starts the chain to them.

## What a report states

A report states that the importer has an import whose module heki cannot name, that may be one
the contract forbids or does not allow, or one it allows only through a relative import.

## Why is this bad?
A contract that passes says nothing about the imports heki cannot follow. `IMP202` reports them
under their own code, so they can be counted, kept in a baseline, and reduced by writing the
module name out, without mixing them with the violations `IMP201` proves.

## Example
```toml
[[tool.heki.import-boundaries]]
name = "core-plugins"
importers = ["pkg.core.*"]
forbidden-imports = ["pkg.plugins.*"]
unresolved = "report"
```

```python
import importlib


def plugin(name: str) -> object:
    return importlib.import_module(f"pkg.plugins.{name}")  # IMP202
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `[[tool.heki.import-boundaries]]`:
  - `unresolved`: `"ignore"` (default) or `"report"`.
  - the other keys: as for `IMP201`.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-read/

# unresolved-guarded-read (MUT206)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Heuristic · Runs when its contract is declared · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Strict mode of a `read-owners` contract (`unresolved = "report"`): reading an attribute named like a target on an object of unknown class.

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs when its contract is declared. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

## What it does
The strict mode of a `[[tool.heki.read-owners]]` contract that sets `unresolved = "report"`:
reports the reads outside the read owners that `MUT203` cannot tie to a target class, so a clean
`MUT203` run says how much it did not check. A read of an attribute named like a target attribute
(`children` for `Reference.children`; for `Reference.*`, a name `Reference`, a project subclass,
or a project base gives its instances in project code, not one only a base outside the project
gives them, [configuration](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#globs-on-objects-of-unknown-class)) is reported
once, at the read,
when its object is of unknown class: an unannotated parameter, a loop variable, the result of a
call heki does not resolve, a value annotated `Any` or `object` (unless an `isinstance` test
around the read narrows it to a class), a protocol whose implementations heki cannot list (one
without members, or implemented by more than eight classes), or a variable of an enclosing
function that a nested scope rebinds (`nonlocal`). `obj.children`, a local alias of it,
`getattr(obj, "children")` and `hasattr(obj, "children")` with a constant name, and `obj.__dict__["children"]` (also
`vars(obj)["children"]`) count, as for `MUT203`.

The rules of `MUT203` for what is allowed apply: allowed readers, exempt methods, functions that
only run inside allowed readers, `forbidden-readers` (the reading function must be one), and
`allowed-protocols`, also for an object heki cannot tie to a class that is typed with a named
protocol declaring the attribute: a class object typed `type[P]` (a parameter, a local, or an
attribute annotated so), or an instance of a protocol whose implementations heki cannot list.
`MUT203` does not follow a read into a parameter that its function does not type, so the callers
decide for such a parameter: the read is reported unless every caller path binds an instance of
a project class outside the targets' classes to it. A parameter some caller binds to an instance
of a target class is reported here: that read is a read of the target that no other rule sees.
With `attribution = "lexical"`, a function that only runs inside allowed readers is not allowed,
and a caller path through an allowed reader counts like any other: the read is the function's
own, and its callers only tell the object's class.

The help names up to three allowed readers that read a target of the attribute's name
themselves, as for `MUT203`, after the contract's `message`:
``allowed readers of `children`: ...``.

## What a report states

A report states that, outside the read owners, the function reads an attribute named like a target
of the `read-owners` contract on an object whose class heki does not know.

Its premises:

- **Named like a target**: the attribute's name matches a target's. Established.
- **Unknown class**: heki did not resolve the class of the object. Established: the claim is about
  heki's own resolution.
- **Outside the owners**: the function is not in the allowed modules and classes, nor runs only
  inside allowed contexts (with `attribution = "lexical"`: the function holding the access is not
  allowed). Established from the contract.

## Why is this bad?
`MUT203` reports what it can back with a class: a read through an object it cannot type is not
followed, so a contract that passes says nothing about those reads. Name-based checkers report
them all; heki reports them separately, under their own code, so they can be counted, ratcheted
with a baseline, and reduced by annotating the objects, without mixing them with the violations
`MUT203` proves.

## Example
```toml
[[tool.heki.read-owners]]
name = "reference-children"
targets = ["Reference.children"]
allowed-readers = ["*GenerationIndex*"]
unresolved = "report"
```

```python
def render(ref) -> str:  # no annotation: heki cannot tell what `ref` is
    return ", ".join(map(str, ref.children))  # MUT206


def size(ref: Reference) -> int:
    return len(ref.children)  # MUT203: a typed read
```

Use instead:
```python
def render(ref: Reference, index: GenerationIndex) -> str:
    return ", ".join(map(str, index.children_of(ref)))
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `[[tool.heki.read-owners]]`:
  - `unresolved`: `"ignore"` (default) or `"report"`.
  - `targets`, `allowed-readers`, `forbidden-readers`, `exempt-methods`, `attribution`,
    `message`: as for `MUT203`.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unresolved-guarded-write/

# unresolved-guarded-write (MUT205)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Heuristic · Runs when its contract is declared · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Strict mode of a `write-owners` contract (`unresolved = "report"`): writing an attribute named like a target on an object of unknown class, or a computed attribute name on a guarded class.

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs when its contract is declared. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

## What it does
The strict mode of a `[[tool.heki.write-owners]]` contract that sets `unresolved = "report"`:
reports the writes outside the write owners that `MUT201` cannot tie to a target class, so a clean
`MUT201` run says how much it did not check. Four kinds of writes are reported, each once, at the
write:

- an attribute named like a target attribute (`fields` for `Model.fields`, any name for
  `Model.*`: a write may add the member) written on an object of unknown class: an unannotated parameter that no project
  caller binds to an instance of a known class, a loop variable, the result of a call heki does
  not resolve, a value annotated `Any` or `object` (unless an `isinstance` test around the write
  narrows it to a class: `if isinstance(obj, Field): ...`), a protocol whose implementations
  heki cannot list (one without members, or implemented by more than eight classes), or a
  variable of an enclosing function that a nested scope rebinds (`nonlocal`). Rebinding
  (`obj.fields = []`), deleting, `setattr` with a constant name, and changing the container the
  attribute holds (`obj.fields.append(x)`, `obj.meta["k"][name] = v`, also through an alias, in
  the function or in a scope nested in it) count;
- an attribute name computed at run time written on an instance of a target class:
  `setattr(model, name, v)`, `model.__dict__[name] = v`, `model.__dict__.update(...)`,
  `model.__dict__ |= other` (also through `vars(model)` or a local alias of the namespace), and a
  `__dict__` key in a name that is no constant: a module-level name bound twice, in a loop, or
  before a star import, rebound by another module, or that a change through `globals()` may
  bind (in a module whose `__getattr__` caches what it serves, one the module body binds on some
  paths only), a class attribute without `ClassVar` or
  `Final` (an instance may hold its own), one a subclass defines again or inherits first from
  another base, a `Final` field of a dataclass read on an instance (or on a class object with
  `slots=True` along the way), and one stored on its class, a subclass, or an instance outside
  the class body (`Model.KEY = "x"`);
- an attribute name computed at run time written on an object of unknown class (an unannotated
  `target` in `setattr(target, name, v)` or `target.__dict__[key] = v`), which may be any target;
- with `unlisted-dict-keys = "report"`, a constant `__dict__` key written on an object of unknown
  class (`field.__dict__["_name_cache"] = v`, `field.__dict__.setdefault(KEY, v)`, `del
  vars(field)["k"]`) that no target of any `write-owners` contract names for some class this
  contract's targets cover: it may be a new key of that class, which `MUT201` reports on a typed
  object.

The rules of `MUT201` for what is allowed apply: allowed writers, exempt methods, a class's own
initialization (`setattr(self, name, v)` in `__init__`), functions that only run inside allowed
writers, `forbidden-writers`, `allowed-protocols` (also for an object of unknown class typed with
a named protocol declaring the attribute: a class object typed `type[P]`, or an instance of a
protocol whose implementations heki cannot list), and, with `fresh-objects = "allow"`, writes that
construct the object they write. A parameter that every caller path binds to an object of a project class is not
reported: `MUT201` reports the write at those callers. For a computed name on a parameter, a
caller binding an object of a target class leaves the write to `MUT205` (`MUT201` has no name to
report at that caller), unless it is that class's own initialization handing over its `self`,
and one binding an object of another class ties it there. The same holds for a `__dict__` key no
target names: a caller binding an object of a class the key would be new to leaves the write to
`MUT205` (`MUT201` sees no `__dict__` write at a caller handing the object to a helper that does
not type it). With
`attribution = "lexical"`, a function that only runs inside allowed writers is not allowed, and a
caller path through an allowed writer counts like any other, while a helper that only a class's
own initialization runs on its own `self` (`self._assign(name)` in `__init__`) stays allowed.
With `own-receiver = "allow"`, a computed name written on the receiver of the method judging it
(`setattr(self, name, v)`) is allowed.

The help names up to three allowed writers that write a target of the attribute's name
themselves, as for `MUT201`, after the contract's `message`:
``allowed writers of `fields`: ...``.

## What a report states

A report states that, outside the write owners, the function writes an attribute named like a target
of the `write-owners` contract on an object whose class heki does not know, a computed attribute
name on a guarded class or on an object whose class heki does not know, or, with
`unlisted-dict-keys = "report"`, a `__dict__` key no target names on an object whose class heki
does not know.

Its premises:

- **Named like a target**: the attribute's name matches a target's, or is computed at run time
  (with `unlisted-dict-keys = "report"`, or is a `__dict__` key no target names for a class the
  targets cover). Established.
- **Unknown class**: heki did not resolve the class of the object. Established: the claim is about
  heki's own resolution.
- **Outside the owners**: the function is not in the allowed modules and classes, nor runs only
  inside allowed contexts (with `attribution = "lexical"`: the function holding the access is not
  allowed, nor runs only inside a class's own initialization). Established from the contract.

## Why is this bad?
`MUT201` reports what it can back with a class: a write through an object it cannot type is not
followed, so a contract that passes says nothing about those writes. Name-based checkers report
them all; heki reports them separately, under their own code, so they can be counted, ratcheted
with a baseline, and reduced by annotating the objects or naming the attributes with constants,
without mixing them with the violations `MUT201` proves.

## Example
```toml
[[tool.heki.write-owners]]
name = "model-store"
targets = ["Model.fields"]
allowed-writers = ["Store.*"]
unresolved = "report"
```

```python
def touch(model) -> None:  # no annotation: heki cannot tell what `model` is
    model.fields = []  # MUT205


def fill(model: Model, name: str) -> None:
    setattr(model, name, [])  # MUT205: the attribute is computed at run time


def fill_any(target, name: str) -> None:
    setattr(target, name, [])  # MUT205: neither the class nor the attribute is known


def read_only(model: Model) -> int:
    return len(model.fields)  # not reported: a read
```

With `unlisted-dict-keys = "report"` as well:

```python
def remember(model) -> None:
    model.__dict__["_seen"] = True  # MUT205: a key no target names, on an object of unknown class
```

Use instead:
```python
def touch(model: Model) -> None:
    model.fields = []  # now `MUT201`, outside `Store.*`
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `[[tool.heki.write-owners]]`:
  - `unresolved`: `"ignore"` (default) or `"report"`.
  - `unlisted-dict-keys`: `"ignore"` (default) or `"report"`: also report a constant `__dict__`
    key no `write-owners` target names, written on an object of unknown class.
  - `targets`, `allowed-writers`, `forbidden-writers`, `exempt-methods`, `fresh-objects`,
    `attribution`, `message`: as for `MUT201`.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unretained-async-task/

# unretained-async-task (EFF107)

Family: Execution Effects (EFF) · Heuristic · Opt-in · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Opt-in: an `asyncio.create_task` result bound to a local variable but never awaited, returned, or stored.

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs only when `select` or `extend-select` names its code or name. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

## What it does
Checks for the result of `asyncio.create_task(...)`, `asyncio.ensure_future(...)`, or
`loop.create_task(...)` that is bound to a local variable but never kept: never awaited,
returned, yielded, stored (in an attribute, a container, a global, or an enclosing scope),
passed to a call (`tasks.add(task)`, `asyncio.gather(task)`), captured by a closure, cancelled,
or asked for its result.

The factories are known by what their names are bound to: an import alias
(`from asyncio import create_task as spawn`) counts, a project function named `create_task` does
not. `loop.create_task` needs a receiver known to be an event loop (`asyncio.get_running_loop()`,
`get_event_loop()`, `new_event_loop()`, or an annotated `asyncio.AbstractEventLoop`).

It does not report:

- a call whose result is discarded (`asyncio.create_task(work())` as a statement): that is
  Ruff's `RUF006`;
- `asyncio.TaskGroup.create_task`, which keeps its tasks;
- receivers of unknown type;
- an argument known not to be a coroutine, from which no new task is made: the result of a
  project function that is a plain `def` or a generator function without decorators other than
  `staticmethod`, `classmethod`, `abstractmethod`, `override`, or `final` (`create_task` raises
  `TypeError` on what it returns, and `ensure_future` returns a future it is handed unchanged),
  or a value typed as a future or a task (`loop.run_in_executor(...)`, `loop.create_future()`,
  `asyncio.gather(...)`, `asyncio.wrap_future(...)`, `executor.submit(...)`, or an annotated
  `asyncio.Future`). An argument of unknown kind (a parameter, an awaitable, a constructed
  object, the result of a decorated function) may be a coroutine and is reported. The argument
  is the first positional one or the one passed as `coro=` / `coro_or_future=`.

A method of the task that is passed to a call, stored, or returned keeps the task too, because
the bound method holds it: `self.addCleanup(task.cancel)`, `loop.call_later(1, task.cancel)`,
`self.stop = task.cancel`.
Being only the receiver of `add_done_callback(...)` or `set_name(...)` does not keep the task:
the callback does not hold it strongly.

## What a report states

A report states that the task an `asyncio.create_task` (or `ensure_future`, or `loop.create_task`)
call returns is bound to a local variable that nothing keeps.

Its premises:

- **Task factory**: the call is one of the factories, known by what its name is bound to.
  Established.
- **Never kept**: no use of the variable awaits, returns, yields, stores, passes, captures, cancels,
  or asks the task for its result. Established from the uses in the function.

Not part of the claim: whether the task is garbage collected before it ends.

## Why is this bad?
The event loop keeps only a weak reference to a task. Once the function that created it returns,
nothing references the task any more, and it can be garbage-collected before it finishes: the
work silently stops halfway.

## Example
```python
import asyncio


async def handle(event: dict[str, str]) -> None:
    task = asyncio.create_task(notify(event))  # EFF107
    task.add_done_callback(log_failure)
```

Use instead:
```python
import asyncio

background_tasks: set[asyncio.Task[None]] = set()


async def handle(event: dict[str, str]) -> None:
    task = asyncio.create_task(notify(event))
    background_tasks.add(task)
    task.add_done_callback(background_tasks.discard)
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix.

## Options
- `lint.extend-select = ["EFF107"]` (or `--extend-select EFF107`) enables the rule. It is
  opt-in: selecting the `EFF` prefix does not enable it.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/unshielded-cleanup-checkpoint/

# unshielded-cleanup-checkpoint (EFF118)

Family: Execution Effects (EFF) · Heuristic · Off by default · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

A cleanup (a `finally` body, an `except` taking the cancellation, an `__aexit__`) that awaits a call reaching an AnyIO or Trio cancellation checkpoint with no shield on the way: in a cancelled scope the cleanup stops there.

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs when `select` or `extend-select` names its code or name, and with `lint.heuristic = true` (`--heuristic`) also by default and for its prefixes and `ALL`. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

## What it does
Checks for cleanup code that awaits a call reaching an AnyIO or Trio cancellation checkpoint with
no shield on the way. The rule is heuristic: it runs when `select` or `extend-select` names it,
and with `--heuristic` (`lint.heuristic = true`).

A cleanup is:

- a `finally` body;
- an `except` clause that is the first of its `try` to take the cancellation: a bare `except`,
  `BaseException`, `asyncio.CancelledError`, `trio.Cancelled`,
  `anyio.get_cancelled_exc_class()`, or a tuple holding one; a clause after one whose classes
  heki cannot tell is left out, and so is a clause after one taking the cancellation
  (`except Cancelled: raise` first);
- the body of an `__aexit__` method.

A checkpoint is an await of a call the catalog lists as one: `anyio.sleep`, the `to_thread`,
`to_process`, and `to_interpreter` calls, `run_process`, `open_process`, `open_file`, the
connections, `Event.wait`, the acquisition of a `Lock`, `Semaphore`, `CapacityLimiter`, or
`Condition` (also by `async with`), `Condition.wait`, a memory object stream's `send` and
`receive`, `Process.wait`, their Trio counterparts, and `run_in_threadpool`. The call is found
through awaited project calls, with the shortest chain of calls down to it. A lock or semaphore
made with `fast_acquire=True` takes no checkpoint while nobody holds it and is not counted.
`lowlevel.checkpoint()` and `checkpoint_if_cancelled()` count only where something runs after
them: awaited last, they hand the cancellation on to the caller on purpose.

It does not report:

- a checkpoint inside a `with` over `CancelScope(shield=True)` or `move_on_after(...,
  shield=True)` (and the other `move_on_*` and `fail_*` calls) on every path to it, in the
  cleanup or in any function on the way, also when the code names the scope by the module that
  defines it (`anyio._core._tasks.CancelScope`); a project function whose checkpoints are all
  shielded reaches none;
- a checkpoint inside a cancel scope that may shield: one made with a `shield` argument that is
  not a constant, one whose `shield` attribute the function sets, or one made elsewhere;
- a checkpoint on a branch the call's constant arguments never take (`await self._stop()` where
  the checkpoint is under `if force:` and `force` defaults to `False`);
- a function every call of which runs it shielded: each awaits it inside a shield, or only
  creates its coroutine (`await _shielded(self._close())`, a task) where heki does not follow
  it; a function with no call heki finds is reported;
- an await of a coroutine stored first (`pending = work(); await pending`), an `async for`,
  and a project context manager entering a shielded scope (not followed);
- native asyncio awaits (`asyncio.sleep`, `asyncio.Lock`): what cancels them is a task's
  `cancel()`, which is delivered once;
- test code.

## What a report states

A report states that when the scope around the cleanup is already cancelled, the await raises
the cancellation at the checkpoint, so the statements after it in the cleanup, and the work of
the call itself, do not run.

Its premises:

- **Cancelled scope**: the cleanup runs while an AnyIO or Trio scope around it is cancelled. An
  AnyIO cancellation is level-triggered: every checkpoint inside the cancelled scope raises
  again until the scope exits. Open: whether the cleanup runs after a cancellation at all (a
  `finally` also runs on a normal exit) is not established.
- **Checkpoint**: the call reaches the checkpoint on some path. Open: one path is enough, and a
  branch decided by state the call does not show is not told apart.
- **No shield**: no shield is on the path, in the functions on the way or in the calls of the
  function holding the cleanup. Open: a caller further up and a caller heki does not see (a
  framework calling an endpoint) may run it shielded.

## Why is this bad?
A cleanup releases what the code holds: it deletes a temporary resource, stops a process,
closes a connection, or puts a worker back into its pool. Cancellation is the usual reason the
cleanup runs, and an AnyIO or Trio scope cancelled once cancels every checkpoint inside it, so
the first await that checks for cancellation raises again. A shutdown loop that stops each
process inside `try: ... except Exception:` ends at the first process, because the cancellation
is not an `Exception`; a pool that pops a stale worker into a call argument and then awaits
neither destroys nor keeps it.

## Example
```python
import anyio


async def delete_group(name: str) -> None:
    await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(delete_container_group, name)


async def run(name: str) -> None:
    try:
        await watch(name)
    finally:
        await delete_group(name)  # EFF118
        log_deleted(name)
```

Use instead:
```python
    finally:
        with anyio.CancelScope(shield=True):
            await delete_group(name)
        log_deleted(name)
```

## Fix safety
No automatic fix. A shield keeps the cleanup running while the scope is cancelled: give a
cleanup that can wait for long a deadline too (`anyio.move_on_after(10, shield=True)`).

## Options
- `lint.heuristic = true` (or `--heuristic`) runs the rule by default; `--select EFF118` runs
  it alone.
- `[[tool.heki.ecosystem]]` entries with `effects = ["checkpoint"]` add checkpoints.


---

Source: https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/rules/write-owner-violation/

# write-owner-violation (MUT201)

Family: Mutation & State (MUT) · Heuristic · Runs when its contract is declared · Severity `error` (a bug) · No automatic fix

Writing a guarded attribute/container (directly, via alias, or via helper) outside declared `write-owners`.

!!! note "Heuristic"

    This rule is heuristic: a premise of its claim can be open ("What a report states" lists them), so a report can be wrong about the code. It runs when its contract is declared. It has not been measured yet. See [Rule Precision](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/precision/).

## What it does
Checks writes to attributes and containers that a `[[tool.heki.write-owners]]` contract
reserves for a set of allowed writer functions. A write is reported when it happens outside the
allowed writers:

- directly (`model.fields = [...]`, `model.fields.append(...)`, `del model.fields`), also by
  calling on the attribute's value a project method that changes its own `self` in place, in
  its body, through its calls on `self`, or through `super()` (`model.bag.add(x)` with
  `def add(self, name): self[name] = 1`): the call changes the value as a builtin container's
  changing method does, whether or not the contract allows the method itself. A method that
  only reads its `self`, or changes only an object it builds, writes nothing;
- through a local alias (`fields = model.fields; fields.append(...)`), also one a scope nested
  in the function reads from it (a nested function, a lambda, a comprehension, or a generator
  expression: `lambda: fields.append(x)`) unless a nested scope rebinds it (`nonlocal`), one
  `getattr` with a constant name loads (`getattr(model, "fields").append(...)`), or what a
  method, property, or
  function returns when it returns the attribute itself on every `return`
  (`model.field_list().append(...)` with `return self.fields`), stores no attribute of that name
  itself, and every class the object may be runs it (no `cached_property`, no class attribute of
  the name coming first); the object must be passed by position (no keyword-only parameter, no
  `*args` unpacking);
- through `setattr(model, "fields", ...)` / `object.__setattr__` (also through a module-level
  name bound once to it: `_set = object.__setattr__`) or `model.__dict__["fields"]` (also
  `vars(model)["fields"]`, `model.__dict__.setdefault("fields", v)`, and a local alias of the
  namespace, also one a nested scope reads from it: `namespace = model.__dict__`, then
  `def fill(): namespace["fields"] = v`),
  also with a string constant for the name (`model.__dict__[FIELDS_KEY]`, imported or not):
  a module-level name declared `Final` or bound once in its module and rebound by no other (a
  module `__getattr__` caching what it serves, `globals()[name] = value`, leaves the names the
  module body binds on every path, since Python calls it only for a missing name, unless a
  decorator wraps it or another module loads it), or
  a class-body name declared `ClassVar` or `Final` and bound once (`self.KEY`, `cls.KEY`,
  `Model.KEY`), which every subclass of the object's class finds along its MRO in the same
  class (none defines it again or lists another base defining it first,
  `class Child(Other, Model)`) and no code stores on the class, a subclass, or an instance
  (`Model.KEY = "x"`; another module may store it on the defining class only for a `Final`
  one); on an instance of a protocol, every class implementing it must hold the same constant.
  A `Final` name of a dataclass (or of a class a `dataclass_transform` builds) is a field, which
  each instance holds itself (`Keys("x").KEY`): it names an attribute only when read on the
  class object of a dataclass whose default no class along the way replaces (one with
  `slots=True` or built by a transform); a name a loop takes from a tuple, list, or set of such
  constants (`for key in ("fields", FIELDS_KEY): setattr(model, key, [])`), or from a module's
  tuple of them (`for key in RECORDS`, imported or not), writes each of them, when no code
  changes the list or set (`keys.append(name)` makes the name unknown), and so does the key of
  each pair a generator gives `__dict__.update`
  (`copy.__dict__.update((key, src.__dict__[key]) for key in RECORDS)`); the name a loop takes
  from the keys or items of a closed `TypedDict` (`closed=True`, or a base that is closed)
  writes each key the class and its bases declare, while an open `TypedDict` may hold more keys
  (a subclass value) and its write stays one named at run time;
- into the entries of the container the attribute holds (`model.meta["kw"][name] = v`,
  `model.meta["kw"].append(v)`, through a local alias of the entry, an entry `get` returns, and
  the entries a loop takes from `values()` or `items()`: `for names in model.meta.values():
  names.clear()`): an `item_mut` write;
- through a helper that mutates the container or object it receives (`helper(model.fields)`),
  reported once at the outermost call site; a helper changing an entry of the container it is
  handed (`box["k"].add(v)`, also through a local alias of the entry) writes it too, an
  `indirect_item_mut` write, and so does a method of the container changing an entry of its
  own `self`, called on the attribute's value (an `item_mut` write at the call). An attribute
  write on an entry is such a change only when heki ties the entry to no project class
  (`for field in fields: field.name = v` with `fields: list`, also in a function the entry is
  handed to that does not type it either): on an entry of a project class
  (`fields: list[Field]`), it is that
  class's write (`Field.name`), judged by the contracts of `Field.name` as the same write made
  directly (`for field in model.fields: field.name = v`) is, also when the helper hands the
  entry to a function typing it (`rename(field, v)`) or writes below one of its attributes
  (`field.tags.append(v)`). A helper that
  sees the object's class (an annotated parameter, `self` of a method) reports its own write
  instead, so a write it routes through the allowed writers stays allowed for its callers; a helper handed the value of an attribute
  (`helper(field.data_type)`) writes that attribute only when it changes the value in place,
  and otherwise writes the value's own attributes. A helper that does not see the class and
  only hands the value on to an allowed writer or an exempt method writes inside the owner.

A target names a class and an attribute; it covers the class's subclasses too (the target's class
family). With `unlisted-dict-keys = "report"`, a constant key written through the namespace of an
object of a class a target covers (`field.__dict__["_cache"] = v`, `vars(field).setdefault(KEY, v)`,
`del field.__dict__[KEY]`) is reported too when no target covering that class names it, in this
contract or in any other `write-owners` contract (`writes `pkg.model.Field._cache` (as a `__dict__` item), a
`__dict__` key no target names`), so a new key needs a target first. A target names the keys its
attribute pattern matches, and an entry target names its container; a key another contract names is
judged by that contract alone, a contract with only `forbidden-writers` allows no writer and names
no key, and a contract allowing every writer (`allowed-writers = ["*"]`) lists keys any function
may write. A computed key, a plain attribute store (`field._cache = v`,
`setattr`), and a write in a helper that does not see the object's class are not such writes. A
target can also name one entry of the container an attribute holds, `Class.attr["key"]`: it matches
the writes of that key (`field.extras["init"] = v`, `field.extras[INIT]` with a string constant,
`field.extras.pop("init")`, `del field.extras["init"]`, `field.extras["init"].append(v)`, and a
store operation called with the key, `set_extra(field, "init", v)` writing `field.extras[key]`,
reported at the call), not a write of the whole container (`field.extras = {}`, `field.extras.update(...)`) or with a computed
key, which are writes of `Class.attr`, as are the entries a loop takes from `values()` or
`items()` and an entry a helper changes. When a contract names both a container and one of its
entries, a write of the entry is reported once, under the entry.

The written object's class is the one heki infers for it, with annotations as hints: a
parameter, local, attribute, or return annotation, including the items of `list[...]`,
`Sequence[...]`, `Iterable[...]`, `Iterator[...]`, `Generator[...]`, `dict[...]`,
`Mapping[...]`, `tuple[...]`, and `set[...]`, and a type alias naming one (`Models: TypeAlias =
list[Model]`); a constructor call, also of a value declared `type[Model]` wherever it is held (a
parameter, or an attribute annotated in `__init__` or the class body); a standard library call
by its declared return type (`importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)` gives a `types.ModuleType`,
though a custom loader may return another object); and what the object comes
from: a loop over such a container (`for model in models`), a subscript (`models[0]`,
`by_name["a"]`), unpacking (`model, _ = pair`), `dict` views and `get` / `pop`, `enumerate`,
`zip`, `reversed`, `sorted`, `iter`, `next`, `list` / `tuple` / `set`, `itertools.chain`, a
display, the items appended to a local list, or a comprehension or generator expression. A
method call or a `@property` / `cached_property` read has the return annotation of the
definition the receiver's class finds first along its MRO, as for a type checker (`typing.Self`
is the receiver's class, and a class method returning `Self`, such as pydantic's
`Model.model_construct(...)`, gives the class it is called on); an attribute annotated with a
type parameter of its class (`obj: T` in `class Site(Generic[T])` or `class Site[T]:`) holds
the argument the instance's annotation gives (`site: Site[Schema]`, also through a type alias);
a name another module binds only under `if TYPE_CHECKING:` (serving it from a module
`__getattr__`) is the class that import names, also as a base class, and a name a module
serves only from its `__getattr__` is what the hook returns for it where heki follows the hook
(a branch testing the name against the literal, a factory read from a module-level dict by the
name and called, also through a function of the module calling what it is handed, and the hook
a project factory returns, `__getattr__, __dir__ = make_hooks(__name__, _EXPORTS)`), as an import
of it would be, and a class object a factory annotated `-> type[C]`
returns is `C` as a `TYPE_CHECKING` import is; a copy (`copy.copy`,
`copy.deepcopy`, `dataclasses.replace`, `model_copy`) has its original's class, calling a `functools.partial` object returns what the
wrapped function returns, and `typing.cast` names the class of its value, its type read as
an annotation (`cast(list[Model], x)` as `cast("list[Model]", x)`): a cast to a subclass narrows
a value known as its base, and a cast to `Any` or to a base class keeps the class the value is
known to have, as an annotated local does. A cast hands back the object it is given, and so does
a project function returning its parameter on every path (`def same(x): return x`, also
`return cast(T, x)`): `cast(list[int], store.items).append(x)` and `same(store.items).append(x)`
change `store.items`, as an alias does. A variable rebound in a loop
(`node = node.parent`) or assigned on some paths only (a walrus inside `and` / `or`) has the
classes of the values reaching it; a value of several classes (`Model | Node`: up to eight an
annotation declares, up to three from different assignments) is each of them, and an
`isinstance` check narrows it
in the code it guards (`if isinstance(x, Model): ...`, `if not isinstance(x, Model): return`,
also inside `and` / `or`), whatever class it had before and under each of its names
(`isinstance(v := x.source, Model)` narrows `v`). An assignment expression in a comprehension binds
the enclosing function's variable with the class of its value, in the items built from it and after
the comprehension, when the comprehension's body runs. A generator expression runs its body only as
it advances, so an unadvanced generator binds nothing. A nested scope that rebinds the variable with
`nonlocal` makes its type unknown. A value typed with a project `Protocol` is
an instance of the protocol and of the project classes that implement it structurally (having
every member it defines; at most eight, counting a class and not its subclasses), also when it
is handed to a helper that does not type it: a target on the protocol and one on an
implementation both cover its writes. An
object whose class heki cannot see (an unannotated parameter or return, `Any`, a value of more
classes than those, a protocol without members or with more implementations) is not tied to the
target.

A private helper (`_name`, or a comprehension, generator expression, or lambda scope) with
project callers hands the responsibility to its callers: the write is reported at the call
sites of the first non-private callers, with the chain of calls as related information. A
private function that only its own recursion calls (`_walk` calling itself, handed out as a
callback) has no such caller and reports its writes itself. One
report stands for every write behind that call (`sites` in JSON), so a Ratchet baseline counts a
second write inside a recorded helper. A write matching several targets of one contract (`A.items`
and `E.items` for a write on an `E`, a subclass of `A`) is one report, under the target
configured first, naming the others (`(also `E.items`)`). A write reached through an allowed writer on one path and
around it on another (or through a forbidden writer on one path only) is reported for the path
the contract does not allow.
Reading a `@property` or `functools.cached_property` attribute calls its getter, so a private
getter hands its writes to the functions reading it; a read never calls a property's setter.

A write runs where the body holding it runs. Calling a generator function only creates the
generator: its writes run where it is iterated (as for `EFF101`), so a generator created by an
allowed writer and iterated elsewhere writes elsewhere, and one handed to an allowed writer that
iterates it writes inside the owner. A generator that is created and never iterated writes
nothing. A coroutine that is never awaited or driven at a project call (handed to
`asyncio.create_task`, `ensure_future`, `gather`, ...) runs on the event loop: a private one
reports its own writes instead of handing them to the function that created it. Functions run on
another thread by an offloading decorator (`@sync_to_async`, ...) are not followed either.

A function that only runs inside the owner's operations is not reported either: it has project
callers, and every path of callers above it starts in an allowed writer, an exempt method, or
the class's own initialization (a mutator method that only the store and `__init__` call). A
function without project callers, one that is also called from anywhere else, or one reached
only through a cycle of other functions stays reported.

With `attribution = "lexical"`, neither of the two rules above applies: a write is judged in the
function whose code holds it, whoever calls that function. The write statement is its function's
own, and so is a call handing a typed object to a helper that changes it without knowing its
class (`fill(model.fields)`, reported with `via` the helper, which never sees the class); a write
a callee makes is reported at that callee. A lambda, comprehension, or generator expression is
part of the function it is written in, and a nested `def` is a function of its own. A class's
own initialization and `fresh-objects` still allow a write, the initialization through the
helpers it passes `self` to included: a helper whose every path of project callers starts in an
initializer handing it its own `self`.

With `own-receiver = "allow"`, a write through the receiver of the method it is judged in is
allowed: the function reported (with `attribution = "lexical"`, the function holding the write)
is a method that is no static method, and the object the member is looked up on may be its first
parameter (`self._cache[k] = v`, `setattr(self, name, v)`), also for a member the class
inherits. Another parameter, an attribute of the receiver, and a nested `def`, lambda, or
comprehension using the enclosing method's `self` stay reported.

With `allowed-protocols`, a write through a value typed with a project protocol the key names
that declares the attribute (`parser._flag = True` with `parser: RenderHost`, `RenderHost`
inheriting the declaration from a base protocol) is allowed, wherever it is judged; a write through
another protocol, the implementation's class, or a value a helper changes without typing it stays
reported. A pattern names the subprotocols of the protocols it matches too, unless
`protocol-subclasses = false`.

A class's own initialization is allowed: a write inside an initializer (`__init__`,
`__post_init__`, `__new__`, `model_post_init`, `__setstate__`) of a class of the target's
family is not reported when the written object is the initializer's own `self`, whether it
writes it directly, through a local alias, through `super().__init__()`, or through helpers it
passes `self` to (`self._init_fields()`, `_setup(self)`). An object that may be `self`
(`self if flag else other`) gets the benefit of the doubt. Writes to objects that are provably
not `self` stay reported: another parameter, an attribute of `self`.

A write that constructs the object it writes is allowed too (`fresh-objects = "allow"`, the
default): the object was allocated in the same call chain, by calling its class, by
`object.__new__(Model)` (also `Model.__new__(Model)` when no class defines `__new__`), by copying
(`copy.copy`, `copy.deepcopy`, `dataclasses.replace`, `.copy()`, `.model_copy()`), or by a
project function that returns such an object (at a call leaving an optional parameter at a
default without elements, such as `None`, the paths returning an element of it return
nothing) or returns the one it is handed, and nothing else can hold it yet: no store into
an object the function did not make, a container, a global, or a closure, no `yield`, and no
call that may keep it ran before the write. Calling the class may keep it too: the
construction keeps what the `__init__` it runs, or a base's reached through
`super().__init__()`, keeps of `self` (`REGISTRY.append(self)`, a helper handed `self` that
keeps it), and a class with a metaclass other than `type` or `abc.ABCMeta`, a decorated
`__init__`, or an `__init__` rebound outside its class body gives no new object. An attribute store into another new object of a
class whose attribute write runs no code links the holder to it instead: the object stays new
until it, an object holding it, or a value read out of one is kept (see
[configuration](https://heki.koxudaxi.dev/configuration/#write-owners)). So does a store into a list, set, or dict
the class's constructor made for a new instance (`copied.children.append(part)`). A project function keeps an object it
stores, yields, or hands to code heki does not follow or to a function that keeps it; reading
or writing it keeps nothing. A
store made only where tests of the function's parameters pass (`if register:`) keeps nothing at a
call whose arguments fail them (`register=False`, or a default the call leaves). Writes
that a helper makes to a new object its caller hands it count as well. A shallow copy shares its
containers with the original, so only rebinding its attributes constructs it
(`copied.data_types = [...]`); `copied.data_types.append(x)` changes the original's list and is
reported. `fresh-objects = "report"` reports these writes like any other.

The help starts with the contract's `message` and then names up to three allowed writers that
write the member the report names themselves: public functions and methods an `allowed-writers`
pattern names (with `forbidden-writers`, every function outside them), by fully qualified name
(``allowed writers of `Model.fields`: `pkg.store.Store.add_field` ``). A write through a helper,
a write that constructs the object it writes (with `fresh-objects = "allow"`), private functions
